Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Medical Record Number: [REDACTED]

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to our outpatient clinic with widespread skin-colored, dome-shaped lesions over the face and neck, which gradually increased in size and number over a year. The patient disclosed his HIV-positive status, with a CD4 + count of 82 cells/mm3. The patient also reported using a standard antiretroviral therapy regimen for the last five years. The clinical diagnosis was made due to the presence of molluscae bodies in some of the skin lesions, and the patient was confirmed with molluscum contagiosum. No systemic modalities of retinoid or other antiviral medication were used previously. The patient was prescribed multiple topical and oral medications, but the lesions showed no significant improvement.

Discharge Diagnosis:
Diagnosis: Molluscum contagiosum

Hospital Course Summary:
The patient was treated with oral isotretinoin 0.5 mg/kg for one month, considering the unavailability of other proven therapies and the widespread location of the disease. Isotretinoin was used because of its property of being a systemic retinoid with intracellular conversion into tretinoin and its effects on cellular proliferation and differentiation. After one month of follow-up, there was objective and subjective improvement in the appearance and count of the lesions. The patient had no adverse effects of oral isotretinoin, except dry lips, which were managed using petrolatum jelly. The remission was maintained even after two months of follow-up.

Condition at Discharge:
The patient was discharged from the outpatient clinic with improved, almost no lesions on the right half of the face, and a few lesions remained on the left half of the face. The patient was advised to continue the prescribed treatment and follow-up appointments with the clinician.

Instructions at Discharge:
The patient was advised to follow-up with the clinician for further evaluation. The patient was instructed to maintain good hygiene and avoid sharing personal items, such as towels and clothing, to prevent the spread of the disease. The patient was advised to continue using petrolatum jelly for dry lips. The patient was advised to continue the prescribed oral isotretinoin dosage. 

Follow-Up Recommendations:
The clinician advised the patient to follow-up with them regularly, as per the national guidelines of Nepal, ensuring optimal ART adherence and monitoring. The patient was advised to contact the clinician immediately if any adverse effects or new symptoms develop. 

Signed,
[REDACTED] (Clinician)

HOSPITAL COURSE SUMMARY:

Admission Date: [DATE]
Discharge Date: [DATE]

FINAL DIAGNOSIS:
Bladder non-Hodgkin's lymphoma of diffuse large B-cell type.

HOSPITAL COURSE:
The patient was admitted with a history of intermittent lower abdominal pain and dysuria for the past 3 months. Urine culture was positive, and ultrasonography showed bilateral hydroureteronephrosis with a thickened bladder wall and a pelvic space-occupying lesion infiltrating the bladder.

A cystoscopy was performed, which revealed a bladder tumor involving the trigone, and transurethral resection of the tumor was done. Histopathological examination revealed the presence of round or ovoid cells with nuclear pleomorphism, detrusor involvement, and lymphovascular invasion.

Based on immunohistochemistry, the tumor was characterized as CD20, bcl2, bcl6, and MUM-1 positive and negative for CD10, synaptophysin, and chromogranin. The Ki67 labeling index was 90%, and c-myc was expressed by 15% of cells, confirming the diagnosis of bladder non-Hodgkin's lymphoma of diffuse large B-cell type.

A PET-CT scan was performed, which showed a metabolically active large pelvic mass involving the bladder, vagina, and rectum along with metabolically active lymphoproliferative disorder on both sides of the diaphragm and multiple active lesions in the stomach, liver, and both lungs.

The patient was initiated on R-CHOP regimen for NHL but died due to multi-organ failure after the first cycle of chemotherapy.

DISCHARGE CONDITION:
Deceased.

FOLLOW-UP:
None necessary.

HOSPITAL COURSE:
The patient was admitted with a complaint of pain abdomen, abdominal distension, and obstipation for 2 days. She had no history of vomiting. Laboratory findings showed a total leucocyte count of 11,790/mm3. Plain abdominal X-ray and abdominal ultrasonography showed dilated bowel loops with to-and-fro peristalsis. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CECT) of the abdomen revealed herniation of the ileal loop through the left obturator canal. The patient underwent emergency laparotomy and intraoperative findings showed mid-ileal loop herniating through the left obturator canal. The herniated bowel segment was reduced and the obturator hernia defect was closed by approximation surrounding tissues with prolene sutures. The patient discharged on the postoperative day 5 without complication and no recurrence of symptoms during follow-up of 1-month.

HISTORY:
70-year-old thin-built female presented to the emergency department with the complaints of pain abdomen, abdominal distension, and obstipation for 2 days with no history of vomiting. The patient had similar complaints 1 year back and managed by conservative treatment. She had no previous medical or surgical history.

On examination, the patient was conscious, and oriented to time, place, and person. She had a temperature of 98°F, pulse rate of 86/min, and blood pressure of 116/76 mm of Hg. She had a nontender, distended abdomen, and all hernial orifices were normal. Per rectal and vaginal examination was also normal.

DIAGNOSIS:
Ileal loop herniation through the left obturator canal.

DISPOSITION:
The patient was discharged on the postoperative day 5 without complication and no recurrence of symptoms during follow-up of 1-month.

Discharge Summary for Patient 2:

Patient Name: [Redacted]
Gender: Male
Date of Admission: [Redacted]
Date of Discharge: [Redacted]
Diagnosis: Esophageal fistula with massive hematemesis; 6 cm saccular thoracic aortic aneurysm distal to the left subclavian artery

Hospital Course:

The patient was a 48-year-old male with a history of hypertension and a percutaneous coronary intervention with drug-eluting stents three years ago. He presented to the emergency with one episode of massive hematemesis. An urgent UGI endoscopy revealed a large depressed ulcer with a red spot located in the middle third of the esophagus along with a diverticulum located in the lower end of the ulcer. Imaging studies revealed a 6 cm saccular thoracic aortic aneurysm eroding into the esophagus.

Surgery was performed through a posterolateral thoracotomy. The aneurysmal segment of the aorta was replaced with a Dacron graft while taking care to preserve as many intercostal arteries as possible while suture ligating the others. The esophageal opening of the fistula was debrided and repaired with interrupted polypropylene sutures, superimposed with a vascularized intercostal muscle pedicle. The patient was placed on broad-spectrum antibiotics postoperatively.

Postoperatively, the patient recovered well and had an uneventful course. He was successfully separated from the partial bypass, and a gastrostomy and jejunostomy were created. He was discharged and advised to follow up with his primary care physician and the treating surgeon as part of a long-term management plan. 

Discharge Medications: None

Instructions: No heavy lifting, straining or strenuous activity for the next 6-8 weeks. Follow-up appointments were scheduled with the primary care physician and surgeon.

Condition at Discharge: Stable

Discharge Summary

Patient Name: Not provided

Hospital Course Summary:

Admission:
A 32-year-old female at gestational age 22+5 weeks presented to the obstetrics department with complaints of abdominal distension, chest tightness, and limb weakness that had been present for approximately four weeks. She was diagnosed with bilateral ovarian tumors by ultrasound, which showed a hypoechoic mass on the right side measuring 9.2 cm × 6.7 cm, a hypoechoic mass on the left side measuring 9.2 cm × 6.9 cm, an anechoic mass beside the uterus measuring 4.3 cm × 3.6 cm, and pelvic effusion.

Hospital Course:
The patient was diagnosed with a bilateral adnexal malignant tumor which was not excluded as metastasis, based on imaging studies. Further investigations revealed the possibility of high-grade B-cell lymphoma, and the immunohistochemical staining results supported non-Hodgkin high-grade B-cell lymphoma with rearrangements of the MYC gene and BCL2 gene. On admission, she demonstrated a hemoglobin level of 66 g/L, hematocrit of 20.4%, reticulocyte of 3.28%, serum albumin of 35.1 g/L, and tumor marker levels of CA125 578.50 U/mL, alpha-fetoprotein 157.84 ng/mL, carcinoembryonic antigen 0.53 ng/mL, CA199 16.13 U/mL, Cyfra21-1 2.60 ng/mL, Fer 749.58 ng/mL, β 2-microglobulin 5.56 μg/mL, neuron-specific enolase 15.84 ng/mL, CA50 7.19 U/mL, CA153 25.70 U/mL, and serum lactic dehydrogenase (LDH) 1160 U/L.

During her hospital stay, she received ultrasound-guided puncture catheter drainage in the abdominal cavity and right thoracic cavity to manage massive peritoneal and bilateral pleural effusion. She underwent whole-abdomen CT, which showed malignancies of bilateral adnexal origin that did not involve the rectum and bladder, multiple soft tissue masses in the abdomen believed to be metastases, tumor involvement in the bilateral middle, and lower ureters. The patient was further evaluated with PET-CT, which discovered multiple enlarged lymph nodes throughout the body with increased metabolism indicative of lymphoma, and thickening of the bilateral pleural wall, pleura, pericardium, peritoneum, omentum, and mesentery with increased metabolism indicating lymphoma infiltration. The exfoliative cytology of hydrothorax and hydroperitoneum showed many lymphocytes without cancer cells.

Discharge:
The patient's condition was stabilized with prompt medical management and specialized care services. She was discharged with instructions to continue follow-up treatment for her non-Hodgkin high-grade B-cell lymphoma diagnosis. She was further advised to adhere to a prescribed medication regimen, maintain a balanced diet, and get regular check-ups with her primary care physician. The patient was also informed of the importance of consulting with healthcare providers for early intervention in case of new symptoms.

Clinical impression:
1. Non-Hodgkin high-grade B-cell lymphoma with rearrangements of the MYC gene and BCL2 gene.
2. Bilateral ovarian tumors which were not excluded as metastasis.
3. Multiple soft tissue masses in the abdomen believed to be metastases.
4. Tumor involvement in the bilateral middle and lower ureters.
5. Multiple enlarged lymph nodes throughout the body with increased metabolism indicative of lymphoma.
6. Massive peritoneal and bilateral pleural effusion.
7. Gastritis.
8. Anemia.

An ultrasound found growths on both ovaries. The right growth measured about 9.2 cm by 6.7 cm. The left growth measured about 9.2 cm by 6.9 cm. There was also a fluid-filled sac near the womb measuring 4.3 cm by 3.6 cm. Fluid buildup was found in the pelvis area.

Hospital Course:
Imaging tests showed the patient likely had cancer in the areas near both ovaries. Doctors could not rule out that the cancer had spread from somewhere else. More tests pointed to a fast-growing blood cancer called high-grade B-cell lymphoma. Special lab tests on tissue samples confirmed this type of cancer. The cancer had changes in two genes called MYC and BCL2. Blood tests at admission showed low red blood cell levels and low blood protein. Several cancer markers in the blood were tested. Some markers were higher than normal, including CA125, alpha-fetoprotein, ferritin, and LDH.

During her hospital stay, doctors used ultrasound to guide tubes into her belly and right chest area. This drained large amounts of fluid that had built up around her lungs and in her belly. A full belly scan showed the cancer started near both ovaries but had not spread to the rectum or bladder. Multiple small masses in the belly were likely cancer that had spread. The cancer was also affecting the tubes that carry urine from the kidneys to the bladder on both sides. A full body scan found many swollen lymph nodes throughout the body. These showed signs of lymphoma activity. The lining around the lungs, heart, and belly organs was thickened. This also showed signs of lymphoma spread. Tests on the fluid from the chest and belly found many immune cells but no cancer cells.

Discharge:
The patient became stable with quick medical care and special treatment. She left the hospital with instructions to continue treatment for her high-grade B-cell lymphoma. She was told to take her medicines as directed and eat a healthy diet. She should get regular checkups with her main doctor. The patient was also told to contact her doctors right away if she notices any new symptoms.

Clinical impression:
1. High-grade B-cell lymphoma, a fast-growing blood cancer, with changes in the MYC and BCL2 genes.
2. Growths on both ovaries that may be cancer that spread from somewhere else.
3. Multiple small masses in the belly that are likely cancer that has spread.
4. Cancer affecting the tubes that carry urine from the kidneys on both sides.
5. Many swollen lymph nodes throughout the body showing signs of lymphoma.
6. Large amounts of fluid buildup around the lungs and in the belly.
7. Stomach lining irritation.
8. Low red blood cell count.

Hospital Course:

The patient, an 81-year-old female with a significant history of prediabetes and end stage renal disease on hemodialysis, underwent coronary artery bypass graft surgery and replacement of mitral valve with postoperative complications. The patient presented with a dehiscence of the sternal wound, which required wound vacuum assisted closure, as well as a sacral decubitus ulcer, and multiple episodes of sepsis and respiratory failure.

Assessment and Plan:

During the first 45 days of admission, the patient's blood glucose was well-controlled with only 2 units total of sliding scale insulin required. However, soon after the start of intravenous ascorbic acid to aid in sternal wound healing, the patient experienced multiple high FSBG levels over 200 mg/dL, resulting in a total of 9 units of insulin treatment in 24 hours and subsequent FSBG levels remaining high over the next few days. Further investigation revealed a marked discrepancy of greater than 100 mg/dL between simultaneous FSBG and BGMP readings, with BGMP readings ranging from 72 to 146 mg/dL. Given the suspicion for falsely high FSBG readings caused by intravenous ascorbic acid, it was discontinued and FSBG values returned to normal. The patient did not experience hypoglycemia while receiving unnecessary insulin treatment.

Summary:

This discharge summary documents the hospital course of an elderly female with a history of renal disease and prediabetes who underwent coronary artery bypass graft surgery and replacement of mitral valve, complicated by postoperative complications. The patient had high FSBG levels after starting intravenous ascorbic acid, which were believed to be falsely elevated, resulting in unnecessary insulin treatment. The FSBG values returned to normal after discontinuation of intravenous ascorbic acid.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Information:

- Age: 2 months
- Gender: Male
- Admitting Diagnosis: Sepsis
- Discharge Diagnosis: Malaria

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 2-month-old male infant, was admitted to our pediatric antiretroviral clinic with the complaint of fever, which was occurring every 2 to 3 days. The mother of the patient reported that the fever was associated with nonprojectile vomit containing recently ingested milk formula. Upon examination, the patient was found to have hepatic and splenic enlargement of 4 cm each. A diagnosis of sepsis was made and the patient was treated with intravenous cefuroxime before complete blood count investigation. Fever resolved 2 days after commencing antibiotics and the patient was discharged home on oral cefuroxime.

The patient was re-admitted a week later with the complaint of fever recurring every 2 to 3 days. A diagnosis of malaria was made upon detection of trophozoites of Plasmodium falciparum in the peripheral blood film. The patient was treated with oral quinine and showed a remarkable improvement in his condition, with the intermittent fever resolving by crisis within 24 hours of administration. The packed cell volume of 26% at readmission increased to 32% on the fourth day of quinine therapy. The child remained well and was discharged home two days after.

Follow-up Recommendations:
The patient is advised to continue co-trimoxazole prophylaxis as previously prescribed and follow up with the pediatric antiretroviral clinic for routine monitoring.

Patient Education:
The mother of the patient is advised to be vigilant in reporting signs and symptoms of fever and to consider malaria as a potential diagnosis in the event of persistent fever. She is also advised to continue the patient's medication regimen as prescribed and follow up with the pediatric antiretroviral clinic for routine monitoring.

The histological examination of the specimen revealed squamous cell papilloma, which tested positive for human papilloma virus (HPV). Oesophageal manometry and 24-hour oesophageal pH monitoring indicated borderline pathological reflux with some proximal penetration. The patient then underwent complete endoscopic excision of the lesion. Histology confirmed HPV-positive squamous papilloma.

The patient's symptoms resolved after the excision, and the patient received continued anti-reflux treatment, including lifestyle changes. A yearly follow-up confirmed complete remission of symptoms.

A yearly follow-up confirmed complete remission of symptoms. The patient received continued anti-reflux treatment, including lifestyle changes.

Date of Discharge: [REDACTED]                                       

Admitting Diagnosis: Extensive stage small cell lung cancer

Hospital Course Summary:

The patient, a 43-year-old non-smoking woman, was admitted with a six-month history of deteriorating dyspnea on exertion. The patient underwent various diagnostic tests, including a chest X-ray, chest computed tomography, bronchoscopic washing, biopsies, magnetic resonance imaging, and positron emission tomography-computed tomography, which led to the diagnosis of extensive stage small cell lung cancer. The patient was started on first-line chemotherapy with cisplatin and etoposide, which resulted in a significant improvement of the tumor. However, after six cycles, the patient developed progressive disease, and second-line chemotherapy with carboplatin and irinotecan was initiated. Unfortunately, the patient developed obstructive pneumonia after two cycles, and the regimen was changed. The patient was placed in the refractory relapse group and started on third-line chemotherapy using CAV (Adriamycin, vincristine, and cyclophosphamide), which was maintained for 11 cycles. The patient developed progressive disease after the 11th cycle and the regimen was unable to be continued. The patient was then started on fourth-line therapy with ICE (ifosfamide, carboplatin, and etoposide), but had to discontinue due to intolerable toxicity. Later, an ICE regimen without etoposide was commenced as a fourth-line therapy, resulting in a partial response to therapy. The patient’s pain gradually disappeared during this regimen, and she refused further treatment. Eight months after completing the fifth cycle of carboplatin and ifosfamide, the patient presented to the emergency department for dyspnea and rib pain, and a chest CT showed an increase in the size of her mass. Palliative treatment with a sixth cycle of carboplatin and ifosfamide was initiated, and her symptoms improved. However, the patient expired due to aspiration pneumonia 11 days later. The patient survived for approximately 27 months after beginning chemotherapy.

Discharge Medications: [REDACTED]

The patient was admitted with extensive stage small cell lung cancer and treated with various chemotherapy regimens, including cisplatin and etoposide, carboplatin and irinotecan, CAV, and ICE. A partial response to therapy was achieved with ICE without etoposide, which resulted in the reduction of the size and uptake of the tumor. The patient was later admitted to the hospital for palliation of symptoms, and dyspnea and chest pain improved after treatment with a sixth cycle of carboplatin and ifosfamide. However, the patient later died from aspiration pneumonia.

Discharge Summary:

Admission Date: 

Discharge Date: 

Patient Name: 

Medical Record Number: 

Principal Diagnosis: Prostatic TB with Intracranial TB 

Hospital Course:

The patient was a 54-year old man who was admitted to the hospital due to persistent fever and weight loss. Upon admission, various tests were conducted, including blood counts, liver and renal function tests, and blood culture for common pathogens. However, no significant abnormality was discovered. 

As a result, the patient underwent a whole body F-18 FDG PET-CECT, which revealed intense FDG uptake in the right lobe of the prostate gland and asymmetric heterogeneous FDG uptake in the left frontal lobe peripherally. Following this finding, an MRI scan of the pelvic region was advised. 

Subsequently, a TRUS-guided biopsy was carried out, which ultimately revealed multiple caseous epithelioid granulomas containing giant cells. This validated the diagnosis of prostatic TB, and the patient was prescribed anti-tubercular therapy (ATT) immediately. 

However, before the patient was scheduled to undergo an MRI brain, the patient developed sudden altered mental state, which lasted for a brief period. The provisional diagnosis for this episode was Ethambutol and Isoniazid induced psychosis. Later, an MRI brain with gadolinium contrast demonstrated asymmetrical exaggerated irregular leptomeningeal enhancement in the left frontal region with enhancing granulomas in the supra and infratentorial brain parenchyma, which represented intracranial TB. 

Overall, the patient responded favorably to the ATT treatment, with a subsided fever and normalized ESR within 2 months. The patient did not experience any other neurological episodes. Serum PSA was observed to be normal after the first three months. 

Discharge Medications:

N/A

Follow-up:

The patient is advised to remain aware of the symptoms of TB and seek help if such symptoms reoccur in the future.

Discharge Summary:

Patient: 39-year-old woman diagnosed with plasmablastic IgA lambda multiple myeloma

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted to our facility in January 2011 with a diagnosis of plasmablastic IgA lambda multiple myeloma, stage III (International Staging System). She underwent four cycles of PAD chemotherapy (bortezomib, adriamycin, and dexamethasone) and zoledronic acid before receiving an autologous peripheral blood stem cell transplant, conditioned with melphalan (200 mg/m2), in August 2011. The patient experienced a symptomatic relapse with a T7 vertebral collapse in March 2013, after which treatment with lenalidomide and dexamethasone was initiated. Due to a loss of response after four cycles of treatment, the patient received VCD chemotherapy (bortezomib, cyclophosphamide, and dexamethasone), achieving a second complete remission. In December 2013, a fully matched sibling hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, after reduced-intensity conditioning regimen, was performed to consolidate the excellent response. The patient experienced another bone marrow relapse, along with a plasmacytoma of tibia in April 2014, following which she was retreated with VCD. This regimen was stopped after two cycles of treatment due to bortezomib-related peripheral neuropathy. The patient was then placed on VBCMP/VBAD chemotherapy (vincristine, carmustine, cyclophosphamide, melphalan, prednisone/vincristine, carmustine, doxorubicin, and high-dose dexamethasone), achieving a third complete remission.

In April 2015, the patient presented with pericardial effusion and echocardiographic signs of cardiac tamponade, which were resolved through pericardiocentesis. In May 2015, the patient presented with massive left-side pleural effusion. Two thoracocentesis revealed plasmablastic cells. Despite this EMM relapse, multiple myeloma was not detected in blood, urine, or bone marrow. The patient was then started on carfilzomib plus dexamethasone, which resulted in a sudden improvement in her general condition and was discharged without pleural effusion.

Follow-Up Recommendations:

The patient is currently receiving the 18th cycle of treatment and remains in complete remission 19 months after the EMM was detected. Further follow-up appointments will be scheduled to monitor the patient's progress.

The patient, a 25-year-old Asian male with no past medical history, presented with sudden onset, worsening pain of the right forearm and hand. He had classical signs of acute limb ischaemia, consisting of pallor, coldness and delayed capillary refill of about 10 seconds, and sensory and motor impairment. A pulsatile mass in the root of the right side of the neck with a bruit and flow murmur was also noted. The patient underwent a hand-held Doppler ultrasound that revealed a diminished ulnar artery signal and a monophasic radial artery signal, along with a normal brachial artery signal. An aneurysm of the subclavian artery was diagnosed with embolic occlusion of the brachial artery.

The patient was treated with intravenous heparin, which resulted in partial improvement of their symptoms. Further investigation with a brachial angiogram and Computed Tomography angiogram revealed a saccular aneurysm in the mid-portion of the subclavian artery, proximal to the clavicle, with a size of 1.1 × 2 cm and a right-sided cervical rib. The images also showed that the brachial artery was occluded due to a thrombus extending from the mid-upper arm to the distal part of the elbow. Intra-arterial thrombolysis was attempted but failed due to extravasation following direct puncture of the axillary artery. Six days after initial presentation, the patient underwent a subclavian artery aneurysm repair with a cervical rib excision and brachial embolectomy. The patient was treated with warfarin for 3 months post-op.

The postoperative Doppler scan revealed good signals in the right ulnar and radial arteries. The patient attended follow-up clinic 3 months post-discharge with no complications and complete resolution of symptoms.

Hospital Course:

The patient presented to our facility with dysmenorrhea and persistent, severe pelvic pain that had been ongoing for 8 years. The patient had a history of laparotomic right adnexectomy for omolateral ovarian endometriosis and had undergone a pelvic adhesions surgical procedure at a different facility in 2009, which was unsuccessful in relieving her symptoms.

Upon admission, an ultrasound showed a right sided double cystic mass, completely separated from the uterus consistent with infraligamentary myomas. After a follow-up ultrasound, a right-sided cystic mass surrounding a smaller echoic mass was identified. This was later confirmed during a diagnostic hysteroscopy and operative laparoscopy, which revealed a unicornuate uterus with a completely separated and distant right horn with no communication with the unicornuate uterus, without any Fallopian tube or ovary, and with a small myoma. Several thick adhesions attached the right horn to the rectosigmoid and right pelvic wall.

After examination, a unilateral hemihysterectomy was performed on the patient. The right horn was removed, and the right round ligament and right vascular pedicle were coagulated and excised up to the uterine artery. Morcellation was performed, and pathologic evaluation showed the presence of myometrial tissue, hypotrophic endometrium, and focal adenomyosis.

The patient was discharged on the third day post-operation with no complications. At a 9-month follow-up, the patient reported relief from pelvic pain with no acute episodes.

 

Hospital Diagnoses:

- Dysmenorrhea 
- Severe pelvic pain 
- Infraligamentary myomas 
- Hematometra 
- Unicornuate uterus with a completely separated and distant right horn 
- Adhesions
- Focal adenomyosis

 

Hospital Procedures:

- Ultrasound 
- Hysteroscopy
- Diagnostic laparoscopy 
- Unilateral hemihysterectomy 

 

Condition of patient at discharge:

The patient was discharged with no reported complications. The patient's medical condition had significantly improved, and she reported no persistent pelvic pain. The patient was advised to schedule a follow-up with her primary care physician for further care.

Clinically, the patient had improved significantly with no further episodes of pyrexia or abdominal pain. Renal transplantation is planned for the patient once he completes treatment for TB. 

Overall, the patient was discharged with an improved condition and treated for TB. Further follow up is necessary to ensure full recovery.

An 8-year-old boy with no significant medical history was admitted to our urgent ophthalmology clinic with a pencil injury to his left eye. The patient was prescribed Vigamox ophthalmic drops 4 times a day for 3 weeks and preservative-free artificial tears 4 times a day for 4 weeks.

Recommendations:
1. Vision screening should be conducted regularly to monitor for any changes.
2. Regular eye exams are advisable, especially in the presence of eye injuries.
3. Patients should avoid penetrating injuries to the eye.
4. Patients and caregivers should provide immediate medical attention in the event of an eye injury.

The patient is advised to follow up with a pediatric ophthalmologist for regular vision screenings and eye exams. Any changes in vision, pain, or swelling should be reported immediately to their primary care physician.

Histology with immunohistochemistry (IHC) correlation suggested a diagnosis of a primary pulmonary angiosarcoma, intermediate grade. The tumor was found to completely occlude the left main bronchus. A fluorine-18 fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography/computed tomography (18F-FDG PET/CT) done as a part of metastatic workup showed a solitary metabolically active endobronchial lesion in the left main bronchus extending into the left lower bronchus causing complete obstruction and collapse of the entire left lung; further corroborating the diagnosis of a primary pulmonary angiosarcoma.

A formal cardiopulmonary evaluation was done, and the patient was taken up for a definitive surgery. Intraoperatively the tumor was found to originate at the bifurcation of the left main bronchus and a sleeve resection was deemed not possible, the patient, therefore, underwent a left pneumonectomy. Her postoperative recovery was uneventful. The patient received 50 gray of adjuvant radiotherapy.

Follow-up Plan:
The patient is on regular follow-up for the past 7 months.

Discharge Diagnosis:
Primary pulmonary angiosarcoma.

Patient Name: Confidential

Age: 19 years old

Gender: Male

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted to the toxicology ward with significant sleepiness and unclear speech in the middle of a drinking bout which had lasted for the previous 3 months. He was diagnosed with pneumonia after several days with rapid deterioration of his general condition. Echocardiographic examination revealed the presence of numerous vegetations on the heart valves. The patient required intubation and continued mechanical ventilation. Empiric antibiotic therapy was applied, even though bacteriological analysis of venous blood, urine, and bronchial secretions showed them to be sterile. After the patient's condition continued to deteriorate, he was transferred to an operating room at the cardiac surgery ward. The surgical procedure was performed to implant valve bioprostheses in the mitral, aortic, and tricuspid positions. The patient was extubated on the 14th day of ICU stay. However, on the 23rd postoperative day, the patient's general condition deteriorated, with high fever. He was diagnosed with sepsis confirmed by numerous bacteriological tests. After targeted antibiotic therapy was applied with maximum doses of imipenem and Brulamycin, no clinical improvement of the patient's condition was achieved. Transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) revealed the presence of vegetation on the aortic valve bioprosthesis. It was decided to replace the previously implanted aortic valve bioprosthesis. On the 46th day after the initial surgery, the patient was once again transferred to an operating room to remove the damaged aortic valve bioprosthesis and reimplant a new one. The patient was transferred in good condition to a cardiac rehabilitation hospital with a recommendation to continue oral anticoagulation for 3 months and antibiotic therapy.

Diagnosis:

The patient was diagnosed with endocarditis due to alcohol addiction.

The patient was hospitalized for severe back pain and difficulty breathing after being injured by being sandwiched against his back on a broken concrete block. The patient was diagnosed with a T12 dislocation fracture with multiple rib fractures and a right hemopneumothorax.

Treatment Provided:
The patient underwent T10-to-L2 instrumented posterolateral spinal fusion surgery with autografted bone to promote early orthostasis and improve breathing. Surgery was successful.

Postoperative Course:
Three hours after surgery, the patient experienced lower leg and back pain along with motor dysfunction of the lower extremities. Immediate CT imaging revealed no protruding fracture fragments in the spinal canal at the T12 level from reduction of the dislocated fracture during the operation. T11 and T12 laminectomy was performed and a large consolidated hematoma was discovered and removed.

Discharge Condition and Plan:
The patient exhibited gradual recovery from symptoms. At the final follow-up six months after revision surgery, motor function had fully recovered, but mechanical allodynia persisted and required medication. The patient was able to walk with a T-cane on day 20 and was discharged home on day 28.

The patient's medications and follow-up plan will be discussed during a follow-up appointment.

This 54-year-old previously healthy man was admitted for subarachnoid hemorrhage with left hemiparesis and hemihypesthesia. He had experienced progressive headache and neck pain with dizziness for the past two weeks prior to admission. The headache was oppressive, holocranial, and had strong postural variation. The patient developed numbness of the left limbs and fell, resulting in an admission to the previous hospital where he was found to have a contused wound in the left temporal area. The patient was transferred to this hospital for further tests and treatment.

Diagnostic Testing:
CT scan revealed a right frontoparietal subarachnoid hemorrhage and a right parietal hematoma measuring 8 mm in diameter (reported as a probable venous malformation). Cranial CT angiography showed hypoplasia of the A1 segment of the right anterior cerebral artery. Digital subtraction angiography found no aneurysms or arteriovenous malformations but revealed a tubular filling defect within the right frontoparietal superficial cortical vein. Contrast material was slow to empty from the left transverse sinus, suggesting moderate intracranial hypertension. Brain MRI showed diffuse pachymeningeal enhancement after gadolinium administration, suggestive of liquoral hypotension, and a small right parietal hematoma in the acute phase.

Treatment:
The patient was treated with nimodipine, subcutaneous heparin, and subsequently with oral anticoagulants. The patient's neurological deficits resolved, but his headaches persisted. Treatment with blood patch brought about complete resolution of symptoms.

Follow-up:
The patient was discharged in good condition and given follow-up instructions for continued care. The recommendations include maintaining regular follow-up appointments with a healthcare provider and following a healthy lifestyle to prevent any future complications or recurrence of symptoms.

The patient died three days later due to refractory cardiogenic shock.

Infective endocarditis (IE) by pseudomonas aeruginosa (PA), complicated with cerebral emboli, meningitis, and endophtalmia.

The patient was advised to continue taking his medications as directed and to follow up with his primary care physician for regular check-ups. Hospital Course Summary:

Subjective:

The patient is a 65-year-old female with relapsing oral cavity squamous cell carcinoma who presented to our facility after experiencing a left parapharyngeal relapse. The patient underwent cervical radiotherapy and chemotherapy and was subsequently referred to our Phase I unit for enrollment in an early-phase trial.

Objective:

During the screening procedure, chest CT scans showed GGOs, suggestive of COVID-19. IgG antibodies against SARS-CoV-2 were positive, indicating a prior exposure to the virus. The patient was asymptomatic, and two consecutive nasopharyngeal swabs resulted negative. The patient underwent experimental treatment with an anti-PD-L1 mAb administered intravenously every three weeks and a daily oral TKI. The initial tumor assessment showed overall stable disease with an enlargement of GGOs affecting bilateral lower lobes.

Assessment and Plan:

Further investigation revealed no evidence of malignancy, and the interstitial proliferation, CD8+ lymphocytic infiltration, and alveolar damage were consistent with immune-mediated pneumonitis. The immunotherapy with PD-L1 blockade likely led to worsening GGOs initially detected during the screening procedure, with the COVID-19 lung injury acting as an inflammatory primer for subsequent ICI-related pneumonia development. The TKI assumption was unlikely to have played a role in the development of lung damage as it was deemed safe and did not suggest any involvement in its mechanism.

The patient underwent a CT-guided lung biopsy, and the pathological examination supported the diagnosis of immune-mediated pneumonitis. The lung toxicity was classified as grade 1, but the patient experienced no symptoms. Since there was clinical and radiological benefit on the underlying tumor, the patient restarted experimental immunotherapy and was on-treatment at the time of discharge.

Plan:

The patient's discharge instructions include strict adherence to follow-up visits with the primary care physician and the oncologist regularly, especially as part of on-treatment follow-up. Further screening to monitor any progress of immune-mediated pneumonitis and continued radiological monitoring of lung changes. Measurements to monitor respiratory function and continued reporting of any respiratory symptoms are also critical.

Prognosis:

The patient's prognosis is good, and she is expected to continue receiving experimental immunotherapy for the relapsing oral cavity squamous cell carcinoma.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Identification:
This is the discharge summary for a 69-year-old woman with a history of coronary artery disease, hypertension, and dyslipidemia who was admitted for rapidly progressive muscle weakness.

Hospital Course:
Upon admission, the patient presented with predominantly proximal muscle weakness, mild back pain, poor appetite, and dysgeusia. Physical examination showed marked hepatosplenomegaly, and laboratory studies revealed severely elevated serum total calcium and creatinine levels indicative of acute renal injury. Subsequent testing revealed suppressed parathyroid hormone levels, negative PTH-related peptide, mildly elevated lactate dehydrogenase, and almost 5 times the upper range of normal for serum angiotensin-converting enzyme activity along with elevated levels of vitamin D metabolites.

Diagnostic Assessment:
Given strong suspicion for multiple myeloma, a skeletal survey was conducted, which revealed a 1.7-cm punched-out lytic lesion of the vertex of the skull. Serum and urine protein electrophoresis with immunofluorescence failed to demonstrate a monoclonal spike or clonal light chains. Serum free light chains demonstrated an elevated serum Kappa free light chain concentration and a normal Lambda free light chain concentration along with an imbalanced Kappa/Lambda free light chain ratio. A bone marrow biopsy with flow cytometry studies were performed and showed a low-grade B-cell lymphoma with a prominent histiocytic reaction. Subsequently, she underwent a lymph node biopsy, which revealed grade 3B follicular lymphoma. Further staging was performed with positron emission tomography, which showed diffuse patchy uptake within the proximal appendicular and axial skeleton in addition to increased uptake of the large lytic lesion of the skull.

Treatment:
The patient was treated with aggressive hydration and Zoledronate, which resulted in resolution of her hypercalcemia and acute renal injury. R-CHOP chemotherapy was later initiated with significant improvement of her other presenting symptoms.

Discharge Instructions:
The patient is advised to follow-up with her oncologist for further treatment and management of her lymphoma. She should continue to manage her other comorbid conditions including coronary artery disease, hypertension, and dyslipidemia. She should be mindful of her diet and stay active to promote optimal health. She should report any new symptoms or concerns to her healthcare provider.

The patient, a 43-year-old man with gluten intolerance and bullous dermatosis, presented with progressive vision loss, photosensitivity, foreign body sensation, and burning sensation in both eyes. The patient underwent a keratolimbal allograft transplantation and cryopreserved amniotic membrane implant in his right eye due to the presence of corneal melt. Despite undergoing IVIG therapy, the patient's dermatologic lesions were the only ones that improved significantly. The left eye slightly improved to hand motion but the right eye displayed LP without color discrimination.

Severe ocular surface disease with retinal and choroidal detachments in both eyes.

The patient has been advised to follow up regularly with the ophthalmologist for monitoring and management of his ocular condition. Additionally, he has been advised to avoid any activities that may cause further damage to his eyes, including prolonged computer and smartphone use, UV exposure, and dusty environments. The patient has been informed about artificial tears and other lubricants that can provide relief for his eye symptoms.

FOLLOW-UP:
The patient will follow up with the ophthalmologist per the provider's recommendations.

The patient is still alive till 48 months after diagnosis without any detection of lymphoma-manifestation.

Hospital Course:
The patient presented with hair loss, skin lesions, and itching on their face, trunk, and limbs. Previously diagnosed with folliculitis and eczema, the patient did not respond to treatment with cetirizine, hydrocortisone, and mupirocin. The patient experienced symmetrical pain in their wrist and knee joints after exposure to sunlight. Upon examination, the patient had large alopecia patches on the scalp, erythematous plaques on the scalp and face with slight scales, violaceous lichenoid papules, and blisters on the back of the hands and feet, and papules on their trunk and arms. Laboratory tests revealed WBC count of 3.31 × 109, RBC count of 3.7 × 1012, HGB level of 110 g/L, 24-h urine protein at 248 mg, and ANA at 1:160 (homogeneous spot), 1:80 (cytoplasm), dsDNA (-). The patient's ESR was 58 mm/h, and BP180 was 8 RU/ml. Pathological examination of the scalp indicated hair follicle angle plug and epidermal atrophy. The scalp pathology and laboratory tests were consistent with SLE. Pathological examination of the upper arm, hand, and back supported the diagnosis of bullous lichen planus-systemic lupus erythematosus (LP/LE) overlap syndrome.

Treatment:
The patient was given hydroxychloroquine sulfate, prednisone acetate tablets, topical halometasone cream, and tacrolimus cream. Two weeks later, the patient's symptoms showed significant improvement. The prednisone acetate dosage was decreased to 20 mg daily, acitretin 30 mg daily, and oral methotrexate 10 mg weekly. Three weeks later, the hair loss stopped, joint pain disappeared, and partial lesions regressed. Upon recent follow-up, the patient's symptoms remained stable, skin lesions disappeared, and there was some hair regrowth. The patient was prescribed hydroxychloroquine sulfate 200 mg daily, acitretin 10 mg daily, and oral methotrexate 2.5 mg weekly for continued treatment.

Discharge Condition:
The patient was discharged in stable condition with improved symptoms and prescribed medication for continued treatment. The patient should continue to follow up with their healthcare provider regularly to monitor their condition.

Patient: 20-year-old male with chronic apical periodontitis and cystic changes in the mandibular central incisors.

Hospital course:
The patient presented with pain and labial swelling in the lower anterior region for two weeks. Clinical examination revealed discolored mandibular central incisors with labial swelling and a sinus opening seen on the labial aspect of the mandibular right central incisor. Radiographic examination revealed a dumbbell-shaped periapical radiolucency associated with 31, 41. A combined approach of orthograde endodontic treatment for 31, 41 followed by periapical surgery was planned. 
The patient was administered local anesthesia, and the access cavity was done using a number 2 high-speed round diamond bur. The cleaning and shaping of the root canals were performed by hand instruments with step-back technique up to 45 ISO size K-file with alternate irrigation of 3% sodium hypochlorite solution and saline. Calcium hydroxide paste was given as an intracanal medicament for one week. The patient was prescribed antibiotics and analgesics to manage pain and swelling.
One week later, the patient was asymptomatic, obturation was done with cold lateral compaction technique, and the access cavity was restored with composite resin. A complete blood picture and coagulation studies report were normal. The general health condition of the patient was good.
Under local anesthesia, a full thickness mucoperiosteal flap was elevated. The granulation tissue was curetted, and the roots were resected and retrograde filling was done with mineral trioxide aggregate. Bone graft was placed due to the large extension of the defect. The mucoperiosteal flap was sutured in place, and the patient was periodically reviewed after 3 months, 6 months, and one year. At one-year follow-up, a radiograph was taken in relation to mandibular central incisors, which confirmed the satisfactory healing of the periapical lesion.
The patient was asymptomatic during the one-year follow-up. The final diagnosis was chronic apical periodontitis with cystic changes of mandibular central incisors and periapical periodontitis of tooth 31, 41. The recommended treatment plan was successful, and the patient was discharged in good health.

- The patient died due to acute exacerbation from chronic heart failure in November 2020, 10 years after the initial gastrointestinal bleeding event.

Impacted canine tooth in the maxillary bone with periapical radiolucent lesions and absorption of the maxillary right medial and lateral incisor roots by canine crown compression with root absorption of the incisor tooth due to impacted canine.

Despite initial management, her condition still declined, and continuous venovenous hemodialysis (CVVHD) was started for renal failure, along with venovenous extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VV-ECMO).

Although the HIT panel returned negative, Argatroban was administered as anticoagulation due to the significant drop in her platelet count on heparin products. Hospital Course Summary:

History:
The patient is a 58-year-old female who presented with a medial canthal basal cell carcinoma in December 2008, which was removed with clear margins via an excisional biopsy. Five years later, there was evidence of recurrence, which was treated with another local excisional surgery. In September 2014, there was another recurrence with bleeding and ulceration, which was treated with Moh's micrographic resection. In September 2015, a solid tissue mass abutting the medial bony orbital margin and medial aspect of the globe was detected, which was treated with orbital excision. 

Hospital Course:
Following treatment for the orbital excision, the patient expressed her desire to avoid exenteration of the affected area. Therefore, a decision was made to prescribe a 6-month course of vismodegib. Throughout the treatment, the patient tolerated vismodegib well, with minor muscle cramps being the only symptom experienced, which were controlled with magnesium. Late in the 6-month course, the patient experienced patches of alopecia on her scalp, and mild dysgeusia and hyposmia, but found that these side effects did not significantly impact her quality of life. 

Outcome:
The patient has been regularly reviewed by the oculoplastic surgeon, and it has now been 29 months since the orbital excisional surgery. There has been no recurrence of the basal cell carcinoma, and the patient has not required any further treatment. 

Discharge Disposition:
The patient has been discharged and will continue to be closely monitored for any recurrence or potential side effects of the treatment. 

Follow-up:
The patient has been advised to attend regular follow-up appointments with her oculoplastic surgeon and oncologist to monitor for any signs of recurrence or complications. Future treatments will be discussed based on the results of these appointments.

Admission Diagnosis: Euglycemic ketoacidosis due to Jardiance use and recent COVID-19 infection
Hospital Course:

The patient was a 23-year-old female admitted to our facility with complains of shortness of breath, dry cough, chills, malaise, and diaphoresis. She had a recent history of COVID-19 infection and uncontrolled diabetes mellitus on dulaglutide and empagliflozin. Upon physical examination, the patient presented with tachycardia and tachypnea. Laboratory data showed significant metabolic derangements, such as sodium bicarbonate (HCO3) of 11 and anion gap 23. Urinalysis was positive for glucose, protein, and ketones. The patient was admitted to the medical floor to manage metabolic acidosis and did not require treatment for COVID-19 infection. On day 2 of hospitalization, HCO3 decreased from 11 to 6, and the anion gap increased to 24. The patient was started on insulin and HCO3 infusion. On day 3, the anion gap decreased to 16, and insulin drip was discontinued and transitioned to subcutaneous insulin. The patient responded well to treatment with clinical improvement of symptoms. Subsequent laboratory data continued to show significant improvements with the closure of the anion gap. Chart review demonstrated that the patient was supposed to be on insulin therapy and was not following up with the endocrinologist. 

Discharge Diagnosis:

Euglycemic ketoacidosis due to Jardiance use and recent COVID-19 infection

Discharge Instructions:

1. Discontinue Jardiance
2. Continue on subcutaneous insulin injections as prescribed
3. Follow up with endocrinology

Follow-Up:

Outpatient follow-up with endocrinology is recommended to monitor blood glucose levels and manage diabetes.

The patient presented to the hospital with painless hemihypertrophy of the right foot and calf. The asymmetry was first noticed at the time of birth and an initial leg length discrepancy of 1 centimeter increased to 1.5 centimeter. He was forced to wear a larger shoe on his right foot as a result. The patient also experienced muscle cramps on the lateral aspect of his foot and suffered from typical hallux valgus deformity symptoms. Physical examination revealed a painless, soft mass on the medioplantar, plantar, and lateroplantar surface of the right foot. Radiographs and MRI imaging confirmed the clinical presentation. Routine laboratory testing revealed elevated blood creatine kinase levels. The surgical procedure involved resection of the plantar hypertrophic portion of the abductor hallucis brevis muscle, subtotal resection of the hypertrophic flexor digitorum brevis muscle, and correction of the hallux valgus deformity through plication of the medial part of the capsule and proximal osteotomy of the first metatarsal. Postoperatively, the foot was immobilized with a below-knee cast for six weeks, followed by a removable cast and orthotic insoles with medial arch support.

The patient's symptoms resolved postoperatively, and his blood creatine kinase levels declined to a normal range.

Hospital course:
The 7-month-old female Boston terrier was presented with chronic vestibular episodes that started when she was 3 months old. During the physical examination, oculo-vestibular reflex testing caused marked vestibular ataxia, a broad-based stance, and a moderate to severe head tilt to the right. Neurological examination showed only mild head tilt to the left during walking and standing. 
Neuroanatomical localization was consistent with pathology related to vestibulo-cerebellum. Differential diagnoses were considered, and the MRI examination revealed no other abnormality in the brain, suggesting that the observed imaging findings were most likely due to caudal cerebellar hypoplasia. Hematological and biochemical analysis were declined.
The owners reported that the dog was stable and have adapted to the episodes, which mainly happened during playing or sniffing, lasting ~20-30 s. Between the episodes, the dog's gait and head posture were normal.

MRI of the brain showed reduced size of the nodulus and uvula of the caudal cerebellum with no other abnormality in the brain. There was no abnormal contrast enhancement. The imaging findings suggest caudal cerebellar hypoplasia as a possible diagnosis, and no treatment was recommended.

The patient was discharged two weeks later with no effort angina and cardiac dysfunction.

Fondaparinux sodium (ARIXTRA) was injected subcutaneously for 7 days without any event. The patient had more than one year follow-up with no reported complications.

Hospital Course:

The patient is an 8-year-old female with tufting enteropathy who presented on three separate occasions with central venous catheter infection due to Bacillus species. The patient had initially presented in the first few months of life with chronic watery diarrhoea and impaired growth, and was found to have tufting enteropathy - a rare congenital enteropathy that requires indefinite dependence on parenteral nutrition from early infancy. 

On each occasion the patient presented with fever after flushing of the central venous catheter. The first episode of infection was treated with 4 weeks of intravenous flucloxacillin because bacteraemia had persisted despite 14 days of treatment.

The patient was transferred to our hospital following the recurrence of fever and rigors, 10 days after stopping the antibiotics. Bacillus species was isolated from central venous catheter cultures both before and whilst on cefotaxime and flucloxacillin, later identified as Bacillus pumilus at the National Reference Laboratory. There were concerns that the patient had previously reacted to systemic vancomycin, so antibiotics were changed to intravenous clindamycin with vancomycin line locks given for 2 weeks. Blood cultures taken both during and after this treatment were negative. Echocardiography showed no evidence of vegetations at the tip of the catheter or in the heart.

Ten days after stopping the intravenous antibiotics the child presented for the third time with fever and rigors. A Bacillus species was again grown from blood taken from the central venous catheter. The central venous catheter was removed after 5 days treatment with intravenous vancomycin and a new central venous catheter was inserted. Subsequent blood cultures were negative and there has been no recurrence of further fever or infections over a 9-month period, suggesting the infection has been eradicated.

Discharge Summary:

The patient is an 8-year-old female with tufting enteropathy on long-term parenteral nutrition, presenting on three separate occasions with central venous catheter infection due to Bacillus species. The patient was treated with multiple courses of antibiotics and required catheter replacement once due to recurrence of fever and rigors.

The patient is being discharged without any active infections or clinical concerns at this time. The patient's care plan will continue to include regular follow-up with the primary care physician and periodic bloodwork to monitor for any potential infections.

The patient and family were counseled on signs and symptoms of catheter-related infections and the importance of prompt reporting to medical professionals if fever or other concerning symptoms develop. The family was also provided with written and verbal information regarding infection prevention measures, such as strict hand hygiene and catheter care, to minimize the risk of future infections.

The patient was discharged home in good condition and was advised to follow up with the primary care physician for routine care and blood work. The patient's parents were instructed to monitor the patient for any signs of infection and to seek prompt medical attention if any concerning symptoms develop.

The patient was a case of ESRD stage five due to chronic glomerulonephritis and hypertension. The patient did not have a history of smoking.

The chest radiograph revealed bilateral pulmonary infiltrate. High-resolution computed tomography of the chest revealed patchy air-space consolidation, ground-glass opacities, small nodular opacities, and bronchial wall thickening with dilation.

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to our institution with progressive neurological symptoms. He had a history of seropositive Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA) that was managed with maintenance methotrexate, hydroxychloroquine and low-dose prednisone. The patient developed fluctuating confusion, word-finding difficulty, right-sided weakness and gait imbalance. An evaluation was done by the neurologist which confirmed the presence of neurological deficits. An MRI scan showed areas of scattered restricted diffusion and enhancement within the cortex and leptomeninges of the left hemisphere near the vertex, suspicious for meningoencephalitis. CSF analysis also demonstrated lymphocytic meningitis with negative, bacterial and fungal cultures. 

The patient was started on antiepileptic medication and a whole-body PET scan was done to rule out underlying malignancy. A bone marrow biopsy was also done to rule out lymphoid neoplasm. An open meningeal biopsy was performed and gross examination revealed thickening and opacification of the meninges. The histopathological findings were consistent with leptomeningeal involvement by nodular rheumatoid meningitis.

Immunosuppressive therapy with monthly cyclophosphamide and high-dose corticosteroids was initiated for 6 months and then the corticosteroids were tapered. The patient's neurological examination improved one month post treatment initiation, although confusion and bilateral postural tremor persisted. Most parkinsonian features also largely resolved following immunosuppressive therapy. 

Repeat MRI 3 months after treatment initiation showed complete resolution of previous findings, and CRP levels also normalized. The patient was eventually transitioned to a long-term care facility due to the persistent behavioral and cognitive deficits with intermittent periods of agitation.

Diagnosis:
Leptomeningeal involvement by nodular rheumatoid meningitis

Course:
The patient was admitted for investigation of progressive neurological symptoms and was treated with immunosuppressive therapy. The patient's neurological examination improved one month post treatment initiation, although confusion and bilateral postural tremor persisted, and most parkinsonian features largely resolved following immunosuppressive therapy. Repeat MRI 3 months after treatment initiation showed complete resolution of previous findings.

Discharge Condition:
The patient has been transitioned to a long-term care facility due to persistent behavioral and cognitive deficits with intermittent periods of agitation.

Hospital Course:
A previously healthy 50-year-old male smoker presented with dyspnea and a dry cough for the past month. Physical examination and blood tests yielded non-diagnostic results. An electrocardiogram showed negative T waves and echocardiography revealed pulmonary hypertension. Enhanced computed tomography revealed no pulmonary embolism. The patient was initially diagnosed with cor pulmonale secondary to chronic obstructive pulmonary disease but was subsequently admitted to our hospital for further evaluation.

Admission:
On admission, the patient exhibited vital signs within normal limits, except for oxygen saturation of 94%. Physical examination revealed cervical lymphadenopathy, and laboratory findings revealed elevated levels of brain natriuretic peptide, D-dimer, lactate dehydrogenase, C-reactive protein, carcinoembryonic antigen, and cytokeratin-19 fragment. Chest radiograph showed bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy. CT revealed lymphadenopathy in the cervical, mediastinal, and upper abdominal regions and lower lung lobes with septal thickening and ground-glass opacities. Echocardiography indicated pulmonary hypertension.

Diagnostic Workup:
Given the subacute course, elevated tumor markers, pulmonary hypertension without apparent etiology, and diffuse lymphadenopathy, PTTM was suspected. An atypical cell of epithelial origin was found on a cervical lymph node biopsy. CT and tumor markers did not allow for determination of the primary cancer site. Upper endoscopy and colonoscopy showed normal results. To reduce hypercoagulability due to PTTM, edoxaban administration was initiated.

Management:
After consultation with a gastroenterologist, a regimen of imatinib, prednisolone, and tegafur/gimeracil/oteracil plus oxaliplatin therapy was initiated. On day 6, mild dyspnea progressed, and oxygen was administered via a nasal cannula. On day 8, the patient's hypoxia suddenly worsened, and he subsequently passed away.

Autopsy:
An autopsy was performed, and macroscopic examination showed no abnormalities in the gastric wall. However, two gastric cancers of pure signet ring cell carcinoma were found in the pyloric region. Lymphovascular invasions were identified in layers from submucosa to subserosa, and multiple lymph node metastases surrounded the stomach. No findings of Helicobacter pylori-associated gastritis were observed. Additionally, pulmonary thromboembolism was not observed, but thickened epithelial cells of small pulmonary arteries were consistent with PTTM, and carcinomatous lymphangiomatosis was also observed.

The patient, a 22-year-old previously healthy female, was admitted to the hospital following a severe facial trauma sustained in a highway motor vehicle accident. The patient was resuscitated with crystalloid and two units of whole blood prior to arrival at the hospital. Upon arrival, the patient was hemodynamically unstable with tachycardia, hypotension, and severe metabolic acidosis. Trauma series computerized tomography revealed facial trauma with ruptured right globe, temporal bone and temporomandibular joint-line fractures, as well as subdural and epidural hematomas with an 8 mm midline shift and effacement of the anterior horn of the right lateral cerebral ventricle. There was also air within the right ventricle, extending to the right axillary vein, but no immediate RV outflow tract obstruction. A multispecialty conference was held to discuss the optimal treatment plan, and the decision was made to proceed with an emergent craniotomy. During the procedure, the patient experienced a brief episode of hemodynamic collapse secondary to obstructive venous air embolism, which was promptly treated with intravenous epinephrine and fluid resuscitation. The patient was stabilized and underwent a right eye enucleation, repair of brow and facial lacerations, complex repair of nasal laceration and cartilage, repair of upper and lower eyelid lacerations, and reduction and fixation of numerous, complex frontozygomatic fractures. The patient was extubated within 36 hours of admission and exhibited no gross neurological deficits. The patient continues to progress with traumatic brain rehabilitation in the outpatient setting.

Severe facial trauma

Procedures
Emergent craniotomy
Right eye enucleation
Complex repair of nasal laceration and cartilage
Repair of upper and lower eyelid lacerations
Reduction and fixation of numerous, complex frontozygomatic fractures
Irrigation and debridement of open wound

Complete resolution of midline shift and no gross neurological deficits exhibited postoperatively

N/A

The patient, a 76-year-old Japanese woman with a history of diabetes, hypothyroidism, and right breast cancer, presented at our hospital after experiencing severe buttock and lower extremity pain for 1 month. Examination revealed positive straight-leg-raising tests, positive Valleix pain point and superior gluteal nerve pain point tests, and negative femoral nerve-stretching tests. X-ray findings showed mild spondylosis. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed a solitary intradural extramedullary cauda equina tumor at L2/3 with low T1, high T2, and uniform contrast enhancement with gadolinium. Myelography showed a total block of contrast below L2/3 and capping of contrast by the mass. The patient underwent an L1–3 laminectomy and tumor extirpation, which successfully relieved her pain. The pathology of the metastasis was adenocarcinoma, and the patient started chemotherapy for breast cancer. 

Hospital Course Summary:

A 76-year-old Japanese woman presented at our hospital with severe buttock and lower extremity pain without a history of injury, 1 month after undergoing conservative treatment. Upon examination, her pain was found to be severe in the buttocks and posterior femoral area, along with positive straight-leg-raising tests and positive Valleix pain point and superior gluteal nerve pain point tests bilaterally. MRI revealed a solitary intradural extramedullary cauda equina tumor while X-ray showed mild spondylosis. The patient underwent an L1–3 laminectomy and tumor extirpation, which was successful in relieving her pain. Pathology revealed adenocarcinoma metastasis, and the patient started chemotherapy for breast cancer. The lower extremity pain relief was maintained and satisfactory during the postoperative course. The patient died 9 months postoperatively due to Trousseau syndrome and brain metastasis from breast cancer.

Patient Name:

Admission Diagnosis: ST-Elevation Myocardial Infarction (STEMI) 

Hospital Course: 

The patient was admitted to our hospital due to 1 hour of severe chest pain. The electrocardiogram showed ST-segment elevation in leads I and AVL. Laboratory results indicated an elevated serum creatine kinase and troponin I. Primary percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) was performed, and the culprit was found to be left circumflex artery occlusion with triple vessel disease. Aspiration thrombectomy and percutaneous coronary balloon dilation were successful in achieving coronary reperfusion. The cardiac surgeon recommended completing the CABG surgery after the acute phase of AMI; however, the patient declined surgery due to her advanced age. 

On the 6th day of hospitalization, the patient experienced sudden chest pain, dyspnea, agitation, and profuse sweating. An electrocardiogram did not show ST-segment elevation, but the patient was found to have atrial fibrillation with a heart rate of 140 beats per minute, which was treated with electrical defibrillation. The patient was diagnosed with pericardial tamponade and underwent pericardiocentesis with ultrasound guidance. Continuous drainage of hemorrhagic pericardial effusion stabilized her hemodynamic condition. 

A subsequent echocardiogram revealed an abnormal cardiac chamber adjacent to the lateral wall of the left ventricle with a myocardial defect (11 mm) in the lateral wall. The diagnosis was congestive hemodynamic impairment caused by the rupture of the left ventricle after acute myocardial infarction, followed by acute pericardial tamponade. While the patient was advised to undergo surgery, she opted for conservative treatment with drug regimens that included dual antiplatelet, statin, β-blocker, and diuretics. 

During her 36-month follow-up, there were no significant changes in her condition. The volume of the pesudoaneurysm increased to 65 × 55 mm only during the initial 2 months of follow-up. After 1 year, color Doppler ultrasound revealed that the blood flow within the aneurysm cavity decreased and echoes of the thrombus were observed. Once the thrombus almost filled the aneurysm cavity after 1.5 years, partial blood flow imaging was seen only nearby the defect of the left ventricular, which was confirmed by myocardial contrast echocardiography. Given the dynamic changes in the pseudoaneurysm, conservative treatment was continued. After 2.5 years of onset of AMI, the patient experienced angina and underwent LAD and RCA PCI. Following medication adherence and no significant changes during the follow up for 3 years, dual antiplatelet therapy was discontinued. 

Discharge Diagnosis: Congestive Hemodynamic Impairment, Pseudoaneurysm of the Left Ventricular, Triple Vessel Disease

Disposition: 

The patient was discharged in stable condition with instructions to follow up with cardiology for routine medication monitoring and outpatient procedures as needed. The patient was informed of the importance of medication adherence and regular follow-up visits.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [REDACTED]   
Date of Admission: [REDACTED]   
Date of Discharge: [REDACTED]   

Hospital Course:   
The 45-year-old patient was admitted to the outpatient department with complaints of a right vulvar mass that was painful and tender. She noticed the tumor a few days back and reported an aggravation of pain during menstruation. No other symptoms like fever, erythema, or discharge were identified, and her personal medical history was unremarkable. Physical examination disclosed a mass on her right labia minor, which was superficially located and very mobile. Ultrasonography revealed a hypoechoic lesion that suggests the presence of Bartholin gland cyst or abscess. The uterus and both adnexae were insignificant. Therefore, a mass excision was carried out for definitive diagnosis and treatment. During surgery, the vulvar mass was located in deep dermis and had a tortuous appearance with soft rubbery consistency.   

Diagnosis:   
Microscopic examination revealed a well-demarcated convoluted or multinodular tumor with solid growth pattern. The tumor was composed mainly of uniform epithelioid round or polygonal cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm and centrally located round nuclei. Extracellular myxoid materials were multifocally identified in stroma. In addition, intracellular vacuolar myxoid changes were also noted. The focal areas were made up of spindle cells with blunt-ended elongated nuclei in part, and in some areas, the tumor originated from the vessel wall. Mitotic activity, cellular atypia, or necrosis pleomorphism were absent. Immunohistochemistry revealed diffuse strong positive and focal positivity for desmin, smooth muscle actin (SMA), smooth muscle myosin heavy chain (Smm-hc), and estrogen receptor (ER). HMB45 was not expressed in the tumor cells. Based on histologic features and immunohistochemistry, the tumor was diagnosed as vulvar epithelioid leiomyoma.

Treatment and Condition on Discharge:   
The patient underwent a mass excision and was discharged without any complications. She was advised periodic follow-up visits. There was no evidence of clinical or radiologic recurrence for 10 months.

Follow-up Plan:   
The patient is advised to visit the hospital periodically as per the follow-up schedule informed by the doctor.   

Summary:   
A 45-year-old female visited the outpatient department with pain and tenderness in a right vulvar mass. Imaging suggested Bartholin gland cyst or abscess, and therefore a mass excision was performed. Histopathological examination revealed the tumor to be vulvar epithelioid leiomyoma. The patient was discharged without any complications and advised periodic follow-up visits. No clinical or radiologic recurrence was observed for 10 months after the surgery.

History of Present Illness: The patient was admitted for elective lower segment cesarean section and ligation due to complaints of breathlessness, chest pain, occasional palpitation at rest, and swelling of both lower limbs since last 7-8 months. The patient was diagnosed one year after her previous vaginal delivery with ruptured aneurysm of right sinus of Valsalva. The patient was advised to undergo surgical correction of the heart ailment but could not afford the surgery and became pregnant.

Hospital Course: The patient was admitted to ensure safe confinement and underwent a successful elective cesarean section. The patient was preoperatively optimised, and high-risk consent for anaesthesia was obtained. The anaesthetic management was uneventful, and the patient was hemodynamically stable throughout the surgery. The patient was shifted to the Intensive Care Unit (ICU) for observation.

Physical Examination: On examination, her pulse rate was 96/minute, and Blood Pressure was 110/70mm of Hg. Pitting type of pedal oedema was present. Respiratory system showed bilateral equal, normal vesicular breath sounds with no rhonchi or crepitations. A loud continuous murmur was present over the whole of the precordium, best heard along the lower left sternal border.

Diagnostic Tests: Routine blood investigations were normal except Hb. (9gm%). Chest radiograph was normal. Electro-cardiogram showed sinus tachycardia. Transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) showed a membranous outpouching of the right coronary cusp (RCC) protruding into right ventricular outflow tract (RVO) with a small perforation (3.2 mm width). There was a continuous wave flow with a left to right (L-R) shunt into the right (RVO) tract below the pulmonary valve. The ventricular chambers were normal in size and there was good left ventricular function at rest.

Treatment: Patient was continued on oral digoxin and lasix. Intravenous ranitidine 50mg and metoclopramide 10mg were given 30 minutes prior to induction for aspiration prophylaxis. Antibiotic prophylaxis was obtained with 2gm of intravenous amoxycillin.

Follow-up Care: The patient was discharged in stable condition with postoperative instructions. The patient was advised to continue on oral digoxin and lasix and referred to a cardiologist for further evaluation and management of her perforated aneurysm of right sinus of Valsalva.

Prescriptions: Oral Digoxin, Lasix.

Instructions: The patient was advised to follow up with a cardiologist for further management of her perforated aneurysm of right sinus of Valsalva.

The patient presented to the emergency clinic with a sudden decrease in vision following a blunt trauma to the right eye with a tennis ball. On presentation, his best corrected visual acuity was hand movement with perception of rays in all quadrants. The patient was managed conservatively with topical steroid eye drops, cycloplegics, and anti-glaucoma medications. The hyphema and vitreous hemorrhage settled down in three weeks, and the patient's visual acuity increased to 20/60. However, the IOP remained high, and prostaglandin analogue bimatoprost 0.01% was added. As the IOP did not show substantial improvement in the following weeks, the patient was advised for filtering surgery under guarded visual prognosis. 
Intraoperatively, there was a vitreous prolapse during deep block excision, which was managed with anterior vitrectomy. On postoperative day one, the visual acuity was 20/125, and the IOP was non-recordable. The patient was treated with topical and oral prednisolone for serous choroidal detachment, and the effusion settled in two weeks. Gradually, the patient's vision and IOP improved, and at the last follow-up visit after three months, the best corrected visual acuity and IOP were 20/25 and 12 mm Hg off any medication, respectively.

Summary:
An 18-year-old male presented with a blunt trauma to the right eye resulting in a decrease in visual acuity and high IOP. The patient was conservatively managed with topical steroid eye drops, cycloplegics, and anti-glaucoma medications, followed by filtering surgery. The intraoperative management included anterior vitrectomy for vitreous prolapse. The patient developed serous choroidal detachment, which resolved with prednisolone treatment. The patient was gradually tapered off prednisolone and showed improvement in visual acuity and IOP at the last follow-up visit after three months.
