History of Present Illness:
The patient, a 52-year-old man with no significant medical history, presented with a dry cough, recurrent streaky hemoptysis and occasional low grade fever for the last one and half years. The expectoration was mucoid, scanty in amount and there was no postural or seasonal variation. Fever was of low grade (up to 100°F), and irregular, without any definite periodicity. 

Physical Examination:
The patient was well built and well-nourished with no clubbing or peripheral lymphadenopathy. Respiratory system examination was essentially normal except impaired percussion note and diminished vesicular breath sound in the left infraclavicular region. Trachea was central in position. Cardiovascular system (CVS) and Central Nervous System (CNS) and abdominal examinations were unremarkable. 

Diagnostic Evaluation:
Complete blood count and blood biochemistry was normal except anemia (Hb: 10.8 gm %) and high ESR (40 mm/hr). HIV serology was nonreactive, and sputum smear failed to show any AFB on two occasions. Chest X-ray revealed nonhomogenous opacity in left upper zone with upward and forward retraction of oblique fissure, left hilar prominence and raised left hemidiaphragm. CECT thorax showed collapse-consolidation with a few air bronchograms and tiny calcification in the left upper lobe. 

Fiberoptic Bronchoscopy:
The patient underwent fibroptic bronchoscopy, which revealed hyperemic and swollen bronchial mucosa of the left upper lobe with a globular mass, which was partially occluding the left upper lobe opening. Biopsy was taken from the mass, white cheesy material was seen coming out of it, and it was sent for HPE. BAL fluid was also sent for Gram stain and C/S, AFB stain and M. Tuberculosis culture. The BAL fluid failed to show any organism in smear, but the bronchial biopsy showed typical caseating epitheloid granuloma. Postbronchoscopic sputum showed AFB in smear examination. The BAL fluid grew Mycobacterium tuberculosis after three weeks. 

Management:
After review of the investigation reports, the patient was started on Category I ATD (2H 3R3Z3E3/4H3R3) under DOTS along with oral prednisolone. Three months post-treatment, repeat bronchoscopy showed restored patency of the left upper lobe bronchus with stenosis.

Discharge Diagnosis:
Tuberculosis

Disposition:
The patient was discharged in stable condition and instructed regarding TB care, including medication schedule, importance of compliance with therapy, and proper precautions to be taken when coughing and in public settings. Follow-up appointment was scheduled with the primary care physician.

Discharge Summary:

Patient: 53-year-old male nurse diagnosed with HCV infection 

Hospital Course:
In January 2011, the patient was evaluated at the Outpatient Infectious Diseases clinic for abnormal liver function tests. His HCV RNA was 660,000 IU/mL, genotype 3a. A liver biopsy showed chronic active hepatitis with Metavir A2 necroinflammatory grading and F2 fibrosis. The patient was considered eligible for antiviral treatment and started therapy with PEG-IFN-α-2a and ribavirin in March 2011. Treatment was well tolerated, and HCV RNA became negative by the fourth week and remained undetectable during the entire 24-week treatment regimen. ALT normalized within the first 3 weeks of treatment. The patient underwent post-treatment follow-up until September 2012, and a new biopsy revealed a mild reduction in Metavir grading and staging (A1 and F1, respectively).

Hospitalization:
Nine weeks after finishing the antiviral therapy, the patient developed symmetrical polyarthritis with joint pain and edema in the wrists, knees, shoulders, and metacarpophalangeal joints, associated with prolonged morning stiffness. MRI detected bone erosions with juxta-articular osteopenia in the wrist, knee, and hand joints, revealing a diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis (RA). Rheumatoid factor and anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody testing were positive. 

Treatment:
The patient was treated with prednisone and NSAIDs for two months, followed by methotrexate and sulfasalazine with a quick and favorable response to treatment. 

Discharge:
The patient was discharged home in satisfactory condition with a prescription for methotrexate and sulfasalazine. Follow-up with Rheumatologist and Gastroenterologist was advised.

Discharge Summary:

Patient 1, a 47-year-old man with a history of spinal injury resulting in complete paraplegia, was admitted to the department of physical medicine and rehabilitation at our university hospital due to spasticity. Despite taking baclofen and diazepam, the patient reported experiencing 3-4 beats of knee extension clonus and spasm of adductor thigh muscles. The spasticity was not controlled and was interfering with the patient's sleep.

The patient underwent pulsed radiofrequency (PRF) procedure on both L2 and L3 DRGs with 5 Hz and 5 ms pulsed width for 360 seconds at 45 V under the C-arm fluoroscopy guide. There were no complications after the PRF. Following the procedure, the clonus of both knee extensors disappeared completely, and the spasticity on both hip adductors was reduced from a score of 3 to 1+. The patient reported significant improvement in quality of sleep and a 50% reduction in spasticity on both hip adductors.

The spasticity returned at nearly the same degree six months after the procedure, and a repeat PRF was performed with similar results, which were also sustained for six months.

Overall, the PRF procedure was effective in reducing the spasticity of the patient's adductor thigh muscles and improving his quality of sleep. The patient was discharged in stable condition and advised to follow up with the clinic as needed.

The patient will continue to follow up with his physicians.

Imaging studies obtained were all negative.

The patient was observed overnight in the hospital and remained asymptomatic and without any further dysrhythmia. He only had chest wall pain, possibly from sternal rub or from any bystander chest compressions that may have been performed when he became unresponsive. Serum/plasma levels of lidocaine and its primary active metabolite, monoethylglycinexylidide (MEGX), were obtained and returned undetectable. Aspirin 325 mg daily was prescribed and a referral to outpatient cardiology was made. 

Condition at Discharge

The patient was discharged with no symptoms and normal mental status.

Denosumab was discontinued and ozone therapy was started, followed by a new surgical procedure of mandibular toilette, with complete resolution of MR-ONJ. The disease is currently stable while off-denosumab for 8 months.

A 77-year-old male patient was admitted to the hospital after undergoing a burr hole irrigation for a left chronic subdural hematoma (CSDH). Despite the hematoma being organized, the patient's neurological symptoms, including motor aphasia and right mild hemiparesis, did not improve. Following a referral to our hospital, a CT scan showed a thick hematoma in the patient's left convexity.

Treatment:
MMA embolization procedure was performed using Embosphere® and three Target Helical Ultra (Stryker), followed by a craniotomy for evacuation of the OSDH under local anesthesia. The patient experienced minimal oozing from the HOM or hematoma itself during the surgery. Following the procedure, the patient's neurological symptoms improved significantly.

Diagnosis:
Left chronic subdural hematoma (CSDH)

Outcome:
The patient showed no evidence of neurological deficits after 1-year follow-up, although a CT scan showed that the hematoma remained.

Recommendations:
Ongoing monitoring of the patient's condition is recommended to ensure the continued absence of neurological deficits.

The patient was referred to an appropriate specialist for further diagnosis and treatment. We recommended that the patient follow up with the specialist on an outpatient basis.

Patient Name: Anonymous

Medical Record Number: XXXXXX

Date of Admission: XXXXXXX           
Date of Discharge: XXXXXXX

Admitting Diagnosis: Incomplete spinal cord injury 

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted to the Spinal Cord Injury Center at Balgrist University Hospital, Switzerland, with an incomplete spinal cord injury. Clinical examination revealed the patient was suffering from central cord syndrome, at-level neuropathic pain, and mechanical allodynia (brush allodynia) on both forearms. Light touch was normal within the cervical segments, and sharp dull discrimination was preserved while the intensity of the pinprick stimulus was only mildly attenuated. The upper extremity motor score (left: 11/25, right: 11/25) showed a profound weakness of elbow extensors, and no voluntary muscle activity in the finger flexors and abductors bilaterally. The lower extremity motor score was normal (left: 25/25, right: 25/25). Biceps and brachioradialis reflexes, as well as knee-jerk and ankle-jerk reflexes were bilaterally exaggerated. The Babinski sign was negative. Muscle tone was normal without signs of spasticity. Coordination and gait showed discrete signs of ataxia.

Diagnostic testing revealed a multi-segmental (C5-C7), longitudinal “snake eye” appearance myelopathy. Ulnar somatosensory evoked potentials (SEPs) and sensory nerve conduction studies were normal. Noxious mechanical stimuli were applied with a 256 mN pinprick stimulator, and CHEPs were recorded, which appeared to be normal at C4 and T4 with high pain ratings to the heat stimulation, but almost complete loss of painful heat sensation and absent CHEPs at the level of C6.

The patient was treated for the duration of their stay in the hospital. Written informed consent was obtained from the patient before conducting any study, and the study was approved by the “Kantonale Ethikkommission Zürich”.

Discharge Status:

The patient was discharged from the hospital in stable condition. The patient’s condition and prognosis were discussed with them and their families, and the necessary education and instructions regarding self-care, follow-up care, and rehabilitation were provided. The patient and their families were advised to seek immediate medical attention if there were any signs of deterioration in their condition.

Follow-Up:

The patient was instructed to follow up with their primary care physician or specialist for ongoing management of their condition. Any changes in the patient's condition should be reported immediately to their healthcare provider.

Signed,

Dr. Anonymous

HOSPITAL COURSE SUMMARY:

Admission Date: [DATE]
Discharge Date: [DATE]

Medical History:
The patient is a 32-year-old woman who presented with a mass in the vulva and intermenstrual bleeding. She had a history of unsuccessful sexual intercourse due to fear of pain, and the mass had gradually enlarged over the past 3 years.

Clinical Findings:
A physical examination revealed a nontender tubular neoplasm outside the intact hymen, with an opening at the distal end. A canal approximately 5 cm long was found in the mass, from which white mucus was secreted. Ultrasonographic evaluation of the pelvis showed a 4.5- × 1-cm stalk originating from the cervix and protruding into the vagina. A mini-hysteroscopy was performed to excise the mass.

Diagnostic Testing:
Hemoglobin level was 9.4 g/dL. The levels of estradiol and progesterone in the luteal phase were 138 pg/mL and 13.77 ng/mL, respectively. Liver and renal functional tests and thyroid hormone levels were all normal.

Treatment:
The patient underwent a mini-hysteroscopy to excise the mass while avoiding damage to the hymen. The patient, a 56-year-old male with a history of dilated cardiomyopathy and atrial fibrillation, presented with epigastralgia and nonsustained VT. Severe anemia and blastoid cells were observed in the peripheral blood sample, and the patient was diagnosed with Ph+ ALL. Dasatinib 50 mg twice daily and prednisolone 100 mg daily were initiated to treat the leukemia. The dasatinib was discontinued after five days due to an increase in nonsustained VT although the QTc interval was not significantly prolonged. Bisoprolol was gradually increased to 3.75 mg daily, and dasatinib was rechallenged. The patient showed a complete hematological response and a 2-log reduction in minor bcr-abl mRNA transcripts in the bone marrow. Three weeks after the retreatment with dasatinib, blastoid cells reemerged in the peripheral blood, and the dasatinib was discontinued due to refractoriness of leukemia. The patient received steroid pulse therapy and furosemide, and VT did not recur after. Although, dexamethasone and the short-term use of mercaptopurine were used, the patient expired from leukemia on the 183rd day after admission.

Contrast enhanced CT performed two days after RFA showed that the enhanced solid lesion in the tumor was smaller in size compared to pre-RFA CT. The patient's pain disappeared for approximately 3 months, accompanied by an improvement in motor function disorder. However, the pain of the left upper limb reappeared due to growth of the tumor, three months after RFA.

The patient was a 30-year-old male who presented to the Emergency Department after being involved in a motorcycle collision. The patient was complaining of a lump in the left inguinal region. Upon physical examination, the left testis was not palpable within the scrotal sac. A laceration was identified on the right side of the perineum. No pelvic fractures were identified. 

Diagnostic Findings:

An ultrasound was performed to evaluate the scrotum and inguinal region. The evaluation revealed that the left testis was located within the inguinal canal, it was normal in size with normal echotexture and no focal lesions. Spectral Doppler examination of the left testis demonstrated decreased amplitude of systolic upstroke and absence of diastolic flow, suggesting partial testicular torsion. A follow-up CT scan was done to exclude any solid organ injury within the abdomen and pelvis.

Clinical Intervention:

Surgical exploration of the left inguinal canal confirmed the dislocation of the left testis along with a thickened spermatic cord that was looped on itself. The dislocated left testis was repositioned into the scrotum and orchidopexy was performed.

Clinical Progress:

Post-surgical recovery was uneventful, and the patient was regularly monitored for any signs of infection or complications. The patient's pain was well controlled with analgesics. The patient was discharged in good condition with an outpatient follow-up appointment. 

Summary:

The patient was involved in a motorcycle collision resulting in a dislocated testis. The testis was located within the inguinal canal and was successfully repositioned into the scrotum via surgical intervention. The patient was discharged in good condition with an outpatient follow-up appointment.

HOSPITAL COURSE:
The patient was admitted to the hospital due to ocular toxoplasmosis in his left eye with signs of posterior uveitis. The patient had a history of ocular toxoplasmosis and IgG positive antibodies for Tg. The patient was previously treated with several medications, which resulted in complete retinochoroiditis improvement. However, the anterior chamber cellularity (Tyndall 3 +) persisted, and new findings such as multiple areas of superficial circular atrophy in 360º, posterior iris synechiae, and ocular hypertension were observed. Viral origin due to the presence of IA zones and hypertensive anterior uveitis, was suspected. Therefore, Acyclovir and corticosteroids were initiated. The patient later presented cortical opacities and posterior subcapsular cataract of the OS with surgery requirement. The patient also presented reactivation of the inflammatory activity in his OS, despite treatment.

FINDINGS:
Further examination of the patient revealed temporal and nasal conjunctival vessel tortuosity, 0.5 + of anterior chamber cells, increased superficial circular atrophy zones in 360º of the iris, some with deeper atrophy stroma fibers visualization, and a small punctate defect of transillumination. The patient also had dyscoric pupil in medium mydriasis and pseudophakia. Fundus observation for OS revealed vitreous syneresis, posterior vitreous detachment, 0.5 + vitreous cells, 0.2 optic disc excavation, and a hypopigmented retinochoroidal scar on the inferior temporal vascular arch.

LABORATORY FINDINGS:
Laboratories and aqueous humor PCR were requested, which showed the presence of VZV and Tg genetic material. The multiplex PCR qualitatively used ruled out HSV type 1, HSV type 2, Epstein-Barr virus, CMV, HHV-6 (Human Herpes Virus), HHV-7, and HHV-8 etiologies. The patient's VZV IgG level was positive.

TREATMENT:
The patient was treated with a combination of oral Pyrimethamine and Sulfadoxine, Acyclovir, and corticosteroids. The topical tropicamide was given until the resolution of inflammation in the anterior chamber was observed.

FOLLOW-UP:

Patient: 4-month-old male intact Labrador

Hospital Course:

The patient presented with several small skin lacerations of the distal limbs, hock, and tail base. On physical examination, the dog was found to be clinically healthy with normal skeletal development. Several seroma-like swellings were noted in the regions of skin trauma (hocks, tail base). Aspirates taken from these swellings revealed moderate numbers of erythrocytes with fewer neutrophils and macrophages with proteinaceous debris. These findings were consistent with a seroma or hematoma formation, and the dog was treated with amoxycillin/clavulanic acid and firocoxib.

Two months after initial presentation, the patient was examined for ongoing seroma formation and joint abnormalities. Evidence of generalized joint hyperextensibility with a range of motion greater than 180° and skin hyperextensibility and fragility was noted. The dog had a skin extensibility test of 23.5% (normal < 14.5%). A complete blood count revealed mild anemia and serum biochemistry showed a mild hypoalbuminemia and hypoproteinemia. Other serum abnormalities included a moderate hyperphosphatemia, mild elevation in ALP, and decrease in creatinine that were all considered within normal limits for a young dog.

Discharge Diagnosis:

The patient was suspected to have a genetic collagen disease.

Treatment:

The patient was treated with amoxycillin/clavulanic acid and firocoxib. The owners elected to humanely euthanize the patient due to the ongoing joint hypermobility and skin lacerations.

Follow-up Plan:

None.

The patient had a painful swelling of his right leg while he was being treated in the hospital for recurrent episodes of ENL. His right leg was swollen with pitting ankle edema while having normal arterial pulses. His respiratory system examination revealed a respiratory rate of 30 per minute and signs of right lower zone pleural effusion.

The patient had lepromatous leprosy following a positive slit skin smear for mycobacterium leprae. He was commenced on World Health Organization (WHO) multi-drug therapy (MDT) regimen for multi-bacillary (MB) leprosy, which was complicated by type II lepra reaction (ENL) with right sided panuveitis and treated with oral prednisolone.

There was no history suggestive of past venous or arterial thrombosis and tendency to develop thrombosis in his family. Neurology revealed a glove and stocking sensory peripheral neuropathy. There was no organomegaly noted on abdominal examination.

Treatment:
The patient was started on enoxaparin and warfarin concomitantly. Thalidomide and anti-leprosy therapy were stopped temporarily while low dose corticosteroid was continued. After one week, the patient's dyspnea and general condition improved.

Follow-up:
The patient was discharged and provided with instructions to follow up with his healthcare provider for ongoing treatment and monitoring.

Discharge Summary:
    
Patient Name: [Redacted]
Date of Admission: January 2003
Date of Discharge: N/A

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS: 
The patient was admitted with a palpable abdominal mass in left hypochondrium and mild abdominal pain. CT revealed a large hypervascularised splenic tumor. She underwent a radical splenectomy surgery due to increased vascularity and possibility of localized malignancy seeding. The histopathology report confirmed low-grade primary splenic angiosarcoma. 

HOSPITAL COURSE: 
During follow-up, the patient complained of severe bone pain, and multiple bone metastases were detected. Palliative radiotherapy and bisphosphonate therapy were given. Over time, new metastatic deposits appeared, and the patient underwent another course of palliative radiotherapy. However, the patient declined the palliative chemotherapy. Subsequently, new metastases in the liver and axial skeleton were identified in 2010. Chemotherapy treatment was offered and, with the patient's approval, 6 cycles of palliative chemotherapy were given. The patient underwent subsequent follow-up, and no progression of disease was detected until 2016, when progression of metastatic lung lesions was noted. CT directed lung biopsy was performed, which confirmed angiosarcoma metastasis. The patient is currently undergoing second-line chemotherapy with paclitaxel weekly.

DISCHARGE DIAGNOSIS: 
Primary splenic angiosarcoma with metastases to bones, sternoclavicular joint, liver, and lungs.

DISCHARGE INSTRUCTIONS: 
The patient is advised to continue with the ongoing second-line chemotherapy with paclitaxel weekly under close medical supervision. The patient is instructed to maintain follow-up appointments as per the treating physician's advice. In case of any emergency, the patient should consult the hospital emergency department and inform them about the ongoing treatment. The patient is advised to avoid smoking, alcohol and exposure to environmental toxins.

FOLLOW-UP CARE: 
The patient requires periodic follow-up appointments with the treating physician to monitor the response to chemotherapy, manage side effects, and evaluate any new symptoms. The frequency of visits should be determined on an individual basis by the treating physician.

SUMMARY: 
A 65-year-old female patient with primary splenic angiosarcoma was admitted with a palpable abdominal mass and mild abdominal pain. She underwent radical splenectomy surgery, which confirmed the diagnosis of low-grade primary splenic angiosarcoma. The patient developed multiple bone metastases, which were treated with palliative radiotherapy and bisphosphonate therapy. Subsequently, new metastases developed in the liver and axial skeleton, for which the patient received palliative chemotherapy with doxorubicin. During follow-up, metastatic lung lesions were noted, and the patient is currently undergoing second-line chemotherapy with paclitaxel weekly. The patient is advised to continue ongoing treatment under close medical supervision and maintain follow-up appointments with the treating physician.

Treatment:

The patient received left radical inguinal orchiectomy and left inguinal lymph node dissection. Adjuvant chemotherapy with a bleomycin, etoposide, and cisplatin regimen was administered soon after completion of surgical interventions. Persistent elevated β-human chorionic gonadotropin levels were observed after a full course of four cycles of monthly chemotherapy with an episode of flare-up, which suggested relapse. Salvage second-line chemotherapy was initiated with a paclitaxel, ifosfamide, and cisplatin regimen thereafter.

The patient tolerated the treatments well without complications and was discharged from the hospital in stable condition. The patient was advised to follow up regularly with his healthcare team for continued monitoring and management of his condition.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: _______

Gender: Female

Age: 56 years

Admission Date: _______

Discharge Date: _______

Diagnosis: Primary Osteoarthritis of the Left Knee 

Hospital Course:

The patient, a 56-year-old female with a body mass index of 23.2, was admitted to our facility as a diagnosed case of primary osteoarthritis of the left knee. The osteoarthritis of the left knee was evaluated as grade 3 based on the Kellgren-Lawrence Scale. The patient had received an intra-articular injection of high molecular weight hyaluronic acid 2 years back which transiently improved pain symptoms. Significant improvement was not noted in the pain symptoms despite the administration of 4 injections of platelet-rich plasma (PRP) a month apart each. The patient also performed prescribed exercises that included strengthening of quadriceps and hamstrings, and stretching of the hamstrings and took precautionary measures in the activities of daily living which provided little relief in symptoms. An ultrasound of the knee joint was done to look for structural changes, and suitable changes for treatment were recommended. 

Treatment:

In view of inadequate response after 8 months of the last PRP injection, intra-articular injection of adalimumab was planned, and 10 mg of Adalimumab was administered under ultrasonography-guidance. The procedure was uneventful, and the patient did not have any transient discomfort or complications following injection adalimumab. The patient was put on Tablet Paracetamol 650 mg (as per need) as a rescue medication, and post adalimumab injection pill count was on an average 2 tablets per week. 

Outcome:

The patient reported noticeable reduction in pain beginning approximately 2 weeks from the date of injection. The 11-point visual analog scale (VAS) for pain intensity was used to evaluate the patient. VAS reduced from 8 (pre-treatment) to 3 at the 1 month follow-up, remained at 3 at the 3 months follow-up and became 4 at the 6 months follow-up. Ultrasonographic examination was repeated at the end of 12 weeks and 6 months, and pre- and post-intervention ultrasonographic findings did not show any change despite significant improvement in symptoms. The patient's knee injury & osteoarthritis outcome score (KOOS) improved from 32.20 (pre-treatment) to 61.20 at the 1 month follow-up, 60.90 at the 3 months follow-up and 57.50 at the 6 months follow-up. The patient was discharged and is under routine care in our outpatient department, and has not complained of any deterioration in symptoms. A formal evaluation of VAS, KOOS, and ultrasound examination is scheduled after 6 months. 

Recommendation:

The patient has been advised to follow the preventive measures to avoid any pain, inflammation, or stiffness in the joint. The patient has also been advised to follow-up with the treating physician regularly to avoid any complications or further injury.

The patient is scheduled for regular follow-up appointments with the pediatric cardiologist and primary care physician to monitor the cardiovascular condition, growth, and development. Disposition:
The patient was discharged in stable condition, improved cardiovascular symptoms, and with a positive outlook for long-term outcomes.

Hospital Course:
A 75-year-old male patient was admitted to the hospital due to the development of acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) following surgery to drain a peritonsillar abscess that had extended down to the hypopharynx. Upon admission, the patient exhibited decreased peripheral oxygen saturation and bilateral pulmonary infiltrates, which were treated with noninvasive ventilation with a positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP). However, the patient's respiratory insufficiency continued to deteriorate, and after three days, the patient was intubated and treated with invasive ventilation. Two days later, the patient was tracheostomized, and CT scans of the lungs showed bilateral patchy infiltrates and dorsal consolidation extending from the cranial to caudal lung regions.

During the first application, the patient's PaO2/FiO2 value increased significantly, and alveolar infiltrates showed impressive reduction. During the second application, the patient's PaO2/FiO2 value increased to more than 500 mmHg, indicating significant recruitment of lung volume without the use of any recruitment maneuvers. After five days of CENPV, the patient was weaned from the ventilator and discharged to the normal ward.

Upon admission, the patient received noninvasive ventilation with a positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) to improve their respiratory insufficiency. However, after the condition continued to deteriorate, the patient was treated with invasive continuous positive pressure ventilation (CPPV) followed by continuous end-expiratory negative pressure ventilation (CENPV), which improved the patient's respiratory status significantly. Following five days of CENPV, the patient was weaned from the ventilator and discharged to the normal ward.

The patient's respiratory condition has significantly improved, and they have been discharged in stable condition. It is recommended that the patient continue to follow up with their primary care provider for further evaluation and monitoring.

The patient is recommended to maintain close follow-up care with their primary care provider. No further follow-up care is required from this hospital.

His CT scan showed an 8 cm by 4 cm medial soft tissue defect with an isolated IIIb open fracture of the tibia.
The patient was given antibiotics and taken to theatre on the same day of injury, where the wound was debrided and temporarily stabilised with an external fixator. On day 3, an acute angulation was performed and the fracture was stabilised with a Taylor Spatial Frame. His Iowa knee score was maximal, and the Olerud and Molander activity score was 85/100. The patient was satisfied with the outcome and would recommend the treatment.

Follow-up:
The patient was advised to engage in physical therapy to aid with ankle stiffness. He was also prescribed medications to manage pain as needed. Discharge Date: N/A

Admission Diagnosis:
Endometrioid carcinoma of the endometrium, FIGO grade 3

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 45-year-old woman, gestation 2, was admitted in April 2018 with a diagnosis of endometrioid carcinoma of the endometrium, FIGO grade 3. The diagnosis was confirmed through an endometrial biopsy. The patient had a family history of gynecological cancer on her maternal side. Magnetic resonance imaging revealed a 4-cm tumor located in the uterine fundus, which had infiltrated the myometrium and extended to serosa, beyond the left fallopian tube. Fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG)-18F positron emission tomography-computed tomography (PET-CT) demonstrated that several lymph nodes, including iliac and retroperitoneal para-aortic, were suggestive of neoplastic involvement. FoundationOne CDx assay was performed on the tumor sample, which showed high microsatellite instability and intermediate Tumor Mutational Burden (TMB) (13 muts/Mb).

Treatment:
The patient was treated with intravenous pembrolizumab (Keytruda) at a dose of 200 mg every 3 weeks. After three cycles of pembrolizumab, the uterine lesion completely regressed. To evaluate the pathological response, the patient underwent laparoscopic hysterectomy, pelvic and para-aortic lymph node dissection, omentectomy, and inventory of the peritoneal cavity. There was no macroscopic evidence of disease, and signs of complete tumoral regression were seen in endometrium, myometrium, cervix, uterine serosa, left ovary, and adipose tissue in adhering to the uterine fundus. Forty-one lymph nodes were dissected, with a micrometastasis identified in one right pelvic lymph node, and an aggregate of isolated tumor cells with signs of partial regression in one para-aortic lymph node.

Discharge Condition:
The patient has completed 24 months without evidence of progression of disease and without adverse effects. The patient was referred to a genetic counselor for risk assessment. A genetic variant was identified in MLH1 gene c.193 G > A (p.Gly65Ser) and classified by a CLIA-certified lab as of uncertain significance (VUS).

Follow-up Care:
N/A

N/A

Discharge Instructions:
The patient was discharged without any special instructions.

Discharge Diagnosis:
Endometrioid carcinoma of the endometrium, FIGO grade 3

Hospital Course:
The patient, an 80-year-old non-smoker woman with a history of hypertension and diabetes mellitus was admitted to the Emergency Department with a one-week history of dry cough and high fever. The chest computed tomography showed bilateral peripheral ground-glass opacities, and the real-time reverse transcriptase-polymerase chain reaction test for severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) returned positive.

Treatment and Response:
The patient was started on supplemental oxygen, favipiravir, and dexamethasone. Three days later, she was admitted to the ICU due to respiratory failure and was put on mechanical ventilation. She continued to receive dexamethasone and was also given antibiotics and remdesivir. The respiratory condition and chest infiltration improved, and she was extubated after seven days of mechanical ventilation. Dexamethasone was later discontinued after 10 days.

Relapse and Co-infection:
The patient developed a fever and quickly progressive hypoxaemia two days after the extubation and was reintubated. Cultures and laboratory tests were performed with no evidence of co-infection. She was then given dexamethasone again with a subsequent improvement in the chest shadows and was tapered weekly. However, her chest shadows worsened again, and her serum β-d-glucan was found to be elevated. She was given antifungal treatment, and the CMV antigenemia assay was elevated. Ganciclovir was immediately initiated, but the patient died four days after the positive CMV antigenemia test result.

Autopsy:
A needle autopsy was performed approximately 3 h after her death, and CMV-infected cells were found. This confirmed the diagnosis of CMV pneumonia as the cause of her respiratory failure and bilateral chest infiltrations.

Follow-up:
The patient's family was informed about her condition and treatment. The discharge summary along with instructions for follow-up care, including any medication changes, and any scheduled appointments were explained to the family.

Condition:
The patient's condition had initially improved but worsened due to CMV pneumonia, leading to her death.

Hospital Course:

The 75-year-old male patient was admitted to our tertiary care center due to prolonged aPTT discovered during preoperative laboratory tests. Prior to admission, the patient reported bilateral parotid enlargement and cervical lymphadenopathies.

Medical History:

The patient had no significant medical history.

Diagnostic Findings:

Biological work-up showed normal kidney, liver, pancreas, and thyroid functions. Acute phase reactants and immunological tests were within normal range. The prolonged aPTT was confirmed with normal PT and found decreased FVIII plasma levels associated with positive anti-FVIII IgG4 autoantibodies. An axillary lymph node biopsy was performed, revealing benign follicular hyperplasia with elevated IgG4/IgG ratio and no evidence of lymphoma. Further laboratory tests showed elevated serum IgG4 levels with other IgG subclasses within normal range.

Treatment:

The patient was diagnosed with IgG4-RD-associated AHA and treated with oral prednisone 1mg/kg/day for both diseases. The treatment led to a regression of parotid and lymph node enlargement, a decrease in serum IgG4 levels, a progressive correction of FVIII and aPTT values, and a suppression of anti-FVIII plasma activity. Prednisone was then slowly tapered and discontinued after 9 months.

Follow-up:

Nine months after treatment withdrawal, the patient relapsed with a new increase in IgG4 serum levels without organ involvement and a decrease in FVIII plasma levels with elevated anti-FVIII autoantibodies but without bleeding. The patient was started on a new course of oral corticosteroids associated with 2 infusions of rituximab 1g, which led to a sustained remission. The patient had a total follow-up of 3 years after diagnosis.

Summary:

The patient was admitted to our tertiary care center due to prolonged aPTT. Diagnostic findings revealed IgG4-RD-associated AHA. The patient was treated with oral prednisone and achieved sustained remission with the addition of rituximab. The patient had a total follow-up of 3 years after diagnosis.

Discharge Summary

Patient Name: [REDACTED]

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted due to facial plethora and distal paresthesia that had been progressively worsening over the previous eight months. The patient was diagnosed with hypertension one year before he sought medical attention. During the physical examination, he was found to have a full-moon face, facial plethora, and a nodule at the cervical area. Thyroid ultrasound and color doppler diagnosis at another institution showed a hypoechoic nodule in the left thyroid lobe measuring 6.7 × 3.2 × 3.5 cm, with punctate calcifications and a predominantly central vascular pattern. A fine-needle aspiration biopsy of this nodule showed pleomorphic cells with a round and hyperchromatic nuclei, gross chromatin, and occasional apparent nucleoli. Bizarre, multinucleated cells with atypical mitoses were also observed. The CT scan of the neck showed a tumoral mass invading the posterior wall of the trachea, with contact with thoracic vertebral bodies and invasion of prevertebral muscles. The chest CT revealed a large, heterogeneous solid lesion, with the epicenter in the left superior mediastinum and absence of a cleavage plane between the lesion and the left lobe of the thyroid.

During hospitalization, the patient developed hypercortisolism and was diagnosed with Cushing's syndrome (CS) after plasma cortisol levels after overnight suppression with 1 mg of dexamethasone were 26.8 µg/dL, and plasma ACTH measurement was 109 pg/mL. Laboratory tests were conducted to screen for multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 (MEN2) and associated carcinoid syndrome, as well as to rule out pheochromocytoma. Elevated blood glucose levels reaching 300 mg/dL were detected, and the patient had hypokalemia refractory to intravenous potassium. As a result, ketoconazole was prescribed, but this was later suspended due to an increase in transaminases levels three times above the reference value.

An open biopsy of the cervical nodule was performed to establish a conclusive diagnosis as the previous cytological examination was inconclusive. The biopsy revealed an MTC. The multidisciplinary team recommended treatment with radiotherapy and chemotherapy with doxorubicin and cisplatin. During control echocardiography, the patient presented ejection fraction of 51%, and doxorubicin was suspended. The patient improved slowly over time, and the tumor volume reduced, but cisplatin had to be suspended due to severe peripheral neuropathy. Subsequently, the patient was switched to sunitinib in combination with prednisone. Sunitinib induced substantial toxicity, leading to an increase in serum glutamate-pyruvate transaminase (SGPT) and gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT) levels twice above the reference value. The dose of sunitinib was reduced to 25 mg/day. Six months after starting sunitinib therapy, the abdominal CT revealed hepatic metastases, the largest of which measured 9.3 × 6.3 cm. After discussing this with the patient and his family, the multidisciplinary team suspended the medication and provided clinical support. The patient died 23 days later.

Discharge Diagnosis:
Cushing's syndrome (CS) secondary to multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 (MEN2) with medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC).

Discharge Medications:
None.

Follow-up Plan:
This patient has passed away. Therefore, no follow-up plan is required.

Invasive squamous cell carcinoma in the setting of severe solar elastosis

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Medical Record Number: [REDACTED]

Hospital Course:

This is a discharge summary for a postmenopausal woman in her 50s who was diagnosed with Stage IIB breast cancer and received neoadjuvant chemotherapy with a combination of DOC, pertuzumab, and trastuzumab after EC (every 3 weeks, 4 times) treatment. The patient experienced several symptoms during treatment, including grade 2 diarrhea, grade 1 fatigue, grade 1 edema, and grade 1 peripheral neuropathy. The patient's medical history included integration disorder syndrome, diabetes mellitus, and hyperlipidemia, all of which were well controlled by medication. The patient was a current smoker (10 cigarettes per day) and a social drinker with normal liver and renal function.

Summary of Treatment:

Dexamethasone, pegfilgrastim, metoclopramide, and Goshajinkigan, a herbal medicine, were administered to manage side effects such as taxane-associated acute pain syndrome and edema, peripheral neuropathy, and nausea. The patient also received 40 mg of the probiotic Clostridium butyricum MIYAIRI to prevent diarrhea, which was controlled with loperamide.
After the second cycle of EC and before the second cycle of DOC + pertuzumab + trastuzumab, the patient's serum triglyceride level mildly increased, then stabilized without any countermeasures. However, after the third cycle, the serum triglyceride level suddenly increased to grade 3 (770 mg/dL) without any symptoms. The fourth-cycle treatment was conducted, and sustained-release bezafibrate 200 mg was administered twice a day from the day, which resulted in a significant decrease in the serum triglyceride level to grade 1 (287 mg/dL) after 16 days. Bezafibrate administration was stopped on day 28 of the fourth cycle, and the level further decreased to the baseline level (212 mg/dL) on day 39.

Course After Chemotherapy:

Surgery was conducted on day 39 of the last chemotherapy cycle, and adjuvant chemotherapy consisting of pertuzumab and trastuzumab was resumed 52 days after the surgery. The lipid levels did not change during adjuvant chemotherapy. The patient experienced grade 1 aspartate aminotransferase, alanine aminotransferase, and γ-glutamyltransferase elevation confirmed in the second cycle of EC and continued to be around the same level until the end of neoadjuvant chemotherapy. No other new medications were administered during chemotherapy.

Diagnosis:

The patient was diagnosed with Stage IIB breast cancer with estrogen receptor-positive, progesterone receptor-positive, HER-2 overexpression positive, and Ki-67.

Condition at the Time of Discharge:

The patient's condition at the time of discharge was stable. The lipid level returned to a baseline level of 212 mg/dL, and the patient did not experience any significant side effects from chemotherapy.

Follow-up Care:

The patient will be monitored for any recurrence of breast cancer and will receive follow-up care according to the standard clinical practice guidelines.

This is a summary of the clinical events regarding a 3-month-old boy who presented with a complex partial seizure. A cranial CT showed an intracranial hemorrhage secondary to the rupture of an anterior communicating artery complex giant aneurysm that underwent spontaneous thrombosis. An MRI and angiography confirmed a suprasellar lesion with a 26 mm diameter compatible with a giant aneurysm. The patient was transferred to the Pediatric Intensive Care Unit where he was treated with phenytoin, mannitol, sedoanalgesia, and connected to mechanical ventilation. An external ventricular drain was inserted. A diagnostic cerebral angiography was performed which confirmed the thrombosis of the suspected aneurysm. A ventriculoperitoneal shunt was placed to address hydrocephalus. The child was followed up in neuropediatric and pediatric neurosurgery clinics. He made a significant improvement and recovered without any complications. Recanalization of the anterior communicating artery aneurysm was not detected in a series of angiographic studies performed at follow-up until five years after the aneurysm rupture. The patient remains neurologically intact, without restrictions, and with no further seizures.

- Physical examination: Tender nodular lesions on both temples and palpable lymph node on the right inguinal area
- Laboratory findings: Elevated total leukocyte, eosinophil, and hemoglobin levels. ESR was slightly elevated

- Histopathological findings: Marked eosinophilic infiltration in arterial wall and perivascular tissue with eosinophilic abscess, focal destruction of vascular wall, and organizing thrombi in the left superficial temporal artery. The right inguinal LN showed reactive follicles and massive eosinophil infiltration, but no evidence of malignancy.

Diagnosis:
Concurrent JTA and HES

Treatment:
- Excisional biopsy of bilateral superficial temporal arteries for JTA
- Intravenous steroid (methylprednisolone) 90 mg per day for HES
- Low-dose steroid (prednisone 10 mg/day) for maintenance after discharge

Outcome:
The patient did not experience a recurrence of JTA after surgical excision during 2 years of follow-up. He was well-maintained without any symptoms due to eosinophilia with low-dose steroid.

Recommendations:
The patient should continue low-dose steroid for maintenance and follow-up with a primary care physician regularly. Further evaluation and management are needed for chronic rhinosinusitis.

Stable and in improved condition.

3. Rhabdomyolysis.

Clinical Course:

The patient, a 67-year-old male, was admitted on 26 September 2007 due to progressive abdominal swelling, weight loss, and asthenia for three months. A multi-sliced chest and whole abdomen CT scan was performed to evaluate the vessels on 28 September 2007. On the same day, the patient underwent surgery to remove a large, paucisymptomatic retroperitoneal tumour. During surgery, the patient suffered heavy blood loss and hypothermia, requiring a splenectomy and suturing with abdominal packing for 'damage control.' Pathology report confirmed high-grade pleomorphic liposarcoma.

The patient was transferred to the ICU for 14 hours where he underwent heating, metabolic correction, and transfusion of concentrated erythrocytes, platelets, and fresh plasma with no clotting factors. After angiography, the patient underwent second-look surgery on 29 September 2007 with packing removal and cauterization of haemorrhaging sites. The abdominal wall was sutured, and two draining tubes were positioned. Postoperatively, the patient had stable haemodynamics, normal diuresis, and a stable Hb level. His ureteral stents were removed after five days, and he required mechanical respiratory support for ten days due to mild ARDS. On 19 October 2007, a control CT scan demonstrated good vascularization of most of the horseshoe kidney and normal urine flux through the ureters to the bladder.

The patient was discharged on 24 October 2007 with systemic treatment initiated (Ifosfamide 9 g/sqm + epirubicin 120 mg/sqm + G-CSF).

The patient was admitted to our hospital due to coffee ground vomit, general paleness and moderate dehydration. Non-variceal upper gastrointestinal bleeding was suspected and an esophagogastroduodenoscopy was performed without any active bleeding being identified. However, a chest x-ray revealed an image of a lower left pulmonary consolidation. Further investigation with a chest CT-scan highlighted a left diaphragmatic hernia with protrusion of the gastric body into the ipsilateral hemithorax. 

An abdominal CT-scan confirmed a seven centimeter left hemi-diaphragmatic defect with herniation of the fundus, body, and gastric antrum as well as the spleen. The patient's severe malnutrition required parenteral nutritional repletion since an advanced nutrition probe could not be passed due to the anatomical alteration created by the hernial defect.

Fifteen days after admission, abdominal laparoscopic surgery was performed revealing a large left diaphragmatic hernia with protrusion of half the stomach, omentum, and the posterior aspect of the spleen. The spleen had a sub capsular tear, and there was a severe adhesion syndrome on the chest wall and diaphragm with entrapment of the inferior lobe of the left lung. A hernial defect of seven by five centimeters was found, with preservation of the hiatus. Reduction of the herniated organs was achieved through abdominal laparoscopy, however, a complete dissection was not possible due to the splenic interposition.

The Thoracic Surgery group performed thoracoscopic surgery with extensive adhesiolysis and decortication, allowing for the extraction of the protruding sac without damaging the spleen. Primary repair without tension was achieved. The patient tolerated a liquid diet 24 hours postoperatively and had an uneventful recovery. They were discharged on the fifth postoperative day with normal food intake. 

Follow-up:

The patient returned for a follow-up appointment six months later, where an abdominal CT-scan showed a satisfactory diaphragmatic hernial correction. No further complications were reported at this time.

The patient, a 32-year-old lady presented with a pathological fracture of the right humerus, previously treated with interlocked, intramedullary nail at an outside facility, with subsequent development of significant pain and nonunion. The patient presented with significant shoulder pain that worsened with motion, with disuse atrophy of the deltoid muscle and an unsightly prominence of the proximal end cap of the prosthesis.

The patient remained relatively pain-free until her 12th annual follow-up, during which identical symptoms recurred. Revision surgery was performed again, involving a reduction in prosthetic length by an additional two centimeters, which resulted in satisfactory pain control that was maintained till her latest follow-up.

Revision surgeries were performed, including a reduction in length of the prosthesis by removal of the end cap and reattachment through drill holes to the scapula with mersilene tape, and ultimately, a reduction in prosthetic length by an additional two centimeters. The diagnosis of limb-shaking TIA caused by left hemisphere perfusion impairment was considered.

Treatment:

The patient was given fluid replacement therapy, antiplatelet therapy, clopidogrel and aspirin, and statins. ICA angioplasty and stent implantation were performed with excellent restoration flow. No neurological dysfunction was observed post-operation, and the procedure was successful in completely resolving his symptoms. The patient was maintained on antiplatelet therapy and statins after stenting, and no recurrences of his limb-shaking TIA and facial muscles involuntary twitch.

Limb-shaking TIA caused by severe left internal carotid artery stenosis.

The benefit of the ICA angioplasty and stent implantation is that it restored blood flow in the left hemisphere and cleared the symptoms. The patient was advised to follow-up regularly with his primary physician for monitoring and management of his diabetes and hypertension. Further follow-up visits were suggested to monitor the progress of the stenosis, and to adjust the treatment plan if needed.

Skeletal survey was not suggestive of the characteristic dysostosis complex. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain showed J-shaped sella turcica, mild widening of the lateral ventricles with thinning of the corpus callosum.

Further enzyme analysis for MPS IIIA showed null activity of the enzyme sulfamidase activity in leukocytes, confirming the diagnosis. The patient was initiated on rehabilitation and behavior therapy for hyperactivity.

Discharge Diagnosis:

Mucopolysaccharidosis type IIIA

Discharge Condition:

Stable

The patient's parents were advised to follow up on the rehabilitation and behavior therapy. Discharge Summary:
Patient: 57-year-old male
Chief Complaint: Anosmia and bilateral nasal obstruction

Hospital Course:
The patient presented with a 2-year history of bilateral nasal obstruction, worse on the right side, and anosmia. He also reported moderate headache. ENT examination revealed a mass originating from the roof of the nasal cavity, bilaterally, overlying the olfactory epithelial mucosal surface. Nasoendoscopy revealed that the surface of the mass was irregular. The patient underwent a CT scan of the nose and paranasal sinuses, which showed soft tissue mass at the olfactory recess and polypoid mucosal thickening bilaterally in the maxillary sinuses. The imaging also showed marked polypoid mucosal thickening of ethmoid air cells, sphenoid sinuses, and nasal cavities. The patient had no history of epistaxis, rhinorrhea, recurrent sinusitis or any neurological complaints.

Diagnosis:
Based on the CT scan of the nose and paranasal sinuses, the patient was diagnosed with a bilateral olfactory recess expansive soft tissue pathology extending to the skull base, which was suggestive of olfactory neuroblastoma. The case was discussed in the multidisciplinary team (MDT) meeting, and it was unanimously decided to subject the patient to excision biopsy rather than a simple biopsy, under general anesthesia. Subsequently, the patient underwent functional endoscopic sinus surgery (FESS) and excisional biopsy of the bilateral cribriform plate mass.

Treatment:
A functional endoscopic sinus surgery was performed to remove both the olfactory mass and all four sinuses with removal of the nasal polyps and septoplasty. Postoperative period was uneventful. Histopathologic examination of the bilateral masses revealed Sinonasal type respiratory epithelium exhibiting submucosal edema, chronic inflammatory cell infiltrate, and thickening of the basal layer. These findings are typically seen in cases of sinonasal polyposis; however, prominent crypting of surface mucosa with pseudoglandular formation isn't a typical feature of sinonasal polyps. A diagnosis of sinonasal polyps with REAH was thus rendered by a subspecialized Head and Neck pathologist.

Follow-up:
The patient was followed up in the clinic with serial nasoendoscopy, his nasal obstruction improved gradually; however, he did not regain his sense of smell. The patient is under our follow-up for more than two years, his nasal breathing is good, and there is no recurrence of sinusitis ± polyposis. The patient, however, continues to have anosmia. Overall, he is satisfied with his current health status with regards to the nasal disease and our intervention. 

Discharge Condition:
The patient's condition has stabilized, and he is being discharged.

The patient's peripheral facial paralysis was classified as House-Brackmann grade III, and the results of the audiogram were normal. Laboratory investigations and brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) were unremarkable. The delivery of pulsed radiofrequency (PRF) to the Gasserian ganglion was recommended to alleviate the pain of the mandibular nerve division of the trigeminal nerve.

The patient received pulsed radiofrequency treatment with a radiofrequency generator, which produced some pain relief, and a second application of PRF was performed a week later. Sensory testing at 50 Hz and motor testing at 2 Hz were performed to ensure the needle was on the sensory target. Infrared thermography was done to follow up lesion changes and provide effective assessment of combined therapy. The peripheral facial paralysis was treated with linear-polarized near-infrared light irradiation. The patient's treatment regimen was adjusted according to response, and gabapentin was initiated at a dose of 300 mg once per day, which was increased by 300 mg every day until a therapeutic dose (600 mg three times daily) was reached.

The patient was discharged in stable condition with instructions to follow-up with his primary care provider and ophthalmologist for further evaluation and management of his medical conditions. Hospital Course:
The 47-year-old male was admitted to the hospital with complaints of nausea, vomiting, and dizziness. Laboratory results during admission showed elevated troponin levels, high serum glucose levels, and an abnormal anion gap and sodium level. An initial EKG revealed ST-segment elevation in V2-V4, which led to an emergent cardiac catheterization. Before the procedure, the patient developed polymorphic ventricular tachycardia leading to ventricular fibrillation, which required defibrillation and chest compressions. Cardiac catheterization showed stenosis in the left anterior descending artery (LAD) which was treated with drug-eluting stents. Two further episodes of polymorphic ventricular tachycardia were observed during the procedure. 

Diagnostic Findings:
An echocardiogram revealed a normal left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) without wall motion abnormalities. The angiographic findings were suggestive of an ischemic etiology. However, a closer evaluation of the patient’s EKG revealed a coved ST segment elevation suggestive of Brugada pattern. The absence of regional wall motion abnormality raised concern for possible sodium channelopathy. Further evaluation indicated that the patient may have Brugada syndrome which was induced by gastrointestinal upset, low sodium levels, and metabolic abnormalities due to diabetic ketoacidosis.

Treatment and Management:
The patient was monitored and received an implantable defibrillator for the secondary prevention of Sudden Cardiac Death (SCD). After a few days, the patient was discharged with a LifeVest wearable defibrillator for continuous monitoring. Follow-up EKG showed no evidence of Brugada pattern. The patient subsequently underwent electrophysiological study with procainamide challenge test that did not show any sodium channelopathy suggestive of Brugada syndrome.

Final Diagnosis:
The patient was diagnosed with Brugada syndrome, which may have been induced by gastrointestinal upset, low sodium levels, and metabolic abnormalities due to diabetic ketoacidosis. The patient was treated with drug-eluting stents to address the stenosis in the LAD and was discharged with a LifeVest wearable defibrillator for continuous monitoring. The patient subsequently underwent an electrophysiological study with a procainamide challenge test that did not show any sodium channelopathy suggestive of Brugada syndrome.

Follow-Up Plan:
The patient is advised to follow up with a cardiology specialist and to adhere to a healthy lifestyle, including managing diabetes and maintaining good health habits. The patient is recommended to have regular check-ups to monitor the condition and adjust treatment plans if needed. Additionally, the patient is advised to report any symptoms or signs of arrhythmias immediately.

The patient was admitted to the hospital with complaints of progressive facial asymmetry, difficulty in speech and mastication secondary to restricted movement of the mandible, and intermittent pain in the right TMJ region. The patient reported progressive reduction in the vertical opening and increasing asymmetry of the face with no history of trauma. Clinical examination revealed marked facial asymmetry, and radiographic imaging showed a large radiopaque lesion of the right mandibular condyle. CT scan confirmed a tumor of the right condyle head, and surgical removal of the enlarged condyle via preauricular approach was planned.

A preauricular incision was carried out, and the lesion including the condyle was removed successfully using a surgical bur. Histopathology showed chondrocytes of the cartilaginous cap arranged in clusters in parallel, oblong lacunar spaces, similar to that of the normal epiphyseal cartilage along with regular bony trabeculae. There was no evidence of cartilage islands in underlying bony trabeculae. These features were suggestive of osteochondroma, and the diagnosis of giant osteochondroma was made.
 
Postoperative recovery was uneventful, and periodic follow-up appointments were scheduled. During the latest visit of the patient, it was observed that his facial appearance and mouth opening had returned back to normal, and he had been symptom-free.

The patient has successfully undergone surgical intervention for giant osteochondroma, and he has been discharged from the hospital with good postoperative recovery. The patient has been advised to continue follow-up appointments as scheduled.

Hospital Course:
A 44-year-old female patient with nodular goiter presented with progressive dyspnea and noisy breathing, and subglottic stenosis was discovered through endoscopy. A CT scan indicated a 4.0 × 3.0 × 1.7 cm hypodense mass in the left thyroid gland, which was later diagnosed as undifferentiated carcinoma with lymphoepithelioma-like features. The left thyroid tumor was accompanied by three enlarged neck lymph nodes in the left level II and level III regions.
FNAC was performed for the left neck lymph node and left thyroid gland for evaluation. The FNAC sample of the left neck lymph node indicated metastatic carcinoma with lymphoepithelioma-like features, and the thyroid FNAC disclosed loosely cohesive clusters of follicular epithelial cells with an abundant dense extracellular matrix.
The patient received debulking surgery, including a total thyroidectomy and bilateral neck lymph node dissection under the impression that a malignant thyroid tumor was present. The histologic slides of the left thyroid tumor and metastatic node indicated undifferentiated carcinoma with lymphoepithelioma-like features, and metastatic papillary carcinoma was recognized in all the right neck lymph nodes. 
The tumor could not be completely removed because of laryngeal invasion. Therefore, the surgeon performed a total thyroidectomy with preservation of the hypopharynx and larynx. Postoperative radiotherapy was provided for the gross residual local disease. 
The follow-up CT scan indicated prominent regressive change in the tumor, and at the time of study, the patient had been living with the disease for 1 year and 10 months.

Treatment:
- Debuking surgery, including total thyroidectomy and bilateral neck lymph node dissection
- Postoperative radiotherapy

Condition at Discharge:
The patient had no noted complications and was discharged in stable condition.

Follow-up:
The patient need to continue regular follow-up with the treating physician for further evaluation and management as required.

Patient: 47-year-old edentulous female with maxillary complete denture

Chief Complaint: Dysfunctional maxillary complete denture

History of Present Illness: The patient presented with an unuseful maxillary complete denture, resulting from cervical radiotherapy. She had a limited oral opening and insufficient saliva quantity and flowability.

Hospital Course: The patient's treatment plan consisted of fabricating complete dentures with proper extension of the flanges. Flexible impression trays were used to obtain preliminary impressions for both arches. Custom trays for the final impressions were fabricated with autopolimerized acrylic resin. Final maxillary impressions were made by using polysulfide material alternately for the first and second halves of the sectional trays. Record bases were fabricated and occlusion rims were prepared. A centric relation record was made, and the record was transferred from the patient to a semiadjustable articulator. The try-in was evaluated to verify jaw relations and teeth arrangement. After patient acceptance, final festooning and flasking of the dentures were completed. The final dentures were manufactured using similar designs to that of the record bases. The prostheses were deflasked, finished, and polished. The patient was provided with instructions for cleaning, inserting, and removing the prostheses. She was recalled for follow-up visits to check for the maintenance and her adaptability with the new dentures.

Outcome: The patient reported difficulty in the insertion and removal of denture initially, but progressively, she became used to it.

Follow-up: The patient will continue to be monitored during follow-up visits to check the maintenance and adaptability of her new dentures.

Date of Discharge: [REDACTED]

Reason for Admission: Right Pancoast tumor

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted to our institution with a presentation of right arm pain due to a right Pancoast tumor diagnosed as adenocarcinoma by fine needle aspiration cytology. A thorough evaluation using chest computed tomography (CT), brain CT, positron emission tomography (PET), and subsequent thoracoscopy showed N0 status diagnosed by CT and PET; the involvement of the right brachiocephalic and subclavian veins was also highly suspected at the pleural inspection (stage cT4N0M0). The patient underwent four cycles of cisplatin and Pemetrexed plus 60 Gy irradiation with partial tumor regression seen on CT while PET scan became negative.

Surgical Intervention:

The patient underwent successful Video-Assisted Thoracoscopic Surgery (VATS) lobectomy for the right upper lobe of the lung. The surgery was preceded by thoracoscopy to evaluate the resectability of the tumor. The procedure was judged feasible and a V-shaped contra-incision was made along the anterior border of the right sternocleidomastoid muscle, extended parallel to the second intercostal space. Through VATS accesses, sections of the right superior bronchus and the remaining fissure were completed, and the “en bloc” specimen was extracted through the apical incision. After lymphadenectomy, the sternum was sutured with metallic stitches and the anterior defect of the thoracic wall was repaired with a synthetic patch.

Outcome:

Postoperative pain remained under control and never exceeded four on the visual analog scale. Neither intraoperative nor postoperative complications were observed and the patient was discharged after nine days. The patient's pathological result was ypT0N0M0. At the twelve-month follow-up, the patient was free from disease and post-thoracotomy syndrome.

The patient is a 61-year-old man with mouth cancer. He had surgery for early-stage cancer in 2011. He came back after not seeing doctors for over 4 years. He now had swollen lymph nodes in his neck and left armpit. A small tissue sample showed the cancer had spread to these lymph nodes. The patient joined a research study. He received three cancer drugs called carboplatin, 5-FU, and pembrolizumab at a dose of 200 mg. After 4 rounds of treatment, the cancer showed some shrinking. However, he came in feeling very tired and had low blood pressure with the top number at 70. Doctors found that his immune treatment caused his adrenal glands to stop working properly. These glands sit above the kidneys and make important hormones. He was given a strong steroid medicine called dexamethasone. Later, he switched to another steroid called hydrocortisone. A scan of his brain showed no swelling near the pituitary gland. The scan also showed no cancer spread to the brain. His tiredness went away after ten days. He then started taking pembrolizumab again. The patient continues to take hydrocortisone.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [REDACTED]

Age: 46-year-old
Gender: Female
Admission Date: [REDACTED]
Discharge Date: [REDACTED]

Admission Diagnosis: Insidious onset severe persistent headache with bilateral hypoglossal nerve palsy.

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted with an insidious onset of severe persistent headache, most prominent in the occipital region lasting for 10 days. Six days after the onset, she experienced dysarthria, difficulty in moving her tongue within the mouth, and difficulty in eating and drinking. On admission, she was found to have a high-grade fever. Neurological examination revealed bilateral hypoglossal nerve palsy with marked tongue atrophy, more prominent in the left side. Her eye movements were saccadic with a broad-based ataxic gait without any other signs of cerebellar involvement. Her blood test revealed a high neutrophil leukocytosis, and her ESR and CRP levels were elevated. Noncontrast CT brain did not reveal any abnormality. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) biochemistry revealed significant elevation of protein with 59 polymorphs and 8 lymphocytes per cubic millimetre with reduced CSF glucose.

Treatment:
The patient was initiated on empirical treatment as for pyogenic meningitis with ceftriaxone and vancomycin for which she had a gradual improvement of general status with improvement of fever, meningism, gaze, and gait abnormalities while tongue weakness and atrophy persisted.

Diagnostic Results:
Subsequently, she underwent MRI of brain and brainstem, which revealed a posteromedial infarction in the lower part of the medulla oblongata without leptomeningeal enhancement and did not show a significant cerebral oedema. Her chest radiograph did not reveal any changes suggestive of pulmonary tuberculosis or sarcoidosis. Syphilis (VDRL & THPA), HIV serology, and autoimmune markers for vasculitis (rheumatoid factor, ANA (IF), and p & c-ANCA) were negative.

Discharge Diagnosis:
Pyogenic Meningitis with posteromedial infarction in the lower part of the medulla oblongata without leptomeningeal enhancement.

Discharge Medications:
No medications were prescribed at the time of discharge.

Follow-up:
The patient was reviewed at one month and three & six months and was found to be free of fever with good general condition and had normal inflammatory markers. However, she had persistent tongue atrophy with difficult speech from which she was gradually recovering with the help of physiotherapy.

Discharge Instructions:
The patient was advised to continue physiotherapy for persistent tongue atrophy. Further follow-up appointments were recommended to monitor her condition.

HOSPITAL COURSE:

The patient was admitted to our hospital due to abdominal pain, which was relieved by conservative management. He had been diagnosed with congenital IPSVS six years prior and was under medication for attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder.

Laboratory tests revealed elevated ammonia levels and a prolonged coagulation profile. Imaging studies confirmed the presence of IPSVS and the hepatic mass.

The patient's parents opted for close follow-up rather than invasive treatment for the IPSVS. However, at the six-month follow-up, the patient's blood ammonia level had risen significantly, and the shunt ratio indicated the potential progression of hepatic encephalopathy. Hence, endovascular treatment was performed to close the shunt.

During the procedure, the patient experienced bleeding from the sheath's tract, which was managed promptly using US-guided compression. Within six days of the procedure, the patient's serum ammonia levels had decreased to within normal range, and he was discharged after nine days.

FOLLOW-UP:

Two weeks post-embolization, an abdominal US showed occluded shunts with a decrease in the size of the hepatic mass. The right portal vein's blood flow had increased markedly, and the spleen size had minimally increased. A follow-up CT scan a month later showed complete embolization of the IPSVS, improved portal flow to the right lobe, and nearly complete disappearance of the hepatic mass.

On discharge, the patient was stable, alert and oriented. His physical exam and vital signs were normal. His medications were reviewed, and he was instructed to follow up with his referring physician.

DISCHARGE DIAGNOSIS:

1. Congenital IPSVS
2. Hepatic mass.

DISCHARGE PLAN:

1. Follow up with the referring physician for routine care and monitoring.
2. Medications to be continued as before.
3. No dietary restrictions.
4. No strenuous physical activity for two weeks.
5. Report back to the hospital if there are any concerns or adverse events.

Hospital Course Summary:

This is a summary of the clinical aspects of the patient's medical history. The patient is a 68-year-old Caucasian lady of British Jewish descent who presented with the long term sequelae of deep XR treatment administered at the age of six months to the right side of her face. The information regarding the childhood treatment is limited, and there are no other details regarding dose and frequency of the irradiation.

The patient's subsequent health developments and interventions are well documented in the case notes within both the General Practice setting and the hospital departments she has visited since. Relatives have reported that during the London Blitz, she was treated for an extensive mole on her face and neck that was present at birth, and that being a frail child, she was not expected to live.

As a child, right facial asymmetry became progressively more apparent due to arrested development of the skull bones and teeth. At the age of 47, a CT scan of the brain demonstrated right-sided cerebellar atrophy with an arachnoid cyst communicating with an enlarged fourth ventricle, and the presence of multiple skull-based meningiomata of the right petrous temporal bone. Within two years, oesophagitis and prepyloric erosions were identified at gastroscopy.

During a four year period from the age of 53, she was diagnosed with several disorders, including neurofibromata of the left jaw and right cheek; sialadenitis of the left parotid resulting in the gland's excision and subsequent Frey's syndrome; bilateral sensorineural hearing loss, worse in the right ear; and an early right cataract.

From the age of 60, there were further developments that were more painful and sinister than had occurred previously. These include the right-sided trigeminal neuralgia; multiple basal cell carcinomata affecting the right temple; sarcoma of the left neck recurring two years after excision; a right-sided cerebello-pontine angle tumour; and a possible bronchogenic tumour pushing against the oesophagus. The latter two neoplasms have been assessed as inoperable and slow-growing on CT appearance, and the lady has elected not to have further investigation, biopsy, or treatment.

As an adult, this lady worked in a leading West End department store until retirement at the normal age. As would be expected, there have been a succession of age-related problems, including hypertension, hallux valgus, lumbar spine degeneration, lymphoedema, and recurrent varicose veins. At present, she remains a cheerful retired lady, troubled by unsteadiness and gradually worsening headaches. She is kept busy with numerous hospital appointments to attend. She also cares for an older step-sister who suffers from dementia.

The patient's discharge medications were prescribed by the attending physician and are available in the patient's outpatient medical record.

The patient was advised to continue regular follow-up with his primary care physician and cardiothoracic surgeon. Further cardiac rehabilitation is recommended in coordination with the patient's medical team.

Discharge Summary:

Diagnosis:
- Left side hearing impairment
- Temporal bone tumor that invaded the middle ear cavity, cerebellopontine angle (CPA) cistern, and left jugular foramen
- Post-operative regrowth of tumor that invaded the dura membrane forming perilesional parenchymal edema in the left cerebellum
- Three consecutive distal anterior inferior cerebellar artery (AICA) aneurysms adjacent to tumor

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted with dizziness and left side hearing impairment. The patient had a history of temporal bone tumor that had been present for approximately 4 years. Pre-operative magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed a mass at the petrous part of left temporal bone. The patient underwent a mastoidectomy at another institute and during the procedure, the dura of the petrosal apex area was damaged causing cerebrospinal fluid leakage. Post-operative MRI showed near total removal of the tumor. However, on follow-up MRI performed 9 months after the surgery, the remnant tumor had regrown and formed a mass at the CPA and the tumor invaded the dura membrane forming perilesional parenchymal edema in the left cerebellum. Cerebral angiography was performed to examine pre-operative vessels and tumor embolization. On angiography, there were newly noted multiple AICA aneurysms adjacent to the tumor. The distal AICA and posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA) were anastomosed, and therefore, endovascular treatment for these aneurysms was thought to be risky.
 
Using a lateral suboccipital craniectomy approach, the patient underwent resection of the tumor mass from the mastoid wall to the dural invasion. After total removal of the tumor, three consecutive distal AICA aneurysms were found. Clipping of the aneurysms was unfavorable because all aneurysms were fusiform and had fragile vessel walls. On pre-operative angiography, we found well-developed collaterals between the distal AICA and PICA, so we trapped the most proximal and distal portions of the aneurysm and resected the middle portion. Post-operative MRI showed that the tumor was totally removed. Radiation therapy was performed with total dose of 4,300 cGy over 20 treatments due to rapid tumor recurrence after the first surgery. 

Condition on Discharge:
The patient was discharged in stable condition with left side hearing impairment.

Follow-up:
The patient was advised to follow up with the healthcare provider for further evaluation and management.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Information:
Name: [Redacted]
Age: 50 years
Sex: Female
Race: South Indian

Hospital Course:
The patient presented to the outpatient department with a productive cough with hemoptysis for the past 2 months. She had a history of pulmonary tuberculosis, which was discontinued within 3 weeks of starting the treatment. She also suffered from diabetes mellitus with peripheral neuropathy for the past 8 years and was taking oral hypoglycemic agents for the same. The patient was diagnosed with an indwelling aspergilloma and was treated with an oral loading dose of Voriconazole followed by an oral maintenance dose. The patient responded well to the treatment, and the hemoptysis resolved after a lobectomy. After 3 weeks, the sputum became negative for acid-fast bacilli. The patient is currently in the 4th month of treatment and is doing well.

Laboratory Results:
Admission baseline investigations showed anemia, and the renal and liver function tests were within normal limits.

Diagnostic Study:
Computed tomogram of the thorax revealed a thick-walled cavity in the right lung upper lobe with an indwelling aspergilloma. 3 sputum samples were tested positive for acid-fast bacilli by Ziehl Neelsen's staining technique. Conventional method of culture on Lowenstein Jensen's medium yielded growth of M. tuberculosis. The anti-tuberculosis drug susceptibility test showed resistance to Isoniazid and Rifampicin but sensitive to Ethambutol, Pyrazinamide, and Streptomycin in their critical concentrations.

Diagnosis:
The patient was diagnosed with pulmonary tuberculosis and an indwelling aspergilloma.

Treatment:
The patient was initially started on a daily dose of Isoniazid, Ethambutol, Pyrazinamide, and Streptomycin. However, after culture demonstrated MDR-TB, Isoniazid was stopped, and oral Levofloxacin and Ethionamide were included in the treatment regimen. Rifampicin was not included due to its interactions with Voriconazole. The patient was given an oral loading dose of Voriconazole 400 mg 12th hourly for 2 doses, which was followed by an oral maintenance dose of 200 mg 12th hourly for 6 weeks.

Follow-up:
After the treatment, the patient was counseled on the importance of adhering to medication and follow-up visits. She was advised to return to the hospital for follow-up visits and monitoring of symptoms.

Summary:
The 50-year-old South Indian woman presented with complaints of productive cough with hemoptysis for the past 2 months.
