Hospital Course Summary:

The patient, a 6-year-old Greek boy, was admitted to our hospital with a painful intumescence of the left inguinal area. Prior to admission, the patient was referred to a general hospital where he was diagnosed with an incarcerated left inguinal hernia. The hernia was subsequently reduced by a local surgeon, but the patient continued to experience discomfort and pain. Upon physical examination, the left inguinal area appeared normal, with only subcutaneous edema and a hematoma due to the reduction manipulations observed. Mild discomfort and pain was present in the left testicle without clinical evidence of testicular torsion. These symptoms persisted for three days before the decision was made to operate on the patient.

During the operation, a lower Spigelian hernia was identified. The hernia sac penetrated from a small defect in the Spigelian fascia within Hesselbach's triangle. The orifice diameter was about 1.5 cm, and the sac extended up to 7 cm and contained a small part of the large omentum which was successfully reduced. Reconstruction of the hernia was performed with non-absorbable sutures.

The patient remained in stable condition throughout his hospital stay and was discharged without any complications. The patient was instructed to rest and was prescribed appropriate follow-up care.

Follow-Up Care:

The patient remains free of symptoms and recurrence for eight years after the operation.

Hospital Course: 

The patient was admitted with presyncope, nausea, and palpitations. An electrocardiogram (ECG) showed new, complete atrioventricular (AV) block. A permanent pacemaker was implanted, which resulted in resolution of her symptoms. The patient subsequently developed intermittent watery diarrhea without blood or mucus and was passing 10-15 bowel movements per day. The patient had painful, recurrent oral and genital ulcers for the previous 10 months and intermittent large joint swelling and tenderness during this period. Furthermore, the patient had an episode of redness of her eyes 2 months before her first admission that had lasted for 2 weeks, consistent with uveitis. The patient had been admitted 3 weeks before her current presentation with chest pain due to pericarditis. An ECG at that time showed normal sinus rhythm, while an echocardiogram showed small pericardial effusion. At that time, tender swelling of the right knee joint was observed. Her physical examination also revealed numerous mucosal ulcers in her mouth and on the labia minora. Her past medical history included 40 pack-years smoking and a right lower limb deep venous thrombosis when she was pregnant with her second child.
 
Diagnostic Assessment: 

Clinical examination did not reveal any evidence of extraintestinal manifestation of inflammatory bowel disease. The patient's pathergy test result was negative. The results of her autoimmune screen, including rheumatoid factor, antinuclear antibody, anti-double-stranded DNA, anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody, and extractable nuclear antibodies were negative. Her human leukocyte antigen (HLA)-B51 was negative, but she had genotype HLA-B35 in her blood. Stool microscopy and culture did not reveal any pathogens. An endoscopic evaluation showed a large ulceration in the terminal ileum that did not appear typical of Crohn’s disease. Her histopathological examination showed changes consistent with vasculitis but no granulomas or transmural inflammation. A computed tomographic enterogram showed no other areas of ulceration or evidence of Crohn’s disease. Based on these findings, the diagnosis of BD was made.

Treatment:

The patient was commenced on prednisolone 50 mg with a slow tapering course, as well as sulfasalazine 500 mg twice daily that was later increased to 1 g twice daily, to which she responded with resolution of her diarrhea and mucosal ulceration. The patient continued to be in remission during once-monthly and then thrice-monthly clinical follow-up.

Outcomes:

The patient was discharged from the hospital and continued to be in remission during once-monthly and then thrice-monthly clinical follow-up. 

Discharge Diagnosis:

Behcet's disease.

Follow-up Care:

The patient will be followed up on an outpatient basis for further management and monitoring of Behcet's disease.

The patient was diagnosed with DKA and received standard treatment for the condition, which included intravenous fluids, insulin therapy, and potassium replacement. DKA resolved gradually after insulin therapy, but the abdominal pain continued.

A further investigation of MRCP revealed the absence of the dorsal pancreatic duct and a short duct of Wirsung running into the major papilla. On the basis of these findings, a diagnosis of complete ADP was evident.
Low-fat diet was recommended, and pancreatic enzyme supplements as well as mosapride citrate were given with meals to facilitate the digestive process. The pain gradually resolved and went away in 7 days after the treatment. 
One month later, a standard mixed-meal tolerance test was performed to evaluate β-cell function. The 27-year-old African-American woman was admitted to the hospital with chest pain, dyspnea on exertion, and a malar rash. Positive tests for anti-nuclear antibodies and anti-double-stranded DNA confirmed SLE-related pericarditis. Transthoracic echocardiography showed severe PH with an estimated RVSP of 92 mmHg and severe right ventricular dysfunction. After initiation of appropriate treatment, the patient showed improvement of muscle weakness and exercise capacity. Repeat transthoracic echocardiography four months later showed a normal right ventricular size and function with an estimated RVSP of 29 mmHg. Repeat right heart catheterization showed a reduction in the mean pulmonary artery pressure, an increase in cardiac output, and a reduction in pulmonary vascular resistance. The patient was started on oral therapy with sildenafil and treprostinil was tapered until discontinuation.

Diagnosis:
SLE-associated PH and polymyositis.

Treatment:
Pulse dose methylprednisolone, intravenous treprostinil, prednisone, and mycophenolate mofetil were prescribed. The patient was discharged on low-dose treprostinil and oral therapy with sildenafil was initiated. Prednisone was tapered over three months.

Follow-up:
The patient showed improvement in her leg weakness and exercise capacity. Repeat transthoracic echocardiography showed a normal right ventricular size and function. Repeat right heart catheterization showed a reduction in the mean pulmonary artery pressure, an increase in cardiac output, and a reduction in pulmonary vascular resistance. The patient continues to be followed up as an outpatient.

Discharge Summary:

Hospital Course:
The 62-year-old male was admitted to the hospital with a complaint of abdominal pain, vomiting, and ambulatory dysfunction. The initial examination showed no abnormalities. The patient was suspected to have viral gastroenteritis, and hence he was hospitalized for dehydration management. The patient's nausea and vomiting improved after admission, but it was noted that he was leaning backwards and to the right when standing or attempting to ambulate on the first day of hospitalization.

Diagnostic Evaluations:
The neurology service was consulted after assessing the patient's condition on his second day of admission. A CT angiogram of the head and neck showed a congenitally hypoplastic left vertebral artery and no other abnormality was observed in the vertebrobasilar system. MRI of the brain showed acute/subacute infarct in the right cerebellar hemisphere. The echocardiogram showed moderate diastolic dysfunction with trace aortic regurgitation.

Clinical Impression:
The patient was diagnosed with acute/subacute infarct in the right cerebellar hemisphere secondary to chronic atherosclerotic disease that had extended and caused APS. The left-sided dysmetria was observed, which further indicated his neurological impairment.

Hospital Treatment:
The patient was monitored on telemetry for several days without any events or abnormalities noted. He was started on a scheduled antiemetic regimen of metoclopramide 10 mg four times daily and ondansetron 8 mg every eight hours that yielded positive results. Within one day, the patient's nausea and vomiting were controlled, and he was able to eat without difficulty. The patient was successfully discharged from the hospital to rehabilitation.

Follow-up Recommendations:
The patient is recommended to follow up with the neurology service as an outpatient and undergo regular checkups to monitor his neurological function and the progression of his cerebrovascular disease. He is also advised to maintain strict blood glucose control and hypertension management. The family members are recommended to observe the patient's activities, as he is more vulnerable to falls.

Patient: 51-year-old female

Admission Date: February 2013

Discharge Date: October 2015

Diagnosis: Recurrent Ameloblastoma

Procedure: Right mandibular resection and reconstruction with nonvascularized free iliac bone followed by dental implant placement and fixed prosthesis

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted to the department in February 2013 due to discomfort in the mandible. She had been diagnosed with recurrent ameloblastoma and had undergone multiple fenestration procedures in the past. The patient was dissatisfied with the outcomes of previous hospital's treatment policy and came to our department for the complete resection of the tumor. 
After thorough evaluation and diagnosis, we proposed a treatment protocol of radical resection and immediate bony reconstruction using nonvascularized free iliac bone graft. The patient underwent right mandibular resection (teeth 43 to 46; length 35 mm) in March 2013 and was closely monitored for tumor recurrence. 
Follow-up examinations showed no signs of tumor recurrence, but the patient continued to experience right-sided difficulty in mastication. Therefore, a fixed prosthesis was recommended. In November 2014, the mini-plate was removed from the grafted bone, and four dental implants were placed. Subsequently, the patient underwent vestibuloplasty (vestibular extension with periosteal separation procedures) and confirmed osseointegration in all four implants. The final fixed prosthesis was worn by the patient in October 2015. 
The patient's oral hygiene has been regularly managed, and no signs of tumor recurrence or abnormal bone absorption or disintegration of the dental implants have been observed. The patient was discharged in October 2015.

Discharge Instructions:

The patient is advised to continue maintaining good oral hygiene and to follow the regular maintenance therapy schedule. The patient should keep all appointments with the department for proper monitoring of tumor recurrence and dental implant health. If there are any concerns or questions, the patient should contact the department for further consultations.

Patient: 61-year-old male with a history of recurrent chest discomfort and palpitations.

Hospital Course:
The patient was referred to our hospital due to frequent ventricular premature contractions, with no positive results found in examinations. RFCA was performed, and the patient experienced dizziness, tightness in the chest, cold sweat, bradycardia, and hypotension afterward. Further examination of the patient showed hydropericardium, and the patient underwent pericardiocentesis drainage to drain off 800 mL blood. The patient's tight chest improved, and their blood pressure increased. However, the patient experienced chest tightness again two hours later, and an additional 750 mL of blood was drained from the indwelling catheter in the pericardium. This time, the patient was given volume expansion and dopamine to sustain normal blood pressure. During the next hour, the patient experienced further circulatory unstability, and a transthoracic echocardiography revealed a left ventricular wall rupture and a hematoma in the left ventricular wall. The patient was then transferred to the operating room for surgical exploration.

Surgical intervention:
The patient underwent median sternotomy, and CPB was established with cannulation of the ascending aorta and right atrium quickly after the pericardium cavity was evacuated. Cardioplegic arrest was used, and further exploration of the heart showed a 6 × 8 cm2 area of contusion in the posterolateral wall with a 5-cm epicardial tear at the center. Teflon-buttressed sutures were used to close the tear, and a pericardium patch with continuous sutures around and bioglue inside was applied to the contusion region. The patient was discontinued from CPB uneventfully with excellent hemodynamic status.

Discharge Summary:
The patient has recovered well from their surgical intervention and was discharged from the hospital on the 15th postoperative day. Final examination showed that the injury region of the left ventricular wall had healed. The patient is advised to maintain a healthy diet and exercise regimen and to follow up with their primary care physician as needed.

Discharge Summary:
Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Medical Record Number: [REDACTED]

Hospital Course:

The patient, a 78-year-old female, was referred to the ophthalmology department of the University Hospital Bonn on an emergency basis with complaints of blurred vision, loss of visual field, and photopsia. She also reported having a dry cough for the past four months that was refractory to symptomatic and antibiotic therapy.

Over the last five weeks, the patient experienced increasing diffuse thrusting, bilateral pain in the area of the mandible, and thrusting pain in the tongue leading to difficulties in swallowing. The patient also reported weight loss, increasing fatigue, subfebrile body temperatures, and scalp tenderness.

Examinations by a dentist, an orthodontist, and an otolaryngologist remained without any findings. The neurological examination remained unremarkable, and chest radiography was without pathologies.

Laboratory results revealed increased inflammatory markers, and ophthalmological examination revealed optic disc edema with cotton wool spots along the upper temporal vascular arch of the left eye. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) of the left macula, OCT of the optic disc, and fluorescein angiography confirmed anterior ischemic optical neuropathy (AION) of the left eye.

Ultrasound examination of all arteries typically involved in GCA according to OMERACT protocol demonstrated a homogeneous, concentric thickening of the intima-media complex in several arteries of the head and neck area. Vasculitic affection with increased intima-media thickness values was observed in the common superficial temporal arteries on both sides, both frontal and parietal branches, as well as in the right facial artery and right axillary artery. A halo sign was also visible in both vertebral arteries, and the deep lingual artery displayed a typical vasculitic halo-sign.

Diagnosis of GCA was made based on the patient’s symptoms, clinical examination, laboratory results, and ultrasound findings, and treatment was promptly initiated. The patient received an initial daily dose of 500 mg methylprednisolone followed by a daily dose of 60 mg prednisolone per os, tapered over 26 weeks according to the GIACTA treatment protocol. In addition, tocilizumab treatment was initiated with a weekly dose of 162 mg subcutaneously due to the widespread affection of the arterial vascular bed.

With treatment, symptoms and laboratory markers quickly improved. Jaw claudication and tongue pain resolved within days, and the patient was dismissed five days later in stable clinical condition. Three months after dismissal, a follow-up examination was performed, and the patient was on 9 mg prednisolone per day and 162 mg tocilizumab subcutaneously per week and free of symptoms. On ultrasound examination, a relevant decrease of IMT values could be observed in all affected arteries.

Six months after the patient’s dismissal, follow-up examinations revealed that the best corrected visual acuity had increased, and funduscopic examination of the left eye showed a decrease of optic disc edema with a pale optic disc and narrow vessels. The patient was on 12.5 mg prednisolone per day and 162 mg tocilizumab subcutaneously per week and free of symptoms. On ultrasound examination, a further decrease in IMT values could be observed.

The patient has been advised to continue with their treatment protocol and to schedule regular follow-up examinations to monitor their condition.

Diagnoses:
1. Giant cell arteritis

Procedures:
None

Stable

Discharge Summary:

Patient: 32-year-old female with chief complaint of pain in upper anterior tooth.

Hospital Course:
The patient reported to the Department of Conservative Dentistry and Endodontics and was diagnosed with an impacted permanent canine and a palatally placed upper permanent right lateral incisor. A radiograph showed loss of lamina dura and slight radiolucency in relation to the periapical area of the upper right central incisor. A CBCT revealed a periapical lesion related to both roots of the central incisor and an additional root positioned more facially than expected. A nonsurgical endodontic therapy was decided after a discussion with the patient. The root canals were cleaned and shaped, copiously irrigated, and obturated with corresponding Protaper gutta-percha and AH Plus sealer. The patient refused restoration of the facial groove with composite resin.

Outcome:
The patient was asymptomatic after 2 weeks and at a one-year follow-up. The patient was satisfied with the treatment outcome and would continue to be monitored by her dentist. 

Impression:
The patient presented with a rare case of an additional root present with the central incisor, which was successfully treated with nonsurgical endodontic therapy.

The patient was diagnosed with Burkitt lymphoma based on the CT chest and lymph node biopsy.

The patient was discharged to an oncology hospice for palliative care. The family was advised to continue the patient's medications as directed and to follow up with their hospice provider. Hospital Course: 
The patient was admitted with a 4-day history of anorexia and abdominal pain followed by a fall and 14 h long lie on the floor, which was complicated with a left flank abscess. The physical examination revealed peritoneal irritation, tachycardia, hypotension, and tachypnea, indicating severe sepsis on a background of chronic kidney disease and obesity. The imaging studies, including portal-venous phase contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis, showed that the patient was suffering from sigmoid diverticulitis complicated by diverticular abscess leading to retroperitoneal perforation and acute appendicitis. 

Surgical intervention was warranted due to the severity of the patient's condition and his high-risk profile, including ischemic heart disease, atrial fibrillation, and stage IV chronic kidney disease secondary to polycystic kidney disease. The patient underwent sigmoid colectomy with rectal stump and end colostomy formation (Hartmann's procedure) and appendectomy. Minimal pus was found in the left paracolic gutter, and the retroperitoneum was not explored during the surgery. Intra-abdominal drains were placed in the left paracolic gutter and pelvis. 

Following the surgical intervention, the patient was extubated on day 1 and managed in ICU for 8 days due to high levels of oxygen requirement secondary to co-existing pneumonia. The patient stepped down to the surgical ward, where he subsequently developed worsening sepsis; further imaging studies revealed an enlarged, complex retroperitoneal collection in the left flank. Two percutaneous drains were inserted into the retroperitoneal collection. However, despite intravenous antibiotic therapy and drainage of the retroperitoneal collection, the patient passed away on post-operative day 40 due to worsening sepsis. 

Summary of Hospital Course: 
The 81-year-old male patient presented with sigmoid diverticulitis, acute appendicitis, and diverticular abscess with retroperitoneal perforation, which led to surgical intervention. During the hospital course, the patient developed co-existing pneumonia, which required management in the ICU and later developed worsening sepsis, culminating in his eventual passing on post-operative day 40.

input:
Medical History:
The patient is a 30-year-old male with no significant personal or family medical history.

Hospital Course:
The patient presented in November 2006 for diagnosis of a large tumor on the left chest wall that had been growing for 4 years. The patient had a previous diagnosis of myositis ossificans circumscripta, but a biopsy in May 2004 showed an intramuscular tumor with mature bone trabeculae, suggesting a diagnosis of "atypical" myositis ossificans or heterotopic ossification. The patient was proposed for surgical removal, but refused and was lost to follow-up until November 2006.

Upon presentation to our institution, the patient had a frozen left shoulder associated with ipsilateral radial and cubital paralysis and cervical pain. Physical examination revealed a voluminous, plane, hard, and immobile mass extended from the basicervical region to the scapulo-humeral joint and from the left side of the chest wall to the axillary region. Radiological imaging showed a huge calcified heterogeneous mass with cystic and solid elements. The mass had a 25-cm transversal diameter, an 18-cm antero-posterior diameter, and a 30-cm cranio-caudal diameter. It included the left scapula, the periscapular muscles and the chest wall, with intercostal invasion to the pleura and muscular extension to the left arm (triceps).

Diagnostic testing confirmed a diagnosis of low-grade extraskeletal osteosarcoma (ESOS) based on pathological samples collected in May 2004 that were re-examined for molecular analysis of MDM2 and CDK4 oncogenes. The disease was stable after 2 API/AI chemotherapy cycles but progressed after 4 additional cycles, with extension of cutaneous nodules and tumor mass associated with the apparition of left pleuritis. Palliative radiation therapy was not possible technically due to the tumor volume. A thoracoscopic talcage was done, followed by trabectedin-based chemotherapy. However, three weeks after the first cycle, the patient deteriorated rapidly and died of respiratory failure secondary to loco-regional extension, 5 years after the initial symptoms.

Discharge Condition:
The patient died of respiratory failure secondary to loco-regional extension.

Discharge Summary:

Patient information: The patient is a 7 year old Caucasian boy (Turkish) who presented with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and lupus nephritis.

Hospital course: The patient was initially treated with intravenous methylprednisolone pulses and oral azathioprine, which led to a reduction of proteinuria and normalization of the erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR). However, due to incompliance, the patient was inconsistently seen by a physician. Three years after the initial presentation, the patient was admitted to the Intensive Care Unit with loss of consciousness and seizures. The MRI of the brain showed subcortical hyperintense lesions, which were regarded as SLE- related cerebral disease. Treatment with intravenous methylprednisolone pulses, plasmapheresis and intravenous cyclophosphamide showed no effect. The decision for the experimental use of antiCD20 antibody-treatment was made and one single rituximab dose was given. The patient slowly regained consciousness over further two weeks and inflammatory parameters normalized. However, kidney function did not improve during the next two years and the disease progressed to end-stage renal failure requiring hemodialysis. Six years later, signs and symptoms of SLE were not present and the patient underwent single kidney transplantation.

Summary of Hospital Course: The patient presented with systemic lupus erythematosus and lupus nephritis, which initially responded to treatment with intravenous methylprednisolone pulses and oral azathioprine. However, due to incompliance, the patient was inconsistently seen by a physician. Three years after the initial presentation, the patient developed SLE-related cerebral disease and was treated with intravenous methylprednisolone pulses, plasmapheresis and intravenous cyclophosphamide, which were ineffective. The patient was subsequently treated with one single dose of rituximab, which resulted in normalization of inflammatory parameters, but did not improve kidney function. The patient ultimately required hemodialysis and underwent single kidney transplantation six years later without any signs or symptoms of SLE.

HOSPITAL COURSE:

This is a summary of the hospital course for a 56-year-old woman diagnosed with stage IIB (pT3pN1M0), moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma of the pancreatic head.

CHIEF COMPLAINT:

The patient presented to the emergency room (ER) with complaints of shortness of breath.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS:

The patient underwent a pancreatojejunostomy (Whipple procedure) with resection of a long afferent limb from a previous gastric bypass and placement of a feeding jejunostomy for enteral nutrition. This was followed by adjuvant radiation to the pancreatic tumour bed with concurrent continuous infusion of 5-fluorouracil. Subsequently the patient began adjuvant gemcitabine on days 1, 8 and 15 of each 28 day cycle. In April 2016, the patient received cycle 3, day 1 of gemcitabine and presented to the ER 10 days later with complaints of shortness of breath.

MEDICAL HISTORY:

The patient had a history of hypertension, pancreatitis, gastro-oesophageal reflux disease with Barrett’s oesophagus and insulin dependent diabetes mellitus. The patient also had laparoscopic Roux-en-Y gastric bypass, cholecystectomy and total abdominal hysterectomy with salpingo-oophorectomy. The patient had prior alcohol abuse and a 60-pack year smoking history.

PHYSICAL EXAM:

Evaluation revealed the patient to have anasarca, bilateral pleural effusions and hypotension (systolic blood pressure ranging from 77 to 87 mm Hg).

HOSPITAL COURSE:

The patient was managed with intravenous fluids in the chemotherapy infusion room and ER for previous episodes of hypotension and oedema with gemcitabine infusions.

DISCHARGE CONDITION:

The patient was discharged in improved condition.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: IA, Mr.
Age: 85
Sex: Male

Hospital Course:
Mr. IA, an 85-year-old male, was admitted to the psychiatric clinic with complaints of complex visual hallucinations and perceived images of people in front of him. He had been managed for bilateral glaucoma for the past 7 years and had been clinically blind for the past 3 years. His recent experiences had been ongoing for about 8 weeks before his psychiatric appointment. On examination, he was found to have bilateral dry macular degeneration and pale optic disc with cup to disc asymmetry greater than 0.4 bilaterally. His physical and neurological examinations were otherwise normal for his age.

Treatment and Response:
The patient was reassured that he did not have a mental illness and was taught how to keep the images away by closing his eyes and repeating blinking when the objects of his hallucination could disappear momentarily and reappear again. His relatives were educated on the nature of CBS and advised to not attribute it to mental illness. Initially, 2 weekly visits were scheduled and were later reduced to 4 and later 6 weekly. There was no improvement in his visual acuity over this period of time, but his visual experiences disappeared 6 months afterwards without using any drug, and he was discharged.

Condition at Discharge:
Mr. IA was discharged with an explanation of the behavioral method used for his condition and the importance of avoiding attributing it to mental illness. He was advised to keep his eyes closed more frequently and to blink repetitively when the visual experiences recurred. His relatives were satisfied with the explanation and advice given and were scheduled to monitor compliance with and effectiveness of the method.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Information:
Name: [Redacted]
Age: 26 years
Gender: Female

Hospital Course:
The patient presented with a ten-year history of vomiting that was not relieved by standard antiemetic and behavioral treatments for cyclic vomiting syndrome. After thorough medical examination, a possible diagnosis of epilepsy was considered as the patient experienced cramping of the tongue, clenched her teeth against her will, and had an abnormal EEG showing spike and wave complexes in the left temporal lobe. Clonazepam was administered, which substantially improved background wave activity and decreased vomiting episodes. Psychological treatment, including relaxation techniques, breathing exercises, drawing pictures, and counseling, was also provided as the patient was suspected of having a mental trigger for her epilepsy.

Patient's Social and Family History:
The patient had a noncontributory past and family medical history. Family dynamics were identified as a possible psychological trigger. In her childhood, the patient was well-behaved, but her mother paid little attention to her as she was busy caring for her sick elder sister. When her sister entered college and was seldom at home, the mother began to nag the patient to do things and was overprotective of her. Through therapeutic sessions, the patient discussed her family's history, and psychological interventions were implemented to encourage independence and support her in moving away from her family.

Follow-Up:
After leaving the hospital, the patient experienced some ictal vomiting during periods of high stress. Still, with empathic support and therapy, her condition improved drastically when she obtained job training and subsequently found employment. Her symptoms disappeared entirely within several months, and she has been in good health without medication for over seven years.

Recommendations:
The patient is advised to continue to avoid triggers that may cause stress and has been encouraged to maintain independence and lead a healthy lifestyle. Follow-up clinical and psychological assessments are recommended to monitor her condition and prevent any relapses or complications.

input:
Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: Not Disclosed
Gender: Female
Age: 80

Hospital Course:
The patient presented with a history of a slow-growing, painless cyst in the right lateral orbital region, which was evaluated through mechanical ptosis, proptosis, and slight hypotropia. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed a round mass with no enhancement by gadolinium, and computed tomography (CT) presented with deformation of the right orbit with bone erosion centering on the frontosphenoidal suture and confirmed the diagnosis of a dermoid cyst. The patient declined surgical removal with boney reconstruction and continued with periodic aspiration. Sclerotherapy was performed after obtaining informed consent and aspirating the fluid multiple times. The first sclerotherapy was performed with 10 mL of 1% lidocaine containing 1:100,000 epinephrine and 10 mL of absolute ethanol was instilled, and the cavity was washed again with 10 mL of saline. Second and third sclerotherapies were performed at intervals of 3 months. After the final sclerotherapy, the cyst had shrunk in size, and no re-expansion was seen during a 1-year follow-up after the last sclerotherapy. The patient complained of visual field disturbance due to redundant skin, and a blepharoplasty was performed concomitant with incisional biopsy of the cyst. Histopathological examination showed that the specimen comprised dermis with well-developed sweat and sebaceous glands, compatible with a dermoid cyst.

Condition at Discharge:
The patient's dermoid cyst was treated successfully with sclerotherapy and incisional biopsy. At the time of discharge, the patient demonstrated no evidence of a recurring cyst.

Follow-Up Plan:
The patient will continue follow-up care with her primary care physician near her home residence and is advised to inquire if any new symptoms arise.

The patient is a 60-year-old, morbidly obese male with a medical history of uncontrolled hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus with microvascular complications, stroke without residual weakness, and obstructive sleep apnea who was admitted to the hospital with a three-day history of severe headache. An initial CT scan of the brain showed no evidence of subarachnoid hemorrhage. However, an MRI scan of the brain revealed generalized volume loss.

On physical examination, the patient had mild bilateral pedal edema, and we were unable to evaluate jugular venous pulsations due to a thick short neck. Neurological examination was unremarkable, and fundoscopic examination did not reveal any papilledema. Electrocardiogram showed low voltage sinus rhythm. Chest x-ray showed mild left pleural effusion and cardiomegaly. An echocardiogram revealed a large pericardial effusion with features of tamponade.

Diagnostic Studies:
The patient underwent emergent pericardial drainage, and the fluid analysis revealed it as a hemorrhagic pericardial effusion. The septic screen was negative, and vasculitis screening with ANA and ANCA was also negative. A PET CT scan did not detect any malignant focus. An MRI scan of the heart showed basal septal mid-wall myocardial enhancement of non-ischemic pattern, likely due to myocarditis or cardiomyopathy.

Diagnosis:
After ruling out secondary causes of hemorrhagic pericardial effusion, such as malignancy, autoimmune diseases, and TB, our patient was labeled as idiopathic myocarditis leading to chronic pericardial effusion based on MRI scan of the heart.

Management:
The patient's headache was relieved after pericardiocentesis, and his blood pressure stabilized after resuming his home antihypertensive medications. The patient was observed in the hospital for ten days with regular echocardiogram studies. He was asymptomatic and discharged with regular follow-up in the cardiology clinic. The cardiologist outpatient follow-ups with repeated echocardiogram studies for a further five months did not show any fluid reaccumulation. The patient was followed for one year after discharge where he remained clinically stable.

Discharge Diagnosis:
Idiopathic myocarditis leading to chronic pericardial effusion.

Follow-up:
The patient will have regular follow-up in the cardiology clinic to monitor the progress of the patient's condition.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [Name]
Age: 56
Gender: Male
Admission Date: [Date]
Discharge Date: [Date]
Length of Stay: [Number] days

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to the hospital with severe headache and intermitting nausea. Imaging-studies showed a tumor in the posterior horn of the left lateral ventricle. A first surgical extirpation of the tumor was performed in 2002 at an external hospital. During postoperative reconvalescence, the patient suffered from several conditions including heparin-induced thrombocytopenia II, pulmonary embolism, deep venous thrombosis, and basal ganglion infarction with consecutive right-sided hemiparesis.

Two years after the meningioma extirpation, the patient suffered from recurring headaches, dizziness, and ataxia. A cerebral CT-scan showed hydrocephalus, for which ventriculoperitoneal shunting was performed in 2004. The patient recovered well after the procedure. In 2005, the patient was diagnosed with a hemorrhaged tumor located in the caudal section of the aqueduct and dorsolaterally to the fourth ventricle. The tumor was removed, and the pathological examination revealed a recurrently hemorrhaged cavernoma with regressive transformations.

In 2008, recurrence of the tumor in the posterior horn of the left lateral ventricle was discovered on MRI scans at the same location as the tumor before (2002). Additionally, another tumor located in the quadrigeminal lamina was detected. In 2009, surgical resection of the tumor in the left lateral ventricle was performed. The pathological examination confirmed the diagnosis of a collision tumor consisting of components of a meningioma and a cavernoma.

Postoperative MRI showed no residual tumor, and the tumor in the quadrigeminal lamina seemed to be regressing. No adjuvant treatment was recommended due to the benign characteristics of both tumor entities and the spontaneous regression of the tumor in the quadrigeminal lamina. The patient was discharged in a stable condition.

Diagnoses:
1. Recurrent atypical meningioma WHO II°
2. Recurrently hemorrhaged cavernoma with regressive transformations
3. Hydrocephalus

Procedures:
1. Ventriculoperitoneal shunting
2. Surgical extirpation of tumor, posterior horn of the left lateral ventricle
3. Surgical resection of collision tumor

Condition on Discharge:
The patient was discharged in a stable condition without any evidence of tumor recurrence in the MRI follow-up.

Follow-Up Plan:
The patient is advised to attend regular MRI follow-ups to monitor any potential tumor recurrence and report any new symptoms to the healthcare provider immediately.

Patient Name: __________     Admission Date: __________     Discharge Date: __________ 

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 34-year-old female at 24 gestational weeks, was admitted to our emergency service with complaints of vomiting, abdominal pain, weakness, and dyspnea. Upon physical examination, the patient showed reduced breath sounds on the left side of the chest and diffuse abdominal tenderness. Laboratory tests revealed several abnormalities including an elevated white cell count, low hemoglobin levels and a low platelet count. A chest X-ray showed free air under the left hemidiaphragm, and a left lateral decubitus abdominal radiograph displayed that the free air moved to the right side. 

During the attempted surgical intervention, an emergency obstetric USG examination was performed which showed the intrauterine fetal demise. The patient was operated on under emergency conditions. A 14 × 8 cm defect was detected in the posterior diaphragm and the spleen was significantly damaged. A large hernia sac was detected in the diaphragmatic cavity. The defect in the posterior diaphragm was closed by primary repair following the insertion of a gastrostomy tube. After the improvement of hemodynamics and oxygen saturation of the patient, a dead fetus was manually delivered via caesarian section and a total gastrectomy followed by Roux-en-Y anastomosis was performed. 

On the 27th day of treatment, the patient died due to brain hypoxia caused by cardiopulmonary arrest. 

Diagnosis: 
The patient's presenting symptoms and pathology were suggestive of an abdominal and cardiothoracic catastrophe, resulting in the intrauterine fetal demise, posterior diaphragm hernia and necrosis of the stomach. 

Hospital Course Summary:
The patient's hospital course was marked by a series of complications from the presenting pathology. Despite surgical intervention the patient developed the intrauterine fetal demise and complications from posterior diaphragm hernia, resulting in the need for a cesarean delivery and complicated surgery to repair multiple organ damage. Ultimately, the patient succumbed to brain hypoxia caused by cardiopulmonary arrest.

Hospital Course:

The patient, a 50-year-old male with a history of a pruritic plaque on his left hand, was admitted to the dermatology department for assessment. The plaque started as a small, erythematous papule that gradually increased in size over several months and became a larger, scaly plaque. The patient also experienced pruritus and a tingling sensation. Topical steroid treatment provided temporary relief; however, the plaque did not resolve. A biopsy was performed due to the unusual morphology of the plaque, revealing spongiotic dermatitis compatible with nummular dermatitis. Further treatment with potent topical steroids provided only temporary flattening of the plaque.

Several months later, the patient returned with ulceration of the center of the plaque and subcutaneous nodules in a sporotrichoid pattern extending from his left fifth digit superiorly to his elbow. Culturing a biopsy confirmed fish-tank granuloma, caused by M. marinum. The patient reported a history of having a salt-water fish tank and had lost several fish weeks after the onset of symptoms, although there was no necropsy.

Antimicrobial susceptibility testing showed sensitivity to amikacin, clarithromycin, doxycycline, ethambutol, moxifloxacin, rifabutin and rifampin, and resistance to ciprofloxacin and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. Treatment with doxycycline and azithromycin provided no clinical improvement after 3 months of continuous therapy. Treatment was switched to moxifloxacin and clarithromycin, and the patient applied local heat to the affected skin for several hours per day using a reusable heat pack. The patient was referred to a plastic surgeon for excision of the subcutaneous nodules on his left hand, wrist, and arm. After 3 months of the new antibiotic regime and excision of the nodules, the patient's ulcerated plaque healed, and the excised subcutaneous nodules did not recur. 

The patient remained in hospital for 17 months before clinical resolution of the disease was confirmed. The patient was discharged following confirmation of resolution of the disease with no further medical follow-up required.

Discharge Summary

Discharge Date: [Redacted]

Diagnosis:

Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA)

Hospital Course:

A 57-year-old Caucasian male was admitted to the hospital with symptoms including dry cough, haemoptysis, fever, night sweats, arthralgia, and recurrent conjunctivitis. Laboratory tests revealed mild anaemia and elevated white blood cell and platelet counts. CT scans showed multiple small pulmonary nodules and lymphadenopathy. Biopsy of the right lung nodule confirmed GPA, which was supported by serological data including ANCA immunofluorescence assay and Elisa anti-proteinase-3 anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies.

The patient was treated with steroids and cyclophosphamide as per EUVAS recommendation. His condition improved initially, but after six months of treatment, the patient's clinical state deteriorated. CT scans revealed progression of pulmonary infiltrations, and LFT and CRP levels had elevated.

Further screening for hepatic diseases was performed, and active viral infections and antibodies against smooth muscle and other antigens were excluded. Cyclophosphamide therapy was continued for another three months to a total dose of CYC 13 g, and finally, the patient went into clinical remission. Azathioprine was started for remission maintenance.

After another four months of treatment with steroids and azathioprine, the patient was hospitalised due to cough, haemoptysis, hoarseness, and fever. CT of lung revealed new infiltrations typical for GPA. The patient was then given pulses of cyclophosphamide every two weeks. Due to persistent symptoms of active disease, it was decided to change treatment to rituximab.

Outcome:

After six months of therapy with rituximab, the patient achieved complete remission (BVAS=0). The patient's LFT was normalised, and he is currently treated with azathioprine and prednisone for remission maintenance. Twelve months after therapy, the patient is still in clinical remission, and his laboratory tests are normal.

Discharge Medications:

Azathioprine, prednisone.

Follow-up:

The patient is advised to continue taking azathioprine and prednisone to maintain remission. The patient should have regular follow-up visits with the treating physician to monitor his condition and ensure compliance with the medication regimen.

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted to KKESH with a complaint of poor vision in the right eye that was detected 3 years ago.

Medical History:

The patient has no prior history of eye problems. She has negative consanguinity and no family history of ocular diseases. The patient has no history of blood loss, ocular inflammations, or ocular trauma. She has not undergone any previous ocular surgeries.

Diagnostic Assessment:

At the initial visit, the patient's best-corrected visual acuity was 20/400 in the right eye and 20/20 in the left eye, with normal intraocular pressure in both eyes. The examination revealed a very early posterior subcapsular cataract in the right eye and intraretinal pigment migration in the midperiphery, waxy disc pallor, and vessel attenuation. The fundus autofluorescence (FAF) imaging showed a decrease in the AF signal in the midperiphery of the right eye. Furthermore, an abnormal parafoveal ring or curvilinear arc of increased AF was observed. The retinal structure was analyzed qualitatively with transfoveal horizontal spectral domain optical coherence tomography scans (OCT). The OCT of the right eye showed FTMH, while the left eye appeared normal. Full-field electroretinography (ffERG) was also performed, and the responses were markedly reduced in the right eye. On the other hand, the ffERG of the left eye was normal.

Diagnosis:

Based on the diagnostic assessment, the patient was diagnosed with URP.

Treatment:

Surgery was recommended, and the patient underwent right 23-gauge pars plana vitrectomy (PPV) with internal limiting membrane (ILM) peeling and gas tamponade. The surgery went uneventful, and the patient was advised to posture face down for 5 days (12 h/day). One week postoperatively, the FTMH was closed. At the last follow-up, 6 months postoperatively, the hole remained closed, and visual acuity (VA) remained at the level of 20/400.

Follow-up Care:

The patient was discharged with instructions to continue follow-up care with her ophthalmologist. She was advised to attend regular checkups to monitor her eyesight and report any changes in vision immediately.  

Discharge Plan:

The patient was discharged in stable condition with instructions to follow the prescribed medication regimen and attend all necessary follow-up appointments as scheduled. The patient was educated on the importance of lifestyle modifications such as proper nutrition, regular exercise, and avoiding smoking to prevent any potential eye problems in the future. The patient was advised to maintain proper eye care hygiene and promptly report any adverse reactions or side effects to her healthcare provider to ensure timely intervention.

The patient, a 70-year-old female with congestive heart failure, atrial fibrillation, and end-stage renal disease, was admitted to the general surgery clinic with a radiographic finding of a CCF. She reported right upper back pain that was unrelated to meals in the clinic. She had no abdominal tenderness and her liver function tests were within normal limits.

The patient was hospitalized for surgical repair of the CCF with cholecystectomy, using the da Vinci Xi robotic system. The evaluation revealed an inflammatory connection between the gallbladder fundus and the proximal transverse colon, which was successfully separated. The gallbladder was dissected in a top-down fashion and a critical view of safety was obtained. Locking robotic clips were applied to the cystic duct and cystic artery, and the structures were transected. The colotomy was closed in a two-layer running fashion.

Outcome:

The patient recovered uneventfully and was discharged on the second postoperative day. Histopathological examination of the specimen revealed no evidence of malignancy, and the patient was seen in the clinic without postoperative complaints.

The patient is a 38-year-old woman who presented with a six-month history of progressive exertional dyspnea and new onset of syncopal episodes. Transthoracic echocardiography reveals an anomalous vascular structure origin from circumflex artery and draining to the main pulmonary artery with significant left to right shunt, mild dilatation of right heart chambers and 60% ejection fraction. Magnetic resonance imaging and coronary angiography confirms the presence of a coronary artery fistula. The pulmonary to systemic flow ratio was calculated as 1.8 to 1. Left anterior mini-thoracotomy was performed, the fistulous tracts were identified, and the fistula on the pulmonary artery side was obliterated with multiple pledgeted 5-0 polypropylene sutures. Transesophageal echocardiography confirmed a successful closure of the fistula, lack of residual shunt and lack of wall motion abnormalities. Electrocardiogram did not show any signs of ischemia. The patient was extubated one hour after completion of the procedure and discharged on the second postoperative day. At 6 and 12 months follow-up, the patient remained free of any cardiovascular symptoms, while echocardiography showed no residual flow. An excellent cosmetic result was achieved.

A 38-year-old female presented with dyspnea and syncopal episodes, and murmur on auscultation. The patient's medical examination revealed coronary artery fistula with significant left to right shunt and mild dilatation of the right heart chambers. The patient underwent surgical correction by left anterior mini-thoracotomy, and successful obliteration of the fistulous tracts was noted under transesophageal echocardiography with no residual shunt or wall motion abnormalities seen. The patient remained symptom-free at the six and twelve months follow-up visits, with no residual flow detected on echocardiography.@endsection

Discharge Summary:

Admission Date: [Date]
Discharge Date: [Date]
Patient Name: [Name]

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 36-year-old female, was admitted to the hospital after jumping from a four-foot high deck and experiencing extreme pain and inability to bear weight on the right limb. The patient had a positive Lachman test indicating a tear in the anterior cruciate ligament (ACL). Radiographs revealed a joint effusion and abnormalities in the patellar tendon morphology.

Diagnostic arthrogram confirmed a complete midsubstance ACL tear. An ipsilateral hamstring autograft was performed during ACL reconstruction. The patient's post-operative course was complicated by complex regional pain syndrome.

The patient had a delayed recovery and experienced stiffness, difficulty with walking, and had developed quadriceps muscle atrophy at a one-year follow-up. Physical therapy was instituted to help prevent postoperative fibrosis.

Given the patient's continued symptoms, close follow-up with an orthopedic surgeon is recommended.

The patient denied other gastrointestinal or genitourinary complaints, illicit drug use, and was not taking any medication. He referred to homosexual relations with a single partner for six years.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [redacted]
Sex: Male
Age: 50 years
Medical Record Number: [redacted]

Hospital Course:

The patient, a 50-year-old married male, was admitted with asymptomatic reddish raised lesions over the face, trunk, and extremities for 1 month with a history of anorexia, progressive weight loss, and mild abdominal pain. On examination, multiple erythematous to skin-colored papules and nodules were present on the face, ears, trunk, and extremities, with a single verrucous lesion over the nose. Hyperkeratotic nodules were present over the palms and soles. Both ulnar nerves were thickened and nontender. Sensations were intact. A differential diagnosis showed papulo-nodular lesions in secondary syphilis, cryptococcosis, histoplasmosis, and Hansen's disease, along with verruca vulgaris. However, routine blood investigations were normal.

Venereal Disease Research Laboratory and Treponema pallidum hemagglutination assay were negative. Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay for HIV 1 revealed a positive result. CD4 count was 11. Slit-skin smear showed a bacillary index (BI) of 5+. To confirm the diagnosis, skin biopsies from multiple sites were performed, and histopathology of all the specimens (papular, nodular, and verrucous) showed perivascular foamy macrophages with polymorphs extending up to the panniculus suggestive of lepromatous leprosy with erythema nodosum leprosum (ENL). Ziehl–Neelsen stain (Fite-Faraco modification) was positive for acid-fast bacilli (AFB) with BI of granuloma of 6+.

Abdominal ultrasonography revealed lymphadenopathy suggestive of abdominal tuberculosis. Mantoux test and sputum (AFB) were negative. Thus, a final diagnosis of lepromatous leprosy with ENL and abdominal tuberculosis in an HIV-positive patient was made.

The patient was started on antitubercular therapy (three daily tablets of a fixed-dose combination comprising isoniazid 75 mg, rifampicin 150 mg, ethambutol 275 mg, and pyrazinamide 400 mg). In addition, WHO-multiple drug therapy (multibacillary [MB]) consisting of daily dapsone 100 mg and clofazimine 50 mg along with thalidomide 100 mg BD and clofazimine 100 mg TDS (reactional dose) was prescribed. Liver function tests were monitored. ART consisting of daily TLE regimen (tenofovir 300 mg, lamivudine 300 mg, and efavirenz 600 mg) was started. Currently, the patient is under regular follow-up with gradual regression of lesions and no further ENL episodes over the past 3 months.

Discharge Diagnosis:

Leprosy with ENL and abdominal tuberculosis in an HIV-positive patient.

Discharge Plan:

The patient is under regular follow-up, and he will remain in close contact with his treating physician. Further follow-up appointments will be necessary to track his progress.

Discharge Summary

Patient Name: [redacted]
Date of Admission: February 2010
Date of Discharge: February 2011
Diagnosis: Aplastic Anemia (AA) (stage 3) and Epstein-Barr virus-associated Lymphoproliferative Disorder (EBV-LPD)

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted in February 2010 due to a bleeding tendency. A diagnosis of AA (stage 3) was made with severe hypocellular marrow without any dysplasia. After a bone marrow examination and chromosomal analysis, a whole-body CT scan was performed, which showed no abnormal findings. The patient had no related HLA-identical donor, so he was treated with immunosuppressive therapy in May 2010 consisting of methyl-predonisolone, CSP, and rabbit ATG according to the guideline for the diagnosis and management of AA of the British Society of Haematology. The lymphocyte count decreased to 0/μL, but it gradually increased after day +13, although it was maintained below 100/μL. There was no recorded infection, and he was discharged with a regulatory blood transfusion dependency. In August 2010, he developed severe anemia and needed frequent red blood cell transfusions. Moreover, the serum LDH increased gradually from a normal range. An occult blood test in stools was positive, and a colonoscopy was performed, which revealed multiple tumors of the ascending, transverse, and descending colons. Biopsy specimens of all colonic tumors showed the proliferation of atypical lymphocytes. Immunostaining revealed that the atypical lymphocytes were CD20+, CD79a+, CD3-, and CD5-. Immunocytochemistry studies showed that EBV encoded small RNAs (EBER) involving in situ hybridization were positive. PET/CT showed no lymphadenopathy other than the colonic tumors. On day +84, the EBV viral load was slightly increased to 140/106 WBC. He was diagnosed with EBV-LPD and received only CSP as immunosuppressive therapy at day +84. The serum concentration of CSP was 333 ng/mL on day +90. CSP administration was stopped on day +97, and after cessation, his symptoms gradually improved, and the serum LDH level decreased to the normal range. His lymphocyte counts gradually increased to 300/μL, and one month after the cessation of CSP, he underwent colonoscopy again, which showed regression of the tumors. Two months after the cessation of CSP, the EBV viral load was below the detectable level. In February 2011, he had achieved a partial hematological response and was independent of blood transfusion. At this moment, 2 years later, no EBV-LPD occurred.

Hospital Discharge:
The patient was discharged in February 2011 with partial hematological response and independence of blood transfusion. No further EBV-LPD occurred.

Discharge Summary:
Patient: 39-year-old female

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to the hospital with complaints of foreign-body sensation and epiphora in her left eye. A slit-lamp examination revealed multiple milky-white soft masses on the corneal surface of her left eye. A slight opacity was suspected in the anterior stroma under the slit-lamp examination. Upon investigation, these masses were classified as having a gelatinous dystrophy-like appearance and were located at the cilia-attached region. An OCT scan revealed a large mass under the thinned epithelial layer with no destruction on Bowman’s layer throughout the region. The fellow cornea exhibited a linear subepithelial opacity that was not stained by fluorescein under a slit-lamp examination, and an OCT scan revealed a high-density spot in Bowman’s layer, which was coincident with the cilia-attached region and linear line observed under slit-lamp examination.

Treatment:
To treat the foreign-body sensation, the patient underwent lamellar keratoplasty. The corneal tissues were excised, and the excised specimens were frozen and cut into sections. These sections were incubated with antilactoferrin antibody and fixed with Congo red. Histological analysis revealed that the eosinophilic material was positively stained with Congo red showing apple-green birefringence under polarized light. The material was also positive when using the antilactoferrin antibody, with this area matching the Congo red-positive region.

Outcome:
Postoperative recovery was smooth, and there was no recurrence of amyloid deposition. Ten months after the operation, the corrected visual acuity of the patient’s left eye was 20/20. Epilation of the cilia is performed regularly.

Medical History: Choroidal melanoma diagnosed in 1989, recurrence in 2011

Hospital Course: Admitted due to grade 2 thrombocytopenia after receiving third-line treatment with ipilimumab for melanoma recurrence. PET-CT showed partial response in liver and splenomegaly. Bone marrow biopsy identified hemophagocytosis with high levels of ferritin, hypertriglyceridemia, low fibrinogen, and anemia. Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HPS) was confirmed as an immune-mediated adverse effect of ipilimumab and other causes were ruled out. Despite corticosteroid treatment, no improvement was observed, prompting initiation of tocilizumab treatment. IL-2 value was 1734 U/mL (normal range: 158-623 U/mL). After four doses of tocilizumab, there was clinical and analytical improvement. A new bone marrow biopsy showed no signs of hemophagocytosis, and PET-CT showed absence of splenic metabolic uptake.

Diagnosis: Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis secondary to immunotherapy with ipilimumab

Management and Treatment: Methylprednisolone treatment was started after ipilimumab was interrupted due to hematological toxicity. However, tocilizumab treatment was initiated when no improvement was observed with corticosteroid treatment. Tocilizumab was administered at a dose of 8 mg/kg every eight hours, for a total of four doses.

Follow-Up: Patient was discharged from the hospital and recommended to continue follow-up appointments with hematology and medical oncology departments.

Complications: None noted.

Overall Condition: Stable at the time of discharge.

Hospital Course Summary:

Admitted to the emergency department (ED) with altered mental status, a 66-year-old man with hypertension and high cholesterol was found to have nystagmus, dysarthria, discoordination, and ataxia. While in the ED, the patient's condition worsened and concerned about a posterior circulation stroke, a head computed tomography angiogram was obtained, which was negative for any abnormality. An electrocardiogram showed a normal sinus rhythm. The patient was evaluated by the neurology consultant team, who determined the patient had a National Institute of Health Stroke Scale of 11, and tissue plasminogen activator was administered for thrombolysis. He was subsequently intubated for airway protection and admitted to the ICU.

While intubated in the ICU, the patient developed status epilepticus and was treated with multiple doses of benzodiazepine and phenytoin, resulting in cessation of seizure activity. A comprehensive urine drug screen by gas chromatography and mass spectrometry was positive for clozapine and clozapine metabolites, in addition to caffeine and bupropion, a home medication. It was concluded that the patient must have accidently ingested the family member's clozapine, as the patient's blood work showed no evidence of abuse or other medications. The patient had never been prescribed clozapine but managed the family member's medication and often took their respective medications at the same time. The patient was extubated on hospital day three and discharged with a normal neurologic exam and no further seizure activity on hospital day five.

In summary, the patient presented with altered mental status and exhibited symptoms of nystagmus, dysarthria, discoordination, and ataxia. Concerned about a potential stroke, a head CT angiogram was performed, and the patient was evaluated by the neurology team. After admission to the ICU, the patient developed status epilepticus, and a comprehensive urine drug screen was performed, which identified the presence of clozapine that the patient had entered. Ultimately, the patient was extubated and, after determining there was no further seizure activity, discharged with normal neurologic exam results.

HOSPITAL COURSE SUMMARY:

Admission Date: ________________ Discharge Date: ________________

Patient Name: ________________ Age: 67 Sex: Female

HOSPITAL COURSE:

The patient was admitted to the hospital due to exertional dyspnea and significant nausea. Upon EMS arrival, the patient had an oxygen saturation of less than 90% on room air, and so was given oxygen supplementation with a nonrebreather. The patient's medical history was remarkable for well-controlled asthma, hypertension, and diabetes. She had no prior history of structural heart disease.

A chest X-ray revealed bilateral predominantly peripherally distributed patchy opacities. The patient's laboratory investigation showed elevations in LDH, CK, and inflammatory markers, but with a normal high-sensitivity troponin T. The polymerase chain reaction test for SARS-CoV2 was positive.

The patient was admitted to the inpatient non-ICU unit and was primarily managed with supportive care. Her oxygen therapy requirement varied from 2-3 L/min during the day and 4-6 L/min of O2 overnight along with nocturnal proning. The patient did not require treatment with investigational pharmacotherapy.

On the fourth day of her hospitalization, the patient had a desaturation to less than 85% oxygen while ambulating to the restroom. The patient was rapidly uptitrated of supplemental oxygen via facemask and transferred to the ICU for closer monitoring and consideration of mechanical ventilation. The patient was nonemergently intubated to avoid further decompensation due to respiratory decompensation. Therefore, the patient required sedation and developed mild hypotension requiring a low dose of norepinephrine support. Her pressor requirement remained unchanged, and her respiratory status was stable on minimal ventilation settings.

A routine EKG was performed on the night of the patient's respiratory decompensation. The EKG showed new repolarization abnormalities without any clinical decompensation or change in her ventilatory or pressor support requirements. Over the following 48 hours, the serial EKGs showed continued persistence of T wave inversions and progressive prolongation in the QT interval. Elevation of high-sensitivity troponin levels were detected at the time of the patient's initial respiratory decompensation and again in the context of the EKG finding, showing biomarker evidence of cardiac injury, which quickly resolved. Echocardiogram showed preserved left ventricular ejection fraction of 61% but with new apical hypokinesis.

The patient's clinical decompensation was believed to be secondary to respiratory decompensation due to COVID-19. Additionally, the subsequent structural and electrical cardiac abnormalities resulted from stress-induced cardiomyopathy. The differential diagnosis also considered coronary ischemia, myocarditis due to viral infection, drug-related QT prolongation, and repolarization changes related to metabolic disarray.

The patient was gradually weaned from ventilator and pressor support over the subsequent 2 weeks. She was managed conservatively without any specific antiviral medications, including hydroxychloroquine. The patient was started on metoprolol and lisinopril for hypertension. Her EKG abnormalities gradually resolved with progressive normalization of her QT interval.

DISCHARGE INSTRUCTIONS:

The patient is discharged for rehabilitation and will follow up with a plan for an outpatient reassessment of her LV function. On discharge, the patient is advised to strictly follow the recommendations of our healthcare providers, including medication management and regular follow-up care.   Overall, the patient's condition has improved, and it is recommended the patient return if they have any concerns or worsening symptoms.

A 30-year-old male patient was admitted to our facility with a solitary palpable mass in his right scrotal sac that appeared 3 months earlier. He had no history of trauma or medical disease. Summary:

The patient underwent an excision for a well-circumscribed, ovoid mass that measured 5.0×3.5×2.0 cm. The cut surface of the mass was yellowish-tan, rubbery, and trabeculated, without necrosis or hemorrhage. Microscopically, the mass was composed of bland spindle cells with haphazardly arranged collagen fibers and numerous mast cells. Some areas showed edematous stroma with hypocellularity. Numerous mast cells were scattered in the stroma. There was no cellular atypia or mitotic activity. Individual adipocytes and adipose tissue were admixed with the spindle cells, which showed immunopositivity for desmin and CD34 and negativity for smooth muscle actin, S-100 protein, and human melanoma black 45. No further follow-up is required.

Hospital Course:
This 7-month-old boy was admitted to our hospital for treatment of respiratory syncytial viral pneumonia, with a history of tracheoesophageal fistula and esophageal atresia surgery performed at 1 day of age. The patient showed recurrent cough and sputum, and was afebrile. The chest radiograph showed increased peribronchial infiltration and air bronchogram. Due to the risk of aspiration pneumonia, oral feeding was discontinued and the patient was given parenteral nutrition via the peripheral venous route.

Extravasation Event:
On day 6 of admission, while the patient was receiving total parenteral nutrition, a 24-gauge intravenous catheter was newly inserted into the dorsal cephalic vein at the dorsum of the patient's right hand. The patient showed signs of irritability, and the obstruction alarm of the infusion pump was triggered. Without any alarm sign, approximately 9 hours after the repositioning of the intravenous catheter, the patient's right hand and arm appeared severely swollen, and capillary refill was absent. There were several blisters observed under the catheter, and an emergency fasciotomy was performed under the suspicion of compartment syndrome.

Treatment and Care:
The patient received orthopedic surgery and fascia suturing, followed by irrigation of the area several times with saline solution. Delayed primary skin closure was performed 8 days after the fasciotomy. A skin graft was scheduled for treatment of the skin necrosis after debriding the necrotic tissue with a moist dressing. Rehabilitation treatment consisting of wrist articulation exercises was started due to the high chance of wrist joint contracture. Skin graft surgery was delayed due to pneumonia, which was diagnosed during the patient's regular wound dressing and rehabilitation treatment. It was performed 4 months after the extravasation event. At the time of this report, skin engraftment had been successfully completed, and the patient was receiving continued rehabilitation treatment.

Discharge Summary:

Patient: 7-year-old female

Admission Dates: [Date of admission] to [Date of discharge]

Diagnosis/Problem: IgG4-related sclerosing mesenteritis

Hospital Course:

The patient, a 7-year-old female, was admitted with a one month history of colicky abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhea, and fever. After being diagnosed with abdominal tuberculosis three years prior and undergoing treatment for 9 months with no improvement, she was readmitted with similar symptoms and signs. She was eventually diagnosed with Crohn's disease based on a computed tomography (CT) scan, but showed no improvement with steroid, azathioprine, and infliximab. Family history was noncontributory for gastrointestinal or autoimmune diseases and there was no history of night sweat, skin rash, joint pain, or recent travel. On admission to the hospital, the physical examination showed evidence of growth retardation. Laboratory findings revealed normal hemoglobin, white blood cell count, and platelet count, and normal electrolytes, coagulation study, and liver function test results. C-reactive protein (CRP) was elevated and serum albumin was low. Her serums IgG1, IgG2, and IgG3 levels were normal, but serum IgG4 was elevated. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy and colonoscopy showed normal mucosa and no ulcerations. Abdominal CT scan revealed diffuse lymphadenopathy and significant fat stranding and inflammation in mesentery of the terminal ileum.

She underwent exploratory laparotomy for a strong suspicion of lymphoma based on CT scan abnormalities. The operative findings showed extensive intraperitoneal adhesions, mesenteric lymphodenopathy, and inflamed omentum. Histopathological biopsies from lymph nodes and the peritoneal membrane revealed extensive perinodal fibrosis, focal dense lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate, and prominent lymphoid follicular hyperplasia in lymph nodes. Immunohistochemistry using antibodies to IgG and IgG4 showed that the plasma cells were predominantly of IgG4 phenotype. Diagnosis of IgG4-related sclerosing mesenteritis was made and the child was treated with colchicine, esomeprazole, prednisolone, and azathioprine.

At 6 months follow-up from the onset of treatment, she was completely asymptomatic, mesenteric mass was reduced, and her laboratory investigations remained normal. She developed pericardial effusion which responds to high dose of prednisolone. Discharge Summary

Patient Name: [REDACTED]

Date of Discharge: [REDACTED] 

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 78-year-old male, was admitted to the emergency room with complaints of dry cough, fever and malaise persisting for 1 month. He was previously treated with amoxicillin with no improvement. His medical history included diabetes and arterial blood hypertension, for which he was on metformin and amlodipine for 7 years. The patient presented with mildly lethargic orientation, febrile with mild tachycardia, hypoxemia, and crackles in the mid- and lower-lung fields on physical examination. Laboratory tests revealed elevated WBC counts, NLR, ESR, and CRP. The chest radiograph showed diffuse bilateral interstitial infiltrates. The HRCT showed diffuse interstitial lung involvement with a ground glass pattern. Blood and sputum cultures were negative for bacteria, urine antigen tests for Legionella pneumonia and Streptococcus pneumoniae were negative. Serum immunology tests for autoimmune diseases such as antinuclear antibodies, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies and anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibodies were all negative. A bronchoscopy was then performed, BAL and TBLB were negative for malignancy, bacteria, nocardia, fungi, and mycobacteria. BAL increased cellularity and had a mixed cellularity pattern. In view of the above findings, a diagnosis of Cryptogenic Organizing Pneumonia (COP) was considered. Treatment with antibiotics was ceased, and the patient was started on prednisone 20mg daily. The patient showed immediate improvement, blood inflammatory markers decreased, and he was discharged after 5 days on prednisone. He was advised to taper off corticosteroids for a total duration of treatment of 6-12 months.

Medical Condition:
Cryptogenic Organizing Pneumonia (COP)

Treatment:
Prednisone 20mg daily

Follow-up:
The patient has had no recurrence of symptoms at follow-up visits after complete clinical and radiological resolution of his condition.

The patient, a 38-year-old male, was admitted to our hospital with complaints of fever and painful swelling in the right proximal leg. He had a history of travel to Malaysia and was suspected to have tuberculosis of the abdomen in a previous hospital, where he was started on antitubercular drugs. He also had an ongoing anorexia with weight loss. On presentation to our hospital, he was in septic shock and was diagnosed with acute osteomyelitis of the right proximal tibia with septic arthritis of the knee joint. He underwent arthrotomy and was found to have a Gram-negative, safety pin-shaped bacteria infection suggestive of B. pseudomallei. He was initiated on six weeks of ceftazidime and levofloxacin, followed by oral eradication therapy with cotrimoxazole and doxycycline for six months. He completed the treatment course without any adverse drug reactions.

Discharge Summary

Patient: 22-year-old male

Hospital Course:
The patient presented with bilateral muscular atrophy and tremor of the distal upper extremities with insidious onset 5 years ago. Cold exposure worsened the symptomatology. Clinical examination revealed symmetrical muscular atrophy of the hands and forearms and reduced muscular strength during flexion, extension, and abduction of the fingers and flexion, extension of the wrist, as well as reduced tendon reflexes from the affected neurotomes. Electroneurophysiology and electromyography showed signs of chronic motor neuron lesion, bilaterally. Magnetic resonance images (MRI) acquired in neutral position showed loss of cervical lordosis and focal cord atrophy at C5-C6 level. MRI acquired in flexion revealed widening of the posterior epidural space. Postcontrast images showed uniform enhancement of the epidural space. The enhancement was reduced in the neutral position. After considering all the findings, the diagnosis of HD was made, and the patient was treated conservatively.

Diagnosis:
Hirayama Disease (HD)

Summary:
The patient's symptoms were consistent with HD, and was diagnosed based on the MRI findings in neck flexion. The patient was treated conservatively and is being discharged at this time. Further monitoring and follow-up are recommended.

Patient: 53-year-old male, professional chef

Admission Date: January 2017

Hospital Course:

The patient, a 53-year-old male professional chef, was admitted due to a severe exacerbation of atopic dermatitis (AD) with involvement of the face, neckline, trunk, and forearms. The patient's medical history was positive for allergic rhino-conjunctivitis and the allergological work-up found the patient to be positive for pollens, foods, and latex. The patient was prescribed oral steroids and anti-histamines, but these did not result in any improvement. Additionally, the patient experienced episodes of diarrhea and frequent severe exacerbations due to exposure to cooking vapors.

The patient followed a pseudo-allergen-free diet and exclusion of grains and tomatoes for six months. A three-day treatment with 6-methyl prednisolone i.v. was administered, which was progressively tapered over the course of three weeks. However, a rapid relapse of the skin legions and severe pruritus was observed.

Treatment with Cyclosporine A (CoA) was started but after three months, the patient saw no significant improvement. An off-label treatment with Omalizumab was proposed and initiated, resulting in clinical improvement after just about two months of treatment as confirmed by a SCORAD of 1 and a clear improvement of quality of life. After one year of Omalizumab treatment, the patient maintains good control for both skin and gastrointestinal symptoms.

Discharge Recommendations:

The patient is advised to implement strict environmental, hygiene, and diet restrictions based on the test results. The patient is discharged from the hospital and may return to work as a chef without complications and eat grains again with no gastrointestinal problems or relapse of dermatitis. The patient should continue reducing steroid doses in anticipation of complete suspension and continue taking CoA at a maintenance dose of 1 mg/kg/day. Follow-up appointments should be scheduled as needed to monitor the patient's condition.

Patient Information:
Name: [Patient name]
Age: 55 years
Gender: Male

Hospital Course Summary:
The patient was referred to our hospital with persistent per urethral bleeding around an 18 French Foley catheter, three days following a VIU procedure for treating a 1-cm long mid-bulbar stricture. The patient had undergone a VIU procedure 10 years earlier. The patient reported a drop in hemoglobin levels from 12 gm% to 4 gm%. The patient's hematological and biochemical parameters, including the coagulation profile, were normal. Ultrasound revealed a normal upper tract, and urethrocystoscopy revealed mucosal edema and a spurter at the 12 o'clock position. Fulguration with electrocautery was performed, and complete hemostasis was achieved. However, the bleeding recurred after 24 hours and did not respond to local compression. Hence the patient was considered for selective internal pudendal artery angiography, which revealed extravasation from the bulbourethral artery at the distal end of the internal pudendal artery.

A medium split-thickness skin graft was performed on the wound, which healed without complications.

A consultation was requested with vascular and plastic surgery, who recommended wound monitoring and a skin graft to address the skin necrosis.

The patient was discharged improved after treatment of his toe discoloration and skin necrosis.

The patient was prescribed amlodipine besylate.

Follow-up:

The patient was advised to follow-up with his primary care physician for further management of his hypertension and any changes to his medication.

Patient Name: [Redacted]
