Date of Discharge: [Redacted]

Hospital Course:

The patient is a 19-year-old female who presented to the Emergency Department with left-sided facial swelling. She had cough, subjective fever, severe fatigue, and swelling of the gums of her left teeth prior to presentation. The gum swelling got worse, and she started having facial swelling. She underwent a COVID-19 test in the community prior to presentation but had not received the results at the time of presentation. The jaw swelling worsened and started draining pus despite taking amoxicillin prescribed by her dentist. She was admitted for further evaluation.

On exam, she was noted to have left face and neck swelling. Lungs were clear to auscultation bilaterally. She had no bruises, petechiae, or lymphadenopathy. The rest of her exam was unremarkable. A maxillofacial computed tomographic scan (CT) showed diffuse soft tissue edema throughout the left face without drainable fluid collection to suggest an abscess. Initial labs showed pancytopenia with a white blood cell count of 2.6 × 103 per microliter, an absolute neutrophil count of 1.8 × 103 per microliter, a hemoglobin of 2.7 grams per deciliter, and a platelet count of 30 × 103 per microliter. Other notable laboratory results were a total bilirubin level of 1.3 milligrams per deciliter, haptoglobin of 22 milligrams per deciliter, lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) of 2218 U per liter, reticulocyte count of 55.3 × 103 per microliter, prothrombin time of 20.3 seconds, international normalized ratio of 1.3, partial thromboplastin time of 15.5 seconds, and fibrinogen of 514 milligrams per deciliter. A direct Coombs test was negative. Parvovirus B19 IgG was positive with a titer of 7.4, but the IgM was negative. She received four units of packed red blood cells (pRBCs) and was started on broad-spectrum antibiotics.

The patient developed a fever with a maximum temperature of 38.5°C after admission. Her COVID-19 test result returned as positive. Since the initial labs were consistent with hemolysis in the context of pancytopenia, a peripheral smear was ordered as well as flow cytometry on peripheral blood and flow cytometry for PNH. A bone marrow aspiration and core biopsy were performed. A CT chest, abdomen, and pelvis did not reveal any adenopathy and was negative for pulmonary embolism.

Flow cytometry was positive for PNH. The peripheral blood smear showed leukopenia with absolute neutropenia and thrombocytopenia. The observed neutrophils and lymphocytes were mature without significant morphological abnormality. Schistocytes were not present. Bone marrow biopsy showed large areas of the marrow that were less than 10% cellular; however, focally, the marrow is 40–50% cellular with erythroid predominant trilineage hematopoiesis. Megakaryocytes were present but markedly decreased without any significant dysplasia. Few mature neutrophils were present. Blasts were not increased. Immunohistochemical stains performed with appropriate controls demonstrated numerous E-cadherin-positive erythroid precursors. There were rare CD34-positive blasts and few scattered CD3-positive T cells and CD20-positive B cells. Terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase (TdT) stain was negative. Bone marrow aspirate showed small hypocellular spicules with erythroid predominance. Some of these erythroid precursors were binucleated and had nuclear budding or irregular nuclear contours. Neutrophil precursors were present but infrequent. Blasts were not increased. A cytogenetics study revealed normal female karyotype (46XX). No mutations were detected by targeted next-generation sequencing.

The patient was treated with 2 doses of 600 milligrams of the C5 complement inhibitor eculizumab as inpatient with improvement in counts. She was seen in clinic after discharge, and she received 2700 mg of the longer acting C5 complement inhibitor ravulizumab a week after the last dose of eculizumab and a 3300 mg dose 2 weeks later. Her last blood counts showed a white blood cell count of 4 × 103 per microliter, absolute neutrophil count of 2.2 × 103 per microliter, hemoglobin level of 7.8 grams deciliter, and platelet count of 50 × 103 per microliter. Haptoglobin was 30, and LDH was normal. In the subsequent visits, the patient's pancytopenia persisted, and she was referred to a transplant center for evaluation.

Discharge Diagnosis:

The patient was diagnosed with pancytopenia in the context of parvovirus B19 infection and positive for PNH.

Disposition:

The patient was discharged with a referral to a transplant center for further evaluation.

Follow-up:

The patient was advised to follow up with a transplant center for further evaluation and management of her medical condition.

Admission: The patient presented with a 2-month history of right upper abdominal pain and multiple nodules over her face and body. She had previously undergone surgical treatment for adrenal tumors and was diagnosed with NF-1.

The abdominal CT indicated multiple masses in the liver and duodenum and diffuse intrahepatic duct dilatation. Treatment: The patient underwent right hepatectomy and duodenal wedge resection.

The resected hepatic mass showed multifocal stromal invasion and a tubulopapillary mucin component, suggesting invasive adenocarcinoma with high-grade dysplasia. The patient's diagnosis was determined to be invasive papillary neoplasm of the bile duct (IPNB) arising from high-grade dysplasia.

Outcome: The patient was discharged without any postoperative complications and remained stable for 8 months after surgery. Follow-up CT scans showed no recurrence during a regular 3-month follow-up period.

Discharge Diagnosis: Invasive papillary neoplasm of the bile duct (IPNB) arising from high-grade dysplasia.

Follow-up: The patient was recommended to have regular follow-up visits with her primary care physician and oncologist.

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 40-year-old woman, was admitted to our clinic due to left back pain that lasted 2 months. Physical examination revealed no abnormalities. Laboratory tests showed slightly increased adrenaline and plasma renin activity (recumbent position) levels. Upon further examination by abdominal enhanced computed tomography (CT), the patient was found to have well-defined bilateral adrenal masses and was tentatively diagnosed as having primary adrenal malignancy. The patient underwent left adrenalectomy and ipsilateral nephrectomy, with postoperative pathology showing proliferating lymphocytes, plasma cells, and tissue cells. An immunohistochemical staining and gene rearrangement test resulted in a diagnosis of EBV-associated nasal type extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma. Subsequently, the patient underwent 18F-Fluoro-2-Deoxy-D-Glucose (18F-FDG) positron emission tomography (PET)/CT examination for staging, which showed heterogeneous FDG uptake in the left adrenal gland region, homogeneously increased FDG uptake in the right adrenal gland, and left thigh subcutaneous lesion. 

Discharge Summary:
The patient was diagnosed with EBV-associated nasal type extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma, resulting in left adrenalectomy and ipsilateral nephrectomy. The patient underwent 7 cycles of chemotherapy (GLIDE regimen) and autologous stem cell transplantation, and two subsequent follow-up FDG PET/CT scans within 1 year showed complete resolution with no abnormal FDG uptake in the initially involved sites after treatment. The patient was discharged with instructions for follow-up appointments and maintenance. The discharge summary serves as a comprehensive document outlining the patient's medical history, treatment, and prognosis.

Patient Name: [REDACTED] 

Date of Admission: [REDACTED] 

Date of Discharge: [REDACTED] 

Diagnosis: Juxtafacet cysts causing compression of the cauda equina nerve roots 

Hospital Course: 

The patient was admitted due to several weeks of a worsening back and left leg pain, and new urinary retention with overflow incontinence. Physical exam was notable for pain-limited weakness of the left leg in all muscle groups and decreased sensation to light touch from the anterolateral thigh down to the dorsum of the left foot and toe. Lumbar MRI scan demonstrated severe thecal sac stenosis at L3-L4 secondary to bilateral, left greater than right juxtafacet cysts causing compression of the cauda equina nerve roots. A non-contrast computed tomographic (CT) scan showed severe L3-L4 stenosis and lumbar flexion/extension films showed no instability. 

After discussion of various treatment options, the patient underwent direct removal of the JFCs with placement of the Coflex® device for dynamic stabilization to avoid a single-level instrumented fusion while attempting to minimize the risk of cyst recurrence. Surgery was performed three days after initial clinic presentation. Decompression of the thecal sac at L3-4 was accomplished via partial inferior L3 and superior L4 laminectomies and mesial facetectomies via a standard midline approach in the usual fashion. The juxtafacet cysts were seen bilaterally and completely excised using microsurgical techniques by the senior author. After decompression, a Coflex® (Paradigm Spine, LCC, New York, NY) implant was placed between the remaining L3 and L4 lamina and spinous processes and the tissues were closed in the usual fashion. Total estimated blood loss was approximately 35cc. 

Juxtafacet cysts were confirmed on pathology. Postoperatively, the patient had immediate improvement in his left leg pain and no complications. The patient was transferred to inpatient rehabilitation on post-operative day 1. At 1-year follow-up, the patient continues with complete resolution of his left leg pain and urinary symptoms.

Postoperatively, the patient had immediate improvement in his left leg pain and no complications. At 1-year follow-up, the patient continues with complete resolution of his left leg pain and urinary symptoms.

Hospital Course Summary:

History of Present Illness:
The patient, a previously healthy 3.5-year-old male, was admitted with complaints of weakness and pallor lasting for five days. The patient had a three-day history of diarrhea two weeks before the admission. A physical examination revealed jaundice, pallor, and splenomegaly. The initial laboratory investigation showed low hemoglobin levels, and polychromasia and spherocytes were observed in the peripheral blood film. The patient was diagnosed with the warm type of autoimmune hemolytic anemia (AIHA).

Hospital Course:
Erythrocyte transfusion was administered, followed by intravenous methylprednisolone. The patient showed an excellent hematological response to the treatment. Oral prednisolone was used for four weeks, followed by a slow taper during the next five months. The patient experienced a relapse after an upper respiratory infection, and prednisolone was restarted with a good hematological response. The dose of prednisolone was reduced, resulting in hematological deterioration. Azathioprine was initiated, but there was a slight hematological deterioration. Rituximab was initiated after informed written consent and given in four weekly doses. The patient showed a stable response two months after the initiation of rituximab. The DAT became negative 12 months later, and the patient remains disease-free without relapses, three years after the first presentation.

Discharge Summary:

Patient was diagnosed with annular alopecia areata (AA) based on clinical examination and histopathological findings. The patient presented with asymptomatic loss of hair in an annular pattern at multiple sites over the scalp for 2 months. Hair loss was more pronounced at the periphery compared to the center of the patch. The patient had no history of similar illness in family members and no history of drug intake or trauma.

On examination, there were multiple well-defined annular patches of non-scarring alopecia ranging in size from 2 cm x 3 cm to 4 cm x 4 cm present at the parietal and occipital region of the scalp. The area was smooth with no associated skin changes. Systemic examination was within normal limits. Potassium hydroxide (KOH) examination of hair showed no fungal elements, and fungal culture with Sabouraud's media at 4 weeks revealed no growth.

Histopathological examination from the hairless region showed a few vellus follicles in mid dermis with a sparse perifollicular lymphocytic infiltrate. The dermis and subcutis also showed several follicular stellae representing former follicular papillae. The total number of follicles was substantially reduced, with no terminal follicles.

The patient was treated with intralesional injections of trimacinolone acetonide (5mg/ml) every 4 weeks, with remarkable improvement in the lesions after 3 months (3 intralesional injections) of follow-up.

The patient was discharged with recommendations for follow-up care and to continue treatment with intralesional injections of trimacinolone acetonide. The patient was advised to schedule appointments with their healthcare provider every 4 weeks for follow-up care and to monitor for any signs of recurrent alopecia.

Medical History:
The patient is a 50-year-old female with a known case of retroviral disease but not on anti-retroviral therapy.

Admission:
The patient was admitted to the hospital with complaints of right flank pain and suprapubic pain for six months which worsened over the past 15 days with dysuria and increased frequency of micturition with nocturia and urgency. She had no hematuria, other lower urinary tract symptoms or fever. Clinical examination revealed suprapubic and right iliac fossa tenderness. She was anemic (Haemoglobin 7.6 g/dL) which was corrected with packed red blood cell transfusions. Her renal function test was normal.

Diagnosis:
Ultrasonogram (USG) of kidney ureter bladder (KUB) revealed 1.2 cm right upper pole renal calculus with 1.7 cm vesical calculus. Plain X-ray of KUB did not show any radio-opaque shadows. Computerized tomography (CT) scan of KUB revealed only bladder calculi.

Treatment:
Cystoscopy and ureteroscopy were performed, and biopsy was taken. Biopsy showed fragments of urothelial mucosa with focal areas of ulceration, and stroma showed dense infiltrate of plasma cells, lymphocytes, and eosinophils. The sections were negative for dysplasia, granulomas or malignancies. Urine routine examination and cytology did not reveal any amyloid crystals. Urine culture was also sterile. After transurethral resection of entire lesion, the patient went home without any major postoperative issues. 

Follow-Up:
The patient was called for follow-up imaging and cystoscopy after six months.

Summary: 
The patient was admitted to the hospital with complaints of right flank pain and suprapubic pain for six months which worsened over the past 15 days with dysuria and increased frequency of micturition with nocturia and urgency. The patient was diagnosed with bladder calculi and underwent cystoscopy and ureteroscopy with biopsy which showed bladder amyloidosis. The patient underwent transurethral resection of the entire lesion without any major postoperative issues. The patient was called for follow-up imaging and cystoscopy after six months.

Discharge Summary
Patient: 19-year-old female
Clinical Visit Date: [insert date]

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to the Department of Orthodontics and Dentofacial Orthopaedics with the chief complaint of forwardly positioned upper front teeth. On extra oral examination, it was observed that the patient had symmetric facial appearance, convex profile, and incompetent lips with Class II molar and canine relation bilaterally. An overjet of 7 mm and an overbite of 70% were noted. Cephalometric findings showed a hypodivergent growth pattern, skeletal Class II malocclusion with protruded maxilla and reduced mandibular length. Furthermore, orthopantomogram findings revealed erupting mandibular third molars. Based on the patient's diagnostic parameters and arch discrepancies, fixed orthodontic mechanotherapy with the extraction of all four first premolars was decided.

Treatment:
Maxillary and mandibular dentitions were bonded using slot brackets, and initial alignment was done with progressing 016 NiTi to 019 × 025 NiTi wires. Later, 019 × 025 stainless steel wires were continued for 1 month followed by the extraction of all four first premolars. Miniscrews were placed in the maxillary arch with respect to the maxillary second premolar and the maxillary molar for retraction of maxillary incisors. Concurrently, mandibular buccal segment protraction was performed using Class II elastics. Customized utility arch correction was done with 016 × 022 TMA wire for deep bite correction along with Class II mechanics. Final finishing and detailing were done with settling elastics. The total duration of treatment was 22 months.

Outcome:
The patient's final orthodontic treatment had satisfactory results with ideal overjet and overbite as well as achieving Class I canine and molar relation. The patient showed improvement in smile esthetics and an optimum soft tissue profile. Post-treatment records show that an adequate level of lip competence was achieved.

Follow-up:
The patient's long-term retention was planned to sustain the correction achieved in her orthodontic treatment. A long-term follow-up protocol was prescribed for monitoring of erupted mandibular third molars and maintenance of occlusion stability. The patient was scheduled for periodic evaluations to minimize the chances of relapse. 

Signed,

Discharge Summary:

Admitting Diagnosis: Altered Mental Status
Final Diagnosis: Pancreatic Cancer with Hypercalcemia, Encephalopathy and Cerebral Spinal Fluid (CSF) Pleocytosis

Hospital Course:

A 67-year-old, right-handed female patient was admitted to the emergency department presenting with altered mental status. Neurologic examination was very limited secondary to sedation. Per family, the patient had a 2-week history of malaise, generalized weakness, headache, incontinence, and eventually altered mental status. On examination, her vital signs included temperature: 98.3°F, pulse: 99/min, BP: 201/94 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation: 98% after intubation. Initial laboratory work demonstrated a normal complete blood count (CBC) and normal coagulation. Blood chemistry was notable for an elevated calcium of 14.5 mg/dL. Liver function tests demonstrated an elevated alkaline phosphatase (ALP) of 208 U/L; renal function laboratories were within normal limits. Cerebral spinal fluid (CSF) analysis showed a white blood cell count (WBC) of 91 with a lymphocyte value of 90, and a protein of 32. CSF testing for herpes simplex virus, coccidioidomycosis, cryptococcus, West Nile virus, and syphilis were all negative. Head computer tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance venography (MRV) were negative. Electroencephalography (EEG) repeatedly showed generalized slowing. On day 2, MRI fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) showed abnormal posterior subcortical signal density with bilateral thalamic pulvinar involvement.

During the hospital course, the patient was admitted to the ICU and underwent aggressive blood pressure management. Her blood pressure was brought down to 140/57 mm Hg over 4 days. Her mentation slowly improved over 1 week; she was extubated on day 8. Repeat blood work showed a normal chemistry with a calcium of 7.4 mg/dL. Her ALP had decreased to 125 U/L. Her brain was followed with serial MRIs. By day 10, her FLAIR abnormality had almost resolved. Repeat EEG showed delta activity. A repeat CSF analysis showed a WBC of 2 and a protein of 24. NMDA receptor antibody was negative both in serum and CSF. Prion study was negative with negative RT-QuIC and no 14-3-3 protein.

The patient was diagnosed with pancreatic cancer, requiring further management. The patient neurologically continued to improve to a close to baseline state. She was discharged home after a 20-day stay in the hospital.

Follow-up and Recommendations:

A 1-month postdischarge phone call revealed the patient had remained at her baseline mentation. Unfortunately, the patient eventually passed away from her pancreatic cancer 5 months later.

Recommendations include close monitoring of the patient's pancreatic cancer and management of hypercalcemia if it recurs. Additionally, neurological follow-up may be needed to monitor any residual deficits or progression of encephalopathy.

The patient was treated with steroid therapy, which was escalated to 500 mg intravenous methylprednisolone for one day. Discharge Summary:

Discharge Date: [REDACTED]

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted to the orthopedic unit for evaluation of a non-healing fracture of the distal shaft of the left humerus. The patient's medical history was unremarkable, and no history of trauma was reported. The patient was initially treated conservatively with a Plaster of Paris (POP) back slab which was then replaced by a POP full cast. However, the X-rays showed no callus formation, and serial X-rays showed delayed union, bone resorption, and generalized osteopenia. The patient was subsequently diagnosed with osteomyelitis and treated accordingly, but her symptoms did not improve. She was referred to our institution for further management.

During the admission, the patient's left upper limb was carefully examined, which revealed global decreased muscle strength and limited motion of the left forearm. The active movements in the affected limb were mildly painful and limited at the shoulder and elbow joint. Wrist movements including gripping were normal, and no neurologic deficits were found. X-rays showed marked disappearance of bone at the fracture site resulting in a gap of 2-3 cm with tapering of bone ends and generalized osteopenia. Subsequent workup including blood tests, bone scintigraphy, and MRI scans ruled out secondary causes of bone resorption and malignancy, respectively. Histopathologic evaluation confirmed Gorham-Stout Syndrome (GSS) of the left humerus.

Treatment:

The patient underwent a fibular graft for the reconstructive surgery of the left humerus, which is consistent with the present literature on suitable treatment of upper extremity GSS.

Follow-up:

The patient was discharged in stable condition with appropriate post-operative care instructions. She was advised to follow-up with the orthopedic surgeon regularly to monitor the healing progress. No new significant symptoms were reported. 

Diagnosis: Gorham-Stout Syndrome (GSS) of the left humerus 

Abbreviations:
X-rays - X-ray radiography 
POP - Plaster of Paris 
AP - Anteroposterior 
MDP - Methyl Diphosphonate 
MRI - Magnetic Resonance Imaging

The patient was not prescribed any medications at the time of discharge.

Community-acquired pneumonia complicated by acute respiratory distress syndrome, acute hypoxemic respiratory failure, new onset atrial fibrillation, and cardiac arrest.

Chronic lymphatic leukemia, arterial hypertension, multiple squamous cell carcinomas of the scalp, hyperglycemia, mildly elevated liver enzymes, coagulopathy, and mild macrocytic anemia.

Upon admission, the patient underwent thoracentesis and pericardiocentesis to relieve his pleural and pericardial effusions. Further diagnostic testing, including bone marrow biopsy and cytogenetic analysis, confirmed the diagnosis of Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML) with complex cytogenetics, including trisomy 8, trisomy 9, and trisomy 21, and positive for JAK2 V617F mutation.

The patient was treated with supportive measures, including oxygen therapy, and was started on chemotherapy for AML. Throughout his hospital course, the patient had ongoing management of his symptoms and was closely monitored by the healthcare team. Clinical examination revealed large tender swelling with a protruding lower lip. Intra-oral examination showed hard swelling of about 50 mm with displacement of teeth leading to malocclusion. Further imaging revealed an iso-dense large destructive cystic mass that was confirmed as a central giant cell tumor (CGCT) through a biopsy. 

The patient underwent a surgical intervention by the chief professor of our department. A unilocular cystic mass without liquid content was excised, and there was a rupture of the external wall of the mandible cortical without iatrogenic fracture. The patient received antibiotics and antalgics daily for 8 days and recovered well postoperatively. 

Recommendations:
The patient was advised for oral rehabilitation and entered into routine follow-up 3, 6, and 12 months later with no signs of recurrence. 

Summary: 
The 8-year-old girl presenting with central giant cell tumor (CGCT) underwent surgical intervention and exhibited no signs of recurrence during routine follow-up 3, 6, and 12 months later. She was advised for oral rehabilitation following the surgery.

Date of Discharge: April 2016
Length of Stay: 162 Days

Admitting Diagnosis
The patient was diagnosed with PRP in 2009.

Hospital Course
Upon our initial assessment, the patient exhibited no features of connective tissue disease. The patient suffered from classic bilateral discoloration of the fingers with mild pain and numbness. Her symptoms were exacerbated by cold weather and stress. The patient was initially treated with aspirin, nifedipine, and prednisolone by another health facility, but no notable improvement was observed.

The patient was admitted to our hospital in July 2010 with severe digital pain and ulceration. Magnetic resonance angiogram of her upper extremities did not show any features of vasculitis, aneurysm, or stenosis. Computed tomography (CT) scanning of the aortic arch demonstrated a normal aorta and normal branches with no obvious vascular abnormality. CT angiogram demonstrated attenuated, irregular right and left ulnar arteries. The patient underwent bilateral selective ulnar angiography and distal angioplasty, which indicated distal disease at the level of the palmar arches. Biopsy of the left little finger showed no significant histopathological abnormalities and was negative for vasculitis.

Prednisolone therapy was discontinued, and the patient was given a trial of sildenafil (12.5 mg) twice a day, as bosentan was intolerable due to side effects (nausea and dizziness). Disease progression was noted and the patient suffered from severe digital pain and bilateral ulceration of the tips of her fingers. These symptoms required another admission to the hospital and treatment with intravenous (IV) heparin infusion and IV iloprost for a total of 7 days, which led to a minimal improvement in her symptoms. Due to persistent symptoms, rituximab therapy was initiated and she received first cycle in 2012 (1 g two weeks apart). Follow-up after 2 months indicated a significant improvement in her signs and symptoms.

Follow-up after six months of rituximab therapy indicated a complete resolution of the digital ischemia. In January 2015, the patient experienced a recurrence of her previous symptoms, which were resolved by a second cycle of rituximab (375 mg/m2 weekly for 4 weeks). As of the most recent follow-up in April 2016, the patient remains in full remission.

Diagnostic Workup
Laboratory investigation for autoimmune analysis and serology and malignancy screening were normal.

Final Diagnosis
PRP

Discharge Condition
The patient is in full remission.

Discharge Medications
N/A

Follow-up
The patient is scheduled for a follow-up visit in three months.

The patient was a 26-year-old female who had been diagnosed with colon cancer six years prior. The patient presented to the hospital for routine control.

Hospital Course:
Upon examination, the patient had no clinical complaints and no apparent physical findings. Further diagnostic evaluation included a contrast-enhanced CCT scan, which identified a perihilar mass with a smooth contour and homogeneous internal structure. Multiple mediastinal lymph nodes were also identified. The patient underwent a positron emission tomography with 2-deoxy-2-[fluorine-18] fluoro- D-glucose integrated with computed tomography (18F-FDG PET/CT), which showed slightly increased 18F-FDG uptake in the identified mass. In addition, the patient underwent magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the thorax, which showed a lesion that was isointense with muscle in T1-weighted images, hyperintense in T2-weighted images, and enhanced homogeneously in post-contrast series. Based on the imaging findings and patient history, the following differential diagnoses were considered: metastasis, primary lung cancer, lymphoma, and sarcoidosis.

Results:
In laboratory tests, it was found that the patient's IgG4 value was elevated to 723 mg/dL (135mg/dL).

Diagnosis:
A surgical lung biopsy was performed, and the diagnosis was reported as IgG4-related respiratory disease (IgG4-RRD).

Condition at Discharge:
At the time of discharge, the patient's condition was stable. The patient was provided with information regarding the diagnosis and advised to follow up with their primary care physician for continued management and care.

Follow-Up Care:
Follow-up care was recommended with the primary care physician for continued monitoring and management of the patient's condition.

The patient, a 26-year-old female with a history of colon cancer, presented to the hospital for routine control. Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted with left shoulder pain and a prominence of his sternoclavicular joint. Imaging revealed a malunion of an anteriorly displaced SCJ fracture dislocation and a Rockwood type IV acromioclavicular separation. The patient elected to proceed with open reduction and reconstruction of his ACJ and SCJ.

Hospitalization and Procedure:
The patient underwent an open reduction and reconstruction of his ACJ and SCJ. Intraoperatively, the Rockwood type IV acromioclavicular separation was addressed first by starting laterally with a vertical incision over the ACJ. Next, the surgical incision was then carried horizontally across the clavicle to the SCJ and the manubrium. Following resection of the fibrous tissue, the medial edge of the clavicle was partially resected to facilitate reduction back to the residual physeal scar. For maintenance of reduction, the anterior sternoclavicular ligament was reconstructed using a semitendinosus allograft fashioned in a figure-of-eight type weave between the manubrium and clavicle.

Postoperative Course:
The patient had no perioperative complications and was discharged from the hospital without issues. He was briefly immobilized for two weeks and then started range-of-motion training followed by strengthening. At his last six-month follow-up visit, the patient was very satisfied with his functional and clinical outcome. He reported minimal pain and only some stiffness with abduction of his shoulder.

Patient Identification:
The patient is a 69-year-old female who presented with a history of severe-stage primary open-angle glaucoma refractory to previous trabeculectomy and on maximum topical medical treatment in the left eye.

Chief Complaint:
The patient presented with an abscess and erosion of underlying conjunctiva and partial erosion of the scleral patch graft (SPG) in the left eye.

Hospital Course:
The patient underwent placement of a Baerveldt glaucoma implant with a SPG in the left eye with vicryl suture tube ligature. After surgery, the patient was treated with moxifloxacin 4 times a day for 1 week and prednisolone acetate starting at 4 times a day and tapered weekly. However, at postoperative week 3, the patient reported irritation and discharge in the left eye and was diagnosed with an abscess and erosion of the underlying conjunctiva and partial erosion of the SPG. She was restarted on moxifloxacin and gentamicin treatment.

Culture results showed coagulase-negative Staphylococcus, susceptible to gentamicin. The patient was scheduled for wound revision with removal of the SPG, conjunctivoplasty, and placement of a new SPG. After revision surgery, the tube remained covered with no recurrence of erosion or infection.

Patient Outcome:
The patient's skin lesions resolved on the regimen of cephalexin. At postoperative week 6 after the revision, there was no recurrence of erosion or infection.

Impression:
The patient had successful surgery for glaucoma implant with SPG placement, but postoperative complications required wound revision and antibiotic treatment.

Follow-up Plan:
The patient will have regular follow-up appointments for monitoring and maintenance of the glaucoma implant.

Hospital Course Summary:

Admission:
A 43-year-old male with primary hypothyroidism was admitted for evaluation of progressive fatigue, weakness, muscle and joint pain in the setting of recurrent fractures.

History of Present Illness:
The patient had been experiencing musculoskeletal pain in several locations including bilateral knees, ankles, left shoulder, left arm, and lower back which affected his overall functional status. He struggled to climb a flight of stairs, often grabbing the railing to pull himself up. A nuclear medicine bone scan showed abnormal uptake in bilateral ribs, vertebrae, right knee, hips, ankles, and feet. A lower extremity MRI showed stress fractures in left fibula, fifth metatarsal, and right tibia.

Course in Hospital:
The patient was started on calcitriol and phosphate supplements which significantly improved muscle weakness. Due to concern for TIO, a positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT) scan with 68Gallium (68Ga)-DOTATATE was performed which showed multiple lytic osseous lesions with increased somatostatin positive uptake seen throughout pelvis, ribs, ankles, and feet. However, after re-review with radiology, multiple areas of increased uptake were considered to be secondary to fractures, and left posterior acetabular lesion was presumed to be the tumor of interest given a remarkably higher standard uptake values (SUVmax) in this lesion compared to other lesions (SUVmax 20 vs. 4–5).

Procedure:
The left acetabular lesion was biopsied and pathology demonstrated a 1.4 cm phosphaturic mesenchymal tumor of the left acetabulum with uninvolved margins. The patient underwent radical resection of the tumor of the posterior left acetabulum with reconstruction of the posterior wall and posterior column of the acetabulum through a Kocher-Langenbach approach. His hip joint was able to be spared utilizing a 3D-printed custom bone cutting guide (CG) and intra-operative O-arm guided surgical navigation (Medtronic© Stealth) utilizing a navigated Sonopet Ultrasonic Bone Cutting Bovie (Stryker). The posterior wall and column of his acetabulum were constructed with a tantalum augment (Zimmer) and a pelvic reconstruction plate and screw construct (Synthes) after tumor removal.

Discharge Summary:
The patient was discharged with normal phosphorus and FGF23 levels, pain-free left hip, no evidence of hardware complication, back to hiking, and walking on the treadmill. Clinical and radiographic follow-up at 6 months postoperatively found him to be pain-free in his left hip, with almost complete resolution of bone pain, and no recurrence of fractures. Phosphorus level also remained normal at 3.4 mg/dL 6 months after surgery.

The redundant patch applied during the previous AVSD closure was removed, and a new pericardial patch was placed. A lifting annuloplasty was performed to augment the posterior leaflet. The peak pressure gradient of the LVOT decreased significantly after the surgical procedure.

After weaning from CPB, the 2D- and 3D-TEE images revealed a fully widened LVOT with resolution of the AML tethering and mild MR.

Immunohistochemical analysis showed diffuse and strongly positive cytoplasmic staining in all tumor cells for CK 8, CD 10, and CEA, as well as an intense canalicular staining pattern for Hep-Par 1. The mitotic index was low.

The patient's recovery was uneventful, and he was discharged on Day 7. He has been regularly followed up with ultrasound and α-fetoprotein every three months, as well as magnetic resonance imaging every six months, for a follow-up period of 27 months without a sign of recurrence.

The results of the CT angiography showed a patent femoro-popliteal bypass graft and a Popliteal Artery Aneurysm (PA), which measured 8 × 5.6 cm at the distal anastomosis compressing the popliteal artery. The patient underwent LLE arteriogram with exclusion of the LLE PA with an 11 × 10 mm Viabahn stent, balloon angioplasty of the popliteal vessel, and placement of a 6 × 80 mm Bard life stent. On postoperative day (POD) 3, the patient was found to have a small hematoma at the femoral-femoral bypass access site, and a sandbag was applied to the area. On POD 4, the patient's INR was therapeutic, and the hematoma was non-expanding or pulsatile, and he was discharged home.

The patient was discharged home with instructions to follow the prescribed medication regimen, monitor for any signs of bleeding or bruising, and follow up with his primary care physician and vascular surgeon within two weeks. He was advised to avoid any strenuous activities and to keep the surgical site clean and dry until the follow-up appointment. Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to the hospital after being trapped by his van which was parked on the sidewalk and falling after being pushed by a taxi bumping against the side of the van twice, resulting in multiple deep abrasions over the body and extremities. Upon arrival, the physical examination revealed tenderness on the symphysis pubis, fracture of L4 and L5 right transverse process, and first sacral vertebral fracture. The patient underwent open reduction and internal fixation of the symphysis pubis separation with plate and screws using Fannenstiel approach.

Postoperatively, the patient experienced a progressive tingling sensation and motor weakness in both legs. The motor power on ankle plantar flexion of both legs were decreased. A sensory examination revealed decreased sensation in the soles bilaterally, rectal tone was decreased and perianal sensation was decreased as well. Postoperative CT examination revealed jumped-and-locked right L5-S1 facet joint, and widened gap of a sacral fracture site resulting in a cauda equine syndrome. Subsequently, a right L5-S1 jumped facet injury was confirmed intraoperatively, and a second open reduction was performed, in which the reduction state was confirmed by C-arm fluoroscopy. After the procedure, the patient showed marked improvement with grade 5/5 and 4+/5 muscle strength in the right and left plantarflexor muscles, respectively, and normal range of movement on the L5-S1 segment.

After 3 months of non-weight bearing due to symphysis pubis separation, the patient ambulated from a wheelchair to full weight bearing, and at the 6 month follow-up evaluation, he could walk without support, sphincter function was intact, but still experienced numbness in the left sole. The patient has since returned to his previous employment.

Final Diagnosis:
Multiple deep abrasions of body and extremities, tenderness on symphysis pubis and fractures of L4, L5, and first sacral vertebral fracture, jumped-and-locked right L5-S1 facet joint resulting in a cauda equine syndrome.

Procedures:
- Open reduction and internal fixation of a symphysis pubis separation with plate and screws using Fannenstiel approach
- A second open reduction for a jumped facet injury

The patient is not being discharged with any medication.

Hospital course summary:

Admitting Diagnosis: Subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH)

Brief Hospital Course: 
The patient was admitted to the emergency department with severe headache and sudden loss of consciousness. Head CT revealed SAH spanning the suprasellar and ambient cisterns, and the left sylvian fissure. Cerebral CT angiogram confirmed vascular lesions in the right Internal Carotid Artery (ICA) and right P1 segment of the posterior cerebral artery (PCA), indicating probable Posterior communicating artery (P1) segment aneurysm. Subsequent DSA demonstrated dilated, tortuous, and redundant right vessels of the supraclinoid ICA and the right P1 segment. Neurological examination revealed decreased consciousness and stiff-neck. 

Diagnostic Evaluation and Procedures: 
The patient underwent Doppler Ultrasonic Probe, ICG Video Angiography, and Flow800 to evaluate the supraclinoid ICA lesion and P1 segment lesion. Based on the findings, we performed proximal occlusion combined with STA-P2 bypass to address the lesion in the P1 segment. Intraoperative ICG video angiography analyzed with Flow800 showed decreased perfusion of the P1 segment lesion after surgery compared to pre-treatment perfusion. Post-operative CTA demonstrated that the bypass was patent. 

Hospital Course and Therapeutic Interventions: 
The patient was treated surgically and her neurological examination improved significantly postoperatively. The P1 segment lesion was still present but had decreased in size when compared with the preoperative lesion. The patient was discharged in stable condition after her 12-month follow-up. 

Summation: 
The patient was admitted to the hospital with severe headache and sudden loss of consciousness, due to SAH probably caused by the PAMs in the right supraclinoid ICA and right P1 segment of PCA. The patient underwent diagnostic evaluations to assess the extent of the lesion and was treated surgically using proximal occlusion combined with STA-P2 bypass. The patient's neurological examination improved significantly postoperatively and was discharged in stable condition after her 12-month follow-up.

Hospital Course:

The patient, a 65-year-old female, presented with a 3-week history of intermittent epigastric pain, nausea, vomiting and weight loss. Her past medical history was significant for poor mobility, high cholesterol and type II diabetes. 8 years previously she had been admitted with E. coli sepsis and diarrhoea and had an incidental finding of a partially calcified gallbladder with no features of inflammation and benign fatty changes in the liver. On the current admission, the patient's general examination was unremarkable, with normal vital signs. However, blood tests showed deranged liver function tests with elevated levels of ALT, ALP, total bilirubin and GGT. Additionally, the patient had hypercalcemia and leukocytosis. Ultrasound showed a large, solid and heterogeneous mass in the gallbladder with dense shadowing and calcific components. A subsequent CT scan showed a 10cm solid porcelain gallbladder invading liver segments 4 and 5, with multiple metastases including enlarged lymph nodes and pulmonary metastatic deposits. 

Management:

To fully assess for management options, the regional hepatobiliary multidisciplinary meeting recommended magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) and a liver biopsy. MRCP showed extensive gallbladder tumour involving adjacent parenchyma, dilated intrahepatic bile ducts, and scattered satellite liver metastases. Bilateral lung metastases were also noted with extensive peri-portal, portocaval and upper retroperitoneal lymph nodes. US-guided liver biopsy confirmed metastatic adenocarcinoma consent with a pancreatico-biliary system, gall bladder or upper gastrointestinal tract primary site. The patient was discharged on a palliative care pathway as further management options were negated by the results.

Discharge:

The patient was admitted two weeks later with diffuse abdominal pain and ascites, which were subsequently drained. However, the patient clinically deteriorated and passed away 4 weeks later.

Procedures: Local anesthesia was given, complete pulp extirpation was done, and antibiotics were placed in the canal. Later, amniotic membrane was obtained and placed inside the canal up to the level of cementoenamel junction, followed by placement of a thick paste of white mineral trioxide aggregate over it.

Radiological evaluation revealed continued root elongation, complete closure in the periapical opening, thick root dentinal walls with narrowing of the canal space, and normal periradicular architecture. 

Recommendation: The patient is advised to maintain good oral hygiene and follow up with regular dental check-ups to monitor the healing progress.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY

Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Gender: Female
Date of Admission: [REDACTED]
Date of Discharge: [REDACTED]
Total Hospital Stay: 35 days

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to the Pediatric Intensive Care Unit (PICU) due to bloody diarrhea caused by enterohemorrhagic E. coli (STEC O111) with verocytotoxins Stx2 and eae. She developed HUS despite treatment and required renal replacement therapy (RRT) by HDF. During the first RRT session, the patient showed cardiovascular instability and neurological signs, leading to a brain CT scan that revealed no abnormalities. After admission to the PICU, the patient showed signs of coma and required mechanical ventilation. EEG revealed diffuse slow-wave activity with theta-delta oscillations of low voltage. 

On day 3, the patient developed life-threatening bradycardia due to severe hyperkalemia, requiring CPR. Continuous veno-vein HDF was performed over three consecutive days, followed by intermittent HDF until day 14. CytoSorb® hemoadsorption was performed three times on day 6, 8, and 10 due to the onset of multiorgan failure coupled to rhabdomyolysis. Brain MRI was performed on day 4, revealing severe post-anoxic damage, thus the patient received two doses of Eculizumab on day 4 and 11. 

The patient received the best supportive therapy, including antibiotics to treat a septic condition due to S. Marcescens. The patient stayed in PICU for 14 days, and laboratory parameters gained normal values within 18 days. On day 27, a further MRI revealed significant improvement of the ischemic hypoxic area at cerebellar level, confirmed by normal electrical activity at EEG monitoring. 

After extubation, the patient had marked bilateral motor deficit with hyporeflexia/areflexia in the lower limbs and hyperextension of the thigh, and intentional tremors of both the upper limbs. Head postural tremors were also observed. However, the diuresis was adequate and the renal function had recovered, and blood pressure was controlled well. The patient received therapeutic plasma exchange (TPE) to treat peripheral polyneuropathy (seven treatments) but there was unsatisfactory functional recovery. The patient was discharged and transferred to a neuro-rehabilitation center for intensive treatment.

Summary:
The patient was admitted to the hospital due to bloody diarrhea caused by STEC O111 with verocytotoxins Stx2 and eae, which developed into HUS. During her stay in the hospital, she experienced cardiovascular instability, neurological signs, and life-threatening conditions such as hyperkalemia and bradycardia. She received RRT by HDF, CytoSorb® hemoadsorption, Eculizumab, and TPE, along with the best supportive therapy. After discharge, she was transferred to a neuro-rehabilitation center for intensive treatment.

Immunohistochemical staining revealed positive Syn and CgA, negative Melan A, HMB45 and α-inhibin, positive S-100 cells and positive CD31 vascular endothelium marker. Clinical follow-up examinations were performed three times after surgery and showed no recurrence or symptoms of paroxysmal hypertension. The patient was admitted with gradually progressive gait difficulty and frequent falls, combined with mental “slowness”, and reduced attention. In addition, urinary incontinence was noted. Clinical examination showed limb bradykinesia and rigidity, myoclonic jerks were observed in the upper limbs, cortical sensory loss, sensory neglect, and primitive reflexes (especially grasping). Neuropsychological testing revealed moderate-stage dementia, including significant frontal, amnestic, and visuoconstructive components, while significant upper limb apraxia was present. The patient was diagnosed with corticobasal syndrome based on these clinical findings.

Neuroimaging revealed an increased Evans index, acute callosal angle, and periventricular caps, suggestive of normal pressure hydrocephalus. Some degree of cerebral small vessel disease was also evident. The spinal taping test resulted in a significant improvement of cognition, but there was no change in gait. Analysis of CSF biomarkers showed reduced Aβ42/Aβ40 ratio, together with increased τP-181 and τT, compatible with the presence of AD.

Overall Assessment and Plan:
The patient met clinical criteria for corticobasal syndrome and had additional findings suggestive of normal pressure hydrocephalus and cerebral small vessel disease. The patient was treated symptomatically for her condition while in the hospital. The patient was discharged with recommendations for outpatient follow-up with their primary care physician and a neurologist. Further diagnostic workup was recommended, including imaging studies and a follow-up evaluation of the CSF biomarkers.

This hospitalization was for a 68-year-old female with arterial hypertension, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, moderate mitral regurgitation, dyslipidemia, and carotid stenosis. The patient was admitted for palpitations and dyspnea. A couple of years ago, the patient had a lacunar infarct of the right lenticular nucleus.

Diagnostic and Therapeutic Intervention:
The patient underwent transthoracic and transesophageal echocardiography, and a non-homogeneous, slightly mobile, round mass was discovered, attached to the ventricular side of posterior mitral leaflet, with central echo-lucent area, and without acoustic shadowing. A cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) was also performed using 1.5T magnet. To confirm the diagnosis, a multidetector computed tomography (MDCT) was performed.

Findings:
The Transthoracic and transesophageal echocardiography revealed a non-homogeneous, slightly mobile, round mass attached to the ventricular side of the posterior mitral leaflet. The CMR showed a mass that appeared isointense with the normal myocardium. Delayed enhancement sequences showed a non-enhanced central core surrounded by a hyperenhanced rim (fibrous cap). The MDCT showed a hyperdense mass with a hypodense center and a calcified peripheral rim.

Assessment and Plan:
Based on the MDCT findings, the patient's diagnosis was highly suggestive of CMAC. The patient was discharged with follow-up appointments scheduled with the appropriate specialists. The patient was provided with instructions to report any concerning cardiac symptoms, including palpitations, dyspnea, or chest discomfort.  Additionally, routine monitoring of hypertension, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, moderate mitral regurgitation, dyslipidemia, and carotid stenosis should be maintained as part of the patient's long-term care plan.

SABR targeted the tumor in his left upper lung with good results and has been unchanged with postradiation fibrotic changes. Currently, the patient has remained on maintenance pemetrexed for more than 48 months with no evidence of disease recurrence.

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 30-year-old male, was admitted to the orthopedic outpatient department (OPD) with complaints of lower back pain radiating to the left lower limb and difficulty in walking associated with low-grade fever. The physical examination revealed tenderness in the lumbosacral area of the spine, reduced power, and sensory changes in the left lower limb. Laboratory investigations showed decreased hemoglobin levels, total leucocyte count of 14800/cumm, and platelet count of 688000/cumm. Magnetic resonance imaging of the lumbar spine revealed T2 hyperintense and T1 iso to hyperintense moderately enhancing soft tissue in the spinal cord, extending within neural foramina with obliteration of neural foraminal fat. The impression of diffuse Kochs involvement of the spine was given along with suspicion of neoplastic etiology like lymphoma. Vertebral bone biopsy from left L3 and L4 region was performed and sent for histopathological examination which revealed actinomycosis of the lumbosacral spine. The patient was started on penicillin group antibiotics and tolerated the therapy well.

Discharge Summary:

Patient: 79-year-old male

Reason for Admission: Progressive dysphagia and weight loss

Medical History: None provided

Hospital Course:

Upon admission, the patient presented with symptoms including hematemesis, melena, fever, cough, and yellow sputum. Blood analysis revealed severe anemia, high leukocyte and neutrophil levels, and a low albumin level. A sputum smear indicated the presence of gram-positive cocci.

An endoscopy identified an elongated lump on 1 side of the vertical axis of the esophagus. The mass extended progressively for 15 cm along the esophageal longitudinal axis and invaded half of the esophageal circumference. Biopsy revealed the tumor to be a malignant melanoma, positive for S-100 and HMB-45, and negative for cytokeratin and carcinoembryonic antigen markers.

Computed tomography showed inflammation of the lungs and no evidence of distant metastasis. Additionally, a physical examination revealed no pigmented lesions at the skin, eyes, rectum, or other locations.

Due to the advanced age of the patient and comorbidities including hypoproteinemia, infection, and severe anemia, surgery, chemotherapy, or radiotherapy were not performed. The patient was discharged without receiving treatment.

Follow-up:

Approximately 1 month after discharge, the medical team was informed of the patient's death.

Outcome:

The postoperative period was uneventful, and the patient was discharged on postoperative day two. The patient is well and has no recurrence or adrenal insufficiency 18 months post-surgery.

Diagnosis:
The final diagnosis was RT. 

Follow-up:
The patient underwent a follow-up of 6 months, and her platelet count remained within the normal range.

Initial check-up excluded organic causes, and the patient was admitted to the psychiatry ward. A second check-up was made, which showed only a mild pleocytosis in the cerebrospinal fluid. The patient underwent 4 cycles of chemotherapy with Carboplatin and etoposide and concurrent radiotherapy, which yielded a complete response. The patient also underwent an endoscopic surgical intervention for an in situ relapse of her bladder neoplasm.

From October 2015 to July 2016, the patient remained stable, but no improvement of the neurological deficit was witnessed since the treatment of the pulmonary neoplasm began.

The patient was discharged in stable condition. Further follow-up will be needed to manage the neurological deficit.

None noted.

The patient requires regular follow-up appointments.

The patient received neurological consultations during her hospital stay.

The patient was discharged to home in stable condition.

The patient is a 30-year-old nulliparous pregnant Japanese woman who was referred to our institution for prenatal evaluation of a fetal abdominal cyst at 19 weeks of gestation.

Hospital Course:
The fetal ultrasonography at 19 weeks of gestation revealed the presence of intermediate- or high-type imperforate anus with rectourethral fistula. Even after informing the parents of possible poor prognosis of the fetus, the parents did not desire termination of pregnancy. The case continually progressed, and at 32 weeks and 5 days of gestation, the male neonate was delivered by cesarean section. The neonate required immediate intubation and high-frequency oscillatory ventilation accompanied by inhaled nitric oxide treatment due to severe respiratory failure with persistent pulmonary hypertension. Regarding imperforate anus, cystostomy was performed on the first day, and posterior sagittal anorectoplasty was performed before discharge. On 36th days after birth, cystourethrography revealed high-type imperforate anus with patent rectourethral fistula, nonobstructive lower urinary tract, and urethral stenosis distal to the rectourethral fistula. The neonate was discharged after the successful procedure.

Discharge Diagnosis:
High-type imperforate anus with rectourethral fistula, fetal urethral stenosis or obstruction, and progressive bowel dilation.

Procedures:
Cystostomy and posterior sagittal anorectoplasty.

Condition at Discharge:
The neonate was discharged in stable condition and is doing well at 19 months after birth.

Follow-up Plans:
The neonate will be monitored for further development of any abnormalities in the future and will have routine check-ups with a pediatrician.

The patient, a 77-year-old woman, presented to our outpatient clinic with a two-month history of dysphasia. Both thyroid lobes were diffusely enlarged with the right lobe being slightly firmer than the left lobe. Palpable masses were found along the right cervical levels II and III. Thyroid function test was within the normal range. A flexible fiberoptic laryngoscopy showed no remarkable findings. 

An ultrasound showed a larger-than-4-cm, irregular shaped, heterogeneously hypoechoic, solid mass occupying the entire right thyroid lobe with suspicious small internal calcifications. The mass directly invaded the right lateral and posterior wall of trachea, and encased the right common carotid artery. A fine needle aspiration was performed revealing suspicious findings for undifferentiated carcinoma. 

Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck showed a heterogeneously enhancing mass compared to adjacent muscle in the posterior portion of the right thyroid lobe, outgrowing towards the posterior wall of the trachea. Subsequent excisional biopsy of the thyroid lesion was done and it was histopathologically diagnosed as diffuse large B cell lymphoma. 

The patient received three cycles of R-CHOP chemotherapy as well as total 3,816 cGy of intensity-modulated radiation therapy (IMRT) which resulted in complete regression on the CT images four months after the initial diagnosis. 

Discharge condition:
The patient has been discharged with significant improvement in her condition.

Follow up care plan:
The appropriate follow-up care plan has been explained to the patient, and she has been advised to return to the outpatient clinic for a follow-up appointment.

The patient presented with dysphasia and diffuse thyroid enlargement with suspicious findings of undifferentiated carcinoma. DISCHARGE SUMMARY

Patient Name: [REDACTED]

Medical Record Number: [REDACTED]

Admission Date: October [REDACTED], 2017

Discharge Date: June [REDACTED], 2019

Hospital Course:

The patient is a 61-year-old male admitted to our hospital in October 2017 for irritable cough without any medical history of interest. A PET-CT was obtained one month later, which showed abnormal increase of glucose metabolism in the lower lobe of the right lung and abnormal high glucose metabolism in the liver, considered as malignant tumor and metastasis respectively. Pathology indicated tumor cells, NapsinA+, thyroid transcription factor-1 (+), alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) (+), Hepa-1 (−), PSA (–), CD10 (−), CD34 showed vessels, CK7 (+), CEA (+), and Ki-67 positive index about 70%. The two tumors were similar in morphology. They confirmed to primary lung adenocarcinoma. The results of gene testing showed EGFR exon 19 deletion mutation. The patient was treated with gefitinib 250mg per os QD in December 2017. The lung focus was observed to have shrunk, considered as partial remission (PR) by clinical evaluation.

However, in April 23, 2018, masses in the lung were larger than before. The gene testing blood was performed again, and the results showed EGFR E19 mutation and MET amplification. The patient was given targeted therapy with gefitinib (250mg per os QD) and crizotinib (250mg per os BID). Lung CT showed the lung focus had shrunk again in June 06, 2018. Moreover, re-examination of chest CT showed recurrent progress of lesions in December 18, 2018. The patient underwent genetic of blood testing again. The results showed that PD-L1 positivity (50%), the tumor mutational burden (high), EGFR E19 mutation and MET amplification. The patient received salvage therapy with immunotherapy (pembrolizumab 100mg intravenous, every 21 days) combined with chemotherapy (pemetrexed 800 mg intravenous + carboplatin 0.4g d2 intravenous, every 28 days, six cycles, then, maintenance of pemetrexed 800 mg alone). CT scan revealed the clinical response with shrinkage of over 30% of the lung lesion on February 27, 2019. Examination of chest CT showed the patient was PR on June 26, 2019. The masses in liver were also significantly smaller than before.

Discharge Diagnosis:

The patient was diagnosed with stage IV non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) with EGFR exon 19 deletion mutation and MET amplification.

Hospital Course Summary:

The patient was admitted to our hospital with irritable cough and was diagnosed with stage IV NSCLC. The patient received targeted therapy with gefitinib, followed by combination therapy with gefitinib and crizotinib. Salvage therapy with immunotherapy and chemotherapy was given, which resulted in significant improvement in the patient's condition. The patient's condition was monitored with regular annual clinical and radiographic follow-ups. At the time of discharge, the patient maintains improved quality of life with no pulmonary symptoms and responded optimally to the treatment.

Wide cleft palate in a patient with Seckel syndrome and intrauterine growth retardation.

The patient was discharged home in stable condition. It is recommended to continue feeding the patient with soft and pureed foods that are easy to swallow. The patient should schedule follow-up appointments with their pediatrician and specialists for further evaluation and management.

None.

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted with symptoms of recurrent episodes of pain in the abdomen and fever with chills for past 2 days. The patient had a history of two episodes of jaundice in the past which were managed conservatively. On admission, the patient was febrile, tachycardic, and icteric. Physical examination revealed tenderness in right hypochondrium. Laboratory data revealed a leucocytosis with elevated levels of total bilirubin and direct bilirubin.

A contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the abdomen showed a mass near the hilum with dilated intrahepatic biliary radicals. The provisional diagnosis of obstructive jaundice with cholangitis was made and percutaneous transhepatic biliary drainage (PTBD) was planned to decompress the biliary system. As a cholangiogram at the time of PTBD was unable to delineate the complex biliary anatomy in this patient, an endoscopic retrograde cholangiogram (ERC) was performed. ERC revealed multiple small ducts draining into the gallbladder with absent right and left hepatic, common hepatic, and CBDs. The gallbladder was found to be draining into the duodenum by a long thin cystic duct.

On elective exploration, multiple small hepatic ducts were seen entering the gallbladder which drained into the duodenum via a cystic duct. Diagnosis of a type IV hepaticocystic duct was confirmed, and a Roux-en-Y cholecystojejunostomy was performed. The postoperative course of the patient was uneventful, and he was discharged on the 10th postoperative day.

Follow-up after 1 month revealed that the patient was nonicteric with a repeat percutaneous transhepatic cholangiogram demonstrating a free flow of bile from liver into gallbladder and then into the jejunum. At 6 months after the surgery, the patient was asymptomatic.

Diagnosis:

The patient was diagnosed with a type IV hepaticocystic duct.

Treatment:

The patient underwent a Roux-en-Y cholecystojejunostomy.

Condition at Discharge:

The patient was asymptomatic at the time of discharge.

Follow-Up:

The patient is required to follow up with scheduled appointments with the treating physician.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [redacted]
Date of Admission: [redacted]
Date of Discharge: [redacted]
Admitting Diagnosis: Scombroid Syndrome with Acute Coronary Syndrome

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to the emergency department due to tongue swelling and syncope following the consumption of fresh tuna fish and clams. The electrocardiogram displayed ST elevation in inferior leads and ST depression in aVL and V2–V3. Antihistaminic drugs, aspirin, and volume expansion were administered, during which a quick resolution of symptoms and ST elevation were observed. Laboratory test findings exhibited leukocytosis with neutrophilia and troponin increase.

Transthoracic echocardiography displayed normal results. The patient was admitted to the cardiology department with the clinical suspect of Scombroid Syndrome caused by fish consumption. For myocarditis to be ruled out, a cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) imaging was conducted, revealing a focal transmural ischemic lesion of mid-distal posterior wall of the left ventricle.

Further studies with coronary angiography indicated an angiographic “minus” during contrast infusion in the middle portion of the right coronary artery (RCA), suggestive of a thrombus. As there were no clear images of a distal embolization, an optical coherence tomography (OCT) was conducted, showing a non-occlusive intraluminal thrombus in mid-RCA.

The patient's clinical course was favorable, as there was no recurrence of symptoms and there was gradual reduction of cardiac biomarkers. The ECG evolution indicated infero-lateral biphasic T waves.

Discharge Diagnosis: Acute Coronary Syndrome

Medications on Discharge: Single antiplatelet therapy, statins

Follow-Up Instructions:
The patient is advised to continue medications as prescribed. Strict dietary restrictions against fish are recommended. Follow up with a cardiologist in three months for a repeat echocardiogram and ECG to assess myocardial recovery. In case of recurrence of symptoms, the patient is advised to seek urgent medical attention.

Hospital Course:
A 65-year-old woman was admitted to our hospital for multiple itchy erythematosquamous plaques on both lower and upper limbs, and psoriasiform scales on the scalp and retroauricular. The patient had been treated with nivolumab 3 mg/m2 every 2 weeks for stage IV melanoma, which had been administered 11 times at the time of presentation. Two years ago, she was diagnosed with a stage IV melanoma positive for the BRAF V600 mutation. She was diagnosed with lymph node, subcutaneous, and brain metastases. Nivolumab was initiated as a third-line treatment, after a BRAF enzyme inhibitor and ipilimumab (CTLA-4 inhibitor).

The patient had a known history of scalp psoriasis, type II diabetes, and hypertension. Her regular medication included lorametazepam, gliclazide, metoprolol, pantoprazole, and momethasone nasal spray. Upon full-body inspection, no other skin lesions were observed. The patient was in good general condition and had no systemic complaints such as weight loss, night sweats, fever, dyspnea, cough, or gastrointestinal symptoms.

Based on the clinical presentation, the patient was diagnosed with a psoriasis vulgaris exacerbation. Local treatment with corticosteroids was initiated. Additionally, the interval of nivolumab was extended from 2 weeks to 3 weeks, as the patient noticed a flare-up of skin lesions after every nivolumab administration. Dosing at 3-week intervals, in combination with the local corticoid treatment, led to successful control of the psoriatic lesions. No systemic corticoids were administered.

The patient had a stable disease for 14 months after the start of nivolumab. Then, she developed progressive brain metastasis with an intracranial hemorrhage and died.

Discharge Diagnosis:
Psoriasis vulgaris exacerbation.

Discharge Instructions:
The patient has been discharged in a stable condition. The patient's symptoms have improved with local treatment with corticosteroids and nivolumab dosing at 3-week intervals. The patient has been advised to follow up with her oncologist for further management of stage IV melanoma. No further follow-up is required at this hospital.

A different technique was employed for a second repair, namely, to refresh the vaginal edges and perform a two-layer closure of the vagina with the subsequent employment of an omental flap. The omental flap was placed in the pelvis and was attached tension-free to the vaginal cuff closure by interrupted sutures.

Diagnosis:
- Deep endometriotic lesion at the top of the vagina with vaginal cuff dehiscence.

Treatment:
- Laparoscopic resection of the endometriotic lesion using Sonicision.
- Repositioning of the small bowel.
- Refreshment of the vaginal edges and two-layer closure of the vagina with the subsequent employment of an omental flap.

Condition at Discharge:
- Stable.

The patient was advised to attend follow-up care appointments, undergo regular check-ups, and adhere to the prescribed treatment plan.

None prescribed.

The patient was advised to avoid sexual intercourse for six weeks following the second repair. Additionally, the patient was urged to monitor for any signs of recurrent vaginal cuff dehiscence. The 2-year-old male patient was admitted to our department due to intermittent hematuria. An ultrasound of the urinary system revealed a solid mass in the bladder cavity and tumor tissue invading the posterior urethra. The patient underwent cystourethroscopy, bladder tumor resection, and cystostomy, after which the bladder tumor recurred three months later. Postoperative pathological diagnosis suggested embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma (ERMS), and the patient underwent alternative chemotherapeutic treatment with VAC/VTC followed by VDC/IE and local radiotherapy. A local recurrence of cystoma was revealed after chemotherapy and radiotherapy were stopped for several months, and the patient underwent cystectomy again followed by VDC/IE chemotherapy and then CBVP chemotherapy. The patient received CAR-T cells after collecting autologous peripheral blood lymphocytes and undergoing preconditioning chemotherapy with CAR-T. The patient experienced a complete remission (CR), and after follow-up, the thickening of the bladder wall disappeared, with no tumor metastasis or recurrence found.

Discharge Summary:
Admitted to our department for treatment of intermittent hematuria, a 2-year-old male patient had a solid mass in the bladder cavity, which tested positive for ERMS. After alternative chemotherapeutic treatments and radiotherapy, the patient achieved a CR and continues to be in CR and stable 3.5 years following CAR-T cell treatment. The patient experienced no CRS manifestations or significant changes in tested cytokines in the peripheral blood or clinical situations. A follow-up test showed that the number of CAR-T cells detected in the patient did not fluctuate significantly, and only 0.02% were observed in the first week after reinfusion. After reinfusion, Helper T Lymphocyte deceases, about 3 weeks after CAR-T cell transfusion, and Suppressor T Lymphocyte increased.

The patient received radiotherapy alone for the liver lesions, and hepatic artery embolization with doxorubicin and cisplatin for the small recurrent nodule on the right liver.

The patient underwent diagnostic evaluation in the form of imaging, such as computed tomography and biopsy, which aided in the diagnosis and monitoring of his liver lesions and pulmonary metastases.

The patient was stable, asymptomatic with a decrease in AFP from 11 460 µg/L to 3.1 µg/L, and no imaging evidence of disease recurrence at the time of his discharge in March 2012.

The patient was advised to follow-up with his physician regularly for clinical evaluations and imaging studies for monitoring purposes.

Not applicable.

The patient was discharged with improvement in his condition, normal liver laboratory results, and no imaging evidence of disease recurrence.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Admission Date: [REDACTED]
Discharge Date: [REDACTED]

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted to our department with sudden-onset stuporous consciousness. A brain CT scan revealed a subarachnoid hemorrhage with a right temporal lobe intracranial hemorrhage and a right subdural hematoma. Following the CT, angiography demonstrated an aneurysmal sac at the right posterior communicating artery. Emergency decompressive craniectomy (DC) and aneurysmal neck clipping were performed. Following recovery there was some sinking of the scalp flap, and the decision was made to proceed with an autologous cranioplasty 61 days after the initial hemorrhage. There were no complications during the cranioplasty procedure, and there was no evidence of cardiovascular instability or cerebral swelling. Epidural and subdural drains were placed and connected to a suction system during skin closure. Following skin closure the drains were connected to a drainage bag to avoid subgaleal and epidural blood accumulation.

However, the patient had a seizure in the recovery room. Emergency brain CT revealed widespread cerebral edema. Increased intracranial pressure (ICP) and cerebral edema were managed with osmotic diuretics, corticosteroids, and antiepileptic drugs. The edema slowly subsided, but new low-density areas were noted on follow-up brain CT 1 week after the cranioplasty. The decision was made to clamp the drain catheters to control the intracranial pressure.

The patient was monitored closely for any signs of complications, and no further episodes of seizure or cerebral edema were observed. The patient's overall condition improved, and she was discharged in stable condition with instructions for continued follow-up care.

Final Diagnosis:

- Subarachnoid hemorrhage
- Right temporal lobe intracranial hemorrhage
- Right subdural hematoma
- Aneurysmal sac at the right posterior communicating artery
- Widespread cerebral edema

Discharge Instructions:

1. Follow-up appointments with your primary care physician and neurologist are recommended to monitor your recovery and manage any ongoing symptoms.

3. Adequate rest and nutrition are essential for your continued recovery.

4. Avoid activities that may increase your risk of falls or head injury.

5. In case of any new or worsening symptoms, seek immediate medical attention.

[DISCHARGE INSTRUCTIONS END]

Patient: 23-year-old female

Chief complaint: Gum swelling and tooth mobility

Medical history: Unremarkable.

Hospital Course:

The patient was presented to the Department of Periodontics, Seoul National University Dental Hospital in 2004 with the chief complaint of gum swelling. The patient was previously diagnosed with generalized aggressive periodontitis and had received scaling and root planning in conjunction with systemic antibiotics. The patient later reported becoming aware of swelled gums and tooth mobility at the age of 13. The patient received periodontal therapy and was referred to the Department of Prosthodontics for further evaluation and treatment.

The objectives of treatment were patient motivation and education, improvement of oral hygiene, improvement of esthetics, and a stable and predictable outcome. All teeth including the canine in the maxilla and left mandibular lateral incisor through right mandibular canine, and left mandibular second premolar were extracted. Initially fixed prosthesis using implants in the maxilla were planned, but rapid and severe bone resorption after extraction was observed. The fixed prosthesis treatment plan for the maxilla was changed to an implant-supported overdenture. Facebow transfer and mounting on the casts on the articulator were performed for the diagnostic wax-up procedure.

Wax denture try-in for the maxilla and zirconia framework try-in for the mandible were done. The final prostheses were delivered. A daily maintenance care by patient's effort was instructed using interdental cleaning aids. A regular maintenance program was instituted with periodontal recall every 3 months following delivery of the definitive restorations.

Discharge Instructions:

The patient was discharged with oral hygiene instructions and a regular maintenance program of periodontal recall every 3 months following delivery of the definitive restorations.

Follow-up:

The patient will need to follow up with her dentist for periodic monitoring and maintenance of her oral health.

The patient was admitted to the emergency department of St. Orsola Hospital in Bologna, Italy with complaints of generalized articular pain, fever, paresthesia of lower limbs and feet soles, resulting into unstable gear, and visual disorders characterized by impaired ability to focus and binocular vision. The patient's clinical history was marked by acute rheumatic pain about 40 years prior. Physical examination revealed the presence of internuclear left ophthalmoplegia with diplopia secondary, right facial-brachial plexus deficit, hypopallesthesia of inferior limbs and superficial weakness of the feet, depressed mood, moderate peripheral edema, basilar wet sounds, and normochromic urine. The laboratory tests revealed nephritic syndrome with normal renal function, positive antinuclear, anti-double-stranded DNA, anti-Ro/SSA, and antiphospholipid antibodies. Serum complement component C3 was slightly reduced, and CD19+ count constituted 38.4% of total lymphocytes (normal range: 7% to 14%). The MRI reported diffuse inflammatory lesions, and EEG was compatible with minimal structural alterations. Lupus anticoagulant antibodies were positive. Renal ultrasound was unremarkable.

The patient's treatment began with prednisone, which led to an increase in proteinuria and admission to the Nephrology Unit of the hospital. Doppler-ultrasound revealed deep vein thrombosis, and sodium enoxheparin treatment was started. As the patient had high percentages of circulating B cells, rituximab was presented as a therapeutic option, and the patient provided written informed consent to the treatment. The patient received 4 weekly infusions of rituximab after premedication with chlorphenamine, hydrocortisone, and paracetamol. 

At the time of discharge, the patient had stable vital signs and was asymptomatic. The patient's symptoms had improved, and she was advised to follow-up with the primary care physician for continued care and treatment.

Diagnosis on Discharge:
SLE with simultaneously manifestations of LN and NPSLE.
