Hospital Course:
The patient is a 65-year-old non-Hispanic/Latino white woman who presented with dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) following radiotherapy and chemotherapy for left-side breast cancer treated in 2007. The patient was in class II/III of the New York Heart Association (NYHA) classification, with a left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) of 35% and a left bundle branch block (LBBB). In November 2011, the patient was implanted with a cardiac resynchronization therapy-defibrillator (CRT-D) device from the right thoracic side. However, the first attempt to implant the left ventricular (LV) lead was unsuccessful and ventricular pacing was prevented until the second attempt, which was successful in February 2012. Subsequently, the patient's status improved, reaching NYHA class I by September 2012. 

Additionally, a 74-year-old non-Hispanic/Latino white man who underwent coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) in 1993, was presented with atrial fibrillation (AF) which resulted in heart failure (HF) in 2005. Following treatment with amiodarone, sinus rhythm (SR) was restored, and the patient became asymptomatic, with an LVEF of 12% and a left bundle branch block (LBBB). In 2005, the patient was implanted with a prophylactic single-chamber implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD). In May 2012, the patient was further upgraded with a CRT-D device due to severe symptoms (NYHA class III) with an LBBB and a LVEF of 20%. During an outpatient visit on July 17, an electrocardiogram (ECG) revealed AF. On July 26, the patient was hospitalized for HF, and HF treatment was modified. On September 9, the patient's clinical status had improved to NYHA class I, with his SR restored by electrical cardioversion on October 10. 

Conclusions:
Based on the three clinical cases presented, an association between the amplitude of the SonR signal and patients’ clinical status based on NYHA classification was observed. In the first case, a patient with DCM related to radiotherapy and chemotherapy who underwent CRT-D device implantation with successful LV lead implantation and progressive improvement. In the second case, a patient with a history of CABG who underwent prophylactic ICD and subsequently CRT-D implantation upgrading with symptoms of AF, HF, and a significant improvement in clinical status. The SonR signal amplitude appeared to decrease when the onset of AF and remained low as long as AF lasted. The SonR signal amplitude subsequently increased following sinus rhythm restoration, reaching its initial value after the persistence of the sinus rhythm.

This 59-year-old woman presented with high fever, cough, and dyspnea after receiving influenza vaccines. She was hospitalized two weeks later due to the sudden deterioration of symptoms, despite antibiotic treatment. Labs, imaging studies, and bronchoalveolar lavage ruled out infection or malignancy. Further evaluation showed diffuse infiltrates in both lungs and prominent proximal muscle weakness. Diagnosis of polymyositis (PM) with diffuse organizing pneumonia was made in January 2010.

Treatment and Progress:
The patient responded favorably to steroid medication, and her general condition and muscle involvement improved significantly from the first week of treatment. A subsequent lung high-resolution computed tomography (HRCT) showed evolution into diffuse interstitial involvement, and hence, mycophenolate mofetil was added at the fifth week of steroid treatment. Currently, PM is slightly active, along with a fibromyalgic/depressive syndrome. The patient was discharged from the hospital following a satisfactory response to treatment and clinical stabilization.

Diagnosis:
Polymyositis with diffuse organizing pneumonia

DISCHARGE SUMMARY:

Patient's Name: N/A
Medical Record Number: N/A
Date of Admission: N/A
Date of Discharge: N/A

HOSPITAL COURSE:

The patient, a 75-year-old Caucasian female, presented to the emergency department with progressive dizziness, weakness, early satiety, and chest heaviness. A review of symptoms was negative for abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, hematochezia, melena, and bone pain. The patient had a remote history of acid reflux disease, history of colonic diverticular disease, and regular use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDS). Physical examination was notable for pallor, tachycardia, and positive fecal occult blood.

Laboratory testing revealed a hemoglobin count of 7.6 g/dL, prompting further evaluation for a gastrointestinal (GI) source for the bleeding. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) revealed erosive gastritis and duodenitis as well as a non-obstructing Schatzki ring at the gastroesophageal (GE) junction. The pathological evaluation of the gastric and duodenal samples was positive for signet ring carcinoma, favoring a presumptive diagnosis of linitus plastica. However, further investigation revealed an invasive lobular carcinoma in the chest wall and peritoneum.

The patient received one unit of packed red blood cells and symptoms improved. She was subsequently started on hormonal therapy with anastrozole, and later on the cyclin-dependent kinase (CDK) inhibitor, palbociclib.

Given the high suspicion for a breast primary, a full thickness biopsy of the inframammary nodular lesions was attempted. Additionally, the patient underwent abdominal laparoscopy with peritoneal biopsies from the diaphragm, falciform ligament, and lower pelvic peritoneum. The patient was emotionally distraught and anxious after receiving the diagnosis. She received appropriate support and counseling from qualified providers.

The patient was noted to have metastatic breast carcinoma with marrow replacement, and has been scheduled for routine oncological follow up.

DISCHARGE DIAGNOSES:

1. Invasive lobular carcinoma in the chest wall and peritoneum
2. Metastatic breast carcinoma with marrow replacement

DISCHARGE INSTRUCTIONS:

The patient has been discharged to her home with instructions to follow up regularly with her oncologist for further management. The patient should report any new symptoms, such as bone pain or neurologic deficits, to her oncologist immediately. The patient should continue taking all prescribed medications, and follow a healthy and balanced diet. The patient should also engage in regular physical activity as tolerated, and avoid smoking and excessive alcohol intake.

FOLLOW UP INSTRUCTIONS:

The patient is scheduled for routine oncological follow up. She should also follow up with her primary care physician as soon as possible for further management of her medical conditions. The patient should obtain all necessary diagnostic testing and imaging as recommended by her healthcare providers.

MEDICATIONS:

The patient is currently prescribed hormonal therapy with anastrozole, and later on the cyclin-dependent kinase (CDK) inhibitor, palbociclib. The patient should continue taking all prescribed medications as directed by her healthcare providers.

SUMMARY:

The patient presented to the emergency department with progressive symptoms including dizziness, weakness, early satiety, and chest heaviness. Further evaluation revealed an invasive lobular carcinoma in the chest wall and peritoneum. The patient received one unit of packed red blood cells and was subsequently started on hormonal therapy with anastrozole, and later on the cyclin-dependent kinase (CDK) inhibitor, palbociclib. She has been discharged to her home with instructions to follow up regularly with her oncologist for further management.

Chief Complaint: Painful oral ulcer

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted with a painful oral ulcer, which had developed 6 weeks prior. She had a history of aphthous stomatitis and received systemic steroid treatment. However, her condition worsened with an erythematous maculopapular rash on her body, conjunctival injection, fever, diarrhea, and weight loss. Leukocytosis and eosinophilia were noted. Stevens-Johnson Syndrome (SJS) was suspected, and she was treated with systemic steroids, which showed slight improvement in skin condition but unresponsiveness in stomatitis.
A skin biopsy showed interface dermatitis and subepidermal blister formation with basal vacuolization consistent with PNP. Additional tests showed IgG deposition on normal human skin, mouse bladder epithelium, and mouse lung epithelium. The patient was ultimately diagnosed with stage IV follicular lymphoma with BO and invasive pulmonary aspergillosis. 
Chemotherapy resulted in a complete remission of lymphoma, which was confirmed through positron emission tomography. The patient's stomatitis and skin rash were well-maintained with a low-dose steroid therapy of 5mg/day for 8 months. However, she developed BO and invasive pulmonary aspergillosis, which led to respiratory failure. 

Course of Treatment:
Treatment included chemotherapy with rituximab, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, and prednisolone, which resulted in complete remission of the patient's lymphoma. The patient was also treated with a low-dose steroid therapy of 5mg/day, which maintained the improvement of stomatitis and skin rash. 

Follow-Up Care:
No specific follow-up care is necessary since the patient passed away from respiratory failure. 

Diagnosis:
The patient was diagnosed with PNP, which was later associated with stage IV follicular lymphoma with BO and invasive pulmonary aspergillosis.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: Not specified in case report
Gender: Male
Age: 34
Medical Record Number: Not specified in case report
Admission Date: Not specified in case report
Discharge Date: Not specified in case report
Length of Stay: Not specified in case report

Hospital Course:
The patient presented with right hypochondrium abdominal intermittent pain and jaundice lasting for 1 month. Physical examination revealed dim and blackish complexion, jaundice, abdominal bulge, and positive shifting dullness. The levels of serum IgG4 were increased in his younger sister, his daughter, and the patient himself.

Laboratory results showed no abnormalities in hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg), hepatitis C virus antibody (anti-HCV), anti-mitochondrial antibody (AMA), anti-nuclear antibody (ANA), smooth muscle antibody (SMA), antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA), blood and urine amylase or tumor markers. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the liver demonstrated liver cirrhosis and mild dilatation in some intrahepatic bile ducts.

A liver biopsy was performed that indicated fibrosis and fibrotic change surrounding the bile ducts, infiltration of abundant lymphocytes and mild levels of plasma cells, and cholestasis in peripheral hepatocytes with local biliary thrombosis in the enlarged portal area. IgG immunostaining of liver biopsy showed that only scattered IgG-positive plasma cells can be observed. IgG4 immunostaining of liver biopsy demonstrated infiltration of few IgG4-positive plasma cells (1–3 cells/ hpf).

At first, IgG4-SC was suspected, and oral steroid therapy was initiated at 40 mg/day, but the jaundice did not improve. The patient's condition gradually deteriorated, and he eventually developed severe complications after steroid therapy. Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) was conducted that showed irregular narrowing of the intrahepatic bile ducts, and endoscopic nasobiliary drainage (ENBD) was performed. A colonoscopy confirmed chronic colitis. The diagnosis of primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC) was strongly suspected based on a lack of response to steroid therapy and ERCP.

The patient underwent liver transplantation (LT) when his vital parameters were stabilized. Histopathological findings of the liver during operation showed fibrotic change, atrophied biliary epithelial cells, and onion-skin fibrosis in the enlarged portal area. IgG immunostaining of liver showed that only scattered IgG-positive plasma cells can be observed. IgG4 immunostaining of liver demonstrated infiltration of few IgG4-positive plasma cells (1–3 cells/ hpf), which were compatible with PSC. After LT, his quality of life improved markedly.

One year after LT, the serum IgG4 levels of his younger sister, his daughter, and the patient himself were above the upper limit of normal (ULN) range. HLA-DRB1∗07:01, 07:01 was found in both his younger sister and the patient himself, and HLA-DRB1∗07:01, 09:01 was found in his daughter. Three years after LT, liver function values show that alanine aminotransferase (ALT) and aspartate aminotransferase (AST) were in the normal range. An abdominal ultrasonography showed no obvious abnormalities.

Summary:
The 34-year-old male patient with right hypochondrium abdominal intermittent pain and jaundice lasting for 1 month was diagnosed with liver cirrhosis and mild dilatation in some intrahepatic bile ducts based on physical examination and laboratory results. IgG4-SC was suspected initially, and oral steroid therapy was started, but there was no improvement in the jaundice. The patient was diagnosed with PSC based on a lack of response to steroid therapy and ERCP and underwent LT when his vital parameters were stabilized. One year after LT, the serum IgG4 levels of his younger sister, his daughter, and the patient himself were above the ULN range. HLA-DRB1∗07:01 was found in both the patient and his younger sister, and HLA-DRB1∗07:01, 09:01 was found in his daughter. Three years after LT, liver function values show that ALT and AST were in the normal range. An abdominal ultrasonography showed no obvious abnormalities. The patient's quality of life significantly improved after LT.

Hospital Course:

The patient, an 82-year-old Asian Japanese female, was admitted to our hospital with shortness of breath and was diagnosed with pneumonia. She had a history of rheumatoid arthritis (RA) and had been previously admitted for pneumonia and bronchiectasis. The initial treatment with intravenous ceftazidime was initiated, and the patient’s symptoms improved almost completely.

On the 14th day of admission, the patient’s respiratory status rapidly deteriorated and a chest computed tomography (CT) scan revealed areas of ground-glass opacity (GGO) bilaterally. Laboratory test values also showed elevated Krebs von den Lungen-6 (KL-6), surfactant protein-D (SP-D), and plasma (1 → 3) beta-D-glucan levels. The patient’s sputum was positive for Pneumocystis jirovecii according to polymerase chain reaction (PCR) and she was immediately treated with sulfamethoxazole/trimethoprim (ST) therapy and high-dose methylprednisolone (mPSL) with empirical antibiotic therapy (ciprofloxacin).

Unfortunately, despite prompt and aggressive treatment, the patient’s respiratory status continued to deteriorate and she passed away on the 16th day of admission due to complications from suspected Pneumocystis pneumonia (PCP).

Summary:

The patient, an 82-year-old Asian Japanese female with a history of RA and previous admissions for pneumonia and bronchiectasis, was admitted for pneumonia and treated with intravenous ceftazidime. However, the patient’s respiratory status rapidly deteriorated and a chest CT revealed areas of ground-glass opacity (GGO) bilaterally. Laboratory test values showed elevated levels of KL-6, SP-D, and plasma (1 → 3) beta-D-glucan, and the patient was diagnosed with suspected Pneumocystis pneumonia (PCP). The patient was treated with sulfamethoxazole/trimethoprim (ST) therapy and high-dose methylprednisolone (mPSL) with empirical antibiotic therapy (ciprofloxacin), but unfortunately passed away on the 16th day of admission.

The patient was admitted to the hospital with complaints of right flank pain, low-grade fever, nausea, anorexia, and unintentional weight loss. Upon physical examination, she was found to have tenderness to palpation in the right upper quadrant and epigastric regions. Ultrasound of the abdomen showed a well-defined complex solid-cystic mass in the neck of the pancreas. Additionally, a routine chest X-ray revealed suspicious mediastinal lymphadenopathy. A CT-guided biopsy of the pancreatic mass revealed polygonal epithelial cells with characteristic pseudopapillary changes, leading to the diagnosis of pseudopapillary tumor (Frantz tumor) of the pancreas. Special stains including vimentin and beta-catenin were positive, thus confirming our diagnosis.

The patient underwent a Whipple pancreaticoduodenectomy for her pancreatic mass and she recovered well post-operatively. On discharge, she was in a stable hemodynamic condition.

Hospital Course:
The 59-year-old African American female was admitted due to a left-sided breast mass, identified as an invasive ductal carcinoma with necrosis. The patient underwent standard neoadjuvant therapy consisting of weekly paclitaxel and 5-fluorouracil, adriamycin, and cyclophosphamide (FAC). The patient underwent a left modified radical mastectomy followed by chest wall radiation due to poor tolerance of the chemotherapy regimen. 

Diagnosis:
The surgical pathological report indicated an invasive matrix-producing (metaplastic) carcinoma with patchy necrosis and 10% ER positivity, PR and HER2/neu negative.

Treatment:
After radiation, the patient started a course of anastrozole, which was later switched to exemestane due to arthralgia. The patient presented with pulmonary metastases and metastatic lymph nodes in the mediastinum and left internal mammary region. A combination therapy of intravenous temsirolimus, intravenous bevacizumab, and liposomal doxorubicin was administered. Repeat positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT) performed after two cycles of therapy showed a decrease in the standard uptake value in one intrathoracic lymph node and complete resolution of the disease in most of the sites on a PET scan. The therapy was resumed with reasonable tolerance and continued with clinical benefit and radiological response.

Discharge Status:
The patient developed grade 4 dyspnea after 14 cycles of therapy, which indicated the progression of the disease, and the therapy was discontinued. The patient was discharged with plans for regular follow-up and care.

Discharge Summary:

Patient was admitted with complaints of high-grade fever and left-sided pleuritic chest pain of 3-week duration associated with anorexia and significant weight loss of 6 kg in the last 1 month. The patient's hemogram showed polymorphonuclear leukocytosis and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 70 mm/h. He had a fasting blood sugar value of 236 mg/dL and a postprandial value of 300 mg/dL with a urine sugar of 2%. A chest X-ray showed right upper zone fibrosis, and an ultrasound of the abdomen revealed a collection of heterogeneous echogenicity near the inferior pole of the spleen suggestive of a perisplenic abscess. 

After several diagnostic tests, the patient was diagnosed with melioidosis, a bacterial infection caused by Burkholderia pseudomallei. He was treated with 2 weeks of parenteral ceftazidime (2 g t.i.d.) followed by oral co-trimoxazole (160/800 mg t.i.d.) for 12 weeks. The patient's fever and arthritis subsided, and follow-up ultrasound showed resolution of the abscess. Chest X-ray showed improvement in the right upper lobe lesion. 

The patient's vital signs were stable upon discharge, and there were no further complaints at the time of discharge. His condition has significantly improved, and he was asked to attend regular follow-up appointments with his primary care physician. His medication list was reviewed, and the patient was advised to continue medication for his pre-existing conditions. The patient and family were instructed to monitor the patient's blood sugar level as appropriate diet and exercise guidelines were given. 

The patient was informed of the importance of following medication and lifestyle guidelines for successful management of the disease and advised to seek medical attention if the symptoms worsen. An additional patient education pamphlet was given upon discharge that outlines important lifestyle modifications and risk management practices for the disease.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Information:
Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Patient Age: 80
Gender: Female

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to the emergency department with complaints of epigastric pain, postprandial fullness, nonbilious vomiting of partially digested foods after eating, and self-induced vomiting. The patient had a weight loss for 12% of her body weight in the last month. She had been evaluated in another hospital outpatient clinic 10 days before presentation, and proton pump inhibitors had been prescribed, but her complaints had increased gradually over time and were more severe during the last week. She denied hematemesis, melena, hematochezia, fever, night sweats, or abdominal pain in the other parts of the abdomen. 

Physical Examination:
On physical examination, the patient appeared anxious. Her skin turgor was decreased. Blood pressure was 120/75 mm Hg, pulse rate 86 beats/min, and body temperature 36.4°C. Heart and chest examinations were normal. Abdominal examination revealed only epigastric tenderness. Blood tests revealed a mild renal dysfunction with urea 128 mg/dL, creatinine 1.77 mg/dL, and hypokalemia (2.8 mEq/L). A plain chest film showed an air bubble with air-fluid level in her right paracardiac region. Enlargement of the common bile duct and main pancreatic duct was detected on abdominal ultrasound. 

Diagnosis and Treatment:
The patient was diagnosed with upside-down intrathoracic stomach related to Morgagni hernia and intrathoracic gastric volvulus. After a total parenteral nutrition was started unsuccessfully, the patient underwent laparoscopic mesh repair of the hernia defect and reduction of the stomach and other abdominal structures to the abdominal cavity. The postoperative course was uneventful, and the patient was discharged on hospital day 12.

Follow-up Plan:
The patient was discharged from the hospital and recommended to follow-up with the gastroenterology clinic for further monitoring.

- Radiographs of the thigh were suggestive of fibrous dysplasia.

- Histopathological examination was suggestive of intramuscular myxoma.
- The patient was managed with weekly oral bisphosphonates for fibrous dysplasia, which was stopped after 1.5 years.
- A regular MRI every 6 months was advised to assess the recurrence and interval enlargement of the remaining two lesions.
- The patient was pain-free with no recurrence at the latest follow-up after 2 years.

Diagnosis at discharge:
- Mazabraud’s syndrome
- Fibrous dysplasia

Follow-up instructions:
- Regular MRI every 6 months to assess the recurrence and interval enlargement of the remaining two lesions.

Discharge Summary

Patient Name: [Name]
Medical Record Number: [Number]

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted with lower extremity edema and proteinuria on urinalysis. A renal biopsy established the diagnosis of lambda light chain amyloidosis. Treatment included melphalan- and dexamethasone-based chemotherapy followed by autologous stem cell transplantation. Unfortunately, despite therapy, total serum-free light chain levels and massive nephrotic syndrome persisted. Nine months later, the patient underwent hand-assisted laparoscopic ligation of both native ureters to decrease daily urinary protein loss and restore plasma oncotic pressure. Post-operative renal ultrasound confirmed mild hydronephrosis. During the 12-day hospitalization, nutritional and functional status improved, and he was dismissed home on long-term hemodialysis requiring minimal assistance for ambulation.

Final Diagnoses:
Lambda light chain amyloidosis with massive nephrotic syndrome and autonomic dysfunction with disabling orthostatic hypotension.

Procedures:
Hand-assisted laparoscopic ligation of both native ureters.

Follow-Up Plans:
The patient will follow up with the nephrologist for long-term management of his renal disease. Hemodialysis will be continued as needed. Further imaging studies may be considered to evaluate the patient's renal function.

Discharge Summary:

Hospital Course: The patient underwent a simple orthodontic preprosthetic treatment to address a scissor-bite between the upper and lower second molars on the right side. A buccal orthodontic button was placed on the crown of the upper second molar and another button on the lingual surface of the lower second molar. An orthodontic elastic was worn all day, except during meals and oral hygiene. The patient was recalled monthly to monitor tooth movements. After a few months, the patient experienced discomfort in the gum at the level of the second lower molar, where the rubber band was applied. A clinical examination showed slight mobility of the lower molar and a periapical radiograph revealed a small periodontal angular defect mesial to the molar. Elastic use was suspended, and the lingual button removed. Further treatment included subgingival root planning under anesthesia, chlorhexidine gel insertion, and a systemic antibiotic therapy. A week later, rather than an improvement, significant mobility of the lower molar was observed and the worsening of the mesial angular defect affecting the root length was noted. Intraoral elastic around the root was discovered during the extraction procedure, which was not visible in the radiological examination.

Condition at Discharge: The patient was discharged after extraction of the second lower molar.

Discharge Medications: None prescribed.

Discharge Instructions: The patient was advised to maintain a good oral hygiene routine, including regular brushing and flossing. The patient was instructed to avoid hard and sticky foods for a few days after the extraction and to avoid using a straw for about a week. The patient was asked to contact the dentist if any signs of infection, such as swelling, fever, or pain, were observed.

Follow-Up Care: The patient is advised to schedule regular dental check-ups to ensure the good health of the remaining teeth and implant success.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [Redacted]

Hospital Course:
A 9-year-old male patient was admitted to our hospital with sudden loss of vision in his left eye for the past 10 days, following an episode of vigorous eye rubbing. On examination, corneal ectasia with Vogt's striae was observed in the right eye along with a superficial corneal scar. The left eye exhibited dense stromal edema along with a central corneal ectasia, indicating acute hydrops. A diagnosis of bilateral keratoconus with left eye acute hydrops was made based on the clinical findings.

Treatment and Procedures:
The patient underwent pneumodesmetopexy with C3F8 in the left eye, with AC paracentesis using a 26-gauge needle under aseptic conditions. Air was first added to completely fill the anterior chamber (AC) and then replaced with 14% of C3F8 to fill two-thirds of the AC. Topical antibiotics and steroids were prescribed, and the patient was advised to remain in a supine position postoperatively.

Outcome:
The patient has been followed up for 12 months, and the corneal edema has completely resolved. The patient currently has a nebular grade corneal scar and the best-corrected visual acuity is 6/9 (with contact lens). Intraocular pressure (IOP) has been normal postoperatively.

Impressions and Plan:
The patient was treated for bilateral keratoconus with left eye acute hydrops through pneumodesmetopexy with C3F8. The patient’s corneal edema completely resolved, and the best-corrected visual acuity has improved with contact lens. The patient has been discharged with long term follow-up recommended.

History of Present Illness:
The patient, a professional ice hockey player, with a history of multiple concussions (2015, 2017, 2018) was assessed for post-traumatic symptoms on December 3rd, 2018, twenty days after the last head trauma. He reported blurred vision, fogginess, fatigue, nausea and sensitivity to light immediately after the last hit. The patient tried to resume Return to Sport protocol but had to discontinue it after reaching the non-contact training level on the ice. The predominant problems were identified in the visual and vestibular domains and were attributed to Visual Vestibular and Cervico-ocular Syndromes.

Physical Examination:
The clinical neurological examination identified impairments in the postural stability during ocular-motor tasks and exposure to OKN stimulation, particularly in situations with eyes closed. Positioning maneuvers for all six semi-circular canals showed no signs of Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV). VID symptoms were identified using Situational Characteristic Questionnaire (SCQ) and specific Visual Vertigo Questionnaire using an Analog Scale (VVAS).

Diagnostic Tests:
Laboratory-assisted vestibular and ocular-motor tests were normal [Video head impulse test, ocular, and cervical Vestibular Evoked Myogenic Potential (oVEMP-cVEMP)]. Vestibulo-oculography showed a pathological binocular cyclorotation to the left, and Sensory Organization Test (SOT) and Head-Shake SOT tests indicated marginal vestibular deficiency. The gaze stability test (GST) and active dynamic visual acuity (DVA) tests were normal.

Summary:
The patient's symptoms were attributed to both Visual and Vestibular dysfunction, causing reduced gaze stabilization and VID. No imaging tests were performed in this case. The patient was provided with diagnostic and therapeutic information and was willing to participate in this clinical case's purpose.

Patient Name: N/A												Date of Admission: August 4, 2015							
Sex: Male																				Date of Discharge: N/A							
Age: 6 years old																		Length of Stay: N/A									

History and Findings:
The patient is a 6-year-old male who presented with quickly progressive binocular vision loss in 38 days. The patient experienced mild night blindness one year prior to admission. The patient's visual function continued to deteriorate over time. On admission to our ophthalmic center, his intraocular pressure was within normal range. There were many small nodules found on the surface of his bilaterally irises. Both of his optic discs were pale, and the retinal vessels were attenuate. The midperipheral fundus appeared mottled bilaterally, but no bone spicule-like pigmentation was found. Physical examinations showed no other abnormalities. 

Diagnostic Tests and Results:
Fluorescein fundus angiography revealed hyper- and hypofluorescence in the posterior fundus with mottled lesions. Results of optical coherence tomography showed thinning and atrophy in the outer retinal segment, leaving the ellipsoid zone of the fovea intact. Scopic and photopic electroretinogram responses were extinguished in both eyes and no flash visual-evoked potential response was detected. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed several demyelination spots of the right frontal and parietal lobes, and bilateral optic nerve enlarged. 

Diagnosis and Treatment:
The patient was diagnosed with retinitis pigmentosa (RP) with IDON. The patient received corticosteroid therapy for 14 days and then tapered off. After treatment, the patient's best-corrected visual acuity gradually increased. The patient also received targeted next-generation sequencing which revealed a homozygous variant in the OFD1 gene with X-linked recessive inheritance. 

Hospital Course:
The patient's condition improved 3 months later with diffuse improvement of light sensitivity in the central visual field. The concentration of thyroglobulin antibodies and anticardiolipin antibody decreased, and visual-evoked potential was normal in both eyes. Electroretinogram remained extinguished. 

Follow-up Recommendations:
The patient should continue monitoring vision and receiving regular ophthalmic evaluations. Further genetic counseling should be considered.

A 7.5-year-old female presented with fever, irritability, myalgia, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain, generalized erythematous maculopapular patches, and a positive COVID-19 exposure. On admission, physical exam revealed erythema of the throat and generalized erythematous maculopapular patches. Lymphopenia and vitamin D deficiency were noted. Testing for COVID-19 was negative. Chest CT-scan, abdominal ultrasonography, stool exam, and cultures of the urine, blood, and stool were normal. The patient was treated with diclofenac and azithromycin prior to admission and was started on ceftriaxone, hydroxychloroquine, zinc, and vitamin D upon admission. On day three, facial edema, tachypnea, and tachycardia developed. The patient was found to have marked hypoalbuminemia and anemia and was given packed cells and albumin. Blood urea and creatinine were elevated, and echocardiography showed low ejection fraction with dilated right and left ventricles. The patient was diagnosed with myocarditis and treated with vasoactive drugs, IVIG, and meropenem and vancomycin with magnesium sulphate for hypomagnesemia. CXR showed bilateral mild ground-glass opacity. On the fifth day, the patient still had persistent tachycardia and tachypnea, and another dose of IVIG was prescribed along with aspirin. Vasoactive drugs were gradually tapered as the patient's hemodynamic status improved. On the seventh day, the patient became afebrile and was discharged after 12 days with normal echocardiography and laboratory tests.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: N/A
Medical Record Number: N/A
Date of Admission: N/A
Date of Discharge: N/A

Hospital Course:

The patient was referred to our pain clinic due to an 8-day history of postural headache, which occurred following acupuncture treatment to manage chronic lower back pain caused by postlaminectomy syndrome. The patient had undergone L4-5 laminectomy 7 years prior. The physical and neurological examinations were normal. The patient was diagnosed with a postdural puncture headache (PDPH) and was placed on bed rest. An epidural blood patch (EBP) was performed, which failed to relieve the symptoms. A brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) was unremarkable, while an MRI myelogram showed an abnormal fluid signal intensity in the left lumbar area, along with the left paraspinal muscle, and soft tissues at the L3-4-5 level, probably due to CSF leakage.

After conservative care, which included bed rest, hydration, and taking acetaminophen, the patient's postural headaches persisted. A repeat fluoroscopically guided interlaminar EBP was performed with minor relief. A transforaminal EBP at the L3-4 and L4-5 levels on the left side was performed. After the transforaminal EBP, the patient's headache and other symptoms subsided without complications.

At the 2-week follow-up, the patient reported being headache-free, and the activities had returned to normal.

Diagnosis:

Postdural puncture headache (PDPH)

Treatment:

Conservative care, including bed rest, hydration, and acetaminophen, was recommended. Epidural blood patches were performed, including an interlaminar approach using autologous blood at the L2-3 level with 15ml, and a repeat of this procedure using the same volume of blood at the L4-5 level. Finally, a transforaminal EBP with 3ml autologous blood was given at each level at L3-4 and L4-5 on the left side.

Follow-up Care:

The patient was discharged after 4 days. At the 2-week follow-up, the patient reported being headache-free, and the activities had returned to normal. The patient was advised to follow-up with their primary care physician if there were any changes in the symptoms.

Date of Discharge: [Redacted]

Reason for Admission: Indistinct reddish lesion on the extensor surface of right lower leg.

Hospital Course Summary:

The patient, a 55-year-old male with HIV, was admitted to the hospital with a vague reddish flat lesion on his right lower leg. The lesion was found to be a result of vascular proliferation with primitive blood vessels dissecting in the superficial and deep dermis. The overlying skin did not show any significant lesions.

Histology examination of the skin lesion revealed spindle cell proliferation within the vertebrae of the surrounding dermis. There were also focal perivascular infiltrates of lymphocytes as well as many plasma cells. There was slight focal atypia of the lining endothelial cells. Immunohistochemical stains showed HHV-8 nuclear staining of the spindle cells, as well as focal staining of some of the endothelial cells lining the abnormal vascular spaces. CD34, CD31, and Factor VIII positive staining outlined the endothelial cells of the abnormal vascular spaces. No spirochetes or other organisms were observed in the Steiner silver stain on both biopsies.

The above clinical picture and characteristic histology were consistent with early patch stage of Kaposi’s sarcoma.

During his hospital stay, the patient was placed on a regular course of antiretroviral therapy, and was monitored closely for any changes in his condition. The patient's overall clinical picture improved significantly, and he was subsequently discharged in good health.

Discharge Instructions:

The patient has been advised to continue his antiretroviral therapy as prescribed, and to attend regular follow-up appointments with his physician. The patient was also instructed to avoid sun exposure and other harsh skin irritants or agents, as they may cause further damage to the skin. In addition, the patient was advised to monitor for the development of any new lesions or skin changes, and to report any changes immediately to his physician.

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted with a complaint of decreased visual acuity of the right eye for 1 month. A stage 2 macular hole in the right eye was noted. His decimal best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) at the first visit was 0.3 in the right eye and 1.0 in the left eye. Furthermore, his intraocular pressure (IOP) was 15 mm Hg in the right eye and 14 mm Hg in the left eye. The axial length was 23.28 mm in the right eye and 23.44 mm in the left eye. No systemic diseases such as diabetes or hypertension were observed. 

Treatment:
The patient underwent phacovitrectomy with a tamponade of 20% sulfur hexafluoride (SF6) gas under retrobulbar anesthesia. At the end of the operation, a subconjunctival injection of gentamicin was administered. 

Follow-up:
On POD1, dot hemorrhages were observed on the temporal side of the optic disk. However, neither retinal whitening nor further hemorrhage was observed on POD3, and the patient was discharged. Fundus examination on POD10 revealed blot hemorrhage, mottled retinal whitening in the macula, and cotton wool spots, and the patient's BCVA was 0.01 in the right eye, which decreased to hand motion during postoperative week 1. 

Diagnosis:
Fundus examination and fluorescein angiography (FA) showed multiple disruptions of the vessels surrounding the fovea and occlusion of the macular branch retinal artery on the inferior temporal side. Slight fluorescence leakage on the nasal side of the optic nerve head was observed. Progression of arteriovenous occlusion around the macula was observed, and the patient's macular hole was finally closed. 

Treatment:
Limaprost alfadex and kallidinogenase were prescribed as antiplatelet and vasodilator therapy, along with an oral steroid. Stellate ganglion block was performed to increase ocular circulation. 

Outcome:
The patient's postoperative BCVA was 0.2.

Patient Name: [patient name]

Gender: [patient gender]

Reason for Hospitalization:

The patient was admitted at 22 weeks’ gestation to the Emergency Department due to miscarriage. Upon admission, the patient presented shaking chills, fever, stomatitis, sore throat, abdominal pain, and minimal vaginal bleeding for the previous three days.

Hospital Course:

The laboratory findings upon admission showed a low white blood cell count and high C-reactive protein levels. After induction of labour, the patient delivered a stillborn female fetus. The patient was treated with meropenem, followed by piperacillin/tazobactam for 6 days.

Medical History:

The patient had a complex medical history of monoarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis completely resolved at 15 years of age. The patient reported bilateral gonalgia six years before the current hospitalization. Laboratory results showed severe neutropenia, but no ANCA titers. The patient had undergone a bone marrow biopsy, which was reported within normal limits. The patient presented with low neutrophil counts in the past six years but had never contracted opportunistic infections. One year before admission, the patient had delivered a male infant with severe mastitis, followed by two episodes of bilateral knee arthritis.

Postmortem Examination:

The postmortem examination on the nonmacerated female fetus revealed intra-alveolar, gastric, and intestinal neutrophils with oedema, microhemorrhages, and acute tubular necrosis (NTA) of the renal parenchyma. The placenta showed necrotizing AC corresponding to a maternal inflammatory response stage 3/3 and grade 2/2. Funisitis was noted with neutrophilic infiltrate of the umbilical vein and the two arteries with extension to Wharton’s jelly consistent with fetal inflammatory response stage 2/3 and grade 2/2. Initial thrombosis was detected in few spiral arteries of the decidua.

Microbiological Analysis:

Autoptical samples were cultured on different media and identified as K. kingae using MALDI-ToF technology. The microorganism grew in pure culture in all the samples.

Medical Treatment:

The patient was treated with Granulocyte-Colony Stimulating Factor (G-CSF) and cyclosporine (200 mg a day) in addition to hydroxychloroquine due to low neutrophil count and recent intrauterine infection.

Discharge Condition:

The patient fully recovered and was discharged after 10 days.

Follow-Up Plan:

The patient will have regular follow-up appointments with her primary care physician to monitor her medical condition.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Information:
- Name: [Patient name]
- Gender: Female
- Age: 45
- Medical Record Number: [Patient's MRN]

Hospital Course:
[Patient name] was admitted to our outpatient department complaining of a painless right-sided neck mass with drooping of the right eyelid for the past 3 years and difficulty in swallowing for 1 year. A physical examination revealed a nonpulsatile, nontender mass just below the angle of the mandible on the right side of the neck. The patient had ptosis and enophthalmos in the right eye and right-sided miosis. The findings were consistent with symptoms of a prevertebral schwannoma.

A magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan was obtained, which showed a large heterogeneously enhancing oval sharply marginated soft-tissue lesion in the prevertebral region of the right side of the neck. The mass was causing marked indentation on nasopharynx and oropharynx measuring about 7.0 cm × 5.4 cm × 3.0 cm. It appeared heterogeneously hyperintense on T2-weighted (T2W) and hypointense on T1-weighted (T1W) MRI images. No intralesional hemorrhage was present. The mass was extending from 1.5 cm below the base of the skull up to 2 cm superior to the carotid bifurcation.

Computed tomography (CT) neck with angiography was performed to assess the vascular status of the tumor and its relation to major vessels. It revealed a well-circumscribed mass measuring about 7.0 cm × 5.4 cm × 3.0 cm displacing internal carotid artery (ICA) and internal jugular vein (IJV) anterolaterally with flakes of central calcification. The mass did not invade the vascular structures.

The patient was taken up for surgery due to the symptoms. During the surgery, the main vascular structures, such as ICA, IJV, and the vagal and accessory nerves, were identified and dissected from the surface of the tumor. A well-circumscribed oval mass was separated by blunt dissection and was found to be arising from a thin nerve branch of cervical sympathetic chain. The mass could not be separated from the cervical sympathetic chain and the base of the skull. Tumor was excised piecemeal along with a part of the nerve. The excised tissue was sent for histopathological examination and was reported to be a benign schwannoma.

After the surgery, the patient's dysphagia was improved significantly, but signs of Horner's syndrome did not improve.

Summary:
[Patient name] was admitted to our outpatient department with a prevertebral schwannoma causing difficulty swallowing and drooping of the right eyelid. After a successful surgery, the patient's dysphagia improved significantly. However, the signs of Horner's syndrome did not improve.

She was again treated with a dosage-adjusted regimen of intravenous steroids plus oral prednisone and cyclophosphamide pulses, resulting in complete recovery of renal function. 

The patient remained in clinical and analytical complete remission for the next five years, except for persistently low C3 levels. In 2013, a genetic study revealed that the patient and her mother carried a mutation in heterozygosis in exon 2 of C3 gene (c.131_146del; p.Leu44Argfs*19), in addition to autoantibodies against C3, complement Factor B (FB), Properdin and Factor I (FI) detected in the patient’s serum. The patient's clinical course showed no relapse, and the treatment plan consisted of low doses of hydroxychloroquine.

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 25-year-old male from Iraq, presented with painful cutaneous swellings, abnormal gait, and recurrent high-grade fever. He had a history of chronic glomerulonephritis and was on hemodialysis twice a week. His renal allograft had failed due to acute rejection, leading to graft nephrectomy. He had previously been treated for pulmonary tuberculosis and chronic active hepatitis C with interferon, which was discontinued due to pancytopenia.

Diagnostic Assessment:
Physical examination revealed subcutaneous masses with reduced joint movements and painful indurated ulcers. Tests showed anemia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, elevated BUN and creatinine, and altered calcium and phosphorus levels. Intact PTH was significantly elevated, while 25-hydroxy-vitamin D3 was within normal limits. Alkaline phosphatase was elevated, and urine aluminum levels were elevated. A radioisotope bone-scan revealed ectopic calcification, and a CT scan showed heterotopic soft tissue calcification.

Diagnosis and Management:
The patient was diagnosed with tumoral calcinosis and treated with low-calcium dialysate, Sevelemer phosphate binder, and desferal chelation for aluminum toxicity. His fever and painful joints improved after eight sessions of dialysis, after which he was discharged to continue further treatment in his hometown.

Follow-Up and Recommendations:
The patient was advised to continue low-calcium dialysate and phosphate-binder treatment and to seek regular follow-up with his nephrologist. He was advised to maintain adequate hydration, adhere to a low-calcium and low-phosphorus diet, and avoid aluminum-containing antacids and medications. He was also advised to avoid activities that could lead to trauma or pressure on the affected areas and to seek medical attention promptly if he developed any new symptoms.

The patient had a medical history of atrial fibrillation, stroke, hypertension, hypotonic urinary bladder, lower back pain, and gastritis.

The patient, a 71-year-old Japanese woman, presented with a 10-year history of left hip pain and 1-year history of left leg edema. Plain radiographs revealed advanced osteoarthritis (OA) secondary to developmental dysplasia of the left hip. Computed tomography (CT) images and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed compression of the femoral vessels by a mass that was absent 8 years ago on a previous radiograph. The mass was diagnosed as a capital drop secondary to OA and total hip arthroplasty (THA) with resection of the mass was performed. Following surgery, the left leg edema immediately diminished and the postoperative course was uneventful. At the latest follow-up, that is, 3 years after the surgery, the patient was able to walk without an aid and was independent in all activities of daily living, with no evidence of recurrence. 

Diagnoses:
Advanced osteoarthritis secondary to developmental dysplasia of the left hip

Procedures performed:
Total hip arthroplasty (THA) with resection of the mass, using a short tapered wedge stem with a 32mm ceramic head and a 48mm cementless cup with a polyethylene liner

Histopathological findings:
Peripheral cartilage layer, with mature trabecular bone present in the central zone. No malignant cells were observed

Discharge condition:
Stable

Functional status at discharge:
The patient was able to walk independently and had no evidence of recurrence.

A 53-year-old female patient, with a history of NHL (diffuse large B-cell lymphoma [DLBCL]), presented with a short history of progressively deteriorating pain and weakness in the right lower limb. The patient had completed chemotherapy (8 × R-CHOPP) with a complete metabolic response in January 2018. Further examination revealed mild swelling over the left maxillary region with few palpable nodes in bilateral upper cervical regions. Neurological examination revealed a significant lower motor weakness in the right lower limb (2/5), and sensory examination revealed mild appendicular acral numbness to light touch. There was also evidence of mild motor weakness in both the upper limbs (4/5) without significant abnormality on sensory examination. Biopsy of the left facial swelling revealed DLBCL (CD20 positive with Ki-67 index >90%). Her cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and bone trephine did not reveal lymphomatous infiltration. A low-dose noncontrast 18FDG PET/CT examination was performed, which revealed hypermetabolic soft-tissue deposits and hypermetabolic lymph nodes in various regions, including left Level II, V, and celiac regions. There was also evidence of hypermetabolic uptake (predominantly linear pattern) over the bilateral brachial and right sacral plexuses and bilateral sciatic, right gluteal, and both femoral nerves. Based on the clinical, facial biopsy and 18FDG PET/CT findings, a diagnosis of recurrent lymphoma with NLS was made. The second-line chemotherapy was started, and after four cycles, she became asymptomatic with a resolution of left facial swelling and normalization of sensory and motor deficits too. An interim 18FDG PET/CT revealed a complete metabolic response too.

Recurrent lymphoma with NLS

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: M.S.
Age: 26
Gender: Female

Hospital Course:

M.S was admitted to the Department of Neurology for progressive weakness of the left lower limb lasting 1 year. She was diagnosed with progressive right facial hemiatrophy at the age of 5 and it remained stable for 5 years.

Clinical Findings:

Upon examination, atrophy of the facial and lingual subcutaneous tissue and muscles on the right side, a definite vertical line reaching the eyebrows on the forehead, hyperpigmentation of the right orbicular area, and pterygium of the right eye was found. Slight monoparesis of the left lower limb with exaggerated tendon reflexes and Babinski’s sign, vascular symptoms such as cooling at the left shank and foot, and lividity of the toes of the left foot were also found. Neuropsychological examination showed no cognitive impairment. ANAs were found to be present (1:100). The level of protein in the cerebrospinal fluid was slightly elevated (53 mg %). No oligoclonal IgG bands were found. The Qalb and Eindex IgG ratios were within normal limits. Ultrasonographic Doppler-duplex examination of the arteries and veins of the lower limbs did not display any pathological changes.

Medical Imaging:

Brain MR showed thinning and atrophy of the upper frontal gyrus, the medial part of precentral gyrus and paracentral lobule of the right frontal lobe on T2-weighted images and discrete hiperintensity of the white matter in the upper part of the right frontal lobe (corona radiata) on T2-weighted and FLAIR images. Single voxel proton MR spectroscopy (1H-MRS) displayed decreased level of N-acetylaspartate (NAA) and increased level of choline (Cho) and mioinositol (mI) in the upper part of the right frontal lobe. Diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) displayed significantly decreased fractional anisotropy (FA) parameter in the white matter of right upper frontal gyrus (61% of FA in the left upper frontal gyrus) and in the upper part of the right corona radiata. Fiber tractography derived from DTI showed the reduction amount of fibers and involvement of the right pyramidal tract. Lumbar-sacral part of vertebral column MR revealed small central intervertebral disc protrusions on level L4/L5 and L5/S1.

Diagnostic Testing:

In the blink reflex (BR) study, the R2 and R2′ latencies were prolonged after stimulation on the left side, but were within the normal limit after stimulation of the right side. The amplitudes of brain auditory evoked potentials (BAEPs) were lower on the right side, without any differences in latencies. Left trigeminal somatosensory evoked potentials (TSEP) had mildly longer latencies than those stimulated and recorded on the opposite side. No abnormalities were found in visual evoked potentials (VEPs) and somatosensory evoked potentials (SSEPs) from the upper and lower extremities (stimulation of median and tibial nerves bilaterally). Electromyographic examination of the left orbicular muscle of eye and neurography of both facial nerves were within the normal limits. Electroneurography and EMG of the four extremities were also within normal limits except for a low amplitude of motor responses in both peroneal nerves (motor conduction velocities were normal). Neurosensory analysis (quantitative sensory tests) discovered abnormal temperature and pain thresholds (cold pain difference between the sides was 4.1°C, heat pain 4.4°C) in the lower left limb. The cold sensation threshold was mainly elevated and the difference between the sides was 8.8°C, while the warm sensation difference was only 2.6°C. There was no sympathetic skin response (SSR) in the left foot. SSR in both hands and the right foot were present with the correct latencies. Heart rate variability (HRV) analysis did not show any pathological findings.

Diagnosis:

The patient was diagnosed with progressive right facial hemiatrophy combined with incomplete Brown-Séquard syndrome and the presence of antinuclear antibodies.

Treatment:

The patient's treatment plan was not described in the case report.

Disposition:

The patient was discharged from the hospital with recommendations to follow up with a primary care physician and a neurologist.

Patient is an 82-year-old Japanese male with a 1-month history of asymptomatic papules and nodules on the abdomen, shoulders, and extremities. Patient presented with skin nodules clustering on the forearms and corresponding skin lesions on the abdomen due to subcutaneous insulin injection therapy for type 2 diabetes mellitus. Laboratory tests showed elevated levels of ESR, CRP, sIL-2R, and HbA1c, without increase in serum calcium and ACE levels.

Skin sampling was undertaken from the abdominal lesion, and the histopathology showed a nonnecrotic, non-caseating epithelioid granuloma with a relatively lower infiltration of inflammatory cells in the lower dermis and adipose tissue.

The patient was diagnosed with sarcoidosis involving the skin, skeletal muscle, and bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy (BHL). A solitary mass in the left gluteus minimus muscle was detected on positron emission tomography screening. Ophthalmological and cardiovascular examinations did not show any granulomatous lesions.

The patient was treated with topical steroid therapy, and the abdominal skin lesion almost diminished. However, the forearm skin lesions often recurred along the venous lines during a 1-year follow-up, and the BHL remained unchanged. The sIL-2R level improved, though.

Follow-up with relevant specialists for the patient's sarcoidosis was recommended upon discharge.

This 40-year-old female presented with chief complaint of maxillary anterior prosthesis issues due to space between pontic and underlying gingiva, concave gingival contour above pontic, and color disharmony. Diagnosis revealed a Class I alveolar ridge defect with moderate buccolingual tissue loss. 

Treatment Plan:

An established surgery plan included combined technique of roll flap and interpositional graft procedure to maximize ridge augmentation and reduce the number of surgeries. The area was anesthetized to perform the roll procedure, which involved a partial-thickness crestal incision, sulcular incision, and a full-thickness rectangular pedicle, followed by the creation of a subperiosteal soft tissue pocket on the labial surface of the deformed ridge. After the roll procedure, a trapezoidal-shaped transplant was created on maxillary left premolar palatal area for onlay-interpositional graft. The de-epithelialized connective tissue region of the graft was inserted into the pouch within the deformed ridge, while the epithelialized section of the graft was positioned above the surface of the surrounding tissue at the crest of the ridge. The procedure was completed by placing sugicel into the palatal wound to control hemorrhage and subsequent suturing.

Discharge Summary:

A provisional prosthesis containing an ovate pontic was modified and placed in position immediately after the surgery. The sutures were removed after 1 week post-surgery, and the healing process was monitored. By 6 weeks post-surgery, the healing in the recipient site matured considerably, and the final fixed partial denture was delivered at 7 weeks post-surgery. 

Observations:

This prosthesis has been observed to have a natural-looking emergence profile, and the alveolar ridge remained stable until about 18 months after surgery.

In this hospital course, a 43-year-old male presented with penile pain during sexual intercourse. The patient also reported months of intermittent headaches with no neurological deficits. On examination of the genitalia, there were three superficial lesions on the dorsal shaft of his penis. The lesions were subsequently excised, and the histopathology revealed circumscribed, encapsulated, nodular lesions consisting of swirled fascicles of spindle cells, which were positive for vimentin and S-100. Characteristics of the lesion were consistent with a diagnosis of penile schwannomas.

Neurology consult was sought for investigation of a temporal headache. Clinical assessment detected no neurological deficits, and a magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain and spine was subsequently performed. This showed a well-circumscribed small nodule at the superior aspect of the cauda equina (filum terminale) at the level of L1–L2, with enhancement in its vertical length. The lesion appeared to arise from the nerve root at this site. The rest of the MRI examination was otherwise normal. Characteristics of the lesion were in keeping with a spinal schwannoma. Ongoing radiological surveillance was decided upon due to the size of the lesion, and the unobtrusive nature of the symptoms our patient was experiencing. 

The patient was observed for two years following initial diagnosis. The lesion remains stable, and the patient did not report any new symptoms. 

Condition on Discharge:

The patient was not admitted to the hospital and was not discharged. The patient is currently being observed and managed through ongoing radiological surveillance. 

Impression:

1. Penile schwannomas
2. Spinal schwannoma

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [redacted]
Medical Record Number: [redacted]
Date of Admission: February 12, 2019
Date of Discharge: March 5, 2019

Admission Diagnosis:
Henoch-Schonlein Purpura (HSP) 

Medical History:
History of haemorrhoidectomy

Hospital Course Summary:
On admission, the patient presented with abdominal pain, hematochezia and rash. Laboratory tests revealed an elevated WBC count, high GR%, high PLT count and elevated GGT levels. Abdominal ultrasound showed cholestasis and cholecystitis, while CT scans showed localized wall thickening in the small intestine along with pericardial effusion, pelvic effusion, and abdominal lymph node enlargement. The patient was diagnosed with HSP according to the 2006 European League Against Rheumatism and the Paediatric Rheumatology European Society criteria. 

On February 13, 2019, the patient had increased heart rate and dark red bloody stool twice again with the total amount of about 400 mL. Laboratory tests showed an elevated WBC count and high GR%. Considering the gastrointestinal bleeding, glucocorticoid therapy was initiated. The patient was initially treated with somatostatin and pantoprazole sodium, followed by octreotide, levofloxacin, calcium gluconate and human albumin. Glucocorticoid therapy with methylprednisolone was also administered twice a day. 

By February 15, 2019, the patient's abdominal pain was effectively relieved and heart rate normalized with an average of 80 beats per minute. However, the patient continued to experience symptoms of hematochezia intermittently. By February 19, 2019, the patient's abdominal pain and hematochezia resolved. Several drugs were prescribed, and methylprednisolone dosage was gradually reduced.

However, the patient was readmitted on March 13, 2019, due to pain recurrence. Laboratory tests showed elevated WBC count and GR%. Methylprednisolone and esomeprazole were given intravenously to relieve symptoms, and the patient showed improvements by April 1, 2019. 

On April 2, 2019, the patient was discharged and advised on a stepwise reduction of dosage of oral methylprednisolone. A follow-up appointment was scheduled to assess the patient's condition. 

Discharge Instructions:
• The patient was advised to continue taking oral methylprednisolone, as prescribed, and to follow the stepwise reduction in dosage.
• The patient was instructed to monitor their condition and report any symptoms such as abdominal pain, hematochezia, rash, vomiting, or fever.
• The patient was advised to maintain a balanced diet, drink sufficient fluids, and avoid foods that may cause gastrointestinal bleeding. 
• The patient was instructed to avoid activities that may lead to injury or trauma, as certain types of physical trauma may trigger a HSP recurrence.
• The patient was advised to promptly notify healthcare providers prior to starting any new medications or supplements, or if any unusual symptoms develop.
• Follow-up appointments were scheduled to monitor the patient's progress and adjust the medication regimen, if necessary. 

Conditions at Discharge:
Henoch-Schonlein Purpura (HSP) 

Medical Recommendations:
Continue taking oral methylprednisolone, as prescribed, and reduce dosage gradually. Monitor for symptoms and avoid activities that may trigger recurrences of HSP. Follow up with healthcare provider for monitoring and medication adjustment.

The patient presented with sudden-onset upper abdominal pain and was found to have a fist-sized mass lesion located between the stomach and pancreas on computed tomography (CT) without contrast. He was initially diagnosed with a malignant tumor with peritonitis carcinomatosa and hospitalized for further examinations and observation. However, the next day, he was found to have intra-abdominal hemorrhage and was transferred to our hospital, a tertiary emergency center, for further diagnosis and treatments.

On arrival at our hospital, the patient was alert and well oriented. A physical examination revealed moderate tenderness in his left upper abdomen with a peritoneal sign. His laboratory data showed mild leukocytosis, moderate anemia, elevated urea nitrogen level, and high serum amylase. The results of a CT with contrast demonstrated an unenhanced, high-density, homogeneous, mass-like lesion located to the ventral side of the pancreatic tail, and a large amount of ascites, which suggested a hematoma and massive intraabdominal hemorrhage. 

An emergency exploratory laparotomy was performed and a 5 cm laceration was found in the mesentery of transverse colon, which arose from the left margin of Treitz's ligament extending in the left direction. Hemostasis was achieved by suture ligations and absorbable hemostat materials were applied on the oozing points. Intraoperative blood transfusion was performed, and the operation was uncomplicated except for temporary paralytic ileus. The patient was discharged in a good postoperative condition on the postoperative day 20.

During the patient's hospital stay, we discovered that he had a history of intractable constipation and had a habit of massaging his abdomen to facilitate defecation, which likely caused the laceration. We advised the patient to avoid massaging his abdomen in the future and to seek medical attention if he experiences any abdominal symptoms.

In summary, the patient with a medical history of prostate cancer, endoscopic polypectomy, and chronic constipation presented with sudden-onset upper abdominal pain and was found to have intra-abdominal hemorrhage due to a mesenteric laceration caused by self-massage for defecation. An emergency exploratory laparotomy was performed to achieve hemostasis, and the operation was uncomplicated except for temporary paralytic ileus. Medical History:
The patient presented with a lateral cervical left mass and expansive lesion in lingual epiglottis versant on the right side. The patient underwent staging procedures including a contrast enhancement CT (c.e.CT) of the head and neck region and a whole-body [18F]-FDG PET/CT.

Hospital Course:
Accurate pre-treatment staging of cervical lymph nodes is essential for proper treatment planning. Moreover, regional lymph nodes involvement is one of the utmost prognostic factors regarding the patient’s outcome. To date, there is still no consensus on the best imaging modality that should be used in head and neck cancer staging, between CT, MRI, and [18F]-FDG PET/CT.

The patient was staged with a c.e.CT that showed a neck paramedian right lesion presenting an intense contrast enhancement and contralateral confluent lymph nodes compressing the jugular vein and ipsilateral small lymph nodes, of unclear nature. An overall radiological report, c.e.CT was doubtful for ipsilateral adenopathy. A whole-body PET scan was acquired, 3 min per bed position, one hour after the injection of a standard activity of 18F–FDG. It was also performed a low-dose CT for the attenuation correction.

PET scan showed an increased FDG uptake of the primary lesion in the right epiglottis and contralateral side. Noticeably, [18F]-FDG PET/CT showed no significant FDG uptake areas in the ipsilateral right cervical chain. The minimal activity of the right-sided lymph node was indistinguishable from the background activity, suggesting its benign nature.

After the staging (T1-N2b), patient underwent surgical supraglottic laryngectomy and bilateral lateral cervical lymph nodes dissection. Histopathology results showed a squamous cell carcinoma of the right lingual epiglottis side, no malignant cells in the right lateral cervical lymph nodes, while metastatic cells in the left lateral cervical lymph nodes were detected (pT1-N2b).

Patient was discharged on (Redacted). Instructions were given to the patient to attend scheduled follow-up appointments with the oncologist and returning to the hospital if any adverse symptoms occur.

Admitting Diagnosis: Chronic low back pain with suspected degenerative disease.

Principal Diagnosis: Small cell carcinoma of the prostate with solitary spinal epidural metastasis (SEM).

Hospital Course:

The patient, a 68-year-old male with a history of hypertension and adenocarcinoma of the prostate, was admitted to the hospital with chronic low back pain. On physical examination, hypoesthesia was detected in the L5 dermatome and MR imaging revealed a space-occupying lesion in the posterior epidural space at the L4/5 level. The differential diagnosis included a sequestrated lumbar disc, complicated synovial cyst, hematoma, malignant lymphoma, and epidural metastasis.

After consultation with a neurosurgeon, the patient underwent excision of the epidural mass lesion. The tumor was proven to be a small cell carcinoma and immunohistochemically the tumor was positive for CD56, synaptophysin, and CK, but with negative PSA. The pathologist indicated that the immunohistochemical findings suggested the possibility of neuroendocrine carcinoma of the small cell type and that the primary site of the tumor cells (adenocarcinoma) could not be identified. 

The patient underwent L4-L5 postoperative radiotherapy and subsequent palliative chemotherapy and radiation therapy for residual prostate cancer. Following excision of the solitary SEM of the L4/5 level, the patient's symptoms were slightly relieved. However, progression of the residual prostate cancer and lung metastasis were subsequently detected, and the patient died 11 months after excision of the solitary SEM.

Discharge Diagnosis:

Small cell carcinoma of the prostate with solitary spinal epidural metastasis (SEM).

Discharge Plan:

The patient has unfortunately passed away due to progressive prostate cancer and lung metastasis. No further follow-up is indicated.

Histopathologic examination of the tumor cells revealed a positive reaction for cytokeratin (CK) and vimentin, while immunostaining for chromogranin A (CgA) and synaptophysin (Syn) was negative.

The patient had several chronic disorders, including a 10-year history of bronchitis and emphysema, and was a smoker with a 30-pack-year history, but had no family history of lung cancer. Diagnoses:

None.

The patient is advised to continue yearly follow-up visits with a local hospital to monitor his condition. He is also encouraged to continue smoking cessation efforts.

Patient Name: [redacted]

Admission Date: [redacted]
Discharge Date: [redacted]
Diagnosis: Diffuse Large B-cell Lymphoma

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted with fever and cervical pain for which she had received antibiotics in the past. Physical examination showed multiple swollen lymph nodes in the left axillary region. CT imaging revealed axillary lymphadenopathy and bone destruction in the axis. The PET scan showed multiple lesions of the bone and bone marrow. Bone marrow aspiration revealed no large lymphoid cells. Biopsy of the left axillary lymph nodes showed absence of follicular structures and diffusely proliferative large lymphoid cells. Immunohistochemical staining confirmed that the large lymphoid cells were positive for CD20, bcl-2, and MIB-1, but negative for CD3, CD30, and EBER. The patient was diagnosed with clinical stage IV DLBCL, with low-to-intermediate risk according to the international prognostic index.

The patient received radiotherapy for the cervical lesions and declined conventional chemotherapy due to the risk of recurrent NTM infection. She was started on CAM and PSL, and her fever improved within a few days. The PSL dosage was initially 20 mg/day for 2 weeks and subsequently 15 mg/day for 2 weeks. The maintenance dosage was 10 mg/day. The patient experienced slightly reduced taste sensation, considered a side effect of long-term CAM use.

The follow-up imaging studies after 6 months showed complete remission with improvements in lymphadenopathy and lesions of the bone and bone marrow. The patient remains in complete remission 7 months after initiation of treatment.

The 67-year-old female patient with a stage 3 macular hole was admitted on [redacted] with a complaint of decreased vision in the left eye for the past one month. Slight disorganization of the photoreceptor layer was noted under the center of the fovea. By 1 year, the patient's visual acuity had improved further to 20/25, and the photoreceptor layer of the fovea had been reorganized on the OCT images.

Diagnosis:
Stage 3 macular hole, macula-spared retinal detachment with multiple breaks.

Treatment:
Pars plana vitrectomy, triamcinolone acetonide-assisted internal limiting membrane peeling, fluid-gas exchange, laser photocoagulation.

Condition on Discharge:
The patient's condition has improved significantly, with visual acuity improving to 20/25, and there being a complete reorganization of the photoreceptor layer of the fovea.

Follow-up Care:
The patient will require regular follow-up to monitor her vision and retina health.

Summary:

Hospital Course:
The patient is a 30-year-old Tunisian woman with a history of multiple surgical procedures. She was born with congenital mental retardation and had no significant family history except for renal nephrectomy in her brother when he was aged 27 years.

Medical History:
The patient was first presented to her medical practitioner at age 26 with altered bowel habits. An endoscopic examination at the time revealed rectal hamartomatous polyps treated with endoscopic polypectomy. The following year she presented with breast nodules on two separate occasions. Surgical excision was performed on each occasion and histology on each of these occasions revealed benign fibrocystic disease of the breast.

Physical Examination:
During a routine follow-up examination at age 30, she was found to have multiple abnormal physical findings. She had craniofacial abnormalities with macrocephaly, a high-arched palate, adenoid facies, additional skin lesions with multiple facial keratotic papules, and papillomatosis, particularly around the eyes, mouth, and nostrils, buccal mucosal papules with a ‘cobblestone-like’ appearance, and cutaneous verrucous papules in the acral portions of the hands, feet, palms, and soles. A breast examination revealed multiple palpable nodules. There was clinical evidence of multinodular goiter, with a prominent nodule measuring 5.5cm in the left thyroid lobe. Additional physical findings included strabismus and skeletal abnormalities with kyphoscoliosis and pectus excavatum.

Diagnostic Tests:
Laboratory investigations including renal biochemistry, liver function tests and thyroid hormones were normal. Results of a complete blood count showed iron-deficiency anemia. Excised buccal papules sent for histologic examination revealed acanthosis papillomatosis with keratosis epiderma. A breast ultrasound examination showed bilateral nodules compatible with fibrocystic disease. A gastrointestinal evaluation with endoscopy revealed esophageal, duodenal, and gastric sessile polyps ranging from 1mm to 9mm in diameter. Biopsies showed hyperplastic and adenomatous lesions associated with Helicobacter pylori and esophageal lesions composed of glucogenic acanthosis. Colonoscopy diagnosed diffuse colorectal polyposis with multiple lesions in the sigmoid and rectum. Biopsies of these polyps showed inflammatory and hyperplastic hamartomatous polyps.

Diagnosis:
The patient was diagnosed as having CS based on the syndrome testing criteria adapted by the US National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN).

Treatment:
A total thyroidectomy was performed and histopathologic examination of the specimen revealed thyroid papillary carcinoma. Our patient received ablative therapy with iodine and was treated with levothyroxine. Her iron-deficiency anemia was managed with iron supplementation. A prophylactic bilateral mastectomy was proposed, but refused by our patient.

Follow-up:
The patient has remained asymptomatic with undetectable serum thyroglobulin levels.

The patient, an 8-year-old female child, was admitted to our department due to diminution of vision in the right eye since 5 years, with headache and vomiting since 6 months. On examination, no perception of light was observed in the right eye with normal vision in the left eye. An MRI revealed a cystic lesion at the right temporo-frontal-parietal region measuring 8 × 9 × 6.5 cm. A small rounded nodule was seen on the medial aspect of the cystic lesion at the paraventricular location. The lesion was reported as a cystic astrocytoma/ganglioglioma. Endocrine workup subsequently revealed secondary hypothyroidism.  

Treatment:
The patient underwent right fronto-temporo-parietal craniotomy for drainage and marsupialisation of the cystic lesion. The cystic fluid was yellowish and machine oil-like, containing cholesterol crystals and flecks mostly over the medial side. Histological examination revealed inflamed Rathke's cleft cyst with a cystic wall lined by a flattened to pseudostratified squamous epithelium with congested blood vessels, chronic inflammatory infiltrate in the form of lymphocyte, plasma cells, and lymphoid aggregates.

Outcomes:
Postoperatively, the patient's recovery was uneventful, and the headache and vomiting subsided completely. The patient is in regular follow-up with postoperative MRI at 6 months without any recurrence.

The patient was admitted with complaints of mastication, speech, and aesthetic issues, along with dryness on the oral mucosa and thermal hypersensitivity. The patient had a history of neck swelling at the age of 12, which was diagnosed as nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) by incisional biopsy. The patient underwent a 6-month period of chemotherapy followed by 3 months of radiotherapy. During the oncologic treatment, tooth brushing was prohibited, and the patient did not perform any oral hygiene procedures. The patient was not referred to a dentist or informed about any oral hygiene instructions until applying to our clinic.

The patient exhibited heavy plaque accumulation, xerostomia, and excessive dental caries. Moderate gingival inflammation was also observed with no periodontal attachment loss. The patient had limited mouth opening with 25mm interincisal distance. Radiographic examination revealed periapical lesions in teeth 14, 24, 25, 26, and 36, impacted teeth 27 and 37, and altered teeth development in teeth 37 and 47 due to oncologic treatment.

A sequential multidisciplinary treatment was planned which included extraction of hopeless teeth, initial periodontal therapy (IPT), endodontic treatments, preprosthodontic periodontal surgery, and full mouth fixed prosthetic restorations. Following treatment, the patient's mastication ability was significantly improved, and he was satisfied with his new appearance.

Discharge Condition:

The patient was discharged from the hospital in stable condition, with appointments scheduled for maintenance visits with 3-month intervals. The patient was instructed to follow adequate tooth brushing and interdental cleaning routines and to quit smoking. The patient was encouraged to chew gums with xylitol and drink water frequently during the day to dissolve the effects of xerostomia. The patient was also advised about the importance of maintaining good oral hygiene to prevent further dental issues.

The patient and the patient's parents were provided with written informed consent detailing all treatments following the case report review. They understood the risks and benefits of each procedure and agreed to the sequence of multidisciplinary treatment recommended.

The patient was advised to continue good oral hygiene practices and quit smoking to avoid further dental issues. Maintenance visits with 3-month intervals were scheduled to ensure proper oral health. The patient was encouraged to seek medical attention if any abnormal signs or symptoms occurred.
