The patient, a 27-year-old pregnant female with a history of congenital heart disease, was admitted to the hospital at 34 weeks of gestation due to pain abdomen for 2 days. On examination, the patient was found to be cyanotic with clubbed fingers and raised Jugular venous pressure, and there was a pansystolic murmur and bilateral basal crepitations present. The patient was diagnosed to have a large perimembranous ventricular septal defect (VSD) with bidirectional shunt and severe pulmonary hypertension (PAH), tricuspid regurgitation, and a dilated right atrium seen on echocardiography.

Treatment:

The patient had been on irregular treatment with sildenafil 25 mg twice a day since 4 months, and given her previous obstetric history, lower segment cesarean section (LSCS) was planned. All risks were explained, and written informed consent was obtained. Prophylaxis against bacterial endocarditis was provided, and an epidural catheter was inserted for pain management during the surgery. Ampicillin and gentamicin were administered as per standard prophylaxis guidelines.

Procedure:

Over a period of 30 min, a total of 7cc of lignocaine with adrenaline solution and 8 cc of bupivacaine with 25 μg of fentanyl produced a block height of T8 tested to touch with blunt forceps. CVP was maintained between10-12 mm throughout surgery. The procedure was uneventful, and after delivery of the baby, furosemide 10 mg was given intravenously. A total of 450 cc of colloid was given.

Postoperative:

After surgery, the patient was shifted to the intensive care unit (ICU) for monitoring and was discharged on the 10th day. Epidural analgesia was maintained with 0.125% bupivacaine and 20 μg of fentanyl every 8 hourly for 72 h.

Summary:

The patient was diagnosed to have a large perimembranous ventricular septal defect (VSD) with bidirectional shunt and severe pulmonary hypertension (PAH), tricuspid regurgitation, and a dilated right atrium seen on echocardiography. She had a history of a stillborn delivery in her previous pregnancy and was advised against conceiving again, but she refused. She had been on irregular treatment with sildenafil, and given her previous obstetric history, LSCS was planned. The procedure was uneventful, and the patient was discharged on the 10th day. Epidural analgesia was maintained for pain management after surgery.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Date of Admission: [REDACTED]
Date of Discharge: [REDACTED]
Admitting Diagnosis: Generalized Bullous Fixed Drug Eruption (GBFDE)
Final Diagnosis: Generalized Bullous Fixed Drug Eruption (GBFDE)

Hospital Course:
A 24-year-old male was admitted to the hospital with widespread dull erythema over the body with superimposed vesiculobullous lesions over the trunk and limbs. The patient had taken multiple medications including cetirizine, paracetamol, and pseudoephedrine prior to the episode. The patient reported having 4-5 similar episodes in the past, each of increasing severity than the previous one. After being treated with cyclosporine, the lesions healed with hypopigmentation within 5-7 days. The patient was discharged in good general health.

Diagnosis:
The patient was diagnosed with Generalized Bullous Fixed Drug Eruption (GBFDE), a rare variant of FDE, characterized by necrotic keratinocytes and subepidermal blistering. GBFDE has been associated with certain drugs, such as cetirizine, that trigger the immune system and lead to the widespread blisters and erosions. 

Treatment:
The patient was treated with cyclosporine, a potent inhibitor of interleukin-2 (IL-2), which suppresses T lymphocyte functions and inhibits the activation of the Fas receptor–Fas ligand system. Cyclosporine's target of action specifically involves T cells and has a superior therapeutic effect over prednisone or intravenous immunoglobulins (IVIG).

Follow-Up:
The patient reported severe burning and erythema in the healed lesions on self-administration of tablet paracetamol for fever after 6 months, thereby confirming the cause of GBFDE.

Prognosis:
GBFDE has been thought to have a favorable prognosis, but a case-control analysis of 58 patients with GBFDE matched by age and extent of skin detachment showed a nearly identical mortality rate to SJS/TEN, which questions the benign nature of GBFDE. Severe cases of GBFDE should be regarded with the same level of urgency as cases of SJS/TEN, and the necessity of offering an effective treatment is of paramount importance.

Discharge Instructions:
The patient was advised to avoid taking medications that might trigger a similar episode in the future. The patient was also recommended to follow-up with their primary care doctor in case of any recurrence of the symptoms.

Hospital Course: 
The patient was admitted to the hospital in September 2017 for coronary artery bypass grafting, mitral valve plasty, tricuspid valve plasty, and aortic valve replacement. A left ventricular lead was surgically placed, and the pulse generator was upgraded to a CRT-D. The HeartLogicTM feature was calibrated and available for clinical use from January 2018. 

Progress Notes: 
In January 2018, the patient was in NYHA functional class II and euvolemic. Laboratory test results revealed an eGFR of 44 mL/min/1.73 m2 and a pro-BNP level of 6474 ng/L. The HeartLogicTM index was 8 which is on the upper limit of normal. On February 5th, the HeartLogicTM alert was issued as the index crossed the programmed threshold of 16. A remote data review showed that the index had gradually increased to 17 over the last 2 weeks. The patient was contacted by phone and denied having any symptoms or signs of fluid retention. Re-evaluation by phone was performed 2 weeks later. Despite the HeartLogicTM index increasing to 25, the patient still reported being asymptomatic, although he admitted to having a larger fluid and salt intake than advised. The patient was recommended to adjust his intake, and the HeartLogicTM index stabilized, but did not decrease. Accordingly, an outpatient visit was scheduled.

At the outpatient clinic, the patient initially denied having symptoms. However, despite cardiac rehabilitation, the patient experienced mild shortness of breath during exercise. Physical examination showed elevated jugular venous pressure and mild ankle oedema. Laboratory testing revealed a decrease in renal function with an eGFR of 33 mL/min/1.73 m2 and an increase in the pro-BNP level to 9650 ng/L. The HeartLogicTM index was 22. The patient was gradually developing signs of fluid retention, and the dosage of bumetanide was increased. After the adjustment, the patient's exercise capacity improved, and the cardiac rehabilitation program was successfully completed. The HeartLogicTM index also declined to 0. 

Follow-up: 
At a follow-up visit in April, the patient had no signs of fluid retention. Laboratory testing revealed improvement in renal function with an eGFR of 42 mL/min/1.73 m2 and a decline in the pro-BNP level to 4173 ng/L. Currently, the patient is in a clinically stable condition (NYHA functional class II), and no decompensated heart failure hospitalizations have occurred. 

Impression: 
The HeartLogicTM index successfully incorporated into a structured heart failure care path. Additionally, the index may be of value in guiding ambulant medication adjustments.

Discharge Diagnosis: Dual infection caused by Mycobacterium szulgai and M. intermedium

Hospital Course:

The patient, a 46-year-old female with a history of laparoscopic appendectomy in 1998, presented with discharging sinuses over the lower anterior abdominal wall for the past two years. The initial incision wound did not heal properly and was later reopened after one month. Despite receiving treatment off and on with multiple injectable and oral antibiotics, there was no definitive microbiological diagnosis prior to admission. The patient did not have any history of local trauma/injury, immunosuppressive drugs/corticosteroids, or tuberculosis.

On admission, a previous surgical scar was noticed on the lower anterior abdominal wall in the midline with a large keloid formed over it. Six sinus openings were noted over the lower anterior abdominal wall with a single sinus discharging pus at the time of presentation. Tenderness was noted over and around the sinuses. Gram variable bacilli and numerous acid-fast bacilli were observed in the discharge. Following culture and antibiotic susceptibility testing, the patient was started on a combination of rifampicin, ethambutol, and clarithromycin.

After one month of therapy, there was no pus discharge from the sinus. The patient was advised to continue the therapy and report back to the hospital after another month. After two months of therapy, the patient was found to be completely all right with no such discharge.

Discharge Medications:

The patient was advised to continue taking rifampicin 600 mg once daily, ethambutol 600 mg once daily, and clarithromycin 500 mg twice daily.

Follow-Up:

The patient was advised to continue with periodic follow-up based upon clinical response and microbiological response.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [Name]
Gender: Male
Age: 7 years
Date of Admission: [Date]
Date of Discharge: [Date]

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to the clinic with a painful tumor in the lateral-middle third of the right clavicle with functional impotence of the limb. The X-ray showed a radiolucent diaphyseal lesion, which resulted in the suspicion of a pathological fracture on active ABC. The diagnostic imaging studies, including computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging, confirmed the presence of a cavitated, multiloculated lesion in the clavicle, and a scintigraphy study was compatible with cystic bone injury and bone remodelling in relation to the prior fracture. A complete resection of the cyst was performed without prior puncture biopsy, and a block resection was carried out. The entire excised cyst was removed, preserving the epiphyseal ends. The reconstruction of the resulting critical bone defect was done by a free autologous bone graft taken subperiosteally from the diaphysis of the ipsilateral fibula. The length of the acquired graft was 3 mm greater than the bone defect length to ensure its compression fit. An intramedullary titanium nail was introduced in a retrograde-anterograde manner to stabilize the graft. The surgery was uneventful, and the histopathological analysis confirmed the diagnosis of ABC, with free resection margins.

After the surgery, the patient was immobilized for three weeks by using a short posterior splint and was kept in a sling for four weeks. Active mobilization of the limb was allowed progressively, avoiding risky sports for six months. The clinical and radiographic evolution was satisfactory, and a satisfactory radiographic incorporation and consolidation of the graft were observed at five months postoperatively. The joint balance of the shoulder was completely restored six weeks after the intervention. The intramedullary nail extraction was performed 14 months after the intervention, without incidents. After 18 months of the intervention, the child presented complete mobility of the shoulder, without pain or deformities, and the complete reconstruction of the donor area of the graft could be verified. Currently, after more than two-and-a-half years of follow-up, the child maintains an optimal functional outcome, without complications or sequels at the level of the clavicle or in the donor area of the fibula, and without signs of recurrence of the lesion.

Diagnosis:
- Painful tumor in the lateral-middle third of the right clavicle with functional impotence of the limb
- Radiolucent diaphyseal lesion with insufflated and well-delimited boundaries
- Pathological fracture on active ABC

Treatment:
- Complete resection of the cyst, preserving the epiphyseal ends
- Impregnation of bone surfaces and resection bed with lauromacrogol solution to reduce the risk of local recurrence
- Reconstruction of the critical bone defect with free autologous bone graft taken subperiosteally from the diaphysis of the ipsilateral fibula
- Stabilization of the graft by means of an intramedullary titanium nail

Hospital Course Summary:
The patient was admitted to our clinic with a painful tumor in the lateral-middle third of the right clavicle with functional impotence of the limb. After diagnostic imaging studies, a complete resection of the cyst was performed without prior puncture biopsy, and a block resection was carried out. Reconstruction of the critical bone defect with a free autologous bone graft taken subperiosteally from the diaphysis of the ipsilateral fibula was done. Currently, more than two-and-a-half years after the intervention, the child maintains an optimal functional outcome, without complications or sequels at the level of the clavicle or in the donor area of the fibula, and without signs of recurrence of the lesion.

A 66-year-old female patient was admitted to the Department of Periodontics, M. S. Ramaiah Dental College and Hospital, Bangalore, with the complaint of burning sensation in the gums and bleeding gums for the past one month.

Medical History:
The patient had no relevant drug history or significant medical history. She had not received any dental treatment before.

Examination Findings:
On extra oral examination, the patient had some obvious skin lesions on the scalp and a hyperkeratotic plaque behind her left ear. Intra oral examination of gingiva revealed reddish marginal, attached gingiva and interdental papilla in both maxillary and mandibular anterior region with desquamation of epithelium present in certain regions.

Diagnosis:
Based on the clinical and histopathologic features, the lesion was suggestive of discoid lupus erythematosus.

Treatment:
Hand scaling was performed as gently as possible in order to minimize tissue disruption. Soft tooth brush and mouth rise (chlorhexidine 0.12%) was recommended. Triamcinolone acteonide oral paste was advised to apply two to three times per day.

Follow-up:
The patient was recalled for follow-up and maintenance.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Information:
- Name: [Name Redacted]
- Age: 65-year-old
- Gender: Female
- Diagnosis: Malignant melanoma of the urethra with positive surgical margins

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to our hospital with a 6-month history of difficulty in voiding associated with a small mass at the urethral meatus. Physical examination revealed a small tan-colored polypoid growth protruding from the external urethral meatus, mimicking a urethral caruncle, without any evidence of inguinal lymphadenopathy. Urethral carunclectomy was performed with uneventful postoperative recovery. The pathological examination of the specimen demonstrated malignant melanoma of the urethra with positive surgical margins. Further investigations revealed the presence of residual tumor in the last 0.5 cm of the urethra with no abnormal findings in either the proximal urethra or the urinary bladder. Thus, a radical urethrectomy with bladder preservation and a continent catheterizable stoma (Yang-Monti technique) was performed to achieve 2.5 cm margins. The patient tolerated the procedure well, and there were no complications postoperatively.

Outcome:
The final pathology report revealed a small focus (3mm) of a residual malignant melanoma with negative surgical margins. Currently, one year after the surgery, the patient is in complete clinical remission with no evidence of disease.

Follow-up Recommendations:
The patient will require long-term follow-up with regular monitoring and imaging tests to detect any signs of disease recurrence. The patient is instructed to perform self-intermittent catheterization and remain continent. Follow-up consultations with an oncologist and urologist are advised to monitor the patient's condition and ensure optimal management.

Patient Name: N/A

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 60-year-old female, was admitted to the hospital with a 4-day history of right upper quadrant pain, which was treated with oral antibiotics for suspected acute cholecystitis. The patient had a past medical history of Type-2 diabetes and hypertension. Upon examination, the patient was found to have a palpable liver edge, right upper quadrant tenderness, and multiple hypoechoic lesions in the liver suggestive of multiple metastases. Further imaging revealed a 6 × 7 cm tumor mass in the right iliac fossa, associated lymphadenopathy, and further large lymph nodes in the aorto-caval and para-aortic regions.

During laparotomy, a large tumor mass was identified, which appeared to originate from the ascending colon. A right hemicolectomy was performed with a primary ileo-colic anastomosis, and histological examination showed that the tumor had replaced the appendix without caecal involvement. Further immunohistochemistry revealed the tumor to be a neuroendocrine carcinoma of small cell type.

After surgical recovery, the patient was transferred to the oncology department for palliative chemotherapy. Subsequently, the patient developed a right flank abscess after one cycle of carboplatin. The abscess was drained percutaneously, and the patient was referred to the palliative care team.

At 2-months after surgery, the patient passed away, and a post mortem was not performed.

Discharge Diagnoses:
- Neuroendocrine carcinoma of small cell type

Discharge Instructions:
N/A (due to patient passing away)

A chest drain was inserted, and more than 700 mL of blood was drained. Subsequent FAST had revealed a pericardial effusion.

A Clamshell thoracotomy was started due to the patient's unstable hemodynamic status, and surgical exploration showed a massive hemothorax in the left thorax, left lung posterior lobe injury, pericardial injury, and hemopericardium with blood clots. A 10-mm defect was found in the right ventricle near the left anterior descending coronary artery. Chemical cardiac arrest was induced using ATP, and the cardiac wall was repaired surgically using a horizontal mattress suture. The patient recovered after the surgery and received intensive care in the hospital for 13 days.

Discharge Summary:

The patient was discharged after a 13-day hospital stay without complications. The postoperative echocardiographic check-ups showed a septal injury, but the patient did not exhibit any symptoms of heart failure.

The patient should avoid strenuous activities and get plenty of rest for at least two weeks. It is essential to monitor for signs of infection, such as fever, inflammation, and excessive wound discharge. The patient should report chest pain, shortness of breath, or lightheadedness immediately.

Follow-up care should include a visit with a primary care provider or specialist, depending on the patient's condition, within one week. They should return to the hospital immediately if new symptoms appear or existing symptoms worsen.

The patient's condition is stable currently, and they have been discharged home with follow-up treatment as suggested above.

Discharge Summary

Patient Name: XYZ
Medical Record Number: 12345

Hospital Course:

The patient is a 31-year-old female with acute monoblastic leukemia in first remission who underwent HLA-identical sibling HSCT following conditioning with fludarabine and busulfan on February 24th, 2014. She developed lower extremity edema at 10 months posttransplantation. Laboratory analyses demonstrated a urinary protein level of 11 g/day, a serum albumin level of 17.4 g/L, and a serum cholesterol level of 10.72 mmol/L. Immunoglobulin detection revealed low levels of IgG and normal levels of IgA and IgM. A renal biopsy revealed that the patient was diagnosed with membranous nephropathy which was considered as a manifestation of cGVHD.

Treatment:

The patient was initially treated with prednisone and CsA. Rituximab was added to CsA and prednisone when the patient did not respond to initial treatment. The patient remained steroid resistant after 8 weeks of treatment, and as a result, MSCs from the bone marrow of a third-party donor were administered. The patient had a response including a rapid fall in urinary protein and improvement in edema 2 weeks after the first MSC infusion. The 24-h urinary protein level and serum albumin level became normal at the sixth and 10th week after the first MSC infusion. CsA and prednisone were tapered at the second week after the urinary protein was normal and withdrawn at the third month.

Outcome:

At the time of this report, the patient has been off medication for 18 months, and no relapse of leukemia or NS has been documented.

Diagnosis:

The patient was diagnosed with membranous nephropathy which was considered as a manifestation of cGVHD.

Follow-up:

The patient is advised to follow-up with her healthcare provider for regular check-ups to monitor for any possible recurrence of cGVHD.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Gender: Male 
Age: 14 years
Date of Admission: [REDACTED]
Date of Discharge: [REDACTED]
Discharge Diagnosis: Dermoid cyst of conus medullaris

Hospital Course:

The patient was initially diagnosed with tuberculosis of the spine by a district registered medical officer and started on antituberculous therapy. However, the patient's condition worsened, and he was transferred to our tertiary care hospital. He complained of lower back pain, weakness, and numbness in his lower limbs. The patient's higher mental function was normal, and his cranial nerves were intact.

Upon further assessment, a reduced bulk of the flexor group of both lower limbs, hypotonia on the left side, grade 3/5 power in both the lower limbs, and areflexia bilaterally were observed. Sensory examination revealed hypoesthesia and decreased light touch and pinprick sensation in the L5/L4 dermatomes of his right lower limb. The sacral dermatomal sensations at S1/S2 levels were also impaired.

Radiological investigations showed a focal, well-defined space-occupying lesion measuring 1.50×0.6cm2, and abnormal signal intensity within the spinal canal, which was intradural as well as intramedullary in nature, compressing the conus medullaris at the D12 and L1 level. The lesion was heterogeneously intense, localized, and well demarcated. The tumor was hypointense at the T1-weighted frequency with a hyperintense signal area at the caudal end.

Surgical resection was performed through a posterior midline linear incision at the D12 and L1 level. The spinal cord was seen to be compressed and overdistended due to an intrinsic lesion, and myelotomy was performed. A well-demarcated, unilocular, grayish white intradural, intramedullary cyst was found involving the conus medullaris and extending from D12 and L1. The cyst was evacuated and near-total excision was done from the neuronal tissue. A histopathological examination revealed the diagnosis of dermoid cyst, which was confirmed by the presence of aggregates of keratinocytes along with keratin flakes.

Post-surgery, the patient showed gradual improvement in motor power to grade 4/5 in both lower limbs and restoration of light touch and pinprick sensation. After a month of follow-up, there were no abnormal neurological sequelae, and the patient was able to mobilize and walk with support.

Discharge Instructions:

The patient has been discharged on [REDACTED]. Please follow up with your primary care doctor or neurologist for further consultation. In case of any recurrence of symptoms, please return to our hospital immediately.

Signed,

Discharge Summary:

Patient: 52-year-old multiparous African American woman

Diagnosis: Urethral diverticulum

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted after presenting with syncope following a 2-day history of heavy vaginal bleeding, passing large clots, and suprapubic pain. Pelvic examination revealed blood clots in the vagina along with a friable, fibrous ulcerated lesion on the anterior suburethral vagina. A computed tomography scan revealed a soft tissue mass within the lumen of the vagina and an enlarged lymph node in the right ovarian chain. On hospital day 2, the patient underwent an examination under anesthesia with repeat biopsies, which revealed non-diagnostic pathology.

During HDs 3 through 5, the patient’s bleeding decreased significantly, and on HD 6, a second examination under anesthesia revealed biopsies negative for malignancy. A Tonsil clamp was placed into the urethra, and the urology service was intraoperatively consulted, confirming the diagnosis of urethral diverticulum. The diverticulum was excised, and a multilayered repair over the Foley catheter was performed.

On postoperative day 9, the patient re-presented with bleeding, and several rejected sutures in the necrotic tissue were removed. Interrupted mattress sutures were placed to reapproximate the tissue. Final pathology revealed benign squamous mucosa.

Treatment:

Excision of urethral diverticulum and multilayered repair over the Foley catheter.

Follow-up:

In the urology clinic 2 weeks later, a voiding cystourethrogram was performed, revealing no extravasation from the urethra or bladder. A physical examination revealed proper vaginal healing and no defects.

Disposition:

Discharged in stable condition.

The patient, a 5-year-old Chinese woman, presented to the emergency department with complaints of cough, fever, headache, vomiting, and altered interactions with her parents. She was admitted to the pediatric intensive care unit and diagnosed with sepsis and pneumonia. Empiric antibiotic therapy, immunoglobulin supply, and restricted fluid administration were given. The patient's condition deteriorated, and she became comatose, hypotensive, and suffered from arrhythmia and hypoxia. Electrocardiogram confirmed prolonged Q–T interval while the thyroid test results were received, indicating untreated hypothyroidism secondary to autoimmune thyroiditis (Hashimoto's thyroiditis). Hormone replacement was immediately started, and the patient was administered levothyroxine via nasogastric tube. She also received vasopressor, mechanical ventilation, and continuous renal replacement treatment. Two days after starting levothyroxine, her consciousness was restored, and temperature returned to normal. She was extubated on the fifth day after the initial hormone administration. The dosage of oral levothyroxine was reduced, and she was discharged on a regimen of 3 μg/kg/d once daily.

The patient was a 20-year-old female with a history of type I (von Gierke) glycogen storage disease, who was transferred to the referral hospital for liver transplant evaluation. She had recently undergone a living-related renal transplant which failed due to renal vein thrombosis. Following an allograft nephrectomy, she developed multi-organ biochemical derangement, fulminant hepatic failure, coagulopathy, metabolic acidosis, renal failure, and anemia. She was admitted with a diagnosis of hepatic coma, with investigations revealing elevated transaminase levels, hyperbilirubinemia, elevated serum amylase, and significantly elevated lactate levels.

Upon admission, a CT scan of her head and abdomen was performed. There was no evidence of intracranial bleeding, however, a lower chest infiltrate was identified, and there was suspicion of hepatic vein thrombosis. Blood cultures were drawn on admission and later found to be positive for gram-positive cocci in pairs and chains, specifically Enterococcus faecalis. The patient was started on cefotetan and vancomycin therapy.

The following day, although her lactate levels and transaminases levels decreased, her lipase levels increased, and bilirubin levels climbed. Blood and sputum cultures from the third day were positive for Enterococcus faecalis.

The patient was stable for a short period of time, but on the fourth day, she became unresponsive, had diffuse edema, and developed metabolic acidosis and shock. Blood and sputum cultures remained positive for Enterococcus faecalis. The decision was made to perform an emergency hepatectomy with portocaval shunt, as the patient's liver was suspected to be the source of her sepsis.

Unfortunately, during the surgery, the patient became bradycardic and started bleeding through her endotracheal tube. Despite cardiopulmonary resuscitation, she did not respond, and arterial blood showed a severe respiratory acidosis with decreased oxygen levels. The patient was pronounced dead and an autopsy was carried out.

Final Diagnosis:

The patient had a history of type I (von Gierke) glycogen storage disease and had recently undergone a living-related renal transplant. Following renal failure, she received a second living-related renal transplant which thrombosed and had to be removed. Subsequently, she developed multi-organ biochemical derangement, fulminant hepatic failure, coagulopathy, metabolic acidosis, renal failure, and anemia. Investigations revealed elevated transaminase levels, hyperbilirubinemia, and significantly elevated lactate levels. Blood cultures were positive for Enterococcus faecalis.

Discharge Condition:

The patient passed away during the emergency hepatectomy surgery, and an autopsy was conducted.

Discharge Summary:

Admission Date: [Date]
Discharge Date: [Date]

Patient:
The patient is a 61-year-old Japanese man who was admitted with coxalgia.

Presenting Issues:
The patient presented with coxalgia, a condition that causes pain in the hip joint. Radiography revealed osseous projections at the knee and shoulder joints. The patient had also developed coxarthrosis and severe pain of the right hip joint. The range of motion of the right hip joint was limited in flexion and abduction.

Treatment:
The patient underwent right total hip arthroplasty using the direct lateral approach. A gigantic femoral head and large diameter of the femoral neck were noted. The soft tissue appeared normal, and an incision was made in the articular capsule. Hip dislocation was difficult because of the gigantic femoral head and caused a trochanteric fracture. The bone substance of the greater trochanter, femoral neck, and femoral trochanter was poor and showed bone fragility. An acetabular cup was implanted by press fit without screws at the site of the original acetabulum. An osteotomy was performed in a more distal than usual part of the femoral neck, and a femoral polished tapered stem was implanted using bone cement. The fractured greater trochanter was fixed with tension band wiring using Kirschner wire and nylon tape. The articular capsule, gluteus minimus muscle, gluteus medius muscle, and tensor fasciae latae muscle were repaired.

Outcomes:
Postoperatively, the implant setting was unproblematic, and the exostosis at the femoral neck had been removed. Walking with full weight-bearing was permitted, and there were no complications such as dislocation or infection. Thirteen months postoperatively, the patient had no coxalgia, but the range of motion of the right hip joint was still limited in flexion and abduction. The patient had no limp and no interference with his activities of daily living. There was an ectopic ossification seen radiographically. The patient had returned to his previous work and had no difficulties with everyday activities.

Follow-Up Care:
The patient was discharged from the hospital with a crutch.

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted to our department due to complaints of mobility on the inferior implant-supported prosthesis and the superior prosthetic bridge, causing difficulty in chewing and speech. The patient reported a history of congenital dental agenesis, with complete mandibular rehabilitation with six implants and a superior bilateral canine to central incisor prosthetic bridge.
Clinical examination and orthopantomography indicated a combined horizontal and vertical osseous deficiency and active peri-implantitis in all six implants previously placed in the inferior arch, confirmed through cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT). Maxillary vertical and alveolar ridge deficiency was also noted. Bimaxillary custom-made implants were proposed, using an innovative design in the mandible including areas of endosseous support for adequate osseointegration.

The patient underwent surgery under general anesthesia. On the maxilla, a crestal incision was performed, exposing the anterior nasal spine, the pyriform apertures, the canine fossae, the zygomatic buttresses, and the posterolateral maxillae. The implant was tested and fixed with osteosynthesis screws. On the mandible, a crestal incision was performed around the arch to the contralateral side. The implant was tested, fixed with osteosynthesis screws, and bone grafting was carried out in the endosseous zone.

Abutments were placed, and flaps were closed. Prosthetic impressions were taken immediately after closure, and a provisional prosthesis was successfully adapted 12 h later, before patient discharge.

Follow-Up:

Over 1 year and 3 months of follow-up time, there were no complications. The patient reported excellent implant stability, adequate masticatory function, no implant exposure, and absence of pain.

Summary:

The patient with severe maxillary atrophy and previous mandibular all-on-6 rehabilitation with current peri-implantitis underwent bimaxillary custom-made implants. The surgery was successful with no complications, and the patient reported significant improvement in implant stability, masticatory function, and absence of pain after 1 year and 3 months of follow-up time.

Patient: 51-year-old woman with a history of myocardial infarction and suspicion of ALCAPA

Hospital Course:

The patient presented with typical chest pain and was found to have ST-T segment changes in I and aVL leads. Additionally, a left anterior descending (LAD) artery was grafted by a left internal mammary artery (LIMA) graft. Neochordae were constructed for thickened mitral valve leaflets with flail anterior segments (A1 and A2), in addition to ring annuloplasty using Sorin Memo 3D annuloplasty ring No. 30 (Sorin Biomedica Cardio S.r.l., Saluggia, Italy). 

Post-surgery, the patient's condition improved with a LVEF of 50% and mild MR, as noted in the transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) performed after cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB). 

After 10 months of follow-up, the patient was asymptomatic and had normal findings on echocardiographic examination.

Conclusion:

The patient was diagnosed with ALCAPA and underwent surgical treatment to close the anomalous left coronary artery orifice and left anterior descending (LAD) artery grafting. Mitral valve repair was also performed. The patient's condition improved post-surgery, and after 10 months of follow-up, the patient was asymptomatic with normal echocardiographic findings.

Hospital Course:
The 45-year-old female with a history of asthma and gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) presented to our clinic with a chronic productive cough. She had previously been treated with levofloxacin, which improved her symptoms but they recurred after discontinuing the antibiotic. Chest X-ray and CT scan revealed infiltrates in both lungs, along with bronchiectatic changes in the lower lobes. Her autoimmune screen came back negative for rheumatoid arthritis and Sjogren's syndrome. Immunoglobulins were elevated; however, alpha one antitrypsin and immunoglobulin E (IgE) were normal. Chronic recurrent aspiration was suspected, and esophageal pH monitoring with manometry confirmed the suspicion of chronic aspiration from severe acid reflux with an elevated DeMeester score. Bronchoscopy was performed to rule out obstructive disease and obtain samples to rule out mycobacterial disease, which were positive for heavy growth of Achromobacter xylosoxidans, subspecies denitrificans. The bacteria was responsive to levofloxacin and other antibiotics such as amikacin, cefepime, ceftazidime, gentamicin, meropenem, piperacillin/tazobactam, tobramycin, and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, but resistant to ciprofloxacin, cefotaxime, and aztreonam.

Management:
Airway clearance techniques with percussion and flutter valve and bronchodilator therapy with hypertonic saline nebulizers were initiated, and the patient was started on a 3-week course of levofloxacin. One month after stopping antibiotics, her symptoms recurred, and again, levofloxacin was initiated for two more weeks with good clinical response. She was referred for surgical intervention to address ongoing injury to the airways and prevent aspiration insult.

Discharge Condition:
The patient was discharged in stable condition.

Follow-Up:
The patient was advised to continue airway clearance techniques with percussion, flutter valve, and bronchodilator therapy with hypertonic saline nebulizers.

Admitting Diagnosis: Vaginal bleeding with complete placenta previa

Final Diagnosis: Complete placenta previa with placental vessels invading bladder, pulmonary emboli, bladder leak

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 38-year-old woman at 24 weeks of gestation, was admitted to the hospital with vaginal bleeding and a history of three previous Caesarean sections. A fetal ultrasound showed complete placenta previa with placental vessels invading the bladder, which confirmed the diagnosis. Various consultations were performed, and prophylactic administration of magnesium sulfate, antibiotics, and steroids were initiated.

On hospital day #2, the patient developed an increased oxygen requirement and tachycardia. A computed tomographic scan of the chest revealed extensive bilateral pulmonary emboli. Inferior vena cava filter placement was performed, the patient was transferred to the surgical intensive care unit, and a continuous heparin infusion was initiated.

On hospital day #6, the patient went into labor and underwent a multidisciplinary procedure. An exploratory laparotomy and repeat Caesarean section were performed, and a viable female neonate was delivered. A total abdominal hysterectomy and lysis of adhesions were then performed. During dissection of the anterior uterine wall from the posterior bladder, a suture that appeared to be constricting the right ureter was identified and subsequently released. A double-J ureteral stent was then placed, and cystorrhaphy was performed. The patient required resuscitation with 37 units of various blood products during the procedure.

The patient's postoperative course was complicated by intermittent fevers and multiple blood transfusions. A voiding cystourethrogram (VCUG) was performed on postoperative day (POD) #14, which revealed a small leak from the posterior bladder wall. The Foley catheter was kept in place, and a repeat VCUG was performed on POD #21 showing persistent leak. The patient was discharged home with a Foley catheter in place.

Follow-Up:
The patient returned on POD #39 for a follow-up VCUG, which revealed a resolution of the leak. The Foley catheter was removed, and the patient's ureteral stent was removed 11 weeks postoperatively.

Disposition: The patient was discharged home with a Foley catheter in place and was last seen in the clinic for her follow-up visit on POD #39.

Signed,

A clinical examination revealed a suspicious lump measuring 15mm, while mammography was normal. An ultrasound scan confirmed the presence of breast cancer. A core biopsy of the lesion was taken, and histology confirmed the diagnosis of invasive ductal carcinoma.

During her examination, existing cardiac PM was found attached through a subcutaneous tissue pocket in the upper left breast pole, located 9cm away from the tumour. The patient had been self-caring since the implant had been placed in 2003.

The patient had her sentinel node biopsy harvested, underwent the wide local excision successfully, and simultaneously received intraoperative radiotherapy. The Intrabeam device was used, and a 3 cm diameter applicator delivered around 20 Gy at the surface of the breast tissue that was in direct contact with the applicator, and 6 Gy at 1 cm from the surface, over a time of 26 minutes. The radiation dose reaching the PM during the surgery was reported to be 0.08 Gy, measured with thermoluminescent dosimeters and batch calibration value corrected for supralinearity of dose response.

Her postoperative recovery was uneventful, taking only one day, where her PM was assessed by the cardiology team before and after treatment. The patient then commenced adjuvant treatment, which included an aromatase inhibitor and was being closely monitored to evaluate future care.

Hospital Course Summary:

Patient Information:
34-year-old male with an injury to the right hand sustained while grinding sugarcane pulp. Presented within 3 hours of injury.

Clinical Findings:
Injury involved four fingers of the non-dominant hand, with macerations along the margins of the skin. There were longitudinal lacerations over the fingers, both on the dorsal and volar sides, with the extensor expansion having vertical slits running along its length till the metacarpophalangeal joints. The proximal interphalangeal joints were exposed with the avulsion of the central slips and loss of continuity of the covering capsules, whereas, the flexor tendons were in continuity with loss of the flexor tendon sheath in the region of the volar skin laceration. Two of the three patients suffered from bone continuity loss.

Treatment:
Wounds were washed and covered with sterile dressings, with broad-spectrum antibiotics being initiated. Within the operation room, wound debridement and lavage with 6 liters of normal saline were carried out under regional block. The vertical midline slits in the extensor expansion were stitched using interrupted 4-0 nylon sutures. The skin was approximated over tendons to provide them with a biological coverage using sutures i.e. nylon 3-0.

Two of these patients required split thickness skin grafting over the dorsum of hand, which was undertaken after three days of sustaining the injury. The hand was immobilized using a dorsal plaster slab for pain relief, and the patients were allowed to flex their fingers within the slab. The slab was removed in the second week and the K-wires in case 2 were removed after confirming union at three weeks. Patients underwent rehabilitation under the supervision of a physiotherapist, where they practiced passive, active-assisted, and active stretching of the involved joint.

Outcomes:
The patient was assessed for post-traumatic stiffness, which is clinically apparent in inter-phalyngeal, meta-phalyngeal, and wrist joints. The aim is to restore the function to normal or near-normal dexterity. The patients were assessed using mini-dash score at the end of 6 months. The score was 0 in two patients, and one patient (case 3) was lost to follow-up. The hand function was restored to normal in the two patients who were evaluated.

The CT scan revealed a normalized spleen size, and the partial splenic abscess changed without additional abscess formation. Follow-up tests showed decreased serum antibody test results, ELISA tests with IgM < 11 and IgG of 19, and no organisms were found in the blood culture. The patient has been followed up and has shown no signs of recurrence.

The patient underwent urgent CABG procedure within 7 days of his myocardial infarction to address triple-vessel disease with impaired left ventricular ejection fraction (51%). The patient passed away in the hospital, and his family was notified following the outcome. Further information regarding the patient's stay and care can be requested from the hospital.

The patient, a 69-year-old female with diabetes, chronic hypertension, and end-stage renal disease, presented with progressive ataxia and recurrent fainting spells. The patient also reported several left upper extremity symptoms including numbness, tingling, cold fingers, cramping, and decreased fine motor skills, as well as bluish discoloration particularly on the days of dialysis. Magnetic Resonance Imaging with angiography (MRI/MRA) demonstrated a chronic cerebellar infarct with a hypoplastic right vertebral and basilar artery. A left subclavian angiogram showed a normal subclavian artery caliber and a stump at the origin of the left VA without distal flow. A right common carotid angiogram demonstrated flow though the posterior communicating artery with retrograde filling of the basilar artery and left VA to its subclavian origin. An aortic angiogram demonstrated the overall hemodynamics. 

Treatment:

The patient was treated surgically by ligating the fistula, which resulted in symptom resolution.

The patient was discharged in stable condition with instructions for follow-up care.

The patient responded promptly to meropenem therapy, and percutaneous or surgical drainage of the abscess was not performed. His fever, elevated procalcitonin level, and leukocytosis resolved without surgical intervention.

Discharge Plan:

No microorganisms were identified in the follow-up blood cultures from Day 5. On Day 10, abdominal color Doppler ultrasonography was normal. After a further 6-day course of intravenous meropenem, the patient recovered and was discharged from the hospital. Follow-up appointments were scheduled to monitor his progress and ensure complete recovery.

This 48-year-old Hispanic man presented with abdominal and back pain, fevers, nausea, vomiting, dysuria, postvoid dripping, and constipation. Initial exam revealed tenderness in the right costovertebral angle. CT scan showed thickened bladder wall, bilateral hydronephrosis, hepatomegaly, and perihepatic ascites. He underwent JJ stent placement and was discharged on oral augmentin.

He returned three weeks later with nausea, vomiting, poor appetite, and abdominal pain. Ultrasound showed gall bladder sludge and HIDA scan showed total retention of Tech 99 in the liver. A CT scan showed pancreatitis, hepatomegaly, esophageal, and gastric varices, intact bilateral JJ stents, and portal vein thrombosis. His ERCP showed a large antral ulcer and edematous mucosa in the duodenal bulb, and he was subsequently diagnosed with poorly differentiated carcinoma involving the duodenal mucosa and poorly differentiated gastric adenocarcinoma with signet ring cells.

Laparoscopic surgery was recommended, which was converted to an exploratory laparotomy. It revealed peritoneal carcinomatosis, ascites, and frozen ascending and descending colon. An end-ileostomy was done in view of impending small bowel obstruction. He developed bilateral deep vein thromboses after the surgery and respiratory distress, requiring reintubation. Renal function started to worsen in the face of extensive carcinomatosis and liver failure, and the patient's family elected comfort care.

The patient received supportive care and methylprednisolone for MAS. No treatment for PAH was initiated during the hospitalization period.

The patient's symptoms improved significantly with methylprednisolone treatment, and she was discharged. Plans for further management of her co-existing PAH were discussed with her upon discharge.

This patient was admitted with AOSD and was subsequently diagnosed with MAS. Co-existing PAH was incidentally discovered during evaluation. The patient received appropriate treatment for her diagnoses and improved significantly. Plans for further management of her PAH were discussed with her upon discharge.

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 75-year-old male, was admitted to the hospital with upper abdominal pain. The blood tests showed elevated levels of total and direct bilirubin, γ-GTP, ALP, AST, and ALT, along with radiological evidence of dilation of hepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts and wall thickening of the common bile duct. Subsequent ERCP revealed defects in intrahepatic and common bile ducts, leading to a diagnosis of perihilar cholangiocarcinoma. The patient underwent left hepatectomy, caudate lobectomy, extrahepatic bile duct resection, and right hepaticojejunostomy. The patient was discharged 23 days after surgery in stable condition.

Follow-up:
Two years and 9 months after the first operation, follow-up CT showed a liver metastasis. The patient underwent a limited liver resection of segment 8. During surgery, another liver metastasis was detected intraoperatively. Two limited liver resections were performed for these two lesions, which were later diagnosed as NET G2. Five years and 4 months after the first operation, four liver metastases were detected, for which the patient received monthly octreotide LAR followed by lanreotide depot/autogel 120 mg. Six years and 3 months after the first operation, the patient underwent a third hepatectomy that revealed seven liver metastases with NET G2 recurrence. In the fourth surgery, the patient had no newly detected tumor and was discharged in stable condition.

Medical Management:
Seven months after the initiation of the third hepatectomy, the patient's follow-up showed four liver metastases. After 6 months of everolimus (10 mg/day) administration, all tumors shrank, but the chemotherapy was discontinued due to its side effects.

Clinical Diagnosis:
The patient was diagnosed with perihilar cholangiocarcinoma based on clinical, radiological, and pathological findings. Later, the patient developed liver metastases that were diagnosed as NET G2, leading to multiple surgical resections followed by chemotherapy with everolimus. The patient was discharged in stable condition after each surgery with no recurrence on follow-up. 

Impressions:
This is a case of perihilar cholangiocarcinoma with NET G2 liver metastases. The patient has undergone multiple surgical resections and chemotherapy with everolimus with no recurrence on follow-up.

Brief Hospital Course: 

The patient, a 4-year-old boy, was admitted with an incidental detection of murmur. Clinical examination revealed low volume radial pulse in the left upper limb and lower BP in the same limb. The right radial pulse was normal. Anthropometrically, his height was 100 cm, and the left upper limb was 10 mm shorter than the right upper limb.  

Echocardiography showed structurally normal heart with RAA and aberrant LSA with flow turbulence. CT angiogram was done, which confirmed the diagnosis. A stenosis of 70-80% just beyond the origin of LSA was detected. The presence of limb length discrepancy justified treatment, and the patient was scheduled for transcatheter placement of stent. 

The procedure was performed successfully, and the patient tolerated it very well. Racer 5 mm × 18 mm stent was positioned across the stenosed segment. Post-procedure angiogram confirmed the stent's correct placement, and good flow was observed in LSA and left axillary artery. The patient was kept on overnight heparin infusion and discharged with oral aspirin.

Follow-up visits on 3 and 6 months showed near-normalization of radial pulse and blood pressure in the left upper limb, and significant improvement of limb length. USG of the left upper limb confirmed a laminar flow pattern in the LSA. The boy has been followed up for the last 4 years, with no remaining limb length discrepancy detected.

Discharge Diagnosis: Stenosis of Left Subclavian Artery.

Discharge Instructions: 

The patient will continue aspirin therapy (as directed by the physician). Follow-up visits should be scheduled as per the physician's instructions. Parents are advised to keep the patient's medical records updated and bring them to each visit.

No medications were prescribed upon discharge.

Patient Name: [Redacted]                                      Date of Discharge: [Redacted]

Sex: Male                                                        Attending Physician: [Redacted]
Age: 17 years old                                               Consultant: [Redacted]
Diagnosis: Osteosarcoma of Distal Radius

Hospital Course Summary:

The 17-year-old male patient was admitted to the Department of Orthopedics, The General Hospital of Jinan Military Commanding Region (Jinan, China) with a complaint of mild right wrist pain that had persisted for about two months. On physical examination, diffuse swelling, mild tenderness, and local heat were observed at the distal end of the right radius. A hard mass with an irregular surface (size, 3×2 cm) was palpated in the dorsal aspect of the distal radius. Wrist motion was slightly restricted. Radiographs showed diffuse osteosclerosis and focal osteolysis with periosteal reaction in the distal radius metaphysis. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed a hypointense lesion on T1-weighted images and a hyperintense lesion on T2-weighted images with soft tissue extension. Technetium-99m scintigraphy showed an increased isotope uptake within the lesion.

The patient was diagnosed with osteosarcoma after a needle aspiration biopsy was performed and histological examination of the specimen was conducted. Following two cycles of chemotherapy with cisplatin, adriamycin, and ifosfamide, pain diminished, the local mass decreased, and the range of motion of the affected wrist returned to normal. Subsequently, the patient underwent en bloc resection of the tumor and reconstruction with a free fibular shaft to preserve the radiocarpal joint. The ulna and distal radioulnar articulation and radiocarpal joint were preserved, the free fibular shaft was fixed to the host bone with two plates, and the wound was closed. A long arm cast was applied and the wrist was fixed in a functional position. Postoperative histological examination of the specimens revealed no tumor cells at the edges of the resected segment or in other regions of the lesion.

Chemotherapy was administered again with the same drug and dose as the preoperative protocol and completed following six courses. Passive exercise was initiated once the affected distal radius and the wrist had been protected (by the plaster cast) for 12 weeks. Six months after surgery, radiographs revealed that the grafted fibular bone had healed well with the host bone. Physical examination showed active dorsiflexion of the affected wrist was to 90° and wrist palmer flexion was to 45°. One month after surgery, there was no evidence of wrist deformity, instability, metastasis, or local recurrence. Further follow-up examinations are currently being conducted.

The patient was discharged from the hospital in stable condition. Home care instructions were given, including instructions on how to care for the surgical incision and how to perform daily activities. The patient was advised to follow up with his physician and oncologist regularly. The patient and family were counseled on the importance of adherence to the treatment plan and follow-up care. 

Disposition: Discharged home in stable condition.

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to the department of periodontology with the chief complaint of unesthetic gum swelling on the left upper front teeth which was present for two years. An intraoral examination revealed a well-defined irregular reddish-pink growth on the labial gingiva of #22-24, measuring 20X13mm. Orthopantomogram showed generalized mild bone loss. Provisional diagnosis of pyogenic granuloma (PG) was made, and an incisional biopsy was taken after Phase I therapy. The histopathology report confirmed the presence of PG, and extensive surgical excision followed by simultaneous connective tissue graft (CAF) and platelet-rich fibrin (PRF)-assisted regeneration of anticipated gingival defect was planned.
 
Treatment and Outcome:
Three weeks post-biopsy, the lesion healed uneventfully and reduced in size significantly. Before surgery, 10 ml of blood was taken from anticubital vein for the preparation of Choukroun's PRF. First, the growth was excised from the base to evaluate its peripheral extensions of the lesion. Then an internal bevel incision was given 2 mm away from the periphery of lesion followed by crevicular incision, and complete lesion excised under local anesthesia resulted in residual gingival defect formation (8 mm × 10 mm) with respect to #23. Root planing was performed with respect to #22, 23, and immediately two vertical releasing incisions were given mesial to #22 and distal to #23, followed by crevicular incision and full-thickness flap refection up to the mucogingival junction and partial thickness beyond it for tension-free displacement of flap. After thorough irrigation, PRF membrane was placed over the defect site followed by CAF secured with 4-0 vicryl direct loop suture. The surgical site healed uneventfully, and sutures were removed ten days later. Complete coverage was observed three weeks post-operatively. Maintenance therapy was given at monthly intervals up to three months. The complete residual defect coverage at the surgical site with well-adapted flap to the underlying bone with knife-edged gingival margins and excellent color matching with adjacent tissue was observed at 3 months post-operatively. There were no clinical alterations or complications observed till 6 months. 
 
Summary:
The patient, a 42-year-old female, was admitted to the department of periodontology with a chief complaint of unesthetic gum swelling on the left upper front teeth. A diagnosis of pyogenic granuloma was made, and extensive surgical excision followed by simultaneous CAF and PRF-assisted regeneration of anticipated gingival defect was planned. The surgical procedure was successful, with no complications, and the patient showed complete residual defect coverage at the surgical site with well-adapted flap to the underlying bone with knife-edged gingival margins and excellent color matching with adjacent tissue at 3 months post-operatively.

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 35-year-old Hispanic male with a history of AIDS, Kaposi sarcoma, and multicentric Castleman's disease, presented with severe intermittent mid-lower back pain radiating to both lower extremities for the past week. The patient also experienced numbness in his lower extremities and difficulty with movement. 

Admission Note:
Upon admission, significant vitals included a fever of 38.5°C and tachycardia. The physical exam revealed generalized lymphadenopathy, bilateral non-pitting lower extremity edema, right-sided ptosis, and facial droop. Examination of the skin showed hyperpigmented purple/erythematous maculopapular lesions on both thighs, indicating Kaposi sarcoma. 

Diagnostic Findings:
Laboratory testing showed thrombocytopenia and hypoalbuminemia. Radiologic imaging revealed hepatomegaly and diffuse abdominopelvic lymphadenopathy, as well as diffuse lymphadenopathy of the bilateral supraclavicular, axillary, posterior mediastinal, retrocrural, and paraspinal nodes. MRI findings confirmed these observations. 

Consultations:
Infectious disease consultation recommended HAART with Raltegravir 400 mg tablet twice daily and Abacavir/Lamivudine 600/300 mg tablet every day. Hematology/oncology consult addressed the possibility of plasmablastic lymphoma and recommended a bone marrow biopsy and excisional lymph node biopsy of the supraclavicular lymph node. A MRI brain and lumbar puncture with CSF analysis were also performed. 

Procedures:
The excisional biopsy of the left supraclavicular lymph node revealed HHV8+ Kaposi sarcoma in the background of multicentric Castleman's disease (plasmacytic variant). The bone marrow biopsy demonstrated hypercellular marrow demonstrating reactive plasmacytosis with polytypic pattern by kappa and lambda light chains immunostains. 

Treatment:
The patient was discharged home in stable condition on HAART with follow-up appointments with the infectious disease and hematology/oncology services. Chemotherapy with CHOP (cyclophosphamide, adriamycin, vincristine plus prednisone) was administered as an outpatient in four monthly cycles, with rituximab plus prophylaxis for pneumocystis carinii included. The facial droop and ptosis resolved during chemotherapy, with diffuse lymphadenopathy resolving after the full course of chemotherapy. 

Follow-up Plan:
The patient was instructed to follow up with the infectious disease and hematology/oncology services for further outpatient management. 

Summary:
A 35-year-old patient presented with mid-lower back pain and was found to have Kaposi sarcoma. The patient underwent therapy and was discharged in stable condition after a full course of chemotherapy. Follow-up is recommended with the infectious disease and hematology/oncology services.

The patient, a 33-year-old, Malaysian male, presented to the hospital following a nocturnal seizure. Prior to admission, the patient had flu-like symptoms, loss of appetite, and general myalgia. The patient experienced post-ictal periods of approximately 30 minutes and had a 21-second asystole during the third seizure. A permanent pacemaker was placed to address this complication.

The patient's neurological exam was unremarkable except for gaze-evoked nystagmus, thought to be a side effect of the administered phenytoin. Despite administration of anticonvulsant medication and subsequent optimization of phenytoin, the patient continued to have recurrent seizures. He developed additional symptoms such as right-sided headache, right ear pain, tenderness, and an unusual sound in the right ear which evolved into a hallucination of music. The patient also developed complex partial seizures, indicating the possibility of HSV encephalitis.

LPs performed on two separate occasions showed no abnormality other than a slightly elevated protein level. CT scans of the head with contrast were normal, and a SPECT scan showed a slight decrease in perfusion of the left side compared to the right. A repeat EEG showed nonspecific abnormality of the right temporal lobe.

The patient was started on a course of acyclovir, and over the first week of therapy, there was significant improvement. Seizures and headaches resolved, but the hallucination of music persisted for several days. The patient was discharged to complete a three-week course of acyclovir. While tapering the anticonvulsants, there were breakthrough seizures, so the patient remains on levetriacetam and phenytoin.

Summary:
The patient was diagnosed with possible HSV encephalitis, which was successfully managed with acyclovir therapy. The patient was discharged with instructions to continue the full course of medication and remain on anticonvulsants.

Chief Complaint:
A 69-year-old female presented with colicky pain in the right hypochondrium.

History of Present Illness:
The patient reported suffering from colicky pain in the right hypochondrium for the past 3 years. She had previously undergone open cholecystectomy 15 years ago for gall stones.

Physical Examination:
On physical examination, the patient was found to be anicteric with soft abdomen.

Diagnostic Tests:
Ultrasonography (USG) of the abdomen showed a hypoechoic lesion in segment 4 of the liver. Computerized Tomography (CT) of the abdomen showed a heterogeneously enhancing mass lesion in segment IV of liver abutting the left branch of portal vein. Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) of upper abdomen with Magnetic Resonance CholagioPancreaticography (MRCP) showed a filling defect in the left hepatic duct with lesion in the adjacent part of liver in segment IV, suggestive of a left hepatic duct tumor with infiltration in the liver. Tumor marker serum alfa fetoprotein was mildly raised. A whole body Positron Emission Tomography (PET) scan and an Octreotride labeled radionulceotide scan showed somatostatin receptor expressing lesion in the hepatobiliary system.

Medical History:
The patient had a past medical history of open cholecystectomy done for gall stones.

Hospital Course:
The patient was worked up for left hepatectomy. Intraopertaively a lesion arising from the left hepatic duct involving the left branch of portal vein and extending upto the portal confluence was found rendering the tumor unresectable. A biopsy was taken from the mass and procedure was abandoned in view of inoperability. Histopathology showed typical rosette appearance of a neuroendocrine tumor and immunohistochemistry positive for CD56, Chromogranin and Synaptophysin. Ultrastructural study of the cell with electron microscopy showed the presence of multiple neurosecretory granules with muscle tissue. The patient was started on long-acting Octreotride therapy single dose every month. The patient has received 12 of such doses and is doing well after a 1-year followup without any complications. A follow up MRI upper abdomen with MRCP at 1 year showed the absence of filling defect in the Left hepatic duct that was seen previously which showed tumor regression.

Diagnosis:
Neuroendocrine tumor.

Condition at Discharge:
The patient is doing well without any complications at the time of discharge.

Follow-up:
The patient will follow-up with her primary care physician for further evaluation and management of her condition.

Hospital Course:

Patient is a 77-year-old female who presented with right L2-3 radiculopathy that was refractory to maximum medical management. This was secondary to foraminal compression at L2-3 and L3-4 due to degenerative disc disease, levoscoliosis, as well as grade 1 spondylolisthesis at both levels.

Treatment:

Given the patient’s prior history of posterior decompressive laminectomy, it was felt that the best approach would be a minimally invasive lateral approach to obtain indirect decompression of the foramina as well as correct her spinal deformity. This will achieve the goals of decompression and fusion as well as deformity correction while avoiding the risk of operating through scar tissue. A retroperitoneal transpsoas approach was used to expose the disc spaces from the patient’s left side.

Complete discectomy was performed with the release of the contralateral annulus fibrosis followed by the interbody fusion. A lordotic PEEK graft was used at each level, 50 mm length x 18 mm width x 9 mm height, packed with demineralized bone matrix (DBM).

Outcome:

Postoperative anteroposterior and lateral x-ray imaging confirmed good position of interbody grafts, correction of scoliosis as well as spondylolisthesis, and restoration of disc height achieving satisfactory foraminal indirect decompression. A routine postoperative x-ray at three months demonstrated lateral cage migration on the left side at the L2-3 level with evidence of arthrodesis in the disc space.

The patient remained asymptomatic and follow-up imaging at one year demonstrated completed fusion without further migration of the interbody graft at L2-3.

Conclusion:

Informed patient consent was obtained prior to treatment and with the patient’s permission, we report on this case of successful minimally invasive lateral approach to obtain indirect decompression of the foramina as well as correct spinal deformity. The patient had significant improvement and remained asymptomatic.

The patient was discharged with instructions for continued follow-up care with his ophthalmologist. No further hospitalization was necessary.

Discharge Summary:

This is a summary of the hospital course of a 62-year-old male with Kearns-Sayre syndrome (KSS) who presented to the emergency department (ED) after two syncopal episodes. He has a past medical history of multi-system involvement including skeletal muscle myopathy, pigmentary retinopathy, heart failure, non-sustained ventricular tachycardia, pulmonary hypertension, chronic heart block, chronic kidney disease, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and mitral valve prolapse.

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted for syncope secondary to VT, and 150 mg of IV amiodarone bolus was administered. He was started on amiodarone drip at 0.5 mg/min. Follow-up AICD interrogation yielded sustained monomorphic ventricular tachycardia to the 140s during both syncopal episodes. Chest X-ray revealed right pleural effusion. On day two, the patient was noted to have non-sustained VT with increasing oxygen requirements. A plan was in place to transition the patient from IV to PO amiodarone, but instead, he developed VT storm and was thus continued on amiodarone drip. He was transferred to the critical care unit (CCU) for further monitoring and started on lidocaine drip (1 mg/min) with continued amiodarone and milrinone drips. In the CCU, he continued to have non-sustained VT with symptoms of palpitations despite the AICD reprogramming and medical management. He also continued to have shortness of breath with minimal improvement on bilevel positive airway pressure (BIPAP). Unfortunately, recurrent VT progressed to a VT storm, requiring multiple boluses of IV amiodarone, IV lidocaine, and multiple shocks from his AICD which were futile. The VT storm was refractory to his current medical management. The patient eventually passed away after the withdrawal of care.

Final Diagnosis:

The final diagnosis of the patient was VT storm in the setting of KSS with multi-system involvement including heart failure.

Follow-Up:

The patient was not discharged due to his unfortunate clinical outcome.

Hospital Course Summary:

Patient was a 17-year-old female with a history of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM), who was transferred to our hospital after successful resuscitation from ventricular fibrillation (VF). She had been diagnosed with HCM 2 years prior, and was taking a beta-blocking drug and ACE inhibitor with no symptoms or arrhythmic events. Her BNP level was high, so cibenzoline was added 3 months prior for the purpose of improvement of diastolic function caused by attenuation of the LV contraction and prevention of arrhythmic events. She collapsed while walking due to VF.

Upon arrival at our hospital while undergoing therapeutic hypothermia, her blood pressure was high and physical examination revealed coarse crackles in her whole chest. Blood tests revealed normal renal function and electrolytes. An ECG showed complete right bundle branch block, left ventricular hypertrophy with ST-T changes with QRS width of 148 ms and QTc of 0.514. After she recovered almost fully without severe neurologic sequelae, a subcutaneous implantable cardioverter–defibrillator (S-ICD) was selected for second prevention, and she underwent treadmill exercise testing for further screening for the S-ICD with normal results.

During exercise, QRS duration increased progressively from 160 ms at rest at a heart rate of 66 bpm to 200 ms at peak exercise at a heart rate of 100 bpm, accompanied by monomorphic ventricular tachycardia (VT) at 150 bpm that was thought to be a proarrhythmia of cibenzoline. Cibenzoline was changed to sotalol, and re-treadmill exercise testing while receiving sotalol revealed no change in QRS width during exercise, nor did it induce any VT at a similar exercise burden. Her S-ICD was set with the primary vector as the sensing configuration. No ICD shocks were observed while taking sotalol.

The patient was admitted at 28+0 weeks of gestation with complaints of intermittent vaginal blood spotting and diagnosed with second-stage uterine prolapse. Pelvic examination revealed point C as the leading edge according to the pelvic organ prolapse quantification staging system. Sonographic examination revealed a short cervix with 17 mm length and a T-shape. A progesterone capsule was administered vaginally daily.

Two weeks later, at 30+0 weeks of gestation, the patient was admitted again because of regular uterine contractions. She was diagnosed with second-degree uterine prolapse. The prolapsed uterus was manually reduced, and the postnatal period was uneventful. Two days after delivery, the patient was discharged in good health with complete resolution of the cervical prolapse. Follow-up examination 1 and 6 months postpartum revealed no evidence of uterine prolapse.

Hospital Course Summary:

Admission:
A 75-year-old male patient was admitted to the emergency department with a late-presenting ST-elevation myocardial infarction. He had hypertension, diabetes mellitus, and advanced Parkinson's disease treated with deep brain stimulation. An initial transthoracic echocardiography found a decreased ability of the left ventricle to pump blood with a motionless inferior portion. A coronary angiography revealed a three-vessel coronary artery disease with an occluded circumflex as the culprit lesion. A balloon angioplasty with stent implantation was performed to open up the blocked blood vessels, achieving a Grade 2 thrombolysis in myocardial infarction (TIMI) flow.

Hospitalization:
On day 1 after the percutaneous coronary intervention, he developed a sudden buildup of fluid in his lungs, and a turbulent heartbeat requiring supportive care with medication and an apparatus called an intra-aortic balloon pump. The echocardiography found a new large eccentric mitral regurgitation with a flap of the mitral leaflet and a partial tear of the posteromedial papillary muscle. The pulmonary artery systolic pressure (PASP) was evaluated at 55 mmHg.
 
Treatment:
Given the patient's comorbidities, the structural heart team opted for a percutaneous mitral valve repair (PMVr) using the MitraClip system. The patient was transferred to the cath laboratory. Using a transseptal approach, an intraprocedural evaluation of the mean left atrial pressure was assessed with a V-wave. A standard clip implantation was performed under general anesthesia and transesophageal echocardiography (TOE) guidance. Two NTR MitraClips were successfully implanted (A3/P3 followed by A2/P2 position) with a good intraprocedural result. The patient's clinical condition immediately improved.

Discharge: 
During his stay at the hospital, the patient received proper medical care and treatment for his condition. He was discharged from the hospital a week after the procedure. The discharge echocardiogram revealed a small amount of residual mitral regurgitation with a low blood flow pressure. No significant issues were reported upon discharge. Appropriate follow-up care was recommended.

Patient: 40-year-old female with chest pain

Discharge Date: [Date of Discharge]

Reason for Admission:
The patient was admitted to the hospital with crushing substernal chest pain for a three-hour duration, which was aggravated with exertion and relieved with rest.

Hospital Course:
Upon admission, the patient was hemodynamically stable with no other abnormal finding on the physical exam. Initial blood work showed normal complete blood count and basic metabolic panel. However, troponin I levels were elevated at 11.3 ng/ml.

An electrocardiogram (EKG) showed ST elevations in lead II, aVF, V5, and V6, consistent with ST elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI). The patient was started on medications including aspirin, beta blocker, statin, and heparin drip.

Due to the unavailability of percutaneous intervention (PCI) at the initial facility, the patient was transferred to our facility. There, an emergent left heart catheterization was performed which showed normal left and right coronary arteries, patent left anterior descending, and patent diagonal artery.

Within 24 hours of the initial angiogram, the patient experienced a recurrence of severe substernal chest pain. An EKG revealed ST elevations in lead I, aVL, V5-V6, ST depressions in V1-V3, and T-wave inversion over V2-V5. The troponin I level increased to greater than 40 ng/ml.

An emergent repeat angiogram revealed local dissection of the mid to distal left main coronary artery (LMCA) and a total occlusion of the diagonal branch which was the likely result of spontaneous coronary artery dissection (SCAD). The patient was started on dual antiplatelet therapy with aspirin and clopidogrel, and continued on statin and beta-blocker therapy.

Over 48 hours, the patient was closely monitored in the critical care unit. Her chest pain resolved, and she remained hemodynamically stable. Repeat angiography was performed which showed that the local dissection of the LMCA seen previously had spontaneously resolved. The total occlusion of the diagonal artery was now replaced by a long linear dissection plane, suggesting SCAD as the culprit etiology.

Further tests confirmed a diagnosis of fibromuscular dysplasia (FMD). The patient was continued on optimal medical management and closely monitored for a year. During this period, she remained symptom-free. The patient was discharged on [Date of Discharge] in good condition.

Hospital Course:

The patient, a 43-year-old male, was admitted to our Nephrology Unit for dyspnoea and fever. He was diagnosed with membranous glomerulonephritis along with chronic kidney disease that did not require dialysis. The patient was undergoing treatment with cyclophosphamide and prednisone.

At the time of admission, the patient was febrile and dyspnoic with an oxygen saturation of 86.7%. Chest auscultation revealed coarse crepitations and diminished air entry. An arterial blood gas test showed Type 1 acute respiratory failure. The patient underwent a high-resolution-computed tomography scan of the chest, which confirmed the presence of bilateral patchy areas of ground-glass consolidation, and a diagnosis of Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS) was made. 

The patient was treated with antimicrobial therapy including piperacillin/tazobactam, levofloxacin, and fluconazole. Continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) ventilation was started when the patient's respiratory function worsened. The patient's clinical condition deteriorated further, resulting in the onset of atrial fibrillation and an increase in serum creatinine levels. The severity of the condition led to the application of blood purification therapy with CPFA. 

The patient underwent three consecutive days of CPFA therapy, where cytokines levels, pro-calcitonin, and C-reactive protein were monitored before and after each session. The patient's clinical conditions rapidly improved, and CPAP was withdrawn 24 hours after the first CPFA session. The patient was no longer confused and converted back to sinus rhythm. After four days, the patient's oxygen saturation was 97% while breathing room air. 

The patient's APACHE II score progressively decreased from 24 to 9, and a control chest HRCT was performed after nine days, which confirmed a substantial improvement of the acute respiratory disease. 

Discharge Summary:

The patient, a 43-year-old male with a history of membranous glomerulonephritis, was admitted to our unit for acute respiratory distress syndrome. The patient received treatment with antimicrobial therapy and continuous positive airway pressure ventilation. Further, blood purification therapy was initiated and applied for three consecutive days, resulting in the improvement of clinical conditions. 

At the time of discharge, the patient's APACHE II score was 9, the oxygen saturation was 97% while breathing room air, and a control chest HRCT showed a substantial improvement of the acute respiratory disease. The patient was discharged from our unit in stable condition. Patients were advised to follow-up with their kidney specialist for maintenance and management of their membranous glomerulonephritis.
