The 70-year-old female patient was incidentally found to have left maxillary sinus mass on a computed tomography (CT) scan of the facial bones performed for trauma. The patient was referred to Otolaryngology for further workup. On physical examination, a palpable mass was noted below the left zygoma, and on endoscopy, the left ostiomeatal complex was compromised secondary to adjacent soft tissue fullness. Contrast enhanced CT of the paranasal sinuses demonstrated a large, soft tissue density mass without significant enhancement in the left maxillary sinus. Bony destruction was noted along the anterior, posterior and lateral walls of the left maxillary sinus, as well as the left orbital floor. A left maxillectomy was performed under general anesthesia. Repeat CT 1 month later showed no evidence of recurrence. 

Medical History:

The patient had a medical history notable for Human Immunodeficiency Virus, Diabetes Mellitus, Hypertension, and chronic sinusitis. There was no history of tobacco or alcohol use.

Presenting Symptoms:

The patient reported having intermittent blood-tinged mucus for over 2 years with episodes of epistaxis over the last month. They also reported 1 week of left facial numbness, and one day of drooling from their left oral commissure.

Diagnostic Findings:

Non-contrast magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the paranasal sinuses showed the soft tissue mass was isointense to muscle on T1 weighted images, extending anteriorly into the pre-maxillary soft tissue.

Pathology Results:

Fine needle aspiration of the mass revealed scant groups of cohesive cells with nuclear enlargement, hyperchromasia, and mild cellular crowding, without high-grade features. Special staining further revealed positivity for cytokeratin AE1/AE3, p63, and p40, but was negative for S100, diagnostic for ameloblastoma. 

Plan:

Resection of the lateral and most inferior aspects of the mass was performed with a Caldwell-Luc procedure, achieving near total resection.

HOSPITAL COURSE

This patient was admitted to our facility for an intense pruritus on her right arm, which had been ongoing for six months. She also complained of right brachial paresis.

The patient has a known history of multiple myeloma.

Computed tomography of the cervical spine, magnetic resonance imaging, and electromyography of the brachial plexus were performed, which showed right cervical disc herniation with nerve root compression of C6-C7 and right brachial plexus inflammation (Parsonage-Turner syndrome).

The patient was treated with methylprednisolone aceponate cream 0.1% and oral hydroxyzine 25mg every 8 hours, which resulted in little improvement of the pruritus. Gabapentin was introduced at 900mg/day, which achieved optimal control after three months of follow-up.

FOLLOW-UP INSTRUCTIONS

The patient was referred to neurosurgery and oncology consultation for additional therapeutic orientation.

SUMMARY

The patient presented with brachial plexopathy, which is attributed to neoplastic infiltration of multiple myeloma. The treatment plan included the application of methylprednisolone aceponate cream 0.1% and oral hydroxyzine 25mg every 8 hours, along with the introduction of gabapentin at 900mg/day. The patient was referred to neurosurgery and oncology for further management.

Discharge Summary

Patient: 31-year old female attended for rehabilitation of maxillary right canine site.

Hospital Course:

- The patient refused the orthodontic path prescribed by previous practitioners for esthetic reasons.
- A large diameter tapered implant was placed to avoid the conventional surgical approach of removing the impacted canine and waiting for implant placement.
- A non-invasive alternative protocol was proposed that depended on a previous successful case. The patient agreed and was informed of the risks.
- The implant was placed with primary stability and the palatal side was filled with a bone substitute.
- The patient will be monitored for healing and progress.

Patient: 80-year old men attended with a failing mandibular tooth-supported prosthesis.

Hospital Course:

- The patient had multiple failing teeth, including an impacted premolar, requiring extensive invasive surgery and a prolonged healing period.
- A non-invasive 2-step solution was proposed, which involved extracting all teeth except canines, placing 5 implants (2 encroaching the impacted premolar), a provisional bridge supported by remaining canines for 3 months, and further implant placement and integrating resulting prosthesis.
- The patient agreed, and 3 out of 7 implants encroached upon the impacted premolar, achieving primary stability. Patients will be monitored for healing and progress.

Patient: 85-year old women attended to rehabilitate her atrophic edentulous maxilla.

Hospital Course:

- The root of an ankylosed impacted canine was found outcropping the crest, occupying a strategic position, necessitating maintenance in order to host an encroaching implant with sufficient primary stability.
- Nine implants were placed left to heal in a submerged way for 6 months.
- The patient will be monitored for healing and progress.

Instructions:

- Continue monitoring the patients' healing progress and manage any complications that may arise. 
- Always provide clear explanations of proposed treatment plans to patients, including their risks and benefits. 
- Ensure that patients are aware of the alternative options available to them if available and appropriate.

Date of Discharge: [REDACTED]

Diagnosis:

- Corneal scarring

Hospital Course: 
The patient underwent penetrating keratoplasty for aphakic bullous keratopathy and corneal scarring. The donor cornea was replaced due to a large dendritic-geographic epithelial ulcer noted immediately after placement. Perioperative administration of intravenous aciclovir was given. Postoperatively, the patient was started on systemic and local antiviral therapy, and local antibiotic treatment. The graft was clear and re-epithelialized at 1 week. Long term prophylactic acyclovir 400 mg was started. However, six months later the patient developed a geographic corneal ulcer involving the graft-host interface with keratic precipitates and corneal edema. The patient was treated with acyclovir 400 mg and topical aciclovir both five times a day for 2 weeks with resolution of the ulcer and residual scarring.

Summary: 
The patient who had aphakic bullous keratopathy and corneal scarring underwent a successful penetrating keratoplasty with the use of a donor corneoscleral disc. The initial donor corneoscleral disc was removed and replaced with a second donor corneoscleral disc which was available. The patient was treated with antiviral and antibiotic medications following the surgery. The patient developed a geographic corneal ulcer, which was treated successfully with antiviral medications. The patient was discharged with instructions for a follow-up within a week.

Hospital Course:
-The patient was admitted to the cardiac catheterization laboratory with sudden onset chest pain associated with anterior ST-segment elevation on the electrocardiogram. The chest pain occurred during a bowel movement and he was found to be in cardiogenic shock upon arrival.
-Emergency diagnostic coronary angiography was performed, revealing severe proximal stenosis in the left anterior descending (LAD) artery. An extravasation of contrast media from the LAD artery into the pericardium was noted, with no flow in the distal LAD artery, resulting in a suspected dehiscence of the left internal mammary artery (LIMA) graft.
-Injection of contrast media discovered that the LIMA graft's flow of contrast only reached the mid-segment and stopped, while the saphenous vein grafts (SVGs) in the right coronary artery (RCA) and circumflex (LCx) artery were patent.
-After diagnostic coronary angiography, the patient experienced pulseless electrical activity cardiac arrest, but spontaneous circulation was achieved with CPR, and an intra-aortic balloon pump was inserted.
-Urgent echocardiography revealed a large global pericardial effusion with right atrial and right ventricular collapse. Emergency pericardiocentesis was performed to aspirate 700 mL of haemorrhagic fluid that contained an organized thrombus.
-Due to on-going haemodynamic compromise and non-availability of cardiac surgery on-site, it was decided to perform percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) to treat the LAD artery stenosis. Following PCI, thrombolysis in myocardial infarction (TIMI) 3 flow was achieved, and no further extravasation was seen at the dehiscence site.
-Assessment of the LIMA graft showed a sluggish flow with extravasation of contrast media into the pericardium, requiring four coils (Tornado Embolisation Microcoils. Cook Medical, Bloomington, IN, USA) for embolization to halt the flow.
-The patient was then transferred to the local cardiac surgery unit and underwent emergency re-sternotomy and evacuation of the blood clots. His haemoglobin level post CABG (4 weeks prior to this admission) was measured at 100 g/L and dropped to 79 g/L following LIMA avulsion. He received 2 units of blood transfusion.
-The echocardiogram post-PCI revealed residual blood clots in the pericardial space that were difficult to extract percutaneously.
-The patient made a full recovery with no neurological sequelae and was discharged after a few days.
-Outpatient review at 3 months confirmed an excellent recovery without report of cardiovascular symptoms. Control coronary angiography was performed at 5 months, and the patient underwent successful PCI to mid and proximal LAD into the left main (LM) artery with LCx ostium optimization.

Discharge Summary:

Admission Date: June 2016
Discharge Date: June 2016
Length of Stay: 2 weeks

Patient is a 54-year-old white male with multiple comorbidities who presented to the emergency room with mental status changes, abdominal pain, dyspnea, and fever. Imaging studies revealed small pleural effusions, ascites, and hepatosplenomegaly with no evidence of portal hypertension or splanchnic thrombosis. Laboratory data were remarkable for hyperferritinemia, hypofibrinogenemia, anemia, and thrombocytopenia along with elevated transaminases and coagulopathy. The patient was suspected to have HLH in light of laboratory and physical examination findings. Additional differential diagnosis workup yielded unremarkable results.

Empiric therapy was initiated with N-acetylcysteine and dexamethasone. The patient continued to deteriorate, with multiple organ failure including renal failure, myocardial injury, and respiratory failure requiring intubation. After 15 days, the patient fulfilled multiple HLH-2004 diagnostic criteria including hyperferritinemia, fever, splenomegaly, cytopenias, hemophagocytosis on biopsy of bone marrow, elevated CD25, and decreased NK cell activity by standardized studies. The patient steadily recovered with the steroid therapy instituted for 12 days and supportive measures. However, he refused further interventions for HLH and chose palliative care, ultimately passing away 2 weeks later.

In summary, the patient presented with mental status changes, abdominal pain, dyspnea, and fever, ultimately developing HLH and multiple organ failure. Despite initial treatment with N-acetylcysteine and dexamethasone, the patient's condition continued to worsen, and he ultimately chose palliative care.

Date of discharge: [REDACTED]
Admitting Diagnosis: Basilar Artery Aneurysm
Discharge Diagnosis: Basilar Artery Aneurysm treated with flow diverting Pipeline stent

Hospital Course:
A 60-year-old male was admitted for investigation of headaches, and a contrast enhanced computed tomography scan of his brain revealed a 20 mm × 10 mm basilar artery aneurysm that was not surgically operable. His past medical history included coronary artery disease, atrial fibrillation, a metallic mitral valve, a prior ischaemic stroke, hypertension and a previous provoked deep vein thrombosis.

The patient underwent a right CCVAB to allow endovascular access to the aneurysm. The mid portion of the right common carotid artery was exposed in the neck above the omohyoid muscle via a longitudinal incision anterior to the medial border of the sternocleidomastoid. The long saphenous vein was harvested from the left thigh, anastomosed in an end to side fashion to the CCA and to the vertebral artery. A contrast enhanced computed tomography scan confirmed patency of the graft on the Day 1 post procedure.

In the early post-operative period, the patient had ongoing hypotension that was likely secondary to cerebral autoregulation of blood pressure post CCVAB. The patient also suffered from a line sepsis, which delayed the second stage of the operation. Six weeks after the bypass procedure, the patient underwent an angiogram from the right common femoral artery. Access to the basilar artery aneurysm was achieved via a coaxial system consisting of a 6F long sheath to the origin of the anastomosis, a 5F intermediate guide within the graft and a 025 microcatheter to deliver a 3 × 35 mm flow diverting Pipeline stent to exclude the basilar artery aneurysm. There were no significant complications, and the patient recovered well.

Discharge Instructions:
The patient is advised to follow-up with their primary care physician and to continue taking any prescribed medications. They are also advised to monitor for any signs of fever, swelling, or redness at the site of the surgery. Additionally, they are advised to avoid any strenuous activities or heavy lifting for at least 4-6 weeks.

Follow-up:
The patient is advised to follow-up with their primary care physician within 2-4 weeks for a routine check-up. The patient should also schedule a follow-up appointment with their surgeon to monitor their condition and to ensure appropriate care.

He was transferred to the local hospital by his coworkers where he regained consciousness within 3 hours and complained of severe pain, weakness, and swelling in his right upper limb. The patient was treated symptomatically for pain and swelling, but the weakness persisted. After 6 weeks of the incident, he was referred to our hospital for further evaluation.

On examination, the patient's vital signs were within normal limits. A large healing scar of the burns sustained due to the lightning strike was visible on his upper back. Right suprascapular hollowing was also noted. Power in rhomboids, spinatii, and serratus anterior were preserved. However, the patient exhibited weakness in his right supraspinatus, infraspinatus, biceps brachii, deltoid, teres major, and pectoralis major (power 2/5 in all muscles). Right biceps, supinator, and triceps jerks were absent. Sensory loss was noted in right C5,6,7 dermatomes. Ophthalmological examination as also the rest of the examination was unremarkable.

The patient underwent further testing which revealed reduced amplitude and normal latency and conduction velocity of the sensory component of the right median nerve and lateral antebrachial cutaneous nerve. Motor nerve study showed decreased amplitude and normal latency and conduction velocity in right median nerve, musculocutaneous nerve, radial nerve, and axillary nerve. Ulnar nerve study was normal. EMG showed profuse fibrillations in right deltoid, biceps brachii and supraspinatus, and some fibrillations in left abductor pollicis brevis and triceps. Rest of the study was normal. Based on the test results, a diagnosis of brachial plexopathy was made which was localized to the upper and middle trunk (C5,6,7).

After receiving symptom-relieving treatments, the patient was monitored and eventually discharged with instructions to schedule a follow-up appointment with a specialist to monitor progress of his condition.

Hospital Course:
The patient is a 65-year-old African American man with a past medical history of diabetes and gout who presented with complaints of right third toe pain and constitutional symptoms, such as intermittent fever and chills. After evaluation, it was determined that the patient had a non-tender third toe with purple/black discoloration which probed to the bone and was swollen and fluctuant. An X-ray was obtained which illustrated that the tip of the distal phalanx was missing, and soft tissue injury was observed. Culture tests showed Escherichia coli and coagulase-negative staphylococci; however, no growth was observed after five days. The patient underwent several debridements due to acute osteomyelitis resulting in third metatarsal head resection. He then developed new-onset right knee pain and was diagnosed with gouty arthritis after turbid and milky fluid was analyzed with nucleated cells and monosodium urate crystals present. Further inspection of his labs showed a gradual rise in white blood cell levels, with predominantly monocytic leukocytosis, and blast cells accounting for 22% of the cells seen. Additionally, pseudo Pelger-Huet bodies were observed in the patient's peripheral blood smear, indicating concerns for an underlying myeloproliferative process. Results of the flow cytometry performed on this sample were indicative of AML, illustrating an Inv(16), which is a favorable prognostic marker of AML. Following the stabilization of the patient's current condition, he was transferred to an affiliated cancer institute for the management of his AML.

Hospital Course: The 73-year-old Caucasian female was admitted with decreased vision and metamorphopsia for 6 months in her left eye. Initial examination showed best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) of 20/80 left eye (LE) and 20/25 right eye (RE). Fundus biomicroscopy revealed the presence of exudative AMD with a subfoveal PED and an associated MH. Spectral domain optical coherence tomography (SD-OCT) confirmed a full-thickness MH with attached edges and a partially detached posterior hyaloid on top of the prominent PED. Intravitreal anti-VEGF-therapy with three loading doses of a monthly bevacizumab (1.25 mg)-injections was started. In the follow-up, the second injection was administered after four weeks, and SD-OCT showed complete closure of the MH along with marked visual improvement to 20/50. During further follow-up, PED recurred, but no reopening of the MH was observed. Continued intravitreal drug therapy with bevacizumab according to Pro Re Nata regimen led to resolution of PED and visual stabilization.

Discharge Diagnosis: Exudative AMD with Subfoveal PED and an Associated MH

Discharge Education: The patient was counseled on the importance of continued ophthalmic checkups and adherence to medication regimen. The potential side effects of the medication and the importance of promptly reporting any new symptoms were also discussed.

Hospital Course:
The patient, an 89-year-old male, was admitted with complaints of cough and haemoptysis. The patient had a history of bronchiectasis in the right middle lobe bronchus for 30 years. One month before admission, the patient suffered a massive haemoptysis, which was controlled through bronchial artery embolization. However, haemoptysis recurred, and the patient was admitted to our hospital. Bronchoscopy performed on the patient showed active bleeding from the right middle lobe bronchus, which was temporarily controlled through haemostatic medications and cryotherapy.

Management:
On the next day, an 8 mm x 3 cm silicon stent was deployed using biopsy forceps after multiple attempts. Another customized stent with a diameter of about 6 mm was placed from the right intermediate bronchus to the right lower lobe bronchus, to avoid stent migration. Bleeding stopped promptly after the placement of stents. The patient received successive antibiotic therapy, and no obvious complication of obstructive pneumonia developed.

Outcome:
One month after the operation of stents implantation, the patient experienced complete atelectasis of the right middle and lower lobe with the complication of right pleural effusion. The patient received further surgery to remove the silicon stent inside the right intermediate bronchus. Thoracic puncture and drainage were done after stent extraction for relieving pleural effusion. Post-operation CT scan reviewed the patient's chest and revealed the right lower lobe recruitment. The patient did not experience any more haemoptysis during the three-month follow-up time and left the hospital ten days after stent extraction.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Age: 45 years
Sex: Female
Admission Date: [REDACTED]
Discharge Date: [REDACTED]
Length of Stay: 7 days

Admitting Diagnosis:
Undifferentiated Spindle Cell Sarcoma Involving the Pancreas

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to the hospital urgently due to the acute onset of severe abdominal pain and collapse. Upon examination, she was found to be in class III haemorrhagic shock with distended and diffusely tender abdomen. She was immediately resuscitated with blood transfusions and intravenous crystalloid boluses. Hematological and basic investigations revealed haemoglobin level of 5g/dl and moderate amount of free fluid with mass around the proximal part of the pancreas, respectively. Following which, an emergency exploratory laparotomy was performed, and the source of bleeding was identified as the nidus, which was situated posterior to the body of the pancreas and had ruptured through the inferior border of the pancreas. The histopathological analysis of the biopsy revealed an infiltrating tumour composed of fascicles of spindle cells with oval, vesicular nuclei with scanty eosinophilic cytoplasm that was diagnosed as undifferentiated spindle cell sarcoma, and the tumour was surgically excised.

Treatment:
The patient was managed in the intensive care unit for 4 days and received a course of Ifosfamide and Doxorubicin for 6 months as adjuvant chemotherapy. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography was performed before the commencement of chemotherapy, which showed a 7 × 4.8 × 4.9 cm mass lesion with a thin wall containing hypodense material, attached to the inferior border of the pancreas. There were no other metastatic lesions identified.

Outcome:
The patient recovered following surgery and was discharged 7 days after admission. She was referred to the oncologist and offered a pancreatectomy with excision of the tumour, which was refused. The patient received six months of chemotherapy and finally succumbed to the disease 18 months after the presentation.

Summary:
The patient was admitted to the hospital with undifferentiated spindle cell sarcoma involving the pancreas that was treated with surgery and adjuvant chemotherapy. The patient was discharged following a 7-day hospitalization but eventually succumbed to the disease after 18 months.

Patient Name: [Name]

Discharge Date: [Discharge Date]

Medical History:
The patient had a history of obesity and underwent anterior cervical discectomy and fusion five years prior.

Hospital Course:
The patient presented to the emergency room with a persistent headache and was admitted to the hospital. A CT scan and MRI of the brain and spine showed extensive pneumocephalus and potential meningitis. After imaging and consultation with the neurosurgery team, the patient was found to have a CSF leak, and surgery was recommended.

The otolaryngology/rhinology team was consulted for further evaluation of the CSF leak. The patient was taken to the operating room for identification and repair of the CSF leak. The location of the potential defect was confirmed with intraoperative surgical navigation, and an area of mucosal thickening was noted. A small, pinpoint fistula with actively leaking CSF was also found in the posterior oropharynx.

The head and neck surgery team was asked to assist with repair of the fistula. An anterior neck approach to the cervical hardware was performed, and the anterior cervical hardware was removed, revealing a profuse CSF leak. The defect was repaired with DuraSeal followed by rotation of the right omohyoid muscle into the site of the defect between the prevertebral fascia and the oropharyngeal mucosa. The patient was then monitored in the neurosurgery intensive care unit.

Outcome:
The patient's headaches resolved, and repeat imaging showed resolution of the pneumocephalus. He remained in the ICU on bed rest with the lumbar drain open at 10 ml/hr for 5 days. The patient was then allowed to mobilize, and the lumbar drain was removed. He was subsequently discharged and continued to do well with no evidence of CSF leak on follow-up imaging.

Follow-up:
A repeat CT myelogram of the spine at 8 months showed no signs of persistent leak. The patient was advised to follow-up with his primary care provider for routine care.

Diagnosis:
CSF Leak

Procedure:
Repair of CSF Leak with anterior neck approach to cervical hardware and DuraSeal repair, followed by the rotation of right omohyoid muscle into the site of the defect.

Medical History: The patient had a medical history of hypertension, high cholesterol, and diabetes mellitus.

Hospital Course Summary:
The patient was admitted to the Coronary Care Unit because of sudden onset of chest pain at rest. ECG abnormalities associated with an increase of cardiac enzymes (hs troponin 70 pg/ml and CK-MB 8 ng/ml) were suggestive of an ACS (non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction). Echocardiogram showed left ventricular hypertrophy, end-diastolic diameter, and mild hypokinesia of the basal segment of the inferior wall with normal systolic function. In the parasternal short axis view, there was an abnormal diastolic flow inside the ventricular inferior wall. This flow was directed from the basal segment of the inferior wall into the left ventricular cavity. In the apical two-chamber view, there was the entire intramural course under the mitral valve posterior leaflet, where it was thrown into the ventricular cavity during diastole.

Treatment: According to ESC guidelines, the GRACE (Global Registry of Acute Coronary Events) risk score of the patient was 146 and early invasive strategy of myocardial revascularization (within the first 24 hours from admission) was indicated. The patient underwent coronary angiography, which revealed 90% stenosis in the middle portion and 70% stenosis in the distal portion of the left anterior descending artery, a double 70% stenosis in the proximal and the middle portion of the circumflex artery and the right coronary artery, dominant, with stenosis of 50% at the end of the proximal portion. Angiography confirmed the presence of a tortuous voluminous coronary fistula: it originated from the interventricular posterior artery and coursed along the posterior interventricular sulcus from the apex to the base of the left ventricle. The patient underwent percutaneous coronary angioplasty with the placement of two drug-eluting stents in the left anterior descending artery and a single drug-eluting stent in the circumflex artery.

Follow up: To complete evaluation, cardiac CT was performed to detect coronary fistula anatomy, its relationships with cardiac structures and its course. CT images documented that coronary fistula originated from the distal portion of the right coronary artery, ran into the left ventricular inferior wall, and drained into the left ventricular chamber under the mitral valve, with a final tract with an intramyocardial course. The patient was asymptomatic at 24-month follow-up.

Disposition: The patient was discharged in good condition.

Hospital Course: A 73-year-old male patient presented with severe postoperative hypertension following coronary artery bypass grafting. The patient had a medical history of type 2 diabetes, dyslipidemia, coronary heart disease, prostate cancer, and long-standing hypertension that had become harder to control during the past 2 years. The patient's family history was unremarkable, except for cases of sudden death among maternal relatives. A CT scan showed a small right adrenal mass, and biochemical testing revealed high levels of normetanephrines with no signs of familial syndromes. A meta-iodobenzylguanidine (MIBG) scan showed intense and moderate uptake of a 2 × 2 × 3 cm mass of the right adrenal gland with no distant metastases detected. The patient underwent adrenalectomy and was diagnosed with pheochromocytoma, confirmed by histology post-operatively. The patient has been discharged and will now continue with outpatient follow-up.

Summary of Hospital Stay: The patient was admitted due to severe postoperative hypertension that was difficult to manage despite medication. After further investigation, the diagnosis of Pheochromocytoma was confirmed by histology post-operative. The patient underwent adrenalectomy, and no complications were encountered during the procedure. The patient has been discharged and will be followed up in the outpatient clinic.

Diagnosis: Pheochromocytoma is a chromaffin cell tumor of the adrenal gland. It causes the excess production of catecholamines, including epinephrine, norepinephrine, and dopamine, resulting in variable symptoms of hypertension, palpitation, headache, sweating, and blurred vision.

Treatment: The patient underwent adrenalectomy to remove the tumor, after which there were no complications. The patient will continue to monitor and manage chronic conditions, including diabetes, dyslipidemia, and hypertension, with appropriate medication and lifestyle changes.

Prognosis: The prognosis is dependent on the size of the tumor, degree of malignancy, and any additional risk factors or comorbidities that the patient may have. In this case, the adrenal mass was small, and the Ki-67 proliferation index was less than one percent. Therefore, the patient's prognosis is positive.

Follow-up: The patient has been discharged and will return to the outpatient clinic for regular follow-up care to manage chronic conditions and monitor for recurrence or metastasis. Appropriate testing, including urine and plasma metanephrine levels, will be done to evaluate the patient's recovery.

Patient is a 43-year-old previously healthy Caucasian male who was admitted due to persistent fever, abdominal pain, posterior chest pain, and earache. He was diagnosed with external otitis and discharged with oral amoxicillin-clavulanate and paracetamol. Laboratory tests at that time showed increased CRP and ALT levels. Following discharge, patient presented with hyperchromic urine, hypocolic faeces, and jaundice. Bilateral laterocervical lymph nodes were found, but no other alterations were detected in the physical examination, chest X-ray, or abdominal ultrasound.
The patient's blood tests revealed an increase in WBC, moderate increase in lipase, and increased bilirubin levels. So, he was given antibiotics, including Piperacillin-Tazobactam and Tigecycline, however, his condition worsened, leading to multiorgan failure and admission to the ICU. Autoimmune profile work-up, immunoglobulin values and lymphocytic typing were normal, while hepatic biopsy showed fragmented liver tissue with accentuated lobular architecture, portals enlarged for sclerosis and lymphocytic inflammatory infiltration, and granulocyte involvement. Subsequently, corticosteroids were initiated, which resulted in an improvement in the patient's condition, as well as a reduction in cholestasis parameters, acute phase reactants, and hepatic cytolysis.
The patient was discharged after 40 days of hospitalization, with tapering corticosteroid therapy. On the 47th day following discharge, the patient underwent a Coronary Computed Tomography Angiography, which was normal. Eighteen months later, the patient was reported as completely asymptomatic.

Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Age: 40
Gender: Female
Date of Admission: [REDACTED]
Date of Discharge: [REDACTED]

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS:
The patient was referred for an evaluation of right periorbital pain, right eye ptosis, and diplopia that had first appeared 20 days earlier. She had restricted adduction of the right eyeball. Initial MRIs showed enlargement of the right medial rectus muscle with mild contrast enhancement, and additional lesions in the right retrobulbar optic nerve sheath and preseptal area.

MEDICAL MANAGEMENT:
The initial diagnosis was orbital IIP, and the patient was started on 60 mg of prednisone daily for 10 days, which greatly improved her symptoms. The dosage was gradually reduced over the next 8 weeks, but her symptoms relapsed when prednisone was reduced to below 20 mg per day. Azathioprine and mycophenolate mofetil also could not be administered because of potential direct hepatotoxicity. The patient was started on 3 mg of tacrolimus while discontinuing prednisolone over 8 weeks. After 6 months of tacrolimus administration, the right periorbital pain had completely disappeared, and the restriction of right eye abduction had resolved. The second follow-up MRIs were obtained at 16 months after the onset, by which time the lesions had nearly resolved. Tacrolimus was gradually reduced over a period of 7 months before being discontinued, and the patient had no further relapse during the 1-year follow-up.

CLINICAL FINDINGS:
The patient had painful tenderness of the right medial orbital region. Routine serological tests, autoimmune screening tests, and CSF studies all produced normal findings. However, her hepatitis C virus RNA level was 1,724,673 IU/mL in the quantification test, indicating active hepatitis C.

DISCHARGE INSTRUCTIONS:
The patient is advised to follow up with their healthcare provider for further management of hepatitis C. If any orbital IIP concerns arise, they are to contact their healthcare provider immediately.

Hospital Course:

The patient, a 65-year-old man with a history of diabetic nephropathy, underwent renal transplantation using his HTLV-I seropositive wife as the donor. Eight months after the transplant, he presented with weakness of his legs, which progressed rapidly, leaving him wheelchair-bound 12 days later. Despite receiving pulsed steroid therapy, he did not regain his leg muscle strength, and was transferred to our hospital.

At our facility, the patient underwent neurological examinations which showed flaccid paraparesis of his legs with diminished deep tendon reflexes. Nerve conduction studies did not reveal any evidence of peripheral neuropathy. His serum anti-HTLV-I antibody titer was elevated, and the CSF protein content was elevated with an increased cell count. Western blotting identified HTLV-I antibodies in his spinal cord fluid.

MRI scans of the thoracic spinal cord displayed T2 high signal intensities with slight swelling. A diagnosis of HAM was made based on these findings. The patient was started on interferon-α treatment, but showed little improvement. Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIg) therapy was added along with interferon-α, following which the patient showed improvement and was able to move his legs more easily. MRI examinations showed spinal cord atrophy. His OMSD improved during his inpatient stay.

Discharge Condition:

The patient was discharged in stable condition with recommendation for continued outpatient follow-up by his primary care physician and neurologist. Instructions were given to continue with interferon-α and IVIg therapy at his follow-up appointment. It was recommended that the patient continue to participate in physical therapy and rehabilitation programs to improve his mobility.

Summary:

A 65-year-old man with a history of diabetic nephropathy and renal transplantation, presented with flaccid paraparesis of the legs. A diagnosis of HTLV-I associated myelopathy (HAM) was made. The patient was treated with interferon-α and IVIg therapy, and showed improvement. The patient was discharged in stable condition with recommendation for continued outpatient follow-up.

Discharge Diagnosis: Syphilis infection, pleocytosis, persistent gait ataxia, and left eye ptosis

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted for evaluation of symptoms of progressive paraparesis, upper and lower extremity paresthesia, ataxic gait, and left upper eyelid ptosis. The patient is a 55-year-old single male with a prior episode of self-limited diplopia. The current symptoms have been progressing for four weeks, and the patient reported persistent low-intensity abdominal pain in the lower quadrants over the previous three to four months.

Neurological examination revealed incomplete left eye ptosis, bilateral small pupils, symmetric paraparesis, lower limbs areflexia, positive Romberg’s sign, lower limbs sensory ataxia, and hesitant, wide stand gait. The cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis showed albuminocytologic dissociation, and brain and spine MRI showed gadolinium enhancement in the cerebral pial layer and dorsal columns of the spinal cord.

The patient was treated with intravenous immunoglobulin for the assumption of Miller-Fischer acute demyelinating polyneuropathy. The VDRL test was found to be positive, and the patient was treated with intravenous penicillin for 14 days. The patient had a mild improvement at discharge but had persistent gait ataxia and left eye ptosis. Neuropsychiatric symptoms were moderately improved with quetiapine and escitalopram.

Clinical follow-up up till the 18th month revealed persistent gait ataxia and left eye ptosis and recovery of muscular strength. Lower limb pain persisted and moderately controlled with gabapentin, titrated up to 2000mg per day. CSF analysis six and twelve months after treatment showed persistent pleocytosis, as well as an 8- and 16-fold decrease in CSF-VDRL titer, respectively. Brain MRI was repeated at six and 12 months after treatment, being similar to the initial one. Brain MRI at 18 months after treatment showed slightly less intense signal enhancement after gadolinium administration in the spinal cord, particularly in the medullary cone.

The patient refused further lumbar punctures and was discharged with the plan of further outpatient management.

Discharge Medications:

- Gabapentin
- Quetiapine 
- Escitalopram

Follow-up Plan:

The patient is advised to follow up with the infectious disease specialist and to continue taking the prescribed medications. The patient should return in case of any worsening of any symptoms or for any other medical concerns.

The patient was advised to undergo surgical intervention to remove the cancerous growth, but he declined the treatment. Due to the stage of the cancer and the patient's unwillingness to undergo surgery, he was referred to palliative care for pain relief and symptom control.

Well-differentiated SCC of the right alveolus and buccal region in relation to 45,46 with lymph node secondaries.

The patient has been advised to regularly follow up with his oncologist for the management of his pain and symptoms. None

Hospital Course:
The patient is an 82-year-old female who was admitted to the hospital as an emergency with gross abdominal distension and lower abdominal pain. She had a six-week history of nonspecific malaise, loss of appetite, and dizziness, along with a longstanding history of constipation. Her past medical history included hypertension and impaired glucose tolerance, while her past surgical history included a previous caesarean section.

On examination, the patient had a nontender, grossly distended abdomen with an indentable mass in the lower left quadrant. Blood tests revealed acute renal failure and microcytic anaemia. A CT scan revealed massive dilatation of the sigmoid colon with faecal material within, resulting in bilateral renal tract obstruction. Following a clinical decision, she underwent a laparotomy, during which she was found to have massive colonic dilatation of the sigmoid and descending colon, with dense perirectal fibrosis throughout the length of the rectum. The rectum was resected at the mid rectum, and a Hartman's procedure was performed. Her renal function normalised, and she made an uneventful recovery. 

On histology from the resected specimen, it was observed that the longitudinal muscle layer was degenerate and absent in many areas of the specimen. The myenteric and submucosal plexuses were degenerate where longitudinal muscle was absent, while polyglucosan inclusion bodies were present throughout the longitudinal and circular layers of the muscularis propria, with almost total degeneration of the longitudinal layer, suggesting a myopathic process. The occurrence of longitudinal loss was in areas where the overlying muscle and mucosa were intact indicating that this was likely to be a primary myopathy. There was also a replacement of myocytes in both muscularis layers with elastosis and fibrosis, along with additional areas of elastosis in the submucosa and widespread smooth muscle metaplasia.

Discharge Diagnosis:
The patient was diagnosed with acute renal failure and massive colonic dilatation of the sigmoid and descending colon, with dense perirectal fibrosis throughout the length of the rectum. Histology from the resected specimen revealed a primary myopathy with elastosis and fibrosis.

Follow-Up Care:
The patient is advised to follow a healthy diet and exercise regimen and to attend regular follow-up appointments with the healthcare provider. She is also advised to take appropriate measures to prevent constipation, such as increasing fibre intake and staying hydrated.

None.

The patient is advised to avoid strenuous physical activity and to take adequate rest for at least two weeks following the surgery. DISCHARGE SUMMARY

Patient:
A 7-day-old male infant with dysmorphic features including microcephaly and microphthalmia, broad and flat nasal bridge, short neck and flat occiput, widely spaced nipples, thumb in palm hand deformity, and both calcaneovalgus foot abnormality, with abnormal heart sound detected.

History:
The patient was born at 40 weeks of gestation with a birth weight of 3,390 grams. The patient was the first baby of a 31-yr-old male and a 28-yr-old female. Both parents were healthy and there was no familial history of chromosomal abnormalities.

Hospital Course:
The patient was transferred to our hospital with tachypnea and poor oral feeding. Routine laboratory data including complete blood count, liver function tests, serum electrolytes, glucose, blood urea nitrogen, and creatinine were within normal range. The metabolic screening tests were negative. The patient was examined by echocardiography and cardiac computed tomography for the evaluation of the continuous murmur. The examinations revealed large PDA with mild hypoplasia of aortic valve and aortic arch. The patient received ligation of the PDA due to congestive heart failure, which alleviated the heart failure symptoms. Chromosome analysis was performed and revealed a mosaic karyotype with abnormalities of chromosome 6 including a ring chromosome and a dicentric ring chromosome.

Outpatient Examination:
At 3 months of age, the patient displayed a significant growth deficiency with vomiting. The patient was checked for malformed lesions by an esophagography and abdominal ultrasonogram. Concerning both foot and hand abnormalities, the patient received stretching exercise therapy comprised of plantaflexion and thumb abduction.

Follow-up:
At 9 months of age, the patient had global developmental delay including motor skills, personal-social interaction, and cognitive-adaptive development. A repeated echocardiogram revealed a closed ductus arteriosus with continued mild hypoplasia of the aortic valve and aortic arch. Brainstem evoked response audiometry test revealed mild right hearing loss; our institution's ear-nose-and-throat department recommended a hearing aid.

Plan:
We recommend the parents that the patient should receive an ophthalmologic examination and brain imaging study. Permission was not granted. The patient is to continue stretching exercise therapy comprised of plantaflexion and thumb abduction for both foot and hand abnormalities in the department of orthopedics of our institution. Follow-up appointment advised with ear-nose-and-throat department.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Information:
- Age: 74
- Gender: Male
- Medical History: Hypertension, dyslipidemia, diabetes mellitus, coronary artery disease, and end-stage renal disease

Hospital Course:
- The patient was transferred to our hospital due to bilateral intermittent claudication that had been ongoing for 6 months before admission.
- The patient had received clopidogrel and cilostazol as medication but refused surgical revascularization.
- Endovascular therapy (EVT) was chosen as the treatment option, and the patient gave written consent.
- EVT was initiated in the right superficial femoral artery chronic total occlusion (SFA-CTO) using the contralateral approach.
- The antegrade approach with the stiff CTO wire resulted in subintimal wiring. Therefore, bidirectional approach with direct distal-SFA puncture was used.
- Retrograde-antegrade rendezvous technique led to wire externalization, but no devices were able to pass the lesion by the antegrade and retrograde approaches.
- Minimal balloon could not pass the lesion, and the needle cracking technique from outside and inside of the vessel could not modify the lesion fully.
- ELA using the Turbo Elite 0.9 mm (Spectranetics, Co., USA) was applied, and it modified the CTO entry-morphology.
- After ELA ablation, the Caravel microcatheter (ASAHI Intecc) finally crossed the lesion using an antegrade approach with the BAlloon Deployment using FORcible Manner (BADFORM) technique, which enabled change of the wire from conventional the 0.014-inch wire to 0.009-inch RotaWire floppy (Boston Scientific) and RotaLink Plus 1.5mm burr ablation.
- Thereafter, we dilated the entire SFA lesion with conventional balloons and simultaneously achieved hemostasis of the distal-SFA puncture point.
- A bare nitinol stent was deployed due to severe dissection of the partial SFA.
- Treating the bilateral iliac arteries with bare nitinol stents followed, resulting in improvement of the right ABI of the patient from being unmeasurable to 0.79, and his intermittent claudication disappeared.
- The ABI and symptoms have remained satisfactory eight months after the current EVT.

Impression and Plan:
- This patient presented with bilateral intermittent claudication that improved after EVT treatment, including ELA and stent deployment.
- The patient's symptoms and ABI remained satisfactory at the eight-month follow-up.

Hospital Course:

An 8-year-old male child was admitted to our hospital with cardiac failure. The patient had a history of TOF repair and left pulmonary arterioplasty two years ago at the referring hospital. Echocardiogram conducted during admission showed the presence of a large residual muscular outlet ventricular septal defect (VSD) likely following VSD patch dehiscence. Cardiac catheterization was performed for further evaluation which confirmed the presence of VSD via angiogram. The right ventricular pressure was high at systole, and angiogram in the main pulmonary artery showed dilated right pulmonary artery while the left pulmonary artery (LPA) was completely occluded.

Intervention:

Radio-frequency (RF) energy was applied to the blind-ending channel of the proximal LPA to recanalize the occluded artery. A 2mm × 10mm coronary balloon was inflated at the atretic segment of LPA and a 6mm × 20mm cutting balloon was used to perform balloon dilatation. A 10mm × 17mm stent was used to address the atretic segment, which was further dilated using an 8mm×40mm Powerflex PTA balloon. The patient was discharged 3 days after the procedure with aspirin at 5mg/kg.

Follow-up:

The patient was readmitted 4 weeks after the procedure for the revision of the VSD patch. Repeat cardiac catheterization conducted three months later shows that the LPA stent is patent and the LPA had increased in size with improved left lung arborization. A localized segment of the left lower lobe artery was stenosed (2.4mm), which was subsequently redilated using an 8mm × 20mm peripheral Flextome cutting balloon.

Outcome:

A Formula 418 Expandable stent was implanted to the stenotic segment distal to the first stent with satisfactory results. The LPA and distal pulmonary arterial tree appear healthy and are of satisfactory size for future growth. Repeat cardiac catheterization conducted four months after the initial intervention showed a reduction of the right ventricular pressure of 41 end-diastolic pressure 8 mmHg (simultaneous aortic pressure: 91/50 mmHg, mean: 66 mmHg).

Conclusion:

The patient was discharged in stable condition with aspirin therapy. The guardian of the patient was instructed to follow-up with their local pediatric cardiologist for routine monitoring and care.

Medical Course: 
During the evaluation, the best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was 20/100 (Plano), N18. Normal values were recorded for pupils, intraocular pressure, and anterior segment examination by slit-lamp biomicroscopy. Fundus examination of both eyes showed a normal optic disc and bright foveal reflex. The patient showed a severe red-green color vision deficiency. The full-field ERG confirmed normal values for the amplitude and latencies of both rod and cone components in both eyes.

The SD-OCT showed an intact external limiting membrane and preserved but flat inner segment-outer segment junction in both eyes. The mfERG waveform showed decreased signal amplitudes and a prolonged latency originating from the central macula with the central rings affected more than the peripheral rings, leading to a diagnosis of OMD.
All available immediate family members received comprehensive eye examination and were found to be normal except the elder brother.

Condition on Discharge: 
The patient was diagnosed with OMD.

Follow-Up Arrangements: 
The clinically unaffected and asymptomatic family members did not agree to undergo further evaluation with SD-OCT and mfERG.

Discharge Medications: None

Final Diagnosis: Oculocutaneous Albinism.

The patient was a 3-year-old male alpaca who presented at Huantaiqi Zoo in Chongqing, China with ruminal tympany that had persisted for approximately two weeks. The animal's nutritional condition ranged from low to normal. Despite treatment with sodium bicarbonate, the patient later succumbed to a fatal infection.

Diagnostic Evaluation:

At necropsy, a high-grade sero-fibrinogenous pleural effusion was observed in the thoracic cavity. The lung displayed a pronounced hemorrhage with topical congestion, and lobular pneumonia was noted as well. A limpid hydropericardium was detected, with plenty of foam present in the trachea. No pathological lesions were found in any other organs.

Treatment:

No treatment was administered, as the patient had already passed away by the time of necropsy.

Results:

Bacteriological examination from the lung, heart-blood, and hydropericardium were routinely performed using blood agar. After incubation, a pure culture of translucent grey colonies with hemolysis was detected. Gram staining was positive for sporadic Gram-negative bacteria.
The isolated strains obtained from the lung and hydropericardium shared 99.50% similarity with M. morganii strains registered in GenBank. According to the above-mentioned identification results, the alpaca was infected with M. morganii resulting in fatal pneumonia.

Post-Discharge Plan:

No applicable post-discharge plan, as the patient had passed away.

The 8-year-old female patient presented for evaluation of a slowly growing, plaque-like skin lesion on her left chest wall. The lesion was approximately 0.5 cm in maximum diameter in size and was too small and with a light violet color. The patient underwent surgical excision and biopsy, and the pathology report described the specimen as having a white-gray nodular lesion with spindle cells developed in a storiform to whorled pattern. The differential diagnosis included DFSP and Dermatofibroma. A confident diagnosis of DFSP was made based on immunohistochemical expression of CD34 and negative FXIIIA and S100. 

After the diagnosis, the patient underwent extensive imaging and hematological testing which were without pathological findings. Although the margins of the removed mass were healthy, we decided to perform extended surgical excision to decrease the possibility of recurrence. The child's postoperative course was uneventful, and she will be examined every 6 months for the next 3 years for palpation of her scar tissue and examination of her regional lymph nodes to exclude recurrence or the possibility of metastases.

The patient was diagnosed with DFSP based on biopsy. Extended surgical excision was performed, and the patient will undergo regular follow-up appointments. Further treatment is not required at this time.

Discharge Summary
Patient: 39-year-old male

Medical History:
The patient had a history of allergic rhinitis. He reported many episodes of lightheadedness and patches of urticaria, with chest tightness that happened either with or shortly after exercise over the previous 3 months. Over time, the episodes had become more frequent and severe and required several treatments to relieve his symptoms. The patient was diagnosed with eosinophilic esophagitis via biopsy. 

Hospital Course:
The patient was given several medications to treat his throat and chest tightness with exercise, but they did not completely resolve his symptoms. He later tried to avoid wheat and all food for up to 12 hours before exercise but to no avail.

To manage his condition, the patient elected to start a trial of omalizumab, which was given in doses of 300 mg every 2 weeks. No food restrictions were given during this time. The patient reported marked improvement, and he was able to exercise three times a week without any symptoms. He had only one episode of mild urticaria, but it happened when he had missed one of his omalizumab injections. The patient continued to exercise normally, reporting any symptoms that he had and was followed up monthly.

The patient later experienced episodes of urticaria, markedly increased chest tightness, and periorbital edema after at least 15 minutes of exercise. He ultimately had an episode of anaphylaxis with urticaria, difficulty breathing, and facial swelling and was admitted to the emergency department, where he received several treatments to relieve his symptoms. After this episode, omalizumab was restarted at the same doses and intervals.

Follow-up and Outcome:
The patient continued on omalizumab with no further episodes of anaphylaxis and no restrictions on his activity level. He is expected to continue being followed up monthly and continue exercising normally.

Hospital Course Summary:

The patient, a 60-year-old male, was admitted to our hospital with a two-month history of fatigue and trace lower extremity edema. The patient was also suffering from arthralgias of both knees and hands. Upon examination, it was found that the patient had been diagnosed with newly proteinuria. The patient's nocturia also stood out, alongside an increased urinary frequency.

Physical examination revealed trace lower extremity edema, however, there were no other abnormalities in cardiac, pulmonary, or abdominal exam. The patient had undergone routine cholecystectomy four months prior to admission. Laboratory examination showed a mild elevation in erythrocyte sedimentation rate. Urinalysis revealed 3+ protein but no nitrites or glucose. Renal function was normal. Urine protein was quantified as 10.68 gr/24h.

Further investigation was carried out to determine the cause of membranous glomerulonephritis. The patient was tested for secondary causes which included anti-double stranded deoxyribonucleic acid (anti-dsDNA) antibodies, antinuclear antibodies (ANA), titers for antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA), complement levels, and tests for cryoglobulins and rheumatoid factor. The patient's results were negative or within normal ranges. Serologies for hepatitis A, B, C, and HIV were also non-reactive.

A thoracoabdominal tomography was performed on the patient, which was normal. The renal biopsy showed that the membranous nephropathy was the cause of nephrotic syndrome. IgG deposition was seen along the capillary wall.

Upon review, there was no evidence of acute or chronic infections, nor any other features of related medical issues. The patient was diagnosed with membranous nephropathy.

The patient was discharged in good condition with a diagnosis of membranous nephropathy. The patient received no medications during the hospitalization of his condition.

Follow-Up Instructions:

The patient should seek medical advice from his physician if trace lower extremity edema or any other symptoms recur.

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 47-year-old woman, was admitted to the hospital with bilateral groin pain, inability to urinate, and bloody vaginal discharge. Clinical vaginal examination revealed the presence of a large necrotic mass filling the whole vaginal tract. Transabdominal ultrasound examination showed a cervico-vaginal mass measuring 112 × 114 mm that protruded from the uterine cavity with a distorted view of the uterus. After consultation and an MRI examination, a large heterogeneous signal intensity of a well-defined submucosal fundal fibroid mass was confirmed. Uterine anatomy was distorted as seen as “V shape” fundus in sagittal plane due to traction of the mass. 

Laboratory tests showed a decreased hemoglobin level of 10.1 g/dL, hematocrit of 30.9%, and elevated CRP level of 37.5 mg/L. The patient's fasting glucose level, AST and ALT liver enzymes were within normal range, but the CA125 level was 152 U/mL. 

At laparotomy, a large uterine mass with complete uterine inversion was confirmed. The mass was taken out via transverse uterine incision after depicting the myoma’s pedicle. Total abdominal hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy was performed due to the patient's request before surgery. The excised specimen revealed a giant mass with extensive necrosis and multiple hemorrhagic foci. Pathology report confirmed 12 × 12 × 10 cm sized leiomyoma including large ischemic necrotic areas. There was no evidence of malignancy. 

The patient was discharged without any complications five days after the surgery.

Discharge Diagnosis:
Uterine inversion with uterine fibroid.

Discharge Condition:
Stable. 

Discharge Medication:
N/A. 

Discharge Instructions:
The patient was instructed to follow up with her gynecologist and primary care physician. She was advised to avoid heavy lifting and intercourse for six weeks to allow for full recovery. She was also instructed to monitor for any signs of vaginal bleeding, pain or fever. If any of these symptoms appeared, she was advised to contact her physician immediately. 

Follow-Up:
The patient was advised to schedule a follow-up appointment with her gynecologist and primary care physician for recovery monitoring.

Her body temperature, plasma creatine phosphokinase, and sodium levels were normalized by the 14th day of admission. The patient was previously diagnosed with panic disorder and treated with medication.

Laboratory data showed HHS with random blood glucose, sodium, and serum osmolality, as well as ketones, proteins, and glucose in urine dipstick analysis. T2-weighted, diffusion-weighted, and fluid-attenuated inversion recovery images of brain MRI carried out on the second hospital day showed high-intensity lesions in the SCC, with decreased apparent diffusion coefficient values, suggesting MERS.

The patient was discharged in stable condition. Further follow-up and monitoring were recommended.

Patient name: not identified

-15-year history of diabetes, medically controlled

Hospital Course:

The patient was referred to us with severe pain and decreased vision in both eyes two days after undergoing cataract surgery on the left eye and one month ago on the right eye. The patient had undergone phacoemulsification under topical anesthesia in both eyes one month apart with uneventful postoperative period after the first surgery. The patient presented with bilateral flat anterior chambers and high intraocular pressure (IOP) four hours after his cataract surgery. The patient was diagnosed and treated as malignant glaucoma and was given intravenous (IV) mannitol 20% (1-2 g/kg body weight), tab acetazolamide 250 mg thrice daily and timolol maleate 0.5% eye drops twice daily in both eyes (B/E), peripheral iridotomy in the right eye and YAG hyloidotomy in the right eye, and posterior capsulotomy in the left eye.

On further examination, visual acuity was finger counting at half meter in the right eye and one meter in the left eye. There was bilateral lid edema, conjunctival chemosis, corneal edema, shallow ACs, mid-dilated pupils, patent peripheral iridotomy in the right eye, in-the-bag posterior chamber pseudophakos with opening in the posterior capsule. IOP was 72 mmHg in the right eye and 68 mmHg in the left eye. Fundus was unclear. B-scan Ultrasonography revealed annular cilio-choroidal effusion in both eyes.

A possible drug reaction was suspected and the systemic drug list was reviewed. Acetazolamide, a sulphonamide derivative was suspected as the possible cause and was discontinued. Topical antiglaucoma medications along with atropine, topical steroids, and antibiotics were continued. Over the next two weeks, the patient's condition improved. Five weeks following the initial surgery, his vision was 20/20, N6 with correction and IOP 21 mm Hg in the right eye and 20 mm Hg in the left eye without medications. ACs were quiet with clear corneas in both eyes and gonioscopy showed open angles in both eyes. Fundus examination revealed healthy optic discs with 0.5:1 cup and resolved choroidals in both eyes.

Disposition: The patient's vision was stable and his condition had improved over the two weeks. The patient was discharged in good condition with instructions to follow up as an outpatient.

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 38-year-old male, presented to our emergency department with a low-grade fever, headache, dizziness, blurry vision, and red eyes over the preceding week. Ophthalmologic examination revealed mild diffuse conjunctival injection and bilateral sluggish pupil reaction. Funduscopic examination displayed optic disc swelling and hyperemia with choroidal whitish lesions. Further evaluation using B-mode ultrasound and optical coherence tomography demonstrated significant bilateral posterior choroidal thickening and exudative retinal detachment. Brain MRI displayed bilateral posterior predominant nodular choroid thickening with post-contrast enhancement, associated episcleral thickening, and enhancement inseparable from the optic nerve sheath at its globe insertion. Bilateral inner ear membranous labyrinth enhancement was noted as well. Finally, diffuse supra- and infratentorial leptomeningeal enhancement predominantly along the cerebellar folia and basal cisterns were observed. Laboratory evaluation for infectious, granulomatous, and other autoimmune diseases was unrevealing. The patient clinical presentation and the associated constellation of ophthalmologic and radiologic findings supported the diagnosis of VKHD. High-dose oral corticosteroid treatment was initiated, and the patient's symptoms improved. The patient was symptom-free at his one-year follow-up evaluation.

The patient completely recovered from the COVID-19 infection, but continued having insulin allergies with her humulin 70/30 insulin injections. Hospital Course:

The patient, a 35-year-old gravida 4 para 3, presented at 16 weeks and 6 days gestation for follow-up ultrasound of a perigestational hemorrhage seen at 10 weeks and 4 days. A large uterine cavity pseudoaneurysm measuring 4.2 × 3.8 × 3.7 cm and appearing to arise from abnormal placentation at the previous cesarean scar was identified. Repeat ultrasound revealed a normal active fetus in breech position compressing the pseudoaneurysm upon contact. An unenhanced MRI one week later confirmed a 4 cm lesion projecting into the lower right uterine cavity at the inferior margin of the placenta. Management options were discussed to include conservative imaging observation versus embolization. Due to high maternal mortality risk from spontaneous hemorrhage, elective termination was also discussed but was rejected by the patient.

Treatment:

A novel use of dynamic time-resolved contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance angiogram (MRA) utilizing a functional MR urography protocol™ was performed for enhanced characterization of feeding arteries and treatment planning/mapping. The MRA revealed two suspected feeding vessels: a branch off the right ovarian artery parasitized to the uterine arcuate artery and a branch off the right uterine artery parasitized to the uterine arcuate and radial arteries. A conventional arteriogram performed with iodinated contrast diluted 50/50 with normal saline demonstrated a prominent right ovarian artery. The right ovarian artery was then embolized with coils. A right hypogastric arteriogram revealed a prominent right uterine artery and a large ovoid lesion opacifying with contrast consistent with the target lesion. The right uterine artery was then embolized. Postcoil imaging revealed no lesion opacification. Ultrasound interrogation the next morning revealed no flow within the lesion. Repeat ultrasound 24 hours later, however, showed recurrence of small blood flow into the lesion, with a significant decrease in lesion size to 3.3 cm, which remained stable prior to discharge 4 days later.

Outcome:

Serial ultrasound examinations throughout the duration of the pregnancy demonstrated appropriate interval fetal growth. The pseudoaneurysm progressively decreased in size, measuring 1.4 × 2.0 cm just prior to delivery. The patient presented with premature rupture of membranes at 33 weeks. Cervical changes and painful contractions necessitated an urgent prophylactic cesarean delivery 13 weeks after embolization. On attempt to deliver the placenta, it was adherent to the uterus, consistent with invasive placentation. The placenta was left in situ and a supracervical hysterectomy was performed. The patient was discharged on postoperative day 3. The baby was admitted to the neonatal intensive care unit secondary to prematurity and discharged home in stable condition at 19 days of life.

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted to our hospital on [Redacted] with complaints of paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia. Further examination revealed a left ventricle tumour, which was confirmed by colour Doppler echocardiography and computed tomographic angiography. The tumour was found to be large relative to the left ventricle, occupying 80% of cavity volume of the left ventricular obstructing mitral valve inflow.

Due to the extensive adhesions of the base of the tumour to the anterior wall and side wall of the left ventricle and its proximity to the mitral valve, chordae tendineae, and other important anatomical structures, the orthotopic cardiac tumour resection was deemed difficult and risky. Therefore, the patient underwent a heart autotransplantation procedure, which involved a median sternotomy incision, instituting cardiopulmonary bypass, isolating the heart, removing the tumour, and returning the heart to its original position.

Histology revealed that the tumour was a rhabdomyoma. The patient was discharged on [Redacted] after 13 days of hospitalization. In 5 months of follow-up, there was no tumour recurrence or arrhythmia observed.

The patient was instructed to follow up with his primary care physician for routine assessments and to notify our hospital if any symptoms recurred. Patient: 56-year-old female with left sided vestibular schwannoma and history of fractionated stereotactic radiotherapy

Hospital Course:
The patient presented with acute onset and progressive hemifacial spasms (HFS) characterized by periorbital twitching. Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed no significant changes since previous treatment. It was decided to perform surgical debulking of the tumor and microvascular decompression (MVD). During the surgery, the tumor was debulked and the facial nerve was dissected from the tumor capsule. The bone was removed, exposing the dura of the internal acoustic canal (IAC), allowing the tumor to spontaneously herniate through the opening. Intra-operative monitoring demonstrated electromyographic lateral spread that was successfully abolished with the decompression. Brainstem auditory evoked potentials (BAEP) remained stable. 

Clinical Findings:
Post-operatively, the patient's HFS improved and eventually abated, and hearing remained unchanged. There were no postoperative complications observed.

Diagnosis:
Upon further testing, the final pathology returned as vestibular schwannoma.

Plan:
The patient was discharged and advised to follow up with her healthcare provider for further monitoring and management of the condition.

Instructions:
The patient should be advised to follow up as per her healthcare provider's instructions. Any concerning symptoms should be reported to the healthcare provider immediately.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [redacted]

Date of Admission: [redacted]
Date of Discharge: [redacted]

Reason for Admission:
Multiple carious teeth management.

Hospital Course Summary:
The 19-year-old male was admitted to the postgraduate department of endodontics for the management of multiple carious teeth. During history taking, it was revealed that the patient was a school dropout due to difficulty in coping with the educational curriculum. The patient's medical history was noncontributory. The patient underwent a thorough dental examination revealing dental caries in relation to teeth 15, 37, and 47 and multiple missing teeth (14, 13, 22, 23, and 36).  An orthopantomograph revealed multiple taurodontic teeth in relation to 37, 46, 47, 17, 26, and 27. The patient was advised to have root canal treatment in 37. The complete endodontic management was performed by one of the authors while the other author took care of post-endodontic restoration and clinical follow-up with the department of oral surgery. Orthograde root canal treatment was performed using nickel-titanium rotary instruments and irrigation was done with 5.2% sodium hypochlorite solution (NaOCl) during shaping and cleaning of the root canal system. Passive ultrasonic irrigation (PUI) activation was employed using # 20/0.00 taper SS non-cutting ultrasonic tip and a 1 min flush of 17% ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA; Smearclear, SybronEndo, CA, USA). The canals were dressed with intracanal calcium hydroxide medicament and the tooth was sealed temporarily with an intermediate restorative material. The patient was asked to return after 2 weeks.

At the second appointment, the canals were made dry with sterile paper points. Following radiographic control of the fit of gutta-percha master cone, the apical part of the main root canals was obturated with vertically compacted warm gutta-percha using the Touch&Heat 5004 device. The coronal portion of the main canal was backfilled with thermoplasticized gutta-percha using the Obtura II gun. The access cavity was sealed with dual-cure composite resin. A full coverage crown was restored on the tooth after 3 weeks’ time. The patient was then referred to the Department of Oral Surgery for surgical correction of prognathic mandible. The surgical intervention was performed in two stages. The first stage involved a bilateral sagittal split osteotomy followed after 3 months by a second stage surgical advancement genioplasty procedure. Follow-up was at 6-months and 2-year intervals. Patient remained asymptomatic at these times.

Diagnosis at Discharge:
Multiple carious teeth management.

Procedures:
Orthograde Root Canal Treatment, surgical correction of prognathic mandible (two-stage process)

Condition at Discharge:
Asymptomatic.

Plan at Discharge:
The patient was advised to maintain good oral hygiene and attend regular follow-up appointments with the Department of Oral Surgery.

Discharge Summary

Patient: 65-year-old female

Admitted: Emergency Department

Admission date: [date]

Discharge date: [date]

Diagnosis: Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS) syndrome with an atypical reactivation of Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) and subsequent diagnosis of angioimmunoblastic T-cell lymphoma (AITCL)

Hospital course:

The patient was admitted to our emergency department with erythematous, confluent, itchy, maculopapular exanthema on her trunk and extremities, which had started 7 days before admission, and with malaise, weight loss, arthralgia, and night sweats, having lasted about 3 weeks. The initial diagnosis was parainfectious exanthema, and topical and systemic steroids (prednisone 50 mg) were prescribed, and the patient was discharged. However, four days later, she revisited our department with facial edema and with the exanthema spread all over her body. Further investigations revealed cervical lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, and sub-erythroderma, and her laboratory tests showed mild leukocytosis, mild anemia, eosinophilia and mildly elevated AST and creatinine levels. EBV PCR and serology were positive, while HHV-6 and −8, HIV, and HBV/HCV were negative. Chest radiography and abdominal ultrasound confirmed lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly.

A skin biopsy, performed at presentation, revealed spongiotic dermatitis with perivascular lymphocytic infiltration with eosinophils, while an inguinal lymph node excision biopsy conducted later showed lymphocyte hyperplasia with effacement of the normal architecture and high vascular proliferation with an increased number of CD23+ follicular dendritic cells. The cellular infiltrate consisted of a monomorphic, small- to medium-sized population of lymphocytes CD3+/CD4+ with coexpression of programmed cell death protein 1 (PD1), and of abundant lymphoid cells partly with a blastic morphology and plasma cell differentiation. Expression of CD79a and, partially, CD20 for the B cells and of CD30 for the large lymphoid blasts was noted. The atypical cells were negative for anaplastic lymphoma kinase. EBER in situ hybridization revealed EBER-positive nuclei, and our patient was finally diagnosed with AITCL.

Treatment and Progress:

In view of the patient's drug reaction, she was treated with intravenous corticosteroids followed by oral prednisone upon improvement. Topical emollients to relieve the skin tenderness were applied. However, despite clinical improvement, she was later diagnosed with AITCL, and underwent CHOP chemotherapy followed by autologous stem cell transplantation. Unfortunately, 3 months after stem cell transplantation, her disease rapidly progressed, and she was put on IGEV salvage chemotherapy. At the last follow-up, the patient was in a poor general condition, and she was admitted to a palliative care unit, where she deceased few days afterwards.

Follow-up Care:

The patient's family was informed of the patient's prognosis, and further palliative care was provided until she deceased few days later.

Follow-up appointments, treatments, and procedures were not recommended, as the patient had passed away.

She also felt tired, lost weight, had joint pain, and had night sweats for about 3 weeks. At first, doctors thought the rash was caused by an infection. They gave her steroid cream and steroid pills (prednisone 50 mg) and sent her home. Four days later, she came back with swelling in her face and the rash had spread all over her body. Tests showed swollen lymph nodes in the neck, an enlarged spleen, and skin that was almost completely red. Blood tests showed slightly high white blood cell counts, mild low red blood cells, high levels of a type of white blood cell called eosinophils, and slightly high liver and kidney numbers. Tests for Epstein-Barr virus were positive. Tests for other viruses including HIV and hepatitis were negative. A chest x-ray and belly ultrasound confirmed the swollen lymph nodes and enlarged spleen.

A skin sample taken at the first visit showed inflamed skin with certain white blood cells around blood vessels. A lymph node sample taken from the groin area later showed abnormal cell growth. The normal structure was damaged and there were many new blood vessels. There were also too many of certain immune cells. The cells were mostly small to medium white blood cells of a specific type. Some cells looked immature and some had features of cells that make antibodies. Special lab tests found markers on the cells that helped identify the cancer type. The abnormal cells did not have a marker linked to another type of lymphoma. A test found virus-infected cells in the tissue. The patient was then diagnosed with angioimmunoblastic T-cell lymphoma, a type of blood cancer.

Sadly, 3 months after the transplant, her cancer got much worse. She then received another type of chemotherapy called IGEV to try to control the cancer. At her last visit, the patient was very sick. She was moved to a comfort care unit where the focus was on keeping her comfortable. She passed away a few days later.

Follow-up Care:

The patient's family was told about her condition. Comfort care was given until she passed away a few days later.

No follow-up visits or treatments were scheduled because the patient had passed away.

Microscopically, sheets of foamy histiocytes, mixed inflammatory cell infiltrations, scattered giant cells, and distorted tubule were also noted.
