Discharge Summary:

Patient: 9-year-old male

Date of Admission: [Date]

Date of Discharge: [Date]

Admission Diagnosis: Continuous pain in the lower left back tooth region for 1 week

Hospital Course Summary:

The patient presented with a chief complaint of continuous pain in the lower left back tooth region for 1 week. Clinical examination revealed large disto-occlusal caries on tooth 36, with exaggerated response to vitality tests (sensibility) with lingering pain. Intraoral periapical (IOPA) radiograph revealed blunderbuss canals for both mesial and distal roots. A diagnosis of irreversible pulpitis was formulated.

Following administration of local anesthesia (2% Lignox with adrenaline, 2% Lignox with adrenaline, Indoco Remedies Ltd, Mumbai, India) and rubber dam application, access cavity was made, and three canals were located. Mesial canal orifices were slit-shape and the distal orifice was large oval-shaped. In the mesial canals, #30 k-file (Mani Inc., Tochigi, Japan) was snugly fit in the middle third. Working length for the distal canal was determined using the bent file technique, and confirmed radiographically. In the distal canal, #80 k-file was loose and going beyond the apex without any resistance. Circumferential filing was done in the distal root, and the mesial root was minimally prepared till #30 k-file. 5 mL of 3% sodium hypochlorite solution (Parcan, Septodont Healthcare India Pvt. Ltd, Maharashtra, India) was used as an irrigant for each canal along with normal saline. Triple antibiotic paste (TAP) (metronidazole, ciprofloxacin, and minocycline) was made as paste slurry and placed inside the canal using lentulospiral (Mani Inc., Tochigi, Japan) and k files.

After 3 weeks, TAP was removed, and irrigation was performed using 10 mL of 3% sodium hypochlorite (Dentwash, Prime Dental Products Pvt Ltd; Thane, Mumbai, India), followed by 10 mL of saline and a final flush of 10 mL of ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA) (Dentwash, Prime, Bhiwandi, Maharashtra, India). Bleeding was induced in the mesial root canals using a #15 k file by taking it beyond the apex. Platelet-rich fibrin (PRF) was separated from the blood corpuscles and squeezed between sterile gauze pieces to remove the trapped fluids. Following which, the PRF membrane was separated into small fragments using sterile scissors. A metal plugger (Manipal instruments, Parkala, India) with a rubber stopper set at 1 mm short of working length was used to pack the first increment inside the distal root. On reaching the desired length, a 0.5 mm diameter metal plugger was used in circumferential tapping manner to pack the PRF, and a flat surface was achieved. Following which, the butt end of sterile No. 80 paper point (DiaDent, Chungcheongbuk-do, Korea) was used to compact the PRF further and to remove any remaining entrapped fluid. Next increment was placed in a similar way after shortening the length. Once the entire canal was filled till the orifice with the PRF, MTA was packed inside the pulp chamber to a thickness of 3 mm. Before temporizing, a moist cotton pellet was placed, and the patient was recalled the next day for the placement of Glass Ionomer Cement (GC type 2, GC Corporation, Tokyo, Japan) seal and Composite restoration (3M Z350 XT, 3M ESPE Dental Products, MN, USA).

The patient received follow-up visits at 6 months, 1 year, 2 years, 3 years and 5 years, during which pulp sensibility tests done using Endofrost (Coltène/Whaledent Private Ltd, Raigad, Maharashtra) were negative for the tooth at all recall visits. Follow-up radiographs at the 2-year recall showed complete closure of the root end along with increased root length. The 5-year recall radiograph showed no signs of pathology, and canals were patent and not obliterated. The patient was completely asymptomatic during all the follow-up visits.

Discharge Diagnosis: Irreversible pulpitis, treated with maturogenesis technique using triple antibiotic paste and platelet-rich fibrin.

Management Plan: None. The patient was discharged in good condition and advised to continue oral hygiene practices.

The tooth was very sensitive to tests and the pain lasted a long time after. An x-ray showed that the tooth roots were not fully formed yet. The dentist determined the tooth pulp, which is the soft tissue inside the tooth, was badly damaged and could not heal on its own.

The dentist numbed the area and placed a rubber sheet to keep the tooth dry. The dentist made an opening in the tooth and found three root canals. The canals in the front roots were narrow and slit-shaped. The canal in the back root was large and oval-shaped. The dentist measured how deep each canal was. The back root canal was very wide and open at the tip. The dentist cleaned and shaped all the canals. A germ-killing rinse and salt water were used to clean each canal. A paste made of three antibiotics was placed inside the canals to kill germs.

After 3 weeks, the antibiotic paste was removed. The canals were cleaned again with germ-killing rinse, salt water, and a solution to prepare the canal walls. The dentist poked past the root tip in the front canals to cause bleeding on purpose. A healing material called platelet-rich fibrin was made from blood. This material was squeezed to remove extra fluid and cut into small pieces. The dentist packed this healing material into the back root first using small tools. The material was pressed down firmly to make a flat surface. More material was added layer by layer until the canal was filled. The same was done for the other canals. A special cement was placed on top to seal everything. A wet cotton ball was put in, and the patient came back the next day. A glass filling material and a tooth-colored filling were placed to close the tooth.

The patient came back for check-ups at 6 months, 1 year, 2 years, 3 years, and 5 years. At each visit, the tooth did not respond to cold tests, which was expected. X-rays at 2 years showed the root tips had closed and the roots had grown longer. The x-ray at 5 years showed no problems. The root canals stayed open and healthy. The patient had no pain or problems at any of the follow-up visits.

Discharge Diagnosis: Badly damaged tooth pulp, treated with a technique to help the tooth roots finish growing using antibiotic paste and a healing material made from blood.

Management Plan: None. The patient was sent home in good health. The patient was told to keep brushing and flossing as usual.

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to the hospital with complaints of worsening headache, nuchal rigidity, and fever. She also reported photophobia, nausea, vomiting, and backache. The patient had a history of nephrolithiasis and denied any allergies or medications at home. There was no family history of hypertension, heart disease, or cancer. The patient had been vacationing in Massachusetts, spending a significant amount of time outdoors and swimming. She reported no insect bites.

During the physical examination, a unilateral vesicular rash was observed extending from T8-T9 dermatomal pattern to under the left breast. Nuchal rigidity was noted, and other exams were within normal limits. The patient was alert and oriented to person, place, and time.

Computed tomography (CT) scan of the head showed no signs of acute infarct, hemorrhage, or mass effect. The CSF gram stain showed no organisms, with a negative India ink stain and negative CSF bacterial cultures. The initial blood cultures were also negative. Tests for Lyme, West Nile Virus, Herpes Simplex Virus 1, 2 DNA PCR, and Varicella Zoster Virus (VZV) were negative.

The patient was started on empiric therapy with intravenous ceftriaxone and vancomycin, oral acyclovir, and dexamethasone. The cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) was sent to the department of health for further testing. The patient was noted to have a white blood cell count of 5.2 × 103 cells/µL with normal chemistries. Subsequent testing showed that the patient's CSF was positive for VZV DNA, and the patient was discharged on oral acyclovir.

The patient reported feeling better with reduced headache and fever, and by the fifth day of hospitalization, prednisone was discontinued. The patient was contacted at home and reported to be in good health, with a resolution of meningeal signs and fever.

Discharge Diagnosis:
The patient was diagnosed with meningitis due to Varicella Zoster Virus (VZV) infection.

Discharge Medications:
The patient was discharged on a course of oral acyclovir.

Follow-up:
The patient was advised to continue taking oral acyclovir and follow up with her primary care physician.

Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Hospital Admission: [REDACTED]
Discharge Date: [REDACTED]

Chief Complaint:
The patient presented to the department of Oral Medicine and Oral Surgery for the removal of fibrous hyperplasia in the mandibular vestibule caused by ill-fitting prostheses resulting in epulis fissuratum and vestibular deepening.

Hospital Course Summary:
During the extra-oral examination, a decrease in the vertical dimension of occlusion was noted. Intra-oral examination revealed hyperplastic mandibular lesion of the anterior alveolar mucosa, extending to the vestibular sulcus. Topical mouthwashes with Fungizone and chlorhexidine were prescribed to treat denture-induced hyperplasia and prosthetic candidiasis. After 3 weeks, no symptomatology was noted. Surgical resection combined with gingival graft was carried out to excise fibrous hyperplasia. The resultant lower boundary of the incision was sutured in position. Free gingival graft was carried out from the palate. The final total prosthesis was delivered to the patient 2 months later resulting in perfect integration of the prosthetic volume.

Findings:
The anatomopathological examination confirmed the clinical diagnosis of epulis fissuratum. Favorable postoperative healing was observed 2 weeks later during the removal of sutures.

Treatment:
Topical mouthwashes with Fungizone and chlorhexidine were prescribed to treat denture-induced hyperplasia and prosthetic candidiasis. Antibiotics and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs were administered for 5 days. Chlorhexidine mouth rinse was prescribed twice a day for 2 weeks. The patient was asked to have a soft diet, limited facial movement for 14 days, no brushing around the surgical site for 3 days after the procedure, and to place an ice pack on the lower lip.

Discharge Instructions:
The patient should continue to follow the prescribed soft diet, use chlorhexidine mouth rinse twice a day, and avoid brushing around the surgical site for 3 days after the procedure. The patient should also place an ice pack on the lower lip as needed. In case of discomfort, the patient is advised to contact the hospital. 

Follow-Up:
The patient should have regular follow-up sessions with the oral medicine and oral surgery department to ensure there is no recurrence of the fibrous hyperplasia and that the total prosthesis remains stable and well-extended. 

Signed, 
[REDACTED]
Oral Surgeon

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: Hungarian viszla
Admission Date: June 2014
Discharge Date: June 2014

Reason for Hospitalization:
The patient was admitted to UCDVH with a black, necrotic, cutaneous lesion involving the umbilical region of the ventral abdomen. The dog was dull, moderately dehydrated, and icteric on presentation.

Hospital Course:
The patient exhibited several abnormal clinical findings, including ecchymoses on the ventral abdomen and ventrolateral aspect of the thorax bilaterally, thrombocytopenia, azotemia, panhypoproteinemia, hyperbilirubinemia, increased creatine kinase, and hepatic enzyme activities. Standard management for AKI was undertaken, in addition to antimicrobial therapy given the possibility of leptospirosis, whilst awaiting test results. However, the patient's condition continued to worsen despite treatment. Euthanasia was performed at the owner’s request.

Medical History:
Tick-borne disease (Babesia spp., Anaplasma spp., Ehrlichia spp. and Hepatozoon canis) polymerase chain reaction (PCR) and Leptospira microscopic agglutination test (MAT) were negative. The patient exhibited microcardia and echogenic material in the urinary bladder consistent with hemorrhage.

Summary:
The patient, a 4-year-old Hungarian viszla, presented to UCDVH with a black, necrotic, cutaneous lesion involving the umbilical region of the ventral abdomen. The patient's clinical findings included ecchymoses, thrombocytopenia, azotemia, panhypoproteinemia, hyperbilirubinemia, increased creatine kinase, and hepatic enzyme activities. Despite treatment with standard management for AKI and antimicrobial therapy, the patient's condition continued to deteriorate. The patient was euthanized at the owner's request. Histopathological examination revealed microthrombosis and necrosis of renal glomerular tufts and, multifocally, of tubular epithelia. Transmural hemorrhage was confirmed in the bladder, and focal hepatocyte necrosis and loss were noted. Retrospective evaluation of post-mortem data confirmed a diagnosis of CRGV.

Admission Diagnosis:  Stage IV poorly differentiated ovarian carcinoma on palliative carboplatin-based chemotherapy.

Hospital Course Summary:

Admission:
The patient was admitted due to a brief syncopal episode with associated lethargy, nausea, light-headedness and increased watery ileostomal output following chemotherapy one week earlier. Clinical examination including central nervous system was unremarkable, and the patient was haemodynamically stable and afebrile.

Medical History:
The patient has a history of hypertension, multiple pulmonary emboli on enoxaparin and paroxysmal atrial fibrillation. In the past, the patient had undergone bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy and hysterectomy, and had an ileostomy due to small bowel obstruction with subsequent fistulae formation and bilateral nephrostomy drainage after radiation-induced ureteric obstruction. She had previously experienced recurrent urinary tract infections, which led to colonisation of her nephrostomies with methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), Staphylococcus epidermidis and Candida albicans. The patient had never received anti-fungal prophylaxis.

Initial Assessment:
Laboratory investigations revealed abnormal levels of sodium, creatinine, haemoglobin, white blood cells and lymphocytes. On day 2 of admission, the patient developed fevers of 38.5°C and was empirically commenced on piperacillin-tazobactam and vancomycin. The isolation of Staphylococcus epidermidis from the nephrostomy fluid was considered colonisation and the nephrostomies were changed. Initial septic screen was non-contributory, including negative faecal microscopy.

Diagnostic Assessment:
Persisting fever during her third week of admission prompted assessment for metastatic disease progression with FDG-PET scan. There was no evidence of metastatic malignant disease detected, but an area of abnormal avidity was identified on the aortic valve. Subsequent transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE) revealed a small mobile echo-density superior to the aortic valve. Transoesophageal echocardiogram (TOE) revealed a pedunculated mass within the ascending aorta arising from the commissure of the right & non-coronary cusp of the aortic valve with a calcified base. Brain MRI identified a contrast-enhancing right parasagittal frontal lobe lesion consistent with an embolic lesion.

Treatment:
Fungi were isolated from repeat blood cultures on day 22 of admission and subsequently identified as Lomentospora prolificans with high MIC to amphotericin (>32 mg/l) and itraconazole (>32 mg/L), and in-vitro sensitivity to voriconazole (0.5 mg/L). The patient was commenced on therapy with voriconazole (loading dose 600 mg IV 12 hourly). Unfortunately, due to her underlying advanced malignancy, disseminated fungal infection and poor clinical status, the patient was considered unsuitable for surgical management. She was managed with palliative intent.

Outcome:
The patient passed away five days after the fungus was isolated on day 27 of her admission.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Identification: Baby S P, 6-year-old girl

Hospital Course:
Baby S P was admitted with a complaint of progressive bilateral breast enlargement, cyclical vaginal bleeding, and pubic hair development. She had a recent increase in height, but no neck swelling, pigmented skin marks, bone pain/fractures, or clitoral enlargement. Her birth and neonatal period were normal. 

On examination, her vitals were normal, and she had no thyroid swelling, café au lait spots, or any bony abnormality. Tanners staging revealed B3P3, with no axillary hair or genital ambiguity. There were no abnormalities noted in her cardiac, thoracic, or neurological examinations. Abdominal examination was normal. 

Investigations showed normal hemogram, liver and renal functions, and thyroid functions. However, her hormonal profile revealed low levels of LH and FSH, and high levels of testosterone and DHEAS. CT pelvis showed a bulky left ovary of size 5.4 cm predominantly solid with follicles seen at periphery and pubertal uterus. 

She underwent laparoscopic resection of right tuboovarian mass, which on histopathological examination was found to be mixed germ cell sex cord stromal tumor. The post-operative period was marked by withdrawal vaginal bleeding lasting for 72 hours. A repeat hormonal profile done on the 6th post-operative day showed reduced estradiol levels.

At the 6-month follow-up, there was no vaginal bleeding reported.

Diagnosis: Mixed germ cell sex cord stromal tumor

Treatment: Laparoscopic resection of right tuboovarian mass

Follow-up: 6-months follow-up showed no vaginal bleeding.

Course and Outcome: Baby S P was admitted for evaluation of progressive bilateral breast enlargement, cyclical vaginal bleeding, and pubic hair development. Following laparoscopic resection of right tuboovarian mass, post-operative bleeding was noted, and a repeat hormonal profile showed reduced estradiol levels. Patient Education: The patient's caregivers were advised to contact the hospital in case of any complications or recurrence of symptoms.

Disposition: Discharged with follow-up appointments.

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 2-month-old male who previously underwent surgical correction for intraventricular defect, was admitted to the hospital after presenting frequent episodes of inconsolable crying, associated with neck extension, stiffening of the arms and trunk, sometimes followed by swallowing and vomiting. Symptoms were attributed to GERD, and therapy with PPI started, however, no improvement was noticed.

In the following weeks, episodes became even more frequents with exacerbation of symptoms. His mother video-recorded an attack, which showed the presence of flexion spasms. The child eventually underwent fundoplication, but no improvement was noticed. Persistence of symptoms and occurrence of spasms of the arms during acute episodes finally suggested the diagnosis of West syndrome.

IS was then confirmed by EEG while MRI was negative. Despite starting appropriate therapy at 8 months of age, clinical signs of mental retardation were present. Although IS is a rare disorder, diagnosis was suspected based on age and patient history with a complete neurological evaluation.

To our knowledge, this is the first report of IS misdiagnosed as GERD. The attention towards GERD in children may reduce attention towards other peculiar clinical conditions, like in cases we presented. We would suggest considering GERD only in those patients with high risk rate for developing GERD like children with cerebral palsy, in those with surgery complications after oesophageal atresia and/or in any child with very evocative GERD symptoms, such as hematemesis and or chronic vomiting with growth failure.

Discharge Diagnosis: West syndrome

Final Condition at Discharge:
At the time of discharge, the patient continued to experience symptoms of West syndrome, but appropriate therapy was initiated. The patient's family was instructed to follow up with the pediatricians for medication management and further evaluations.

The patient, a 59-year-old Japanese male with a history of mid-ventricular obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) presented with an asymptomatic thrombus in the apical aneurysm. The patient declined hospital admission and elected to receive treatment at an ambulatory clinic, where anti-coagulation therapy with dabigatran was initiated. The patient showed an approximately two-fold increase in activated partial thromboplastin time and an increased internationalized ratio of the prothrombin time. However, there were no significant alterations in the levels of D-dimer, thrombin-anti-thrombin III complex, and fibrinogen. During the course of treatment, weekly echocardiographic examinations demonstrated a gradual decrease in thrombus size, from 15.0mm×17.0mm to 6.8mm×6.0mm after two weeks. No thrombus was detected after three and four weeks of treatment. No systemic thromboembolic events were reported during the four-week treatment period. Dabigatran administration was continued even after the resolution of the thrombus. 

Diagnosis:

The patient was diagnosed with an asymptomatic thrombus in the apical aneurysm. 

Treatment:

The patient elected to receive treatment at an ambulatory clinic and was initiated on anti-coagulation therapy with dabigatran administration (150mg b.i.d.). Weekly echocardiographic examinations showed a gradual decrease in thrombus size, and after four weeks of treatment, the thrombus appeared to have been resolved. No systemic thromboembolic events were reported during the four-week treatment period. 

Follow-up:

The patient was advised to continue with dabigatran administration. Follow-up appointments were recommended to monitor the patient's condition. 

Discharge Medications:

Dabigatran (150mg b.i.d.) was continued even after the resolution of the thrombus.

No specific follow-up plan was mentioned in the case report.

The patient is a 23-year-old Hispanic female who presented with chest pain, dyspnoea, and fatigue. Initial investigations indicated that she may have pericarditis; however, this was ruled out after further evaluation.

Subsequent clinical findings indicated a possible cardiac cause, and an electrocardiogram (ECG) revealed ST depressions and a poor R-wave progression in the lateral precordial leads. Chest X-ray showed mild pulmonary artery congestion without pleural effusion, and a normal cardiac silhouette. Troponin T levels were elevated, and the patient underwent an urgent coronary angiography.

Coronary vasculitis with 90-95% stenosis of the proximal left anterior descending artery, 100% occlusion of the left circumflex artery, and 100% occlusion of the right posterior lateral branch with a ‘string of beads’ appearance. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (CMRI) showed a transmural delayed enhancement in the apex, without any viability, subendocardial delay enhancement in mid-septal, and inferolateral walls with significant viable myocardium. The CMRI results favored myocardial infarction and ischemic cardiomyopathy (ICM).

During her hospital course, the patient experienced significant hypotension and QTc prolongation, which limited the effectiveness of her medications. She was diagnosed with heart failure and underwent right heart catheterization. She could only ambulate about 10 feet on a flat surface at a slow pace without experiencing significant dyspnoea.

After a second coronary angiography showed disease progression, it was decided that the patient was unlikely to recover without a heart transplant. She underwent heart transplantation on hospital Day 16.

Pathology results of the explanted heart showed concentric intimal fibrosis with associated moderate lymphocytic inflammation of the thickened intima of all major epicardial coronary arteries. Acute multifocal microinfarction of the left ventricle was also observed.

The patient's post-transplant biopsies have not shown evidence of rejection or vasculitis, and five months after transplantation, she no longer reports any symptom-limiting activities.

Diagnosis:
- Coronary vasculitis with ischemic cardiomyopathy
- Heart failure

Treatment:
- Intravenous methylprednisolone and cyclophosphamide
- Oral hydroxychloroquine
- Heart transplantation

Follow-Up:
- The patient continues to be followed by a transplant cardiologist and rheumatologist.

Admitting Diagnosis: Transverse fracture of the left little finger proximal phalanx with ulnar displacement of the phalangeal head and an undisplaced fracture of the basal metaphysis of the middle phalanx

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted to the emergency department with a history of hyperextension injury to the left little finger while playing football. Radiographs of the hand confirmed a transverse fracture through the neck of the little finger proximal phalanx with ulnar displacement of the proximal phalangeal head and also an undisplaced fracture of the basal metaphysis of the middle phalanx. The fracture was manipulated to a satisfactory alignment under adequate analgesia and digital anaesthetic block. The injury was stabilized with neighbour strapping and a dorsal extension block splinting at 30 degrees flexion.

Post reduction radiographs revealed an improvement in the position of the head of the proximal phalanx with unchanged appearance of the middle phalangeal fracture. The PIPJ alignment was satisfactory. Clinically the injury was stable and there was no change in the neurovascular status. The patient was further followed up in the fracture clinic and reduction was assessed both clinically and radiologically with serial radiographs for 2 weeks since the injury.

At 4 weeks, dorsal extension block splinting was discontinued as clinical healing was confirmed. The patient was discharged to physiotherapy and further assessed at 8 and 12 weeks. By 12 weeks, the injury had fully healed with mild ulnar deviation at the proximal phalanx but with complete restoration of function.

Impression:

The patient presented to the emergency department with a transverse fracture of left little finger proximal phalanx with ulnar displacement of the phalangeal head and an undisplaced fracture of basal metaphysis of middle phalanx. The fracture was manipulated and stabilized with neighbour strapping and a dorsal extension block splinting at 30 degrees flexion. The patient was further followed up in the fracture clinic and reduction was assessed both clinically and radiologically. By 12 weeks, the injury had fully healed with complete restoration of function despite mild ulnar deviation at the proximal phalanx. The patient was discharged to physiotherapy.

Discharge Summary

Patient Name: N/A
Medical Record Number: N/A
Admission Date: N/A
Discharge Date: N/A

Hospital Course Summary:

A 36-year-old Japanese man with a 14-month history of HIV infection was admitted to the hospital with various symptoms, including fever, pulsating headache, lumbago, nausea, and vomiting. Although he was receiving highly active anti-retroviral therapy (HAART) consisting of lamivudine, azidothymidine, and lopinavir plus ritonavir for pneumocystis pneumonia, his CD4-positive lymphocyte counts in peripheral blood did not increase beyond 200 cells/mm3. Consequently, three months before admission, abacavir was prescribed, but it was also ineffective. Prophylaxis against Pneumocystis jirovecii was started, and atovaquone was administered as sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim and pentamidine had caused hepatic and renal insufficiency, respectively.

Initial physical examination suggested purulent meningitis since there was an increase in neutrophil count in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). However, broad-spectrum antimicrobials did not cure meningitis. Later, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) indicated the possibility of meningitis with granuloma formation, such as tuberculosis. However, the PCR assay targeting mycobacterium tuberculosis was negative. Therefore, bone marrow aspiration biopsy was performed, revealing the presence of microcalcification by Von Kossa's stain. The PCR assay with toxoplasma-specific primer was performed using the nucleic acid extracted from formalin-fixed and paraffin-embedded tissue (bone marrow aspiration) section, which confirmed the specific PCR product of T. gondii.

Anti-T. gondii therapy consisting of pyrimethamine, clindamycin, and leucovorin was administered and later sulfadiazine desensitization was performed. Also, anti-tubercular treatment had been continued due to suspected tuberculosis from MRI. The patient's fever improved during treatment, but his other clinical symptoms remained. Finally, anti-T. gondii therapy consisting pyrimethamine, sulfadiazine, and leucovorin plus prednisolone had an effect on improving his clinical symptoms, and he was referred to another hospital in his home city at his request.

Disposition:

The patient's clinical symptoms were relieved, and he was stable enough to be referred to another hospital in his home city for further evaluation and treatment.

Recommendation:

The patient should continue anti-T. gondii therapy consisting of pyrimethamine, sulfadiazine, and leucovorin plus prednisolone as prescribed by his doctor. Additionally, he should visit his doctor for follow-up and regular check-ups.

Abbreviations:
HIV: human immunodeficiency virus
HAART: highly active anti-retroviral therapy
CSF: cerebrospinal fluid
PCR: polymerase chain reaction
MRI: magnetic resonance imaging
